The spot is located in Marzi, which is known as the valley of wheat. When Tucci swung by the bakery, he tried pane di cuti, a 100-year-old recipe. For Tucci and his hungry parents, she also made morsello, a bread bowl filled with sausage and broccoli rabe. This portable meal was once a favorite among farmers and hunters who wanted to carry a not-so-little slice of home with them wherever they went. Today, this dish is often served at weddings and celebrations. At Osteria della Cipolla Rossa (Red Onion Inn), run by Michele Pugliese and Romana Schiariti, the specialty is the unapologetically simple red onion spaghetti. The key ingredient is the region’s renowned sweet red onions, called cipolla rossa, which only grow along the small stretch of coastline surrounding the city of Tropea. The onions are so sweet that, during the episode, Tucci bit into a raw one as if it were an apple. Il Principe di Scilla is a family-run restaurant in Scilla, Italy, that is all about the local swordfish, the most respected or prized sea creature in Calabria — and for a region surrounded by water on three sides, that’s really saying something. “It’s like prosciutto and smoked salmon had a love child,” Tucci said as he sampled the fresh raw swordfish with restaurant owner Johnny Giordano. Tucci also tried scialiatelli alla ghiotta, which is like a swordfish ragu. “It’s nothing short of incredible,” Giordano said of the pasta dish. In the dishes at Qafiz, tucked in the Aspromonte mountains, chef Nino Rossi uses local ingredients. He prepared for Tucci the signature dessert that helped the restaurant snag a Michelin star: fire. Inspired by the idea of renewed growth after the 2021 wildfires, the aptly named dish is made of meringue flavored with charcoal, sliced apple and white chocolate foam. “It’s like a million different flavors in there,” Tucci said as he dove in for seconds. La Collinetta, located in the mountain town of Martone, is run by farmer and chef Pino Trimboli. When Tucci visited, Trimboli made lamb in clay, an ancient Greek dish. The lamb is surrounded by wet clay before it’s baked to seal in the delicate flavors and juices. This ancient technique comes with a tradeoff: Each dish takes over four hours to cook. But Tucci said the resulting “fall off the bone” lamb was worth the wait. Stay tuned for updates as Tucci travels to two more regions of Italy. Earlier this year, Tucci traveled to Piedmont, Umbria, Venice and London. For a guide to all the places he visited during season one, click here.

item.title: The European capital of cool that keeps getting cooler
item.description:
Source: CNN Travel Score: 3.10
Lisbon is in the midst of a renaissance. The latest European capital of cool’s affordable rents, great nightlife and gorgeous streets – which wind high into the hills from the River Tagus – have seen younger travelers arrive in their droves in recent years, enjoying extended stays thanks to dedicated “digital nomad” visas. As a result, the city has taken on a youthful, multicultural and international vibe, helping to pull in tourists from around the globe in the process. It isn’t just those looking to live and work here that are driving this change, though. Walk the streets of Portugal’s buzzing capital and it’s impossible to escape the sense of confidence around the place. Locals have truly begun embracing their Portuguese identity, unashamedly showcasing the best of traditional food and culture, from delicious pastel de nata pastry in the Belem district to the aching sounds of Fado singing in Alfama. It all goes to make up what Lisbon citizens call “alma” or soul, something that’s utterly unique to this wonderful place. Visitors can see this on special nights such as June 13’s The Feast of St Anthony, perhaps the biggest night in the Lisbon calendar, when locals celebrate their patron saint with long processions that go on late into the night, preceded by epic meals of sardines and local wine in the streets. But “alma” goes beyond just one night. Come here at any time of the year and there’s a feeling that life is to be lived in public. That might be on the bohemian streets of the Bairro Alto neighborhood, where restaurants spill out onto narrow lanes. Or at ultra hip spots like Park, a bar atop a multi-story parking lot that has become a byword for hipster cool, not to mention incredible views. Everyone is welcome and the atmosphere remains vibrant well into the early hours. ‘Intense people’ “Alma” isn’t just about hanging out with friends or enjoying languid meals outdoors, however. It’s also found in traditional music, especially Fado. Marrying poetry and singing and born on the streets of Lisbon’s beautiful Alfama and Mouraria neighborhoods, it is more than simply an expression of sadness and melancholy. It is rather, explains Fado singer Gisela João, an expression of Portuguese intensity and tradition. “I think Fado, it’s the most true… as we can be expressing the personality of [the] Portuguese country, Portuguese people,” she says while walking Alfama’s streets. João is not the archetypal Fado singer of old. She does not wear a black dress and she is also younger than most stereotypical Fado singers too. “Why should I dress as a girl that grew up in the ’40s and ‘50s?” she asks. “It’s not who I am.” She is, though, very much steeped in the music’s history. “I moved here because I came to sing in a Fado restaurant,” she says. “In this street, for example, I remember that you would walk on the street and you would listen: Fado going out of the windows like here, one singing here, another one here… It was like you were in the middle of Fado.” She is also keen to debunk the idea that sadness is what defines Fado. “For me, [Fado] is about poetry and the poem for me, a really nice poem, is a poem that can talk about [the] life of everyone… when I sing it is when I feel that I can express myself.” This is evident in João’s beautiful voice, which echoes around the neighborhood. It is a sound that is quintessentially Portuguese. “We are really intense people,” she says, laughing. “We care a lot. You come to Portugal and it’s really normal that you meet someone and that person immediately invites you to go to the house, to have dinner, to be with the friends and the family and organize a big party just to receive you… We are dramatic!” An age of discovery Lisbon can feel as if it’s half on land and half at sea, with the wide sweep of the River Tagus leading out to the vast Atlantic. This, after all, is a country that remains fiercely proud of its 500 years of seafaring history. Lisbon’s famous Padrão dos Descobrimentos, Monument of the Discoveries, which stands in the Belem neighborhood on the banks of the Tagus, pays tribute to the country’s great explorers. Henry the Navigator is depicted alongside historic figures including Vasco da Gama and Ferdinand Magellan, a tribute to Lisbon’s place at the heart of maritime discovery in the 15th and 16th centuries. Ricardo Diniz, an intrepid solo sailor turned corporate coach, is continuing this long tradition, bringing the past into the present day. “We’re very proud of our past. We achieved something incredible over 500 years ago, and we are reminded about this every single day,” he says, pointing from the deck of his boat out across the water. “We are on the ocean. We have this incredible river.” When he returns after long journeys out to sea, he says his pride swells as Lisbon comes into view. Diniz says that while the water is key to Lisbon’s traditions as well as its present and future as a modern city, the changes in recent years have been driven by people from outside talking about just how great this place is. “In the last five years, especially, many people who come from abroad to Lisbon are surprised at what they find,” he says. “I think they are the true ambassadors of our city and our country, people from abroad talking beautifully about Portugal.” A city of confidence Speak with the locals here and it won’t be long before they remind you of the great explorers and the Age of Discovery some 500 years ago. However, there wasn’t always much to be said about its more modern past. Much of that has changed in the last 20 years, though, as that sense of confidence has come to be felt across the city with Lisbon’s resurgence as a tourist destination and a place to work and play. That’s particularly clear in Lisbon’s food scene. Acclaimed chef Jose Avillez has championed Portuguese fine dining for years. Fifteen years ago he began introducing that most humble of local dishes, the sardine, to his high end restaurant. They are, he says, “… very, very special, because it’s something that we have only three, four months, a year, maximum. “When Portuguese [people] arrive at a contemporary Portuguese restaurant… he expects to have modern food, but to have the soul of Portuguese food. So we have a lot of respect for the sardines.” You can’t avoid coming back to that sense of soul when in Lisbon. It is, explains Avillez, all about a respect for tradition while bringing dishes into the future. “I would say that Portuguese cuisine that is transmitted from grandmothers to granddaughters, from mothers to daughters is the art of bringing the flavors with simplicity, with love. [That] is what we try to do, even if you do it very creatively with a lot of creativity - if it’s fine dining, it’s a two-Michelin star, whatever, what you need to bring to your guests is something delicious. And, I will say 90% of the time, quite simple.” That’s certainly true of Avillez’s cuisine, from his simple sardine recipes to his delicious steak. And, of course, no meal in Lisbon would be complete without a famous pastel de nata, the custard tart which comes from Belem. These small treats have gone global in recent years, but they taste at their very best right here in this brilliant city. Lisbon’s renaissance is something to behold, especially with something so delicious to hand. A place that has changed in so many ways in the 21st century, but has managed to stay true to its roots, its past and its fascinating history.

item.title: Where to Stay in Great Smoky Mountains National Park for Mountain Views and Fall Foliage
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.17
Frequently named the most visited national park in the US, Great Smoky Mountains have universal appeal—travelers come from all over the country (and the world) to enjoy the natural beauty of this part of North Carolina and Tennessee. Hikers, anglers, photographers, road-trippers, birders, families, and thrill-seekers can all find reasons to make the trek. Whether you want to see the namesake fog blanketing the peaks—many of which tower well over 6,000 feet—breathe in the crisp air, or glimpse the famous wildflowers and fall foliage, there’s plenty to do, and some excellent places to spend the night once you get here. From the historic LeConte Lodge—the only lodging within the park’s boundaries—with its hard-to-come-by reservations and hike-in access to some of the South’s most luxurious hotels—Blackberry Farm and The Swag are legendary in the hospitality world—there’s something for every type of traveler. Whether it’s your first time exploring the park or you’re planning a return trip, you have options for where to set up your base camp. You can opt for a rustic cabin rental, a kid-friendly resort, or a stylish glamping site depending on your mood. Read on for some of the best places to stay near Great Smoky Mountains National Park for your next nature-filled adventure. How to plan a trip to Great Smoky Mountains National Park How do you get to Great Smoky Mountains National Park? Great Smoky Mountains National Park sits along the border of North Carolina and Tennessee. If you’re flying into the area, McGhee Tyson Airport (TYS) in Knoxville, Tennessee, and Asheville Regional Airport (AVL) are among the most convenient options. From TYS, it’s a 30- and 60-minute drive, respectively, to the park’s main entrances in Townsend and Gatlinburg, Tennessee. The drive from AVL to the entrance in Cherokee, North Carolina, will take you a little over an hour. When is the best time to visit Great Smoky Mountains National Park? Undoubtedly, the best time to visit Great Smoky Mountains National Park is in the fall. If you time it right—keep an eye on the foliage reports—you’ll witness the splendor of all the reds, oranges, and yellows. The changing colors typically start to appear in late September, and they peak between mid-October and mid-to-early November, depending on the weather and elevation. This time of year also tends to be the busiest season in the park, so keep that in mind when you’re planning a trip (book early and visit mid-week if possible). How long should you visit the Great Smoky Mountains? Because of the size and plethora of things to do within the park, you’ll want to plan for multiple days of exploration—I’d recommend at least three. That way, you can drive the scenic loops, complete a few hikes, and check off all the major sites without rushing. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: The Distinctly Brazilian Flavor of São Paolo's Japanese Cuisine
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.90
At Aizomê, a stylish Japanese restaurant shrouded by a thick wall of trees just off São Paulo’s main thoroughfare, Avenida Paulista, the food is both recognizable to devotees of Japanese cuisine and distinctly Brazilian. You might find pirarucu, an enormous Amazonian riverfish, in saikyo yaki, a traditional Japanese sweet-miso preparation more commonly used on black cod. Ponzu incorporates tucupi, a tart yellow sauce made from fermented wild manioc, a root native to the Amazon. “I’m third generation,” says owner Telma Shiraishi, who was born and raised in São Paulo and whose grandparents hail from the Wakayama and Iwate prefectures of Japan. “It doesn’t make sense for me to make a cuisine that is 100% Japanese, bringing 100% of ingredients from Japan.” Over the past 20 years of leading Aizomê, Shiraishi has been on a journey to determine how these two cultures come together in one place. What began as an effort toward a fiercely traditional Japanese eatery has evolved into a cuisine that better reflects her own experience, which she calls Nipo-Brazilian, blending Japanese and Brazilian techniques, influences, and ingredients. Of Brazil’s 214 million people, an estimated 2 million people are of Japanese descent, making it the largest community outside of Japan. The vast majority live in São Paulo. It’s a history that reaches back to 1907, when the two countries signed an agreement permitting Japanese migration to meet labor needs on coffee plantations in the southern Brazilian states of São Paulo and Paraná. Eventually those immigrants founded agricultural settlements or moved into major cities. The São Paolo neighborhood of Liberdade, often referred to as the city’s Japantown, has been the nucleus of the Japanese Brazilian community since then. When the first Japanese restaurants emerged, they largely catered to members of their own community. For decades, Japanese cuisine faced stereotyping and suspicion—Brazilians were highly wary of raw fish—but later American imports like huge sushi boats, or rolls that included cream cheese, widened the appeal. For Shiraishi, these restaurants “helped break down prejudices” and accustomed palates to the likes of soy sauce and raw fish. Now even that era feels like the past: South America’s largest city has grown to contain a kaleidoscope of options when it comes to Japanese restaurants. There is high-end omakase and kaiseki, a raft of izakayas, specialist ramen, udon, tempura, and tonkatsu joints. The scene has hugely diversified, including both truer interpretations of original dishes and a marriage of Brazilian flavors that builds on, rather than flattens, Japanese roots. There are currently 3,000 Japanese restaurants across São Paulo, and they aren’t confined to Liberdade either; they stretch throughout the city, allowing the former enclave to take on a pan-Asian personality. Shiraishi’s Nipo-Brazilian approach isn’t new, but speaks to the way that Japanese immigrants, since they first arrived in the early 20th century, needed to adapt to local ingredients: Papaya root instead of burdock; water hyacinth stalks replacing lotus roots. Shiraishi recalls her grandmother making sushi with chard leaves, which are far more plentiful in Brazil, instead of seaweed. Unlike the Philadelphia rolls and all-you-can-eat buffets, which Shiraishi felt “didn’t have any connection…to what I grew up eating,” the items now on her menu are reminiscent of the food she was raised on. This spirit lives on in Aizomé’s multicourse tasting menu, and Shiraishi continues to scour the country for ingredients that highlight the history and evolution of Japanese food in Brazil. Guests might eat chayote marinated in cachaça, a Brazilian spirit, and soy sauce. Mapará, another Amazonian fish, often replaces eel. Her dashi uses dried Brazilian fish rather than katsuobushi, and when possible, local wild mushrooms over shiitake. “The only ingredient [which] we don’t have something similar in Brazil is kombu,” says Shiraishi, referring to the umami-rich sea kelp used in much of Japanese cuisine. A rising interest in Japanese food beyond sushi has fueled another distinctly Brazilian boom: izakayas. While these casual pubs have existed in the city for decades, it's only in the past 10 years that they have become some of the city’s most popular hangouts. Izakaya Matsu, an excellent bar in Pinheiros, is perennially packed. In Liberdade, Izakaya Issa and Kintaro have thrived since the 1990s. Wagner Higuchi runs the latter, a tiny bustling bar that his parents founded in 1993. On a warm, breezy evening, the kind where paulistanos like to spill out onto the streets with ice-cold beers, patrons at Kintaro squeeze side-by-side, drinking Japanese beers and shochu with Yakult, while tucking into an array of dishes served in small aluminium containers. The food, says Higuchi, is a mix of traditional—think braised burdock root and carrot, a side dish that dates back to the Edo period—and those from the “colony,” which is how Japanese Brazilians refer to the agricultural settlements of the early 20th century, when the Japanese first settled and adapted to local ingredients, such as a vinegary marinated tilapia. Higuchi took over from his parents in 2018 and now runs the bar; his aunt and nephew man the kitchen. “We focus on homemade Japanese food,” says Higuchi. “We evoke the fond memories of our Japanese descendants, the famous ‘batchan’ [grandma] food. It’s important to maintain these traditions because the flavor of this food is unique.” Higuchi adds that a Japanese person visiting from Japan might find some of the dishes unusual, “but for a descendant who remembers the food from home and batchan’s cooking, it can bring back wonderful memories.” On the northern edge of Avenida Paulista, the elegant, minimalist Kanoê represents another recent shift: toward classic Japanese fine dining. In 2024, the Michelin Guide returned to São Paulo, and a number of Japanese spots, including Kan Suke, Kazuo, Kuro, and Kanoê, were awarded a star. Many are run by Brazilian-born chefs of Japanese heritage who spent time in Japan in an effort to master the art of sushi. Kanoê is an exclusive omakase, packed each night despite its hefty price tag—the tasting menu costs $268. Inside, though, chefs expertly slice the finest fish—from Brazil, Japan, and beyond—and serenely cook over induction stovetops. Most revered is the rice, whose provenance is a closely guarded secret and whose result is deeply vinegary and warm enough to melt the most delicate tuna imaginable. On a buzzy Saturday night, sitting across the counter from several supremely confident and concentrated chefs, the pairing of rice, Spanish bluefin tuna, and Niigata salt is arguably the greatest mouthful of sushi in the city—the kind that makes strangers turn and smile to tables beside them. São Paulo–born owner Tadashi Shiraishi (no relation to Telma) spent years cooking in Japan, Europe, and the US, honing his craft to become one of Brazil’s great sushi chefs. Though deeply rooted in Japanese tradition, he likes to break rules. Tuna is served first because most guests are too full to enjoy the fatty fish at the end of an omakase. It’s a masterstroke, highlighting the fish’s richness before more delicate scallops and hamachi. These types of high-end Japanese restaurants have emerged, in part, thanks to an increasingly wealthy and well-traveled Brazilian populace, says Tadashi, allowing São Paulo’s sushi scene to compete with the world’s gastronomic capitals, like New York. “São Paulo is one of my favorite places to eat Japanese food," he adds. Though Tadashi uses some Brazilian-grown ingredients, his restaurant has never been explicitly focused on creating Japanese Brazilian cuisine. Rather, he explains, it has always been about studying and preserving aspects of traditional Japanese cooking to share with a Brazilian audience. “The restaurant aims to operate within principles closely linked to Japanese tradition, respecting technique, seasonality, hospitality, and the creation of flavor within this framework.” Food among diasporas, perhaps inevitably, can veer further from its origins as people adapt to new countries and cultures intertwine. As with Indian food in the UK or Mexican cuisine in the US, Japanese food in São Paulo is today defined by a multitude of interpretations. There are, Tadashi says, “formats more adapted to Brazilian tastes [and] those closer to traditions and techniques originally developed in Japan, but with a more personal touch.” Indeed, Japanese cuisine in Brazil has never been more popular or varied, from the experimental to the fiercely traditional. There are temakerias in gas stations, beach kiosks selling sushi, and, still, all-you-can-eat sushi rodízios in every town. “The new generation, they don’t want to eat McDonald’s, they want sushi,” says Telma, referring to the ongoing—and yet, in this case, usurped—Brazilian adoration for international chains. This year Telma will open a new spot in Saúde, a neighborhood in the city’s south that is now home to one of the largest Japanese Brazilian communities. “As a community of descendants, we have to tell our story.” Thanks to the continued efforts of São Paulo’s vast array of Japanese Brazilian chefs, the options are better—and the story told louder—than ever before.

item.title: The Best Beaches in Miami, From Nature Reserves to Sceney Beach Clubs
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.21
Miami has always known how to turn a day at the beach into a scene. This rings especially true along the sandy patches belonging to Miami Beach’s top hotels, which have been upping the stakes with cushy amenities and experiences designed to warrant hefty membership fees for locals—and generate enough revenue to keep their beach clubs at the top of their game. The good news for travelers? Book a room at such hotels—think CNT Triple Crown Winners 1 Hotel South Beach and Faena Miami Beach or the new and improved Delano Miami Beach—and many of those same privileges typically extend to hotel guests, no membership required (though nightly rates will cost ya!). Of course, you don’t need a hotel key, annual dues, or an impending inheritance to experience Miami’s best beaches. Miles of public shoreline remain gloriously democratic, whether you want to join the beautiful bodies and colorful lifeguard stands of South Beach, bike beneath the palms of Key Biscayne, kayak through mangroves at Oleta River State Park, or ditch your swimsuit altogether at liberating, clothing-optional Haulover Beach. Consider these 18 picks less a ranking of sand and more a guide to Miami’s many ways of doing the beach, popular year-round thanks to a balmy climate that makes summer feel seemingly endless. Read our complete Miami travel guide here, which includes: - The Best Things to Do in Miami - The Best Restaurants in Miami - The Best Things to Do in Wynwood - The Best Hotels in Miami How we choose the best beaches in Miami Every review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that activity. When choosing things to do, our editors consider landmarks and experiences that offer an insider’s view of a destination, keeping authenticity, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. item.title: The Best Fall Foliage in the USA: A Guide to Where to Go This Autumn
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.82
It’s a rare occasion that vast swaths of the United States experience a season in a similar way—but the sepia-toned mosaic of fall foliage soon to sprawl across the country in a few short weeks proves that fall is the one exception to that rule. Starting as early as late September and extending well into November, you can expect to find some combination of red, gold, yellow, and orange bathing the trees from coast to coast. But anyone well-versed in leaf-peeping—or the colloquial nickname given to any tourist with a proclivity for fall foliage gazing—knows that some states and regions have more colorful and sweeping offerings than others. So for any looking to leaf-peep-maxx this upcoming fall, we took the liberty of rounding up the states, parks, and areas from across the country where you can expect to find the most vibrant fall tableaus come this October. Blue Ridge Mountains, North Georgia Way down on the south of the eastern shore you’ll find a range of mountains absolutely awash for fall. The Blue Ridge Mountain region of North Georgia makes up a smaller enclave of the greater Appalachian Mountains—and though you can’t go wrong with any stop along the Appalachian Trail when it comes to fall foliage, this little corner right on the border between Georgia and Tennessee is especially ideal for the changing seasons. The Southern climate makes things a little milder, without having to sacrifice the fall grandeur. The area skews more towards nature aficionados, with plenty of nature paths and mountain trails to climb. One particular favorite includes Brasstown Bald, where you can catch the best view of the leaves in peak color. Where to stay in the Blue Ridge Mountains: - A charming Victorian B&B: Blue Ridge Inn Bed & Breakfast - A peaceful mountain escape: The Copperhead Lodge The Berkshires, Massachusetts When it comes to the idyllic pastoral regions of New England, Massachusetts’s Berkshires are right up there with the likes of New York's Adirondacks. One look around and you can see exactly how the lush area inspired writers like Edith Wharton and artists like Norman Rockwell (and if you don’t, just take a quick trip to the Norman Rockwell Museum). Other highlights for our Berkshires guide includes shopping at stores like Fluff Alpaca, hiking up Monument Mountain’s three different trails, grabbing some coffee beans from West Stockbridge’s famous No. Six Depot, and ordering a bite off the farm-to-table menu at Prairie Whale. Pair all of that with the area’s bustling boutique hotel scene in Lenox, Massachusetts, and you’ve got one must-see stop on your Great American leaf-peeping tour. Where to stay in the Berkshires: - For an artistic flair: 33 Main - A motor-lodge-turned luxury hotel: Life House Stowe, Vermont Nestled in the embrace of Vermont’s Green Mountains, Stowe might be known for its slopes and skiing—but it’s also one of the best places to catch a verifiable sea of fall foliage come October and November. This is your quintessential idyllic northern New England escape. While it’s had its fair share of development, there are plenty of locals who reside in the town year-round. Pre-game leaf-peeping by exploring the microbrewing scene or shopping for some top-of-the-line maple products at Shaw’s General Store. It’s also something of a hikers paradise, with absolutely no small shortage of trails for the ambitious explorers and gentler strollers alike. No matter what you choose, there’s sure to be one fantastic view. Where to stay in Stowe, Vermont: - For a hygge vibe: Field Guide - A spa-retreat: AWOL Stowe - A traditionally intimate ski lodge: Edson Hill Great Smoky Mountains, Tennessee and North Carolina The Great Smoky Mountains that trail up the border between Tennessee and North Carolina earned their name from the natural, gauzy fog that often drapes across the region. It gives the area an ethereal, almost otherworldly quality during any time of year. Add in a mosaic of fall foliage and it's no wonder why this spot is home to some of the best fall foliage in the USA. See the sights from the famous Cades Cove loop or hike the Laurel Falls Trail or any of the many paths along the mountains. You’ll also find a range of different lodging options in the area—including glamping experiences, cabins, farms, and more. Where to stay in the Great Smoky Mountains: - An irreverent farm getaway: Blackberry Farm - A sprawling ranch: Cataloochee Ranch - A one-of-a-kind glamping stay: Under Canvas Great Smoky Mountains Aspen, Colorado Aspen is one of those cold weather destinations that’s spoken of with an undeniable air of prestige—the same way you would speak of Lake Como in the spring, or the French Riviera in summer. Like Stowe, it’s most famous for its skiing, but it’s got its fair share of foliage to show off around fall. Especially ideal for those who have a taste for the finer things in life, Aspen’s also a prime luxury shopping destination. Shop high end designer brands like Prada or Gucci, and grab a chic cowboy hat from Kemo Sabe. And you can’t forget the decadent fare available at eateries like Bosq, White House Tavern, Matsushia, and more. Where to stay in Aspen, Colorado: - An Aspen mainstay: Hotel Jerome Sun Valley, Idaho Another skiing staple, Sun Valley has long charmed celebrities and nature-lovers alike. It’s renowned for its skiing but offers golden escape during the shoulder season of fall. Sun Valley’s especially great for any leaf peepers who happen to also be fans of Ernest Hemingway. The famous Lost Generation author loved the region and even finished his book For Whom The Bell Tolls in the Sun Valley Resort’s suite 206. Hemingway’s admiration of and attachment to the area is immortalized with with a memorial and free audio walking tour. Where to stay in Sun Valley, Idaho: - A historic ski resort: Sun Valley Resort - For a laidback lodging: Limelight Ketchum North Cascades, Washington New England often takes the cake when it comes to fall foliage, but don’t write off the Pacific Northwest. One drive along the Cascade Loop will show that this craggy region has its own verdancy amid the snow dusted mountains. Often referred to as the American Alps, there are plenty of peaks and summits to see the leaves—such as the Washington Pass overlooking the Liberty Bell Mountain—while hiking trails like the Maple Pass Loop and Blue Lake offer some of the best opportunities for leaf-peeping. Where to stay in North Cascades, Washington: - A floating cabin: Ross Lake Resort Laurel Hill, Pennsylvania There are plenty of trails and state parks you can take advantage of to gaze at the Pennsylvania foliage. There’s Mount Davis, Ohiopyle State Park, Laurel Hill state park, and so much more. You really can’t go wrong with any of them. But we’d recommend conducting your leaf peeping from inside, specifically inside one of famous architect Frank Lloyd Wright’s most well-known works. Dubbed Fallingwater, this quintessentially mid-century modern structure sits atop a waterfall and is entirely ensconced in a forest of trees—making its airy interiors the ideal framing for the lush colors of fall. Where to stay in Laurel Highlands Pennsylvania: - A sprawling estate: Nemacolin Franconia Notch State Park, New Hampshire Rounding off the New England stops, this nature reserve is nestled in the middle of New Hampshire’s White Mountain National Forest. Here, you’ll find parts of the larger Appalachian Trail, as well as hikes up well-known peaks like Artist Bluff—which afford panoramic views of the area’s famous Echo Lake. The body of water sits at the base of Cannon Mountain and perfectly reflects the prism of color around it, even more so when those colors are the rich reds, golds, yellows, and oranges of fall. Where to stay in Franconia Notch State Park, New Hampshire: - A mansion inn: The Franconia Inn Adirondacks, New York You just need to watch one episode of Gilmore Girls to know that New England is one of the top best places to see fall foliage, and the Adirondacks is one of the region’s best fall exports. Located just about four hours outside of New York City, this mountain area encompasses much of New York’s storied “upstate” region—where people escape from the city to ensconce themselves in the privacy of cozy cabins, lake houses, and more. Here, you’ll find over 3,000 lakes and ponds—such as the famous Lake Placid—and the Adirondack High Peaks. Grab a quick drink at Raquette River Brewing or fill up on French-Canadian comfort dishes at Woodshed on Park, before heading out to take in the vivid leaves. Where to stay in the Adirondacks: - For a luxurious lake island resort: The Sagamore Resort - A rustic log cabin experience: The Point - A Lake Placid classic: Great Adirondack Hotel Columbia River Gorge, Northern Oregon Just above California and below other fall foliage fave Washington, the Northern Oregon region similarly offers plenty of mystically foggy places to peep some leaves. What’s even better is you get the best of both worlds with forests and beaches colliding to make up this scenic coast. Travel through the Columbia River Gorge to see all the leaves, then take a road trip out to Cannon Beach to top the adventure off. Where to stay in Northern Oregon: - A water-front property: Cannery Pier Hotel & Spa Shenandoah National Park, Virginia Just off the Blue Ridge Parkway, and not too far from the border of West Virginia, Shenandoah National Park extends about 197,439 acres across Virginia’s Blue Ridge region. It’s got breathtaking views and nature, making it ideal to catch some of the best fall foliage in the USA. After all, there's a reason we named it one of the best national parks to enjoy during the fall. Shenandoah is mostly visited for hiking, with over 500 miles of trails—many of which you can find along the area’s Skyline Drive—that offer ample opportunity to take in nature, no matter the time of year.

item.title: 15 Oregon Coast Airbnbs for Pacific Sunsets, Storm Chasing, and Eclectic Beach Towns
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.35
There are few places in the United States as breathtaking as the Oregon Coast, where towering spruce trees make way for vast blue horizons at what feels like the edge of the Earth. An exquisite marriage of colors, the Beaver State’s famous shoreline stretches from the Columbia River in the north to the California border in the south, lending itself to a misty, nature-filled getaway. Whether you’re interested in exploring the tide pools and gazing at the hordes of seabirds that congregate around Cannon Beach’s Haystack Rock, or staring down Thor’s Well (otherwise known as the “Drainpipe of the Pacific”) over in Yachats, these 15 Oregon Coast Airbnbs offer cozy respites for all kinds of outdoor excursions. Some are vacation spots in and of themselves, with amenities like cedar hot tubs and barrel saunas; others’ main focus is the dreamy ocean views. From A-frame cabins and tiny floating homes to glass-walled lookouts and lighthouse-shaped properties, these are the best Airbnbs for an unforgettable Pacific Northwest escape. Our top picks: - Best for solo travelers: Tiny home on Tillamook Bay - Best for views: Nehalem home five minutes from the beach - Best for families: Cabin with views of Twin Rocks - Best for beach access: Arch Cape home with a sauna and hot tub FAQ: Which Oregon Coast vacation rentals offer the best views? For truly cinematic views, Manzanita’s hillside homes provide a sweeping overlook of seven-mile Neahkahnie Beach. For quieter vistas, Oceanside and Yachats deliver raw, less-developed coastal scenery with panoramic reach. How do I get to the Oregon Coast? Most travelers begin in Portland, Oregon, which is served by Portland International Airport. From there, a rental car is essential—there’s no comprehensive train or bus network along the coast. The northern coast (Cannon Beach, Manzanita, Seaside) is about a 1 hour and 30 minute drive west via Highway 26. The central coast (Lincoln City, Depoe Bay, Newport) is reached via Highway 18 or 20 in around two to three hours. Highway 101, the coastal route, winds southward all the way to California—ideal for a slow, scenic drive with stops along the way. Be prepared for occasional fog, winding roads, and in remote stretches, limited cell service. When is the best time to visit the Oregon Coast? The Oregon Coast has no high season in the traditional sense—each season offers a distinct atmosphere. Its summer season (July to September) brings the most sun and mild warmth, perfect for beach walks, kayaking, and long coastal hikes—but also the most visitors. Fall (October to early November) is quieter, with crisp mornings, fiery foliage inland, and excellent conditions for storm-free trail adventures. Winter (late November through February) invites travelers seeking solitude and drama—this is storm-watching season, when towering waves crash under moody skies, best enjoyed from a fireside perch. Spring (March to May) is fresh and green, with fewer crowds, migrating gray whales, and tide pools alive with seasonal marine life. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Kyler Alvord.

item.title: The Most Beautiful Italian Coastal Towns
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.12
Most first-time visitors to Italy tend to concentrate on cities like Rome, Florence, and Venice, but if you ask us, off-the-beaten-path Italian coastal towns are some of the most beautiful places in the country. After all, Italy has nearly 5,000 miles of coastline, and some of the country’s coastal settlements predate the Roman Empire. From Liguria all the way down to Calabria, not to mention the Adriatic Coast and the islands, there are charming seaside villages that offer a wide variety of experiences. You might want the glamour of world-famous resort towns like Portofino, Capri, and Taormina, where your dolce vita fantasies can come to life. Or perhaps you’d prefer more under-the-radar towns like Maratea and Carloforte, where you can get an authentic taste of local life. In Italy, most coastal towns come alive in the summer, when visitors from around the world hit the beaches. If you want to avoid the crowds, plan to visit coastal towns in the off-season, but keep in mind that some of them all but shut down in the winter. Spring and fall are usually a good compromise. Read on to learn about 25 of the best Italian coastal towns, with Condé Nast Traveler-approved recommendations of where to stay. item.title: Planning a Fall Foliage Trip? Book These Amtrak Routes
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.08
A fall foliage train ride is the quintessential autumn getaway. US rail routes glide through some of the nation’s best scenery, including dense forests, glittering lakeshores, and rippling foothills. Even better: unlike a road trip through these colorful landscapes, a rail journey allows travelers to be completely absorbed in the bright red, orange, and yellow hues flicking past the windows. Amtrak trains stop in foliage-rich destinations across the US and Canada. And while the journey itself is certainly a highlight of the trip, travelers will also find seasonal attractions upon arrival at many of the routes’ stops, like apple picking, hikes through vibrant woodlands, and cozy stays at historical inns. Consider this your guide to booking a fall foliage train ride, from the best time to book for peak colors to the top Amtrak trains for reveling in all autumn has to offer. Simply buy your ticket, sit back, and enjoy Mother Nature’s awe-inspiring spectacle. This story has been updated with new information since its original publish date. What is the best time to plan a fall foliage train trip? Don’t forget that when planning a fall foliage trip, timing is key. You’ll want to visit your destination of choice when the changing leaves are decked out in their peak colors. There are several reliable online tools for predicting when the leaves will be the most vibrant. If you’re not sure where you want to visit, start with the Smoky Mountains fall foliage map, which shows predictions for the progression of the entire country’s leaves based on date. Another good choice is the Farmer’s Almanac, which lists the dates each state is predicted to reach peak foliage. Once you have your dates squared, these are the best Amtrak routes and destinations for an unforgettable fall foliage trip. Vermont Train line: Vermonter On its way from Washington DC to St. Albans, Vermont, Amtrak’s Vermonter train ambles through lush northeastern forests and charming small towns. (The entire 13-hour journey crosses nine states, from the Mid-Atlantic to New England.) Once in Vermont, you’ll have your pick of picturesque villages with plenty of fiery trees to view. The train's first stop in Vermont is a solid choice for a fall weekend getaway: the historic town of Battleboro. This pretty hamlet sits right on the Connecticut river in the foothills of the Green Mountains, so expect undulating blankets of colorful foliage in every direction. The train station is right in town, so most activities and amenities are accessible by foot. Stop by a local café or browse the shops lining Main Street. Rent a kayak from one of the local outfitters and gaze over the water toward hills filled with vibrant leaves. Or, head to nearby Fort Dummer State Park (about a 45-minute walk along South Main Street) for easy hiking trails and lookout points over crimson-tinged maple, oak, and birch trees. Peak time for foliage: Early to mid-October Michigan Train line: Pere Marquette Amtrak’s Michigan Services are a series of rail lines running all throughout the Wolverine State. For an autumn sojourn, plan to hop aboard the Pere Marquette, a daily route that runs from Chicago to Grand Rapids. The train winds up Michigan’s west coast, offering brief but sweeping views of Lake Michigan and bisecting lush, Midwestern farmland dotted with trees resplendent in their autumn wardrobes. Once in Grand Rapids, the city’s 200+ local parks offer up-close views of nature’s shifting kaleidoscope. Among the highlights are Blanford Nature Center, which offers extensive walking trails through an old-growth forest of blazing red sugar maples. Don’t miss the Calvin Ecosystem Preserve and Native Gardens, with its network of scenic trails through more than 100 acres of forests and wetlands. The 1,500-acre Millennium Park is just five minutes from downtown Grand Rapids, yet is home to an 18-mile network of treelined trails that wind along lakes and rivers. After you’ve had your fill of forest-bathing, be sure to explore the local brewery scene for seasonal craft beers—after all, Grand Rapids is known as “Beer City, USA.” Fall-themed activities are available throughout the city as well. Don’t miss apple picking from century-old orchards at Robinette’s Apple Haus and Winery. Extend the historical charm to your accommodations with one of the area’s charming bed and breakfasts, like The Leonard at Logan House, which was built in 1914. Peak time for foliage: October 6 to 15 Wisconsin Train line: Empire Builder As Amtrak’s Empire Builder stretches from Chicago, across all of the Upper Midwest, and into Washington state, it offers plenty of foliage-centric destinations to choose from. Just under a four-hour ride from Chicago is a perfect locale for soaking in autumn’s glory: Wisconsin Dells. Head to Dells of the Wisconsin River State Natural Area for views of trees in their seasonal finery among numerous pines and set against Cambrian sandstone cliffs, canyons, and unique rock formations. Back in the center of town, a leisurely stroll along the scenic River Walk offers a chance to behold the bursts of color while weaving your way along the water. Unwind from all that hiking at one of the area’s local breweries. Then check into Sundara Inn & Spa, one of the first destination spas in the Midwest with treatments like Reiki and CBD massages. Peak time for foliage: Mid-October California Train line: California Zephyr Travelers looking for an extended fall train journey would do well to board Amtrak’s California Zephyr. The line stretches all the way from Chicago to Emeryville, California, in the Bay Area. But the scenery becomes especially dramatic once the train reaches Colorado and traverses the unique landscapes of the West. After passing through Denver, expect to ascend the Rockies, glide over Utah’s salt flats, past red rock canyons, and along the Sierra Nevadas. Hop off the train in Truckee, California, the gateway to the Lake Tahoe region, which transforms into a wonderland of colorful foliage come October. Here, visitors are treated to displays of yellows and reds as quaking aspens, willows, and cottonwoods morph into rich golds, ambers, and chartreuses, and oaks and dogwoods that add splashes of maroon and crimson, all contrasting with the mighty pines and deep blue lake. There’s no shortage of outdoor activities to soak in the autumnal atmosphere, either. Everything from mountain biking and kayaking, hiking and horseback riding will immerse travelers among the vivid trees. For a full outdoor experience, try camping at one of the numerous state-run sites along the lake’s perimeter, or opt for a bit of pampering at a resort and spa like the Hyatt Regency Lake Tahoe. Peak time for foliage: October 15 to 31 Maine Train line: Downeaster Amtrak’s Downeaster line weaves north from Boston through Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Maine, where it ends in the city of Brunswick. Expect smatterings of New England leaves to be on display throughout the journey. Hop off the train in Portland, about a two-hour ride from Boston. While there’s plenty to do in the city itself, we recommend taking a quick 15-minute ferry ride across Casco Bay to Peaks Island. The quaint island can be navigated by visitors without a car. Grab a bike or a golf cart at one of the rental shops in town or simply use your own two feet: the area is quite walkable. There’s one hotel on the island, The Inn on Peaks Island, and plenty of waterfront dining, making it a great choice for a quick overnight or weekend stay. Take a bike ride around the two-mile island loop to absorb the incredible views. The island has a mix of deciduous and evergreen trees, so you’ll get to see bursts of oranges and rubies as well as rich, dark greens, all set against a sparkling waterfront. Peak time for foliage: Early to mid-October Virginia Train line: Cardinal Whisking passengers through the Blue Ridge and Allegheny Mountains, the Amtrak Cardinal train offers a visual feast of fall colors. The U-shaped route curves down from New York City, swooping through 11 states and the District of Columbia before terminating in Chicago. Charlottesville, Virginia, is a stop along the way that’s perfectly situated for reveling in autumnal scenery. Seated smack dab in the middle of the Blue Ridge Mountains, the city is a fall wonderland come October. There are plenty of places in town to spot vibrant leaves, including the bosky campus of the University of Virginia and the historic Downtown Mall, which is pedestrian-only. But for the true leaf-peeping extravaganza, you’ll want to rent a car and head to Shenandoah National Park, about an hour’s drive away. Hike the easy 1.6-mile Stony Man loop to an awe-inspiring lookout point with a vista of the rolling hills of deciduous trees all around. Peak time for foliage: Mid- to late October Montana Train line: Empire Builder Spanning eight states across the Northwestern US, the Empire Builder line operates from Chicago to Seattle and cuts through prime landscapes for foliage viewing. Leaf enthusiasts will want to hop off at Whitefish, Montana—a Rocky Mountain town that’s known for its access to Glacier National Park. Though the colors are spectacular, don’t expect to see rich reds or oranges. Here, it’s bright yellow tones that rule the day. Across the rolling hillsides and along the area’s scenic rivers, you’ll find brilliant honey-hued aspen trees and gold-tinged larches, a unique type of pine tree with needles that change from green to flaxen and fall away when the weather turns crisp. For the ultimate scenery, rent a car for a day and drive a quick 40-minute jaunt to Glacier National Park. There, you’ll see the resplendent larch trees framed by the park’s snow-capped peaks above and its sparkling lakes below. Drive the famous Going-to-the-Sun Road, which is less crowded in the fall months, to get a look at the most iconic views. Note that portions of the 50-mile road begin to close down in the third week of October, so be sure to check the official road status page for the latest information. Peak time for foliage: Mid-October Massachusetts Train line: Lake Shore Limited In the fall months, the Berkshires are a true leaf-peeping paradise. The rolling mountain landscape becomes an undulating patchwork quilt of searing scarlets, terracottas, vermillions, and more. Amtrak’s Lakeshore Limited route puts fall travelers right in the colorful action, with its stop in Pittsfield, Massachusetts. During the four-hour trip from Boston, the route passes through open countryside and picturesque towns until it enters Western Massachusetts after Springfield. Then, the train follows the Westfield river and trundles through dense forests bedecked in autumnal grandeur. Pittsfield station is located in the heart of the downtown district, so travelers can step off the platform and straight into charming shop-lined streets and walkable accommodations like the Hotel on North. Farther afield, there are cozy inns like The Old Inn on the Green in New Marlborough and 33 Main in nearby Lenox. Explore the region’s surrounding farms, like Bartlett’s Orchard for u-pick apples and extensive farmer’s markets at Berkshire Grown. For a deep-dive into the region’s vast foliage, try a longer hike along Yokun Ridge, which offers eight-miles of trails that connect Pittsfield and Lenox, with three lookout points over the tie-dyed treetops. Peak time for foliage: October 5 to 21 Connecticut Train line: Northeast Regional One of Amtrak's most popular routes, the Northeast Regional train also doubles as a fall foliage express come October. Spanning from Virginia all the way to Boston, almost every stop is a chance to spot tie-dyed treetops. Hopping off in Connecticut—we recommend the charming town of Mystic— is a great bet to experience the wondrous effects of Mother Nature’s paint brush. Located right in Mystic is the Denison Pequotsepos Nature Center, which offers numerous hiking trails winding through forests of stately oaks, red maples, and American beech trees aflame with color. Heading a bit farther north (40 minutes by car) to the Pachaug State Forest will afford even more chances to soak in a bevy of autumnal hues. On its many miles of trails, you’ll meander through a cathedral of trees in metamorphosis. For a truly awe-inspiring view over the treetops, hike to the Mount Misery Overlook. Contrary to its name, this vista is sure to delight the foliage-minded among us. At 441 feet high, the lookout is the highest point of elevation in the area, meaning a bird’s eye view of the forest’s colorful canopy. At the end of the day, treat yourself to a seaside tipple at Mystic’s waterfront bar Red 36 or dinner at The Shipwright’s Daughter, which offers seasonal fare from local purveyors. Peak time for foliage: Mid- to late October Minnesota Train line: Borealis One of Amtrak’s newest lines is also among its best fall journeys. Launched in 2024, the Borealis train runs between Chicago and St. Paul-Minneapolis through historic small towns, Mississippi River bluff landscapes, and verdant farmlands of the Upper Midwest. Trees are plentiful along the route, with oaks, maples, birches, and more awash in a palette of oranges, yellows, and reds. Foliage-seekers can alight in the town of Winona, Minnesota, located on an island in the Mississippi—where visitors hike, kayak, or fish amid craggy river bluffs carpeted with ever-changing treetops. Key sites include the 3,000-acre Great River Bluffs State Park, whose hiking trails offer broad vistas over the colorful canopies and across the Mississippi and Black rivers; Sugar Loaf Bluff, a distinctive rock formation with hikes and advanced rock climbing; and Lake Park, with easy, paved trails encircling Lake Winona. Enjoy the foliage from the serenity of the river with a guided boat tour. Be sure to stay at a hotel with scenic views, too, like the boutique Hotel 44 Degrees North, located in the heart of downtown with rooms that overlook the river bluffs and forests. Peak time for foliage: October 5 to 20 Montreal Train line: Adirondack Restarting operations just in time for fall trips across the Canadian border is Amtrak’s full Adirondack line, which stretches from New York City to Montreal. The route was shuttered for six weeks over the summer in order to complete track modifications. It reopened to the public in early September. That’s good news for autumnal fanatics, as this foliage-rich route—lined with maples, oaks, birches, and more—becomes postcard-perfect each October. Expect multicolored arboreal panoramas to fill the giant picture windows as you weave through the Hudson River Valley, past Lake Champlain, and along the hills of the Adirondacks. Notable stops along the way include Hudson and Saratoga Springs in New York, but we recommend riding the entire 10-hour route to Montreal to absorb the full force of the fall ambience. Once in Montreal, there are plenty of options to continue the leaf-appreciation tour. Mount Royal, the famous mountain peak overlooking the city, will be a riot of color. Less than an hour outside the metro area are dazzling nature reserves chock full of morphing trees, like the Morgan Arboretum and Parc-Nature du Cap-Saint-Jacques. Peak time for foliage: Early to mid-October

item.title: Decoding Ho Chi Minh City's Vibrant Fashion Scene
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.04
A mosaic of skyscrapers, colonial mansions, and aging shophouses, Qun 1—or District 1—forms the heart of Ho Chi Minh City, still referred to by its former name, Saigon. Once the cultural and administrative hub of French Indochina, the area has evolved into Saigon's luxury corridor, where international boutiques, art galleries, Michelin-starred restaurants, and some of the city's most expensive retail real estate now cluster within a few dense, walkable blocks. In the last decade District 1 has also become the clearest stage for Vietnam's fashion transformation. For years the country was known globally as a manufacturing powerhouse, producing garments for brands like Nike and Calvin Klein, but few outside the region could name a Vietnamese designer. That has changed. A new generation of labels—drawing from Saigon street culture, contemporary art, and heritage textiles—has repositioned Vietnam from production base to cultural exporter. That shift is increasingly visible with domestic brands like Latui Atelier and Lsoul appearing on such celebrities as Katy Perry and Blackpink's Jennie, while Ho Chi Minh City itself has emerged as a shopping destination for international travelers. Fueling this renaissance is the country's youthful optimism: Vietnam is one of the world's fastest-growing economies, and more than half its population is under 35. A new era of creatives and consumers is forging a fashion identity that is distinctly Vietnamese yet globally minded. Along streets like Đng Khi and Lê Li, locals and clued-in tourists hunt homegrown labels in stores once dominated by Western brands. From youth-driven collectives to refined tailoring studios, here's a curated guide to shopping in District 1. The multibrand retailers The new luxury anchor of the scene, Rue Miche is often compared to Dover Street Market for its gallery-like staging of local talent. The original boutique on Phùng Kh c Khoan street was joined in late 2025 by Rue Miche L'Édition, a roughly 50,000-square-foot flagship in the basement of the sprawling Union Square mixed-use complex. Since opening, the store has amassed nearly 90 Vietnamese labels across both locations; standouts include Americana-inspired Aah Midnight Club and Latui Atelier, known for shredded denim and provocative cuts. Built on a philosophy its founders sum up as “beautiful fashion and beautiful people,” the fast-growing, sustainability-minded concept store Compound Garment now houses 22 local brands within two adjacent shophouses on Nguyn Công Tr. Showcasing labels that share a visual language of oversized silhouettes, gender-fluid styling, and streetwear-inflected design, it's the most reliable read on what young Saigonese are wearing. The OG of multiconcept retailers in Vietnam since 2017, the New Playground boasts 70-plus Vietnamese labels, including Hades and Dirty Coins, across two District 1 locations (plus one in Hanoi). The original 26 Lý T Trng mainstay, with 40-plus stores, feels like a street market crossed with a concept mall kitted out in industrial mesh, neon, and Gen Z energy. The indie standouts At Gia Studios, fourth-generation tailor Lâm Gia Khang, a Project Runway Vietnam alum, translates regional craftsmanship into globally fluent looks. Traditional materials like Lãnh Mỹ A, a black dyed silk, appear in sharply modern cuts: double-breasted blazers, flowy trousers, and draped skirts. Now stocked at Lane Crawford and Ssense—and recently worn by Zoe Saldaña and Emma Stone—it's among Vietnam's most internationally recognized labels. Gia means “home” or “family”; fittingly, the designer's mother oversees production. On the more experimental end, Parsons-trained designer Tom Trandt's Môi Điên (literally, “crazy lips”; figuratively, “outspoken”) has built a cult following around pleating, sculptural minimalism, and gender-fluid silhouettes that feel both futuristic and traditional. Since launching a decade ago, the label has mined Vietnamese folk imagery, street culture, and dead stock textiles for its collections. Rather than treating the men's traditional áo dài as ceremonial dress, photographer-artist Thiên Minh's Mêman reframes it for everyday life. The label works primarily in Japanese linen and neutral palettes, producing collections that reinterpret Vietnamese heritage through a practical minimalist lens. New-school rebels Keep Fashion Weird is the motto of Duc Studio, whose voluminous, deconstructed pieces evoke a sense of daring. Think full-print riffs on Vietnam's national dress, the áo dài, and handcrafted denim and layered silhouettes. Designer Nguyn Minh Đc started the label in 2019 and entered ready-to-wear in 2021. A puffy bag of his was later spotted on Bella Hadid; more recent pieces have been worn by astronaut and activist Amanda Nguyen and the Vietnamese rapper Hieuthuhai. Nguyn Trng Lâm's Lsoul focuses on hyperfeminine glam: corsetry, lace, and shapes that seem engineered for svelte pop stars. To wit, the members of the pop group Blackpink and singer Madison Beer have all worn the brand, which also recently debuted a runway collection at Shanghai Fashion Week. The label Victim of the Prime launched at a small District 1 boutique in 2022; two years later it opened a larger flagship store right around the corner. The gender-neutral aesthetic is clean, youthful, and slightly cerebral—the brand's slogan is We're All Victims of Something Bigger Than Us. This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: Labor Day Weekend Is a Gold Mine for Travel Deals—Here Are the Best Ones We've Found

Whether you’re chasing snow-capped mountains or solitude in a charming small town, this is the perfect excuse to plan a road trip. Flight deals Save on flights to Asia with Cathay Pacific's celebratory sale From now until September 15, Cathay Pacific members can save up to $88 off on flights to Hong Kong and beyond, score up to almost 2,000 bonus Asia Miles, and utilize exclusive savings on selected flight and hotel bundle packages to Hong Kong. For even more flight savings, post-booking, the first 100 customers can unlock 28% off their next eligible round-trip Economy flight (valid for departures between January 8 and May 23, 2027). To get started, sign up as a member if you aren't already—it's free! Then book with promo code CX80US for $88 off per ticket to destinations across Asia, and code CX80HKUS for $80 off per ticket to Hong Kong. Save on travel packages with JetBlue Vacations With JetBlue's Labor Day travel deals, you can save big on your next vacation package. Whether that means bundling a flight and hotel, flights and a cruise, or any combination in between, this new promotion ensures you'll score up to 50% off flights, as well as up to $525 off all flights and hotel packages when booking a vacation bundle. To qualify, travelers must book a round-trip JetBlue Main Fare flight combined with a hotel or cruise for travel by February 10, 2027. Bundle and save on domestic travel with Southwest Airlines Southwest Airlines has teamed up with MGM Resorts to launch Getaways by Southwest, offering travelers significant savings on flight and hotel packages. Jet-setters looking to explore major domestic destinations can save up to $250 on select five-night domestic packages, while international travelers heading to hot spots like Cancun and Punta Cana can slash up to $500 off their select bookings of five nights or more. Whether you are aiming for the bright lights of Las Vegas, the beaches of Hawaii, or a tropical Mexican escape, this partnership bundles your essential travel needs into a single, budget-friendly price. Train deals Score big on trips for groups via Amtrak Vacations For a slower, more scenic take on group vacations across the US, consider train travel. Amtrak is still offering its Share Fares promotion this September, with routes that bring you and the people you love closer to some of the country’s most iconic destinations. Right now, travelers can save up to 60% off for a group of eight passengers on the same reservation. Smaller groups are also subject to discounts—parties of seven can score 54% off all tickets, groups of six can take 47% off all tickets, and so on. Just use promo code V291 when you book—and remember that all tickets need to be under one reservation. This article has been updated with new information since its original publication date.

item.title: What does the EU's new hand luggage rule mean for travellers? Here’s everything you need to know about the updated air passenger rights
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.21
On Tuesday 1 September, Members of the European Parliament confirmed changes to air passenger rights that were first reported earlier in 2026. These rules have been in place for more than 20 years, since 2004, and aim to protect passengers against disruption to their travels. While many of our rights, such as compensation if flights are delayed by a certain number of hours, will simply be upheld by the latest vote, there are some changes due to come into effect, too. Extra costs for hand luggage have been something that’s plagued travellers for decades, but new regulations are set to change that. After more than a decade of negotiations between the Council of the EU and the European Parliament, a landmark agreement has been reached. What is the new rule for hand luggage? New rules will include the right for passengers to carry one personal item such as a small bag or backpack with them onboard without incurring an extra cost. Airlines will also be required by law to display air fares that include carry-on luggage while booking to improve transparency and comparability between airlines and tickets. Airlines may still offer cheaper tickets who travel without hand luggage, MEPs say. A small catch to be aware of, however, is that this regulation applies to EU airlines only. This means that on non-EU airlines, like easyJet and Jet2, passengers may still be bound to the old regulations – except on flights returning to the UK from an EU country. Which other rights have been introduced? Several new rights are set to improve passenger safety and protection. These include rules to make it easier for passengers to claim compensation and access assistance in case of delay or cancellation, as well as new regulations reinforcing rights for persons with specific needs, such as persons with disabilities or reduced mobility and pregnant passengers. Air passenger rights changes to know - The right to carry on board, without extra cost, one personal item, such as a small bag or backpack - Passengers will no longer be charged for correcting spelling errors or for a printed version of a boarding pass if they have already checked in - Passengers will be able to take the return flight of a two-way ticket even if they did not use the first flight - Clearer and quicker reimbursement for flight disruption and travel delays - Passengers with disabilities and reduced mobility will have the right to compensation, rerouting and assistance if they miss a flight due to the airport’s failure to help them reach the gate on time - Any person accompanying a child below the age of 14 will be entitled to an adjacent seat without paying extra. The same right will apply to passengers with disabilities and reduced mobility, and to pregnant women. “I’m proud that, after 13 years of negotiations, we reached a landmark agreement to strengthen EU air passenger rights,” announced Alexis Vafeades, minister of transport, communications and works of the Republic of Cyprus. “This modernised framework will deliver certainty, fairness and stronger protection for millions of European air passengers. The agreement strikes a fair balance for our airlines, helping preserve connectivity that is vital to the EU’s internal market and its citizens.”

item.title: Is your vagus nerve the real reason travel wrecks you?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.89
Scroll far enough on social media and you'll hit a quick fix promising to calm your nervous system in seconds. The vagus nerve in particular has become wellness shorthand for ‘calm on demand’ but there's actual science behind how you do it properly – and it goes far beyond a 15-second clip. So, what is the vagus nerve? Essentially, the longest cranial nerve in the body, travelling from the brainstem down through the neck and chest into the abdomen, brushing past the heart, lungs and gut. It's the main line of the parasympathetic nervous system – rest, digest, repair – as opposed to the sympathetic system that gears you up to handle a threat. “If you think of your body as a car, the autonomic nervous system is the drivetrain and brakes,” says Lou Atkinson, clinical wellbeing lead of Yōjō, a health and wellness platform specialising in vagus nerve stimulation or VNS. “The sympathetic nervous system is the accelerator, while the vagus nerve is your essential braking system, slowing your heart rate, initiating digestion and lowering inflammation.” Activating the vagus nerve can help us feel calmer, but the issue with quick fixes is that we are treating the symptoms of nervous system dysregulation – like anxiety, insomnia, a need to control everything – rather than the dysregulation itself. “If we treat the symptom without ever getting to the root cause, it becomes a tireless battle managing something that cannot dissipate unless we leave the state we're in,” explains Sarah Baldwin, a Somatic Experiencing Practitioner. What happens to our nervous system when we travel? Travel obliterates almost all our comforting routines and habits. “It’s essentially a stress-test for your autonomic nervous system, and vagal tone takes the hit," says Human Potential Coach and Breathwork Practitioner, Rob Rea. “Crossing time zones desynchronises the body's rest-and-digest rhythm from local day and night – a large part of why jet lag brings poor sleep, a racing heart and low mood, not just tiredness.” Short nights, dry cabin air, dehydration, alcohol and caffeine all tip the body further towards fight-or-flight, leaving less room for recovery. For some, it goes way deeper than jet lag. Leaving a familiar environment removes our daily safety anchors, and unresolved stress can resurface as anxiety or hypervigilance amid the unpredictability of new places. “Long after we’ve arrived, and the danger has passed, the body can keep replaying that same protective response – that’s why so many of us feel anxious or shut down for reasons we can't quite explain, especially when travelling,” trauma psychotherapist Emmy Brunner says. “Release isn't about forcing it – it happens through small, repeated doses of safety, not pushing through.” In practice, this looks like having a vagus nerve toolkit you can turn to when you need it most. "Splash cold water on the face – cold exposure activates the vagus nerve and can pull you out of a spiral almost instantly,” Brunner advises. Another tip she says is to: “Slowly look around the room and name a few things you can see – it reminds the nervous system it's present and safe." Another surprising method that works is quiet humming. “It stimulates the vagus nerve directly through the vocal cords,” says Atkinson. If you feel too conscious doing this in a public place, longer exhales also help engage it: "Breathe gently through your nose, inhale for four seconds and exhale for six," says Rea. "Let the breath become quieter rather than bigger, and continue for two to five minutes." Making travel easier on our nervous systems Perhaps the best advice is to think of nervous system work as part of your pre-travel prep, along with your packing and booking. “People often wait until they're deeply dysregulated to start regulating, but the earlier you start, the better,” Baldwin advises. She recommends getting outdoor light at both ends of the day to recalibrate your circadian rhythm, before, during and after your trip. As is having a piece of home with you. “Bringing something familiar, a candle, a journal, a photo and orienting to a new room by consciously noticing its colours and sounds both help signal safety, too,” she adds. For frequent flyers wanting something more hands-off, wearable vagus nerve stimulators like yōjō deliver gentle electrical pulses to the ear's auricular branch, nudging the body into rest-digest mode without requiring meditation mid-flight – wearable while working, watching a film or trying to sleep. But ultimately it’s about incorporating vagal nerve work into your daily life. “The goal is not a quick fix; it’s to discharge small amounts of activation to lessen our dysregulation by even 5 per cent,” Baldwin says. Our nervous systems need something called disconfirming experiences. “These are moments where we show, not tell, our nervous systems that the thing it thinks is dangerous is actually safe,” she says. After doing that, our nervous system has enough data points to see that the perceived danger is actually safe, and we no longer experience the anxiety we once did. None of this promises to make flying enjoyable – particularly if you struggle with it. But understood and practised properly, vagal tone could be the deciding factor in whether a trip leaves you restored or wrung out. That’s worth knowing, next time you're stuck in seat 34C convincing yourself it's turbulence, when it’s actually your nervous system on overdrive. - Emmy Brunner’s residential retreats combine hypnosis and somatic practice. The Compass, a four-week online course, fuses evidence-based clinical tools with belief and identity repatterning. - Sarah Baldwin’s online programs Navigating Your Nervous System and Nervous System Essentials can be found here. Listen to her podcast, You Make Sense Podcast, on Apple or Spotify. - Rob Rea’s Autumn Equinox Day Retreat will be at 1 Hotel Mayfair, London. Follow him online.

item.title: Art exhibitions in Paris for September 2026: from Musée du Luxembourg to La Collection at Musée National Picasso
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.82
That back-to-school feeling which September brings is always bittersweet. We’ve kissed the summer coastlines goodbye and dusted off our autumn wardrobes, stepping into crisper days ahead. It is a time for a cultural reset, and the Parisian art scene eagerly obliges. The end of August has seen the curtain call of many blockbuster exhibitions, only for September to usher in an array of exciting new ones. Renaissance titans of art like Tintoretto and Pop Art icon Andy Warhol rub shoulders with niche, yet equally beguiling exhibitions – like Bruce of Los Angeles at Acne Studios’ inaugural gallery and a radical exploration of street art inside the Beaux-Arts splendour of the Petit Palais. We update this column monthly so you can always keep track of the best upcoming exhibitions in Paris. The best exhibitions in September 2026 1. La Galerie Dior The luminous museum La Galerie Dior is described as “a place of art and memory” and celebrates Parisian couture and the heritage of the iconic brand. Monsieur Dior was originally a gallerist and was continually inspired by art and architecture as both a collector and designer. The brand continues to be involved in art. The visionary creative director, Maria Grazia Chiuri, has always ensured that inspiring women are perpetually at the forefront of their leadership and vision at Dior. Experience their history through exquisite archival sketches, photographs and original looks as well as sources of inspiration from the artistic to the botanical. Address: 11 Rue François 1er, 75008 Paris Website: galeriedior.com Price: From €12; concessions available Dates: Closed on Tuesdays 2. Claude Monet’s Water Lilies at Musée de l'Orangerie One of the most beautiful corners of the city is the Musée de l'Orangerie, built alongside the Jeu de Paume in the Jardin des Tuileries. It is synonymous with the hypnotic Water Lilies (Les Nymphéas), a series of eight extended canvases by Claude Monet, which were generously donated to the French state after WWI as a symbol of peace. As with Monet’s studio in Giverny, natural light floods into the galleries and illuminates the paintings. Also on display until 20th July is an exploration of Henri Rousseau’s enigmatic oeuvre. In collaboration with the Barnes Foundation in Philadelphia, the l’Orangerie will uncover the painter’s unique style alongside his savvy navigation of the late 19th-century art market. After moving to Paris, he often tailored his works to the whims of the wealthy but this show proves he was far from a shallow name. It builds a rich, three-dimensional picture of an artist who remained singular even while playing the necessary games of the Parisian elite. Address: Jardin des Tuileries, 75001 Paris Website: musee-orangerie.fr Price: From €12.50; concessions available Dates: Closed on Tuesdays 3. La Collection at Musée National Picasso Musée National Picasso-Paris is an opulent museum inside Hôtel Salé, which is devoted to the Spanish artist and the artists with whom he worked. 5,000 works of art are held within their collection, including preparatory sketches as well as his prolific photographic archive and correspondence. Their new exhibition, La Collection, offers a new perspective on the work of Picasso. The museum is located on the picturesque rue de Thorigny in Le Marais, not far from Centre Pompidou. Explore smaller galleries nearby like Perrotin and David Zwirner. Address: 5 rue de Thorigny, 75003 Paris Website: museepicassoparis.fr Price: From €16; concessions available Dates: Until 12 March 2027 4. Musée Rodin Only a short walk from the Eiffel Tower and Grand Palais, Musée Rodin was opened in 1919 and has since been devoted to the work of the prolific French Sculptor Auguste Rodin. Get lost in the classical architecture with exquisite rocaille details. The sculpture garden is also exquisite and offers a quiet escape during the summer months. The museum featured in Midnight in Paris, directed by Woody Allen. Carla Bruni had a cameo as a tour guide. Address: 77 Rue de Varenne, 75007 Paris Website: musee-rodin.fr Price: From €13; concessions available Dates: Closed on Mondays 5. Rodeo: Bruce of Los Angeles In June of last year, Acne Studios opened its first permanent gallery space within the historic arcades of Paris’ Palais-Royal. This September it will showcase a series of 77 vintage photographs by Bruce of Los Angeles, one of 20th-century America’s most prolific chroniclers of the male form. Curator Vince Aletti draws out Bruce’s distinct visual language, which toes the line between the sculptural, the erotic, and the refined. Though best known for his photographs of male performance athletes flexing and posing to the camera, Rodeo turns the lens towards working cowboys across American ranches, captured in relaxed and unforced moments. In an era where cowboy imagery has been thoroughly romanticised, the captivating allure of Bruce’s photographs lies in their unvarnished authenticity. Address: 124 Galerie de Valois, 75001 Paris Website: acnestudios.com Price: Free Dates: Until 7 October 2026; Closed Monday-Wednesday 6. We are [STILL] here The bold and storied street art of Paris has made its way inside the grand walls of the Petit Palais to claim its rightful place within the history of art. Featuring 75 street artists from France and beyond, the exhibition conveys the themes, moods and dynamics of our times through an urban medium which reacts to, and quite literally becomes part of its surroundings. We are [STILL] here showcases various techniques and subjects that, while entirely contemporary and self-sufficient, share a surprisingly deep lineage with classical art movements. Address: Avenue Winston Churchill 75008 Paris Website: petitpalais.paris.fr Price: Free Dates: Until 20 September 2026 7. Timeless Tintoretto From 11 September, Musée Jacquemart-André - one of Paris’ most beautiful mansion-museums – will immerse its visitors into the sumptuous world of Jacopo Tintoretto, a leading figure of 16th-century Italian Mannerism. This will be the artist’s first major French retrospective, whose bold, vibrant, and at times controversial paintings were well ahead of their time. Based in Venice, Tintoretto made a name for himself through large-scale public commissions of the city’s most prestigious buildings. In this exhibition, forty rare paintings and works on paper are brought together from both public and private collections worldwide, with the aim of illuminating Tintoretto’s remarkable and widespread talent, and an oeuvre that firmly defies categorisation. Address: 158 Bd Haussmann, 75008, Paris Website: musee-jacquemart-andre.com Price: €14; Concessions available Dates: Until 24 January 2027 8. Andy Warhol: The Line and the Image Andy Warhol’s cult icon status and instantly recognisable oeuvre is a double-edged sword.
