While it solidifies his position as one of the most famous artists in modern history, it can make it difficult to find fresh ways to be surprised by his ubiquitous screen prints. Enter the Musée du Luxembourg, who tackle this challenge head-on with an exhibition dedicated to Warhol’s lesser-known yet deeply important works on paper. They have collated nearly 150 line drawings complemented by paintings, photographs and archival documents in order to demonstrate the Pop Artist’s delicate process of draftsmanship, invention and seriality. This is a captivating new perspective on a figure that everyone feels they know, yet few have seen through this lens. Address: 19, rue de Vaugirard, 75006, Paris Website: museeduluxembourg.fr Price: €19; Concessions available Dates: Until 10 January 2027 9. Adya & Otto van Rees, At the Heart of the Avant-Garde Dutch-born, Parisian-based couple Adya and Otto van Rees were major players in the city’s avant-garde art scene but fell undeservedly into obscurity in the years following their death. Now, Musée de Montmartre shines a long-overdue spotlight on this couple’s life, love, and professional careers. Influenced by and influencers of their neighbours and friends, Picasso, Braques, and Mondrian among others, this exhibition brings together more than 100 works showcasing the van Rees’ bold and experimental style which traverses multiple artistic disciplines and schools of thought. Address: 12 Rue Cortot, 75018, Paris Website: museedemontmartre.fr Price: €16; concessions available Dates: Until 13 September 2026

item.title: Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The sophomore season expands beyond English country piles to Mafia-held Italian palazzos
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.81
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The second season of Guy Ritchie’s hit Netflix series, The Gentleman, is here. The first series introduced us to Eddie Horniman (Theo James), a young British aristocrat who had inherited his father’s grand country estate, only to discover that behind the family money was a secret cannabis empire. In Season 2, Horniman, now the Duke of Halstead, is keen to expand the operation, alongside his business partner, Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario). This will take them out of the English countryside and subterranean criminal worlds of the East End and Liverpool, and thrust them instead into the world of the Mafia, as they attempt to go international and do business with the dangerous Capo dei Capi, Marco Moretti (Sergio Castellito). “The madness of Italy’s beauty, its culture, its history and its traditions were something I felt would fit perfectly into our show,” says Ritchie. “I had wanted to expand the canvas of The Gentlemen in this season. Italy was just an obvious choice. British gangsters colliding with the Italian Mafia just feels so right for our world. Some fruit hangs low and looks so tasty you just can’t resist for very long.” Here are some of the key locations used in the filming of The Gentleman Seasons 1 and 2, from Ritchie’s Ashcombe Estate to Lake Maggiore in Italy. Is The Gentlemen based on a real-life story? Both the film of the same name and the two seasons of The Gentlemen are not based on a true story, though of course, they borrow elements from the criminal underworld and its cast of characters. The situation that Eddie Horniman and his family find themselves in – of having to find new ways to monetise their vast aristocratic estates – is a reality, however. There are no real life examples of aristocrats running cannabis empires that we know of though. The main thrust of the action in Season 2 of The Gentlemen takes place in Lake Maggiore, connecting Horniman and his business partner Katie Glass to Italy’s criminal gangs – the mafia. Historically, the area has not been known as a mafia heartland – unlike regions like Sicily, for example – but it does have a relationship with organised crime. In particular, the ’Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, have reportedly used the area for cocaine and weapons trafficking, thanks to its close proximity to the Swiss border. Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The Badminton Estate, Gloucestershire While some scenes of The Gentleman were filmed on stage sets at Alperton Studios in Wembley, London, the exterior of Halstead Manor, the fictional home of the Horniman family, is The Badminton Estate. The real-life home of the Duke and Duchess of Beaufort is a popular filming location and wedding venue in the south Gloucestershire countryside. Viewers with a keen eye may recognise the property from Netflix favourite Bridgerton and movies including Pearl Harbour and 28 Days Later. The sprawling estate has been occupied for thousands of years, and the remains of several Roman villas surround the main home. The medieval property was owned by the Boteler family before Edward Somerset, fourth Earl of Worcester, purchased the manors of Great and Little Badminton in 1612. It’s his son, Sir Thomas Somerset, who made significant alterations to the original house, and the property has captured the imagination of high society and even the royal family over the centuries – Charles II stayed in the house, and the late Queen Elizabeth II was a regular visitor to the annual Horse Trials. “Badminton felt immediately right for Halstead,” says supervising location Manager Iggy Ellis, “because it’s a proper, lived-in home rather than a National Trust museum. So inside, there’d be some walking sticks by the door or a few shotgun rounds from where they’d been out shooting. There were cracks and tired bits, as you’d get in every family home. But there was also oil painting and history and majesty. It felt perfect for our story.” Ashcombe Estate, Wiltshire In episode one, Ritchie made his own country estate, Ashcombe Park, available for filming a shooting party scene. “That was a lot of fun but tricky at times too,” says production designer Martyn John. “You’re in the middle of nowhere with no phone signal or internet. We had to take everything in; so, flowers, food, dogs, guns and also… frozen partridges.” Ashcombe is a working farm set in 1,100 acres of rolling chalk land, and is named after the ash trees and the valleys (‘combes’) that monopolise much of it. It has been the family home of Ritchie since 2001 (when he bought it with ex-wife Madonna for £9 million), and was previously the home of photographer Cecil Beaton. Loseley Park, Surrey Much like in season one, some of the exterior and interior scenes at Halstead Manor were filmed at Loseley Park, a historic home just outside of Guildford that is now used as a wedding venue. “Where possible we tried to maximise every location because when you move around it costs money that could be on the screen,” explains supervising locations manager Iggy Ellis. “So we used a cottage in the grounds of Loseley for the exteriors of gamekeeper Geoff’s cottage and built the interior in the studio because we needed lots of camera space and somewhere for Geoff’s menagerie of animals.” Swakeleys House, Ickenham Another multi-purpose location was Swakeleys House, a 17th-century mansion in Ickenham. “It was a great find because we were able to use it for so many things,” explains Ellis. “From the rehab centre where Freddie is recovering from the cocaine habit he acquired in the first series to the interior of the prison where Bobby Glass is meant to be serving time.” Built in 1638, it is an excellent example of the ‘Artisan Mannerism’ architectural style, a form of Jacobean architecture that features decorative classical flourishes such as gable ends. It was the home of Sir Edmund Wright, Lord Mayor of London, and was visited twice by the famed diarist Samuel Pepys. The Adelphi Building, London The Adelphi Building off The Strand was transformed into an auction house for a scene in which Susie Glass bids millions for a Botticelli painting, which is later snatched by a gang on e-bikes outside. “I wanted to use that network of streets around the Savoy Hotel, including a secret little tunnel that cuts between John Adam Street and the riverside,” explains Ellis of the chase. “It takes at least three months’ notice to get London streets closed for filming, and there were some careful negotiations with everyone from Westminster Council to building owners and the Savoy Hotel itself. But that amazing chase really is one of the things I’m most proud of.” The Grade II-listed Adelphi has retained many of its original 1930s Art Deco features, including its impressive stone facade, classic columns and Gilbert Ledwood sculptures. Today it is predominantly used as an office space, and houses the publisher Condé Nast, whose titles include not only Condé Nast Traveller, but also Vogue, Tatler and GQ. Villa Rusconi Clerici, Lake Maggiore Villa Rusconi Clerici became the glamorous palazzo home of Mafia heiress (and Eddie’s love interest) Contessa Isabella Savanza de Parme, known as Bella. “We spent three full days looking at several amazing palazzos, including one on Lake Como,” shares John. “But as soon as I saw the one at Lake Maggiore, I knew this was the one. It was in a much less touristy area and it had such great light and glittering water. You could point the camera anywhere and it just looked beautiful.” The interiors too were perfect for Bella’s home. “I wanted a house or a villa which reflected the taste – if not the scale – of Eddie’s country estate, Halstead Manor” says Ellis. “I wanted these two aristocratic families to merge, stylistically. So, you have all the antiques and the paintings that reflect tradition and ancestry, but also modern pieces because, despite the centuries-old history of both families, there’s a new generation in charge now.” Villa Rusconi Clerici is a beautifully preserved 19th-century palazzo on the Piedmont shore of Lake Maggiore, and unsurprisingly is popular as a wedding venue. The villa that exists today was built for a Hungarian colonel and revolutionary, Stefano Türr, who was married to one of Emperor Napoleon’s cousins and became intrinsic to the unification of Italy. The interiors are Art Nouveau in style, including a grand staircase featuring a wrought iron balustrade. Grand Hotel Majestic, Lake Maggiore The Grand Hotel Majestic stood in for the fictional The Grand Hotel, where a wedding takes place later in the series. First built in 1870, it was one of the finest examples of luxury hospitality in the area, and was immediately popular with the international elite. Unsurprisingly, considering its location on the shores of Lake Maggiore, it is often chosen as a wedding venue for modern couples, much like in the show. One of its chief assets is the view across the lake to Borromeo Island, with actor Theo James pictured standing on one of the balconies looking out across the water in one scene. While the interiors are French in style, with parquet flooring and chandeliers, the grounds are also particularly lavish, with centuries-old trees and flowers, and there’s even a small private beach. Chiesa San Leonardo, Lake Maggiore The 16th-century church Chiesa San Leonardo also features in the new season. Located in the lakeside village of Pallanza, the church features striking columns of pink Baveno granite, as well as 17th-century wooden sculptures and altars. There’s also a 65-metre high bell tower, as well as access to the lake from a dramatic staircase. Where was The Gentleman Season 1 filmed? Stoke Court, Buckinghamshire The Badminton Estate gets much of the credit for appearing as the exterior of the fictional Halstead Manor, but some of the interior scenes used Stoke Court in Buckinghamshire. Stoke Court is home to the study, where Freddie shoots Liverpudlian drug dealer Tommy after a memorable scene featuring a chicken costume, Halstead Manor’s boot room, drawing room and orangery. The real-life property is best known for its association with mid-18th-century poet Thomas Gray, who holidayed there during his childhood. Wrotham Park, Hertfordshire Wrotham Park in Hertfordshire plays the part of the home of extravagantly wealthy drug lord Stanley Johnson, aka Bridgewater House. The neo-Palladian English country house was designed by Isaac Ware in 1754, and it’s where we see Susie Glass and Stanley engage in a polite-ish war of words over his desire to take over her father’s empire. London The Gentleman’s filming locations depict two sides of the coin: lavish country houses owned by the landed gentry and hideouts used by the criminal underworld. For the latter, the locations team looked to London. Locations used across the capital include The Reform Club in Pall Mall, which doubled up for Pinky’s Club, and Billingsgate Market, which is mentioned by name in the series as the headquarters of the Liverpudlian drug group. The exterior shots of the Croydon Tower Block were taken at Brandon Estate, while the boxing ring is the now-closed party venue Printworks in Rotherhithe.

item.title: Flying with children is about to get cheaper and easier thanks to new EU rules – here's everything you need to know
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.45
Ever found yourself fuming that in order to ensure you get a seat next to your child on the way to your family holiday, you have to pay extra for a seat for each of you – on top of what's probably an already hefty ticket price? You're not alone. But changes to EU air passenger rights will make this annoyance a thing of the past, as the right for children under the age of 14 to sit next to an accompanying adult free of charge will be protected. In September 2026, Members of the European Parliament approved changes to rules on air passenger rights that have been protected since 2004. There's a slate of changes due to come into force, but the parents among the Condé Nast Traveller team were particularly intrigued by the promise that a free adjacent seat will be guaranteed for a child under the age of 14 and the adult accompanying them. That means airlines cannot split up families at seat allocation, and cannot charge you extra to sit together. Why under the age of 14? For most airlines, children under 14 cannot travel without an accompanying adult on the same flight. The change means that adding extra fees to allow parents and children to sit together – which can quickly add up as they're charged per person – will be a thing of the past. The rules come into effect 12 months and 20 days after their publication in the Official Journal of the European Union – around August 2027, just in time for any end-of-summer holidays. Other rights that will come into practice next August thanks to these include: - Making it easier to claim compensation if your flight is delayed or cancelled - Transparent pricing that displays ticket prices including cabin baggage by default - Personal items stored under the seat should be free of charge

item.title: Best eSIMs for travellers 2026: How to beat airport Wi-Fi and extortionate roaming fees for good, tried-and-tested by our editors
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.21
On the list of additional costs that can trip up travellers, the dreaded roaming data charge is one of the most irritating. While there are usually phone plan kiosks or the odd SIM card vending machine at the airport, by the point you’ve reached the arrivals lounge, you’re a captive audience and beholden to whatever rate is offered. You also might need data before leaving the airport: I’m still scarred by the charge I incurred in the connecting terminal in Singapore when the WiFi wasn’t working and I needed to let my partner know I’d arrived. But there is a way to beat the charges before you’ve even left the country – and that’s by using an eSIM. Often, purchasing a dedicated travel SIM works out cheaper than buying the additional data bundles offered by your UK phone network, especially for frequent fliers and those headed further than Europe. Plus, by using a digital SIM rather than a physical one, there’s no need to wait for it to arrive or worry about losing your regular SIM card while it’s not in use. Below, we’ve outlined the best eSIM services to know in time for your next trip, along with the price for a week’s worth of data for a long-haul flight to Indonesia as a price comparison guide. The best eSims for travellers at a glance: - Best overall: Ubigi - Best for digital nomads: Saily - Best for customisable data top-ups: aloSIM - Best for heavy data users and longer stays: Holafly - Best pay-as-you-go eSIM: Roamless - Best value eSIM: Airhub - Best for app-free setup: easySim - Best for short trips: GoMo World - Best for security and extra perks: Yesim - Best for essential app-only coverage: Honest Mobile - Best for rewards and younger travellers: Global YO - Best for business travel: Maya Mobile Ubigi Best eSIM overall - Pros: Top-up possible without WiFi or data remaining, worldwide data plans, 5G available - Cons: Little pricier than some of the other services on our list for some countries - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £6 Ubigi is a comprehensive data service for over 200 countries, with data plans from 500mb to unlimited. There are one-off, monthly and annual services, so digital nomads, business travellers and holidaymakers alike will all be covered. If you run out of data, you can top up without being connected to WiFi even without any remaining data, which is an additional safety boon that other services on this list can't always match. 5G connectivity is also available at no extra cost where possible. You can also save 10 per cent on prices on your first order with the code CNTRAVELLER. Editor review: I used a Ubigi eSim when I travelled to Yellowstone from London recently. I think the tell that a service like this is working well is to realise you don’t think about it at all. My internet in the States was just as speedy as when I’m in the UK, and worked as soon as I landed at Denver airport to await my transfer. I appreciate this as a lot of airports charge for WiFi or make you hunt down one of those tedious booths for a code before you’re granted the privilege to log on – if you can’t find one or it’s out of order, as happened to me in Hong Kong one time, then you’re either stuck internetless or have to suck it up and pay your network’s extortionate roaming fee. By activating my eSim immediately upon landing, I didn’t have to worry about connecting to the airport WiFi at all. But the main boon was being able to top up via the app even without being connected to WiFi. Wyoming is very large, very empty, and free fast WiFi was often in short supply. I was grateful to be able to top up without WiFi on one day trip – I didn’t realise I was running low on data before leaving and would have had a whole day without connectivity otherwise. This would have been anxiety-producing as a solo traveller very far from home! Charley Ward Saily Best eSIM for digital nomads - Pros: Good variety of plans, regional and global plans available - Cons: A little more expensive than some of the others listed - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6.89 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £6.89 If you’re looking for data abroad, you’re sorted with Saily, whether you’re going on a quick three-day hop to longer three-month treks. You can buy per country or per region – handy if you’re island hopping across Asia, for example – and there are even worldwide plans for the most intrepid travellers. We like how seamless this service is, especially. You can purchase the data in the UK and when you arrive at your destination, it’ll switch on automatically, so you’re never without data and prevents being hit by accidental roaming charges in the airport. Saily has unlimited data plans in 37 destinations including the US, Japan, France, Spain, Italy and Thailand, plus an unlimited European data plan that works in 36 European countries. The app also has various tours and experiences bookable within the Saily app dependent on where you're headed. New users can use code CNT10 for 10 per cent off all mobile data plans worldwide. aloSIM Best for customisable data top-ups - Pros: Easy-to-use app, transparent pricing, flexible data top-ups without hidden fees - Cons: Data-only plans (no traditional phone calls or SMS) - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: Approx. £8.20 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: Approx. £6.70 If you prefer straightforward, data-only coverage without signing up for unnecessary bells and whistles, aloSIM is a reliable contender. It operates across more than 170 countries, is easy to set up via the minimal mobile app – which allows you to calculate and purchase the exact amount of data you’ll need before stepping onto the plane; not something that can be said of all of the brands featured here. Installation is instant via a quick QR code scan and topping up takes mere seconds in the app should you run out of data or your trip is extended. One note: this brand’s eSims don’t support traditional voice minutes or SMS. However, for seamless 4G/5G connectivity for internet-based messaging apps, navigation, and streaming, it’s a worthy choice. Holafly Best for heavy data users and longer stays - Pros: Unlimited data packages in most destinations, 24/7 customer support, customisable plan durations - Cons: Considerably higher price point if you’re taking short trips, limited hotspot capabilities on some plans - Price for 7 days of unlimited data for Indonesia: Approx. £20.40 - Price for 7 days of unlimited data for USA: Approx. £20.40 For travellers who refuse to count megabytes or hunt down hotel WiFi, Holafly is the go-to provider. Rather than capped data tiers, Holafly built its reputation on offering unlimited data plans across 180+ destinations – essentially, wherever you are in the world, this is the eSim for you. You can tailor your package to the exact length of your trip – whether that’s three days or a full month – ensuring you never pay for extra days you don’t need. It is undeniably pricier upfront than fixed-data alternatives, but for remote workers, heavy video streamers, or anyone who relies heavily on maps and ride-hailing apps on the move, should find the peace of mind worth the investment. Roamless Best pay-as-you-go eSim - Pros: Pay-as-you-go data options ensures no wasted data, voice calls available, well priced - Cons: Although potentially more convenient, pay-as-you-go plans can work out more expensive than fixed plans - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6.70 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £6.70 It’s a problem I’ve had when travelling a couple of times: you have to top up your eSim a day or so before the end of your trip, but then leave the country without using all the new data, thus wasting it (and, therefore, the money you paid for it). Not so with Roamless, which has pay-as-you-go options that won’t expire after 30 days. That means if you don’t burn through all your data on your trip, you can use it on your next getaway, even if you’re not returning to the same destination. The brand also has regular data packages for over 200 countries worldwide from free 500MB packs up to to 20GB, as well as packages including call-time, all for a very reasonable price point that’s lower than some of our other favourites on this list. You can save 20 per cent on your first purchase with the code CNT20. Airalo - Pros: 200+ destinations, regional and global deals, great connection - Cons: highest prices on our list, most packs are data-only - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6.50 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £8.50 Habits are hard to break, and I must admit I was sceptical about using my first eSIM. But after one-too-many surprise phone bills, I finally decided to take the leap during a sunny Croatia break, and where better to start than the world’s first and largest eSIM provider: Airalo. Steady Wi-Fi for around twenty minutes is necessary for installing the eSIM, so I’d recommend doing so before you travel, but you can activate the actual data plan within minutes once you land. Airalo’s easy-to-follow setup guide clearly directed me through the process, and I quickly found myself connected to my new data plan – with noticeably improved connection. I was staying in an off-grid beach village near Dubrovnik, and while my travel buddy struggled for internet access in our hotel room, my connection was fast and reliable at all times. Editor review: The sim is all based around Airalo’s no-frills mobile app, where you can flick through the loaded catalogue of national, regional, and global packs. My 3GB package (priced at £7.50) turned out to be plenty for a five-day trip, but the app also provides instant data top-ups in case you run out. It’s worth noting that almost all Airalo packages are data-only, so text and calls have to be supplied through your original provider, but for me, this feature was ideal. With the eSIM neatly slotting alongside my physical sim, there was no need for the confusing chore of switching phone numbers, and so this eSIM lived up to the hassle-free hype in all areas. Layla Quaedvlieg. Airhub Best value eSIM - Pros: Yearly and monthly subscriptions, unlimited data and voice options available - Cons: None that we can see - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £4.75 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £2.37 This is our best value eSIM option – Airhub is a great service for frequent travellers and digital nomads especially. The app is intuitive and easy to use, and there are plenty of different plans available for trips of all lengths. One perk this service offers over the others we like is the yearly and monthly subscriptions, which make financially savvy options for those on longer trips – for example if you’re stationed somewhere for work or taking advantage of that post-Covid ‘work from anywhere’ lifestyle. There are also plans that include voice minutes and SMS services, which is an additional boast that the other services here can’t match. Editor review: On a recent work trip, I realised how useful the combined voice and data plans can be when travelling. In the UK I rarely make traditional voice calls, but on this particular trip I needed to connect with a contact that didn’t use WhatsApp, so I couldn’t make a call over the internet. I’ve a spend cap on my regular sim which, as I learned, prevented me from making calls abroad. I was left in a frustrating situation where I wasn’t quite sure how to get hold of the guy. The problem was resolved by downloading this eSim, and also meant I didn’t have to spend time removing and then re-adding the spend cap on my regular plan when I got home. If you travel a business and make a lot of calls, I’d recommend this eSim. Charley Ward EasySim - Pros: Diverse range of data plans, many plans work across multiple countries, no need for an app - Cons: No family feature for managing multiple eSIMS per account - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £8.50 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £8.50 Editor review: EasySim is part of the EasyJet family of brands, so they know a thing or two about roaming. True to form, it’s one of the most comprehensive services on offer, with a good range of plans at some of the best prices we’ve seen. Some may not like the lack of an app, but the website is easy to use and does the job perfectly well. As a bonus, this service covers a wide range of phones. Not all the options on this list are compatible with my Motorola – an admittedly niche handset – so the compatibility here adds an additional sweetener to this service for me. GoMo World Best eSIM for short trips - Pros: Low starting prices - Cons: Fewer cross-country compatible plans than EasySim, calls, SMS and MMS services aren’t currently provided - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: No 3GB plan available; 1.5GB for £3.99 or 15GB for £20 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: No 3GB plan available; 1GB for £3.99 or 15GB for £20 As someone who travels regularly for work, and often only for a few days at a time, I’ve sometimes found myself paying over the odds for week-long data plans when I’m only away a few days. Case in point on a recent trip to the Maldives, where I was beholden to the airport’s singular 10gb data SIM offering despite only being in the country for three days. So, if you’re one for regular short hops, GoMo World’s smaller plans are ones to consider for maximum cost-saving benefits. Yesim - Pros: Coverage in 200+ destinations worldwide and a ‘refer a friend’ rewards system to save money on data plans. - Cons: Connection speeds limited to local carrier availability - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: 3GB £9 for 30 days, 5GB £11.70 for 15 days, 10GB £19.80 for 30 days - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: 3GB not available, 500MB for 0.45p for 3 days, 10GB £14.40 for 30 days, 15GB £16.20 for 30 days This Swiss-based eSIM provider boasts excellent reviews on Trustpilot and with good reason. The broad, global coverage offers fast, consistent internet activity in over 200 countries, is easy to use and set up, and is reasonably priced with no hidden extras. The built-in VPN technology offers enhanced security and reassurance when travelling, while the fast customer support service is there ready to answer any questions or fix problems, should they arise, with ease. We’re impressed by the virtual phone number rental capability, too – a rare addition among eSIM providers. Honest Mobile - Pros: Perfect if you’re only planning on using apps rather than making calls. - Cons: Doesn’t support internet calling or streaming - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: from £3.75 per month for unlimited data roaming - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: from £3.75 per month for unlimited data roaming This smart SIM automatically switches to EE, O2, or Three when your main SIM loses signal and provides free, unlimited global roaming for over 200 essential apps, including Google Maps, Skyscanner, and Uber, across 180+ countries. This eliminates the stress of data caps and roaming charges while on your travels. It’s a great idea for keeping costs low, just be careful to stick within the limits of what this eSIM can offer. Maya The best eSIM for business travel - Pros: Money-back guarantee for 180 days, high-speed internet connection, global packages - Cons: None as far as we can see - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: From £5.39 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: From £7.19 For a solid choice with no hidden fees, Maya is a good option. No contracts, 24/7 customer service, and a money back guarantee for up to 180 days. This means that if disaster strikes and your trip is cancelled, you can request an immediate refund with no extra charges. The SIMs are compatible with IOS and Android devices, and with at least two (if not more) networks available in each destination, the 4G/5G internet truly is high-speed. We love their new global eSIM package too, which includes across 119 destinations and starts from as low as £4.79, as well as the special business options, revolutionising the company work trip with shared data pooling. FAQs How we tested the best eSims To find the best travel eSIMs, our editors tested a variety of eSims across a range of long-haul and short-haul trips – from quick European city breaks to multi-stop journeys through Asia and North America. We evaluated how straightforward the provider’s app and setup process was, measuring how quickly we could download, install, and activate data profiles before departure. Once on the ground, we put network reliability, download speeds, and signal strength to the test in a variety of locations, including busy airport arrival lounges, remote countryside, and dense city centres. Finally, we compared overall value for money, flexibility, data-top-up ease, and customer support responsiveness. What is an eSIM? In plain English, it’s a virtual sim card that you install via an app rather than by inserting a physical card into your phone. They are activated remotely, so there’s no need to visit your local phone shop or wait for it to arrive. In your phone’s settings, you’ll be able to toggle between your existing physical sim card and the eSim, even being able to use both simultaneously, such as using one for mobile data and the other for calls and texts. This is handy if your eSim plan is data only but you’d still like the phone and SMS capability while away. It means that, if you download and install the eSim before you head off, you can activate it in the airport when you land and beat pricey roaming charges forevermore. The setup is simple. After registering online, all it takes is a quick scan of a QR code and you’re good to go. If you run out of data, you don’t need to download a new one – just top up your existing plan. Each eSIM has its own inclusions, from calls, texts, and internet streaming, to exclusive access to essential apps like Google Maps, so make sure to check in advance which plan best suits your needs. If that’s not enough to convince you, the entirely virtual setup means that they are also kinder to the planet than the plastic chips of traditional SIMs. Is my phone eSim compatible? Most Apple iPhone, Google Pixel, and Samsung Galaxy models released in the UK since 2018 are eSIM compatible. For other smartphones, the quickest way to check eSIM compatibility is by dialing *#06# on your phone's keypad – a screen pop-up including an EID number indicates your device is eSIM-friendly. You will also need to make sure that your device is not locked to a single network. If this is the case, provided you’ve reached the end of your original contract, you can ask your provider to unlock it for free by requesting a Network Unlock Code (NUC). Do I need a different eSIM for each country I visit? No. All eSIMs are suitable for use worldwide, so you’ll only need to install one eSIM. Do check, however, that the eSim provider you select has data plans available for the country you want to visit – all of the brands below have hundreds of countries available, so this shouldn’t be a problem in the vast majority of instances. Some plans are suitable for use in multiple countries, too, which is good if you’re taking a longer trip hopping from place to place – like if taking a cruise, for example. Airalo, for instance, has packages valid for use in up to 137 countries, from Jamaica to Japan.

item.title: The Indonesian island that time forgot is one of travel’s most exciting new destinations
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.07
There are not many places left in the world like the tip of Rote. It’s a fragment of coastline on an island off West Timor, which itself is a far-flung extremity of the eastern Indonesian archipelago, closer to Darwin than Jakarta. Aussie surfers started coming here 40-odd years ago, arriving for Rote’s long, clean waves, magicked up by a rare blend of wind, swell and bathymetry. There are other elements that give Rote its dream-come-true energy: tropical weather, white sand beaches, dense fringes of coconut palms, lingering sunsets, a steady trade wind in the dry season that keeps the mosquitoes down. Rote is, alluringly, always on island time. Crucially, it’s not easy to reach – good for surfers who don’t much like sharing a wave. The long journey to get here is why Rote has stayed Rote, one of the most wonderfully inconvenient places out there. Amid all this remoteness, the first top-end resort has just opened, Nihi Rote & Hospitality Academy, sister property to Nihi Sumba, west of here. Both these hotels – a few hundred miles apart – front one of the most coveted waves in the world. When I visit, the hotel is still taking shape. At the eastern end of the bay is a clutch of thoughtfully designed, thatched, low-rise villas, each with a swimming pool; the interiors in mine use local materials such as lontar palm and ikat textiles. The gathering place is beach club Nammo, with its poolside restaurant and watersports instructors, smack in front of Bo’a break. Here I wait for the tide to turn before paddling out. When Nihi Rote launches fully in October, there will be 21 villas, three pools, a spa, a pump track and a golf simulator. It is also planning to build and sell multimillion-dollar residences alongside the property. One night I’m invited to Rote Hospitality Academy, where Timorese trainees have prepared an endearing evening of traditional song and dance, storytelling and a feast of coconut rice with lemongrass, rendang beef stew and grilled fish with sambal. Sitting around the firepit, toes in the sand, the students share stories with me about the cuisine; traditional string instrument the sasando, made of bamboo; and their struggles with learning to swim. For many, it is their first job, or their first job in hospitality, and it’s been a fast-track whirlwind. Before the hotel opened, they had already hosted a big-splash 50th birthday party for its owner, Michael Schwab, son of investment firm founder Charles Schwab. “We’ve never seen anything like this on Rote,” says one student. Change is not always easy, especially in a place that, until recently, relied on seaweed farming and fishing. I feel a pang as I drive past Rote’s cinder-block and tin-roof huts, women on the porch pausing to wave as they plait each other’s hair, sepia-tinged frangipani blossoms strewn on the ground. Rote has long been open to outsiders – and that is increasingly rare in this world of ours. “Do you live here?” This is a regular refrain from locals as I freewheel around town. It is always uttered with a smile – on the harbour, at a café, down on the beach. When I reply that I am passing through, they say: come and live here, you are welcome, bring your family. Many have taken up such invitations, seduced by the island’s stress-free go-slow rhythm. “We were also passing through,” a South African surfer tells me, echoing my line. “But that was two years ago.” He and his partner have had a baby, bought some land and are now building a cottage. I borrow a bike to explore the main coastal road, sealed but potholed and set back from the seafront, with sandy lanes trailing down to the beaches. Village merges into village, and the only demarcations are bollards painted “Selamat Datang” – welcome – or a trio of life-sized crucifixes, prettily decorated despite being a symbol of execution: one is painted lavender, another strewn with flowers. The churches here are enormous and numerous, towering vaulted monuments, one resembling a gigantic Noah’s Ark. Catholic, a man tells me, then to be contradicted by his wife: no, Presbyterian. Another says Methodist. The pastor tells me Calvinist. Tropical Christianity, let’s agree on, and fervent. At Easter, I’m told, crowds enact the Stations of the Cross, parading through the streets in the garb of Roman soldiers. The rest of the year there’s not much more than a scrap of traffic. One day I drive 40 minutes and count two motorbikes and one water bowser. I reach the end of a road that peters out into scrub, nothing beyond and nowhere for me to go. Although there are few vehicles, there are scads of roadside vendors selling petrol in fancy glass bottles that look more like love potions. Lines of laundry flap. Animals are everywhere: languorous cows, silky-haired goats atop bathroom-tiled gravestones and broods of chickens crossing the road, I could only assume, to get to the other side. This easy-going scene belies the region’s bloody colonial history. Timor was fought over by the Dutch and Portuguese – a battle rooted in the sandalwood and spice trade – resulting in its split into East and West. The British muscled in, but only for a few years, and the Japanese occupied the area during the Second World War. Remnants of history and cultural heritage are not obvious at first glance; some can be seen in the weaving of tessellated tenun ikat textiles, and the Ti’i Langga, resembling a ten-gallon cowboy hat made of lontar palm, worn by men, with a phallic spike on the brim. The best way to explore Rote, with its offshore islands, reefs and consistent breaks, is by boat. At one rocky outcrop I find a vast cave of screeching fruit bats; I drop into the water with a mask and snorkel, and fast-float in the choppy current to spy triggerfish and parrotfish. I was told oceanic manta ray and whale sharks congregate here, so I focus my eyes towards the deep, which falls away fast; the next strike of land is Australia. I check out surf sites, ending up on the far side of Ndana Island, Indonesia’s most southerly point. Nobody is around. I spend most of my time crashing and splashing, but nothing can beat the occasional moment standing aloft, feeling the push of a wave, the water so clear I can see fish dashing about the coral. A couple of haggard, sun-smashed Aussie surfers arrive close to the end of the day, so I bow out of the wave, instead bobbing about straddling my board to watch the colours of the sky shift. Back on land I meet locals and newcomers with surf shacks, market stalls and motorbike hire shops. Hotelier Mick Fogarty is just opening on Rote, after more than 30 years in Bali running the fabled Mick’s Place on Bingin Beach. When I ask him if he feels an ache about leaving Bali, he says “no” before I’ve finished the question. He and his Danish wife, Sascha Hansen, have three pretty self-catering bungalows, and, sensibly, used the best land to build a house for themselves. “We were going to build a restaurant but then thought, why don’t we build a home,” says Fogarty. That sums up the spirit of those who come to Rote. “Everyone moves here for the lifestyle,” he continues, “not to turn a profit, just to sustain a life.” After sunset, when everyone lopes back from the beach, there are a few couples hitching their gear onto motor scooters and a few families carrying babies, bags and boards, toddlers in tow. Everyone’s sandy with wet, tangled hair. It’s a strong, fit, healthy scene: “no drugs, no nightclubs”, as I keep hearing on repeat. One hotel owner points out, “Many of the people here already had their 20 crazy years, so now we can all chill.” Another labels Rote a “retirement village for surfers, who come for peace and quiet”. Carla Lázaro Ferro from the Canary Islands calls it differently. She lived here, then moved to Berlin, where she found herself “crying for Rote”. “Here you feel you can give back; life is more meaningful, more chaotic, more free,” she tells me. On my last night, I sleep out on the deck of my villa at Ferro’s dreamy resort, Bo’a Vida, overlooking the Bo’a wave and the Timor Sea. Here on the southern edge of Indonesia, the stars glow like light bulbs, even on the horizon. Only the dazzle of the rising moon dims them. I feel as far away as I could be. Shacks, bungalows, resorts and more NIHI Rote & Hospitality Academy Following the success of its sister resort in Sumba (to the west of Rote), this 21-villa property on Bo’a Beach opens the renowned surf sites to top-end travellers. Villas are a mix of one-bedroom, duplex and family-style set-ups, and larger residences are planned. The westerly rooms have the best views of the Bo’a break. An on-site training academy allows guests to give back to the community. Bo’a Vida Owner Carla Lázaro Ferro opened a thatched shack 15 years ago atop a rocky outcrop at the end of Bo’a Beach, overlooking the legendary wave of the same name and the sunset beyond. Now she has six climate-conscious villas, five of which were designed by her husband, award-winning architect Álvaro Carrillo Eguilaz, with stone paths meandering down to slips of sand and the yoga sala. Ferro also runs Indika café in town, which serves fruit bowls until 5.30pm, when everyone heads out to catch a wave. Rote Island Huts Nat and Matt Thistlewaite came here from Australia in 2011 after finding the island of Rote on Google Earth. They arrived with the aim of creating a nonprofit holiday retreat that channelled income into local education and the community. There are five simple huts: three are family-style with bunks, all have beachfront access. It’s a heartening enterprise and they are now preparing to hand over management to local Rotenese, as they always intended. Sardine Beach Rote Pika and Pascal Chevillot, a Slovenian and a Frenchman, used to own Sardine, one of Bali’s top restaurants. Here on Rote they’ve created a spectacular three-villa property in five acres of gardens on one of the island’s best beaches. The rooms use lontar palm and coconut leaf to create traditional roofing, panelled walls and sconces. Pascal’s breakfast is a real event, with Parmesan omelettes and smoked Spanish mackerel. I notice a copy of Tao Te Ching on a side table, which just about sums up the place. Mick’s Place Rote Aussie Mick Fogarty and Sascha Hansen from Denmark are the creators of these three delightful beachfront bungalows with private courtyards in a glade of coconut trees. The couple are strong on sustainability, harnessing solar power, reusing grey water for the gardens and lending bicycles for guests to get around on. The lap pool is set to be the gathering place. Minimum one-week stay. 81 Palms Close to the T-Land break at Nemberala Beach, Spaniards Julia Davila Solana and Jose Miguel Murgui have built six A-frame cabins on the soft sand, plus they’ve recently opened four smaller bungalows at their new Next Door property. The Spanish restaurant is the best place for dinner in Rote, with former Michelin-starred Murgui in the kitchen cooking up gazpacho, tapas and seafood paella. Natural World Safaris (01273 691642) can arrange an 11-day trip combining a B&B stay at COMO Uma Ubud on Bali and a seven-night full-board stay at NIHI Rote & Hospitality Academy on Rote, from £5,800 per person. The price is based on two people sharing and includes all transfers and domestic flights. International airfare is excluded.

item.title: Where was 'Vigil' filmed? A look at all three series of the thrilling BBC drama ahead of series three
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.55
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Vigil filmed? An average of nine million viewers tuned into the first series of Vigil, as Tom Edge’s police drama captivated audiences with its sharp twists and turns in 2021. The first series saw Suranne Jones star as Detective Chief Inspector Amy Silva, supported by talent including Rose Leslie and Gary Lewis, as the action went from land to sea. The first series was such a success that a second followed, with six episodes that transported viewers to the Persian Gulf in December 2023. Now, we see Amy Silva on a third adventure to the Arctic. “The first series of Vigil was written as a limited series, so in both series two and three we have had to reinvent the show whilst retaining its DNA,” said series creator, writer and executive producer. With this in mind, we’re eager to see how the dynamics and lives of the characters have changed in the two years since we last encountered them. This is the lowdown on where each series of Vigil was filmed. Season 3 When a member of a covert British special forces mission is murdered at a remote Arctic research station, DCI Amy Silva and DI Kirsten Longacre are sent to catch the killer and defuse a potential international confrontation. For the Arctic shoot, production moved between Scotland and Svalbard, the remote Norwegian archipelago midway between mainland Norway and the North Pole. “Svalbard was amazing,” says Suranne Jones on filming. “Rose and I felt like we were just on top of the world because we went to places that tourists don’t normally visit since we were filming in such remote locations. There were reindeer outside the breakfast room every morning, we got to drive the snow buggies, and we really had to layer up – the problem was when we got back to Glasgow we were too hot because we still had to film with all our layers on.” The lead actor recalls how welcoming the crew and people of Svalbard were as she sampled moose stew and reindeer and visited a husky café home to retired sledge dogs. Suranne notes how the cast were kitted out with heated gloves and gilets and would settle down beside the fire of an evening; unsurprising considering Svalbard’s average September temperatures of 1°C to 3°C. When asked about her favourite day of filming, Naomi Yang (who plays Shen Jia) said: “There was one day in Svalbard where a very small team of us went to a glacier. I was hiking in my crampons up this glacier. We were with someone with a rifle, because we had to have a rifle with us all the time in case it was needed to scare off polar bears. The glaciers are very blue, due to the way the light is reflected I just remember all of us just being like ‘wow, we can't believe we're in this’.” Season 2 Following the renewal of Vigil for a second series, filming took place across Scotland and Morocco during spring 2023. The second outing follows Silva’s team to the Al-Shawka Air Base in the Kingdom of Wudyan, a fictional location supposedly located in the oil-rich Persian Gulf. As a Royal Air Force prototype combat drone is compromised and kills several soldiers, the team set about trying to find the perpetrator. In an interview ahead of series two’s release, Romola Garai (who plays Acting Squadron Leader Eliza Russell) said, “We were in Casablanca and then Rabat so there’s a completely different aesthetic to the first series. We’ve got these vast desert landscapes of openness and heat haze, people disappearing into a massive horizon – rather than being locked up in a tiny submarine, as we saw in series one. It’s a totally different experience for the viewer as we explore a different world within the military.” As Silva embarks on a journey to the Kingdom, her partner Longacre stays behind in Scotland to lead the investigation there. According to Uni-Versal Extras, Scotland locations to look out for across the series include Glasgow, Luss, North Ayrshire, Lanark, Blantyre, Cumbernauld and Motherwell. Season 1 We first meet DCI Amy Silva and the team when a crew member of the Trident nuclear submarine HMS Vigil is found dead. The police are granted access to investigate, but there’s a catch – the UK’s nuclear deterrent must remain unbroken, meaning the submarine stays on patrol. Despite the death being written off as an overdose, foul play is suspected, but the confined space of the submarine hides many dark secrets. Due to their classified nature, the production team weren’t granted access to real blueprints for nuclear submarines. Filming inside a real submarine would also have been logistically impossible, or at least extremely challenging, so a full-size replica was constructed in BBC Dumbarton Studios in Scotland. The scale of the set, which took up an entire sound stage, reportedly stunned the actors. “The set just blew my mind,” said Surenne Jones. “The size of the subs in real life are extraordinary – they're like four floors, with a bomb shop and missile room. The details that the designers put in is quite something, especially as they couldn't get blueprints of real submarines to work from, because you're not allowed to have them. So they had to be talked through what was there by people who had first-hand knowledge of submarines, and then come up with their own design off the back of that.”

item.title: 9 charming family-friendly hotels in the Cotswolds, approved by our parent editors and their children
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.45
There’s a reason Americans travelling to the UK repeatedly stick the Cotswolds at the very top of their Blighty bucket lists. They can’t resist the siren call of its bucolic-and-considered countryside, its honey-hued thatched cottages and pretty villages, torn out of a children’s storybook and soft with the centuries. The region’s undulating landscape, carved by oaks, preened hedges plump with wild blackberries, and postcard country lanes, hosts several boutique hotels that city folk and their broods break for, really, whenever they can. They, along with the wide-eyed American tourists, gawk at its misty hills, its rose gardens and handsome manor houses, never far from a pub whispering tales of Ye Olde England under beery breath. The key here is knowing which ones are genuinely family-friendly – aka not the Cotswold-Notting Hill rendition of rural, where muddy wellies in the house prompt shrieks of horror. No, family-friendly hotels in the Cotswolds must master the art of accepting the wild unpredictability of young children, the pain points of their weary parents desperate for a break and a blast of fresh air, all while keeping things chic for those without them (or, crucially, away from them). Which is no easy feat. A few have prevailed. From spa hotels with an Ofsted-registered creche and Play Barn to honey-hued manor house hotels tempting exhausted parents with complimentary babysitting hours, here are the most family-friendly hotels in the Cotswolds. Editor's picks of family-friendly hotels in the Cotswolds: Best all-rounder: The Fish Best for babies and toddlers: Calcot Manor & Spa Best for families with teens: Estelle Manor Best for three generations: Lucknam Park Best kids' club: Woolley Grange Hotel How we choose the best family-friendly hotels in the Cotswolds Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. For more information on how we review hotels and restaurants, please look at our About Us page. These are the best family-friendly hotels in the Cotswolds. More inspiration on where to stay in the Cotswolds

item.title: I’ve spent years tracking Nordic wellness trends, and this low-impact Finnish ritual is about to take over
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.34
I can smell the embers of a Nordic trend in the making from miles away. After all, even before the Swedish ethos of lagom (optimal balance) captured the world a few years ago, I’d been unpacking this Nordic mindset around wellness and lifestyle in my storytelling for years. I would go on to write an international bestseller, Lagom, with over 15 foreign editions. From Swedish massages to Finnish saunas, the region is synonymous with wellbeing. While Denmark gave the world hygge (intentional presence), Norway friluftsliv (open-air living), Finland sisu (grit), and Iceland birthed “Viking wellness” with hot baths and cold dips, the reality is that all Nordic cultures share these values under different names. What makes lifestyle trends from the region particularly appealing globally is the foundations on which they’re built. From sustainability-focused mindsets and a return to simplicity to curb undue stress, to government-sanctioned free access to nature (think Allemansrätten in Sweden), which fosters symbiotic relationships with the outdoors, and overall accessibility for everyone because they are egalitarian countries. The Nordic communal goal is a focus on holistic well-being that can be sustained over the long term by every individual, from professional athletes in their prime to elders. The latest Nordic wellness trend, however, has rather practical origins. Ever wonder how cross-country skiers train when there’s no snow? Introducing Nordic walking; not to be confused with hiking with trekking poles. According to its governing body, the International Nordic Walking Federation (INWA), which was founded in 2000, Nordic walking is now practised in over 40 countries for health, fitness, recreation, social connection and competitive sport. As early as the 1930s, competitive cross-country skiers used poles with running shoes for summer training. But it was physical education (PE) teacher Leena Jääskeläinen who brought the concept to the general public in 1966, making it the first documented use of ski poles outside competitive training. “I started Nordic walking in 1998 because it is a fun, social and efficient form of physical activity,” shares Aki Karihtala, president of INWA. “It takes people back to nature.” At the time, he headed the Sports division at Finnish Sporting goods company Exel, the world's largest cross-country ski pole manufacturer. It was Karihtala himself, alongside his team at Exel, who coined the term Nordic walking, which has been widely adopted “regardless of age, religion and culture, because there are no boundaries,” notes Karihtala, highlighting its accessibility. In 1997, Exel designed the first Nordic Walker® poles specifically for the activity. A year later, over 500,000 Finns, in a population of roughly five million at the time, had tried Nordic walking. It's said to be especially effective because it engages the whole body while reducing pressure on your knees with ergonomically designed poles. The federation developed its progressive INWA 10 Step Method™ to teach people the simple technique safely and effectively. Finnish trend and branding expert Katja Presnal is a newer convert to Nordic walking. “I’ve studied trends for over 20 years,” shares Presnal. Her personal lifestyle digital platform was read by over 100,000 monthly readers and millions annually. The irony of Nordic wellness being the hottest lifestyle trend at the moment isn’t lost on Presnal, who grew up in the Turku archipelago surrounded by bays and lush forests. According to Presnal, after two decades of travelling, she stopped “preaching trends” and started “walking the walk” by purchasing a 100+-year-old former dairy tucked away in the Finnish countryside for a slower, more intentional way of life surrounded by nature, lakes, and walking trails. “It was about making everyday life a wellness regimen and creating my own 365-day retreat,” adds Presnal, noting that these were the type of slow living wellness experiences her family would seek in places like Tuscany while travelling. “So I have, in essence, returned to my Nordic wellness roots, which in hindsight was the richness of my childhood.” The low-threshold accessibility, from a physical and financial standpoint, is what makes Nordic Walking perfect right now for newbies like Presnal. Another benefit Presnal notes is connectivity with people. “People are now discovering Nordic lifestyles,” explains Presnal. “You don't recognise your Nordic way of living as something special that could become a global trend or could be taught and shared with somebody because it's just a part of who you are.” How to try Nordic walking You don’t have to wait for the annual World Nordic Walking Day held every May. You can start by: - Finding a local event hosted by over 13 country associations from the Nordics and Baltics to Croatia, Japan, and Australia and joining a group walk with an INWA instructor. - Choosing your favourite local trail and walking at your own pace. - Trying one of INWA’s 25 Nordic Walking Ideas, from themed walks to charity challenges.

item.title: The Great Depopulation
item.description:
Source: Derek Thompson | The Atlantic Score: 5.30
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. Why has the number of births declined everywhere, all at once? Some blame technology, particularly smartphones and social media. Others blame a kind of 21st-century weltschmerz—a sadness about the state of the world and our uncertain future in it. A long essay in The New York Times by Anna Louie Sussman, titled “Why So Few Babies? We Might Have Overlooked the Biggest Reason of All,” argues that today’s generation is too anxious about the future to make the irreversible commitment of having a child. So who is right? Is this about phones and technology, or is it a reflection of modern anxiety about the world? Or, perhaps, both? Birth rates have been declining in developed countries for a long time, as child mortality has declined, as women’s education has increased, as female labor-force participation has soared, as contraception use has proliferated, and as modern notions of feminism have empowered women to take more control over their bodies and their economic futures. And birth rates have continued to decline as smartphone usage has surged, as housing prices have increased, as time spent at home on the internet has grown, and as socialization and coupling have declined. The decline is accelerating faster than almost anybody predicted. As John Burn-Murdoch recently observed in the Financial Times, United Nations demographers predicted that there would be 350,000 births in South Korea in 2023; the real figure came in at 230,000. The total fertility rate has fallen below the replacement level of 2.1 births per woman in almost every country in North America, South America, Europe, and southern and eastern Asia. “Only two things are important right now in life: fertility and deep learning,” the University of Pennsylvania economist Jesús Fernández-Villaverde said at the conclusion of a recent lecture. “Everything else is noise. Once you start thinking about these, it’s hard to start thinking about anything else.” I recently spoke with Fernández-Villaverde about why the birth rate is dropping, why it matters, and just how steep the decline is likely to get. This interview has been condensed and lightly edited for clarity. Derek Thompson: Why is fertility important? Jesús Fernández-Villaverde: The number of children born today will determine how our society will look in 30 to 40 years. The year 2023 was a unique year in the history of humanity, because it’s the first time our total fertility rate as a planet fell below replacement rate. That has never happened before in 200,000 years. That means the world population will peak in another 30 years or so if the trend continues. Thompson: Tell me what replacement level means and what total fertility rate means. Fernández-Villaverde: Imagine you have a population of 1 million people. How many children need to be born for that population to be constant at 1 million in the long run? It turns out that for every woman in that population, you need 2.1 kids. Why 2.1 and not 2.0? Two reasons. First, there are a little more boys born than girls, around 105 boys for every 100 girls, if you don’t do anything like selective abortions. Second, not all girls who are born will move on to become mothers themselves. They will die of accidents or other reasons before they enter their fertile ages. So you need every woman to have 2.1 kids on average to keep population constant. That’s the replacement rate. The total fertility rate is an estimate of how many children women will have in a given population. When we look at the U.S. right now, the fertility rate is around 1.57. That means the average American woman is having 1.57 kids. Because the replacement rate is 2.1, a way to think about it is that we have a shortfall of slightly over 0.5 kids. There is a subtlety I want the audience to understand. The total fertility rate is an estimate. It’s slightly different from what we call “completed fertility.” Completed fertility is when I go back to women who are already 50 years old and see how many kids they actually had. The problem with completed fertility, which is what we really care about in the very long run, is that by definition it takes decades before we can compute it. So if we are going to make any forecast about the future, we cannot rely on completed fertility. Thompson: Given your educated estimate, what is the decade when the global population will start its structural decline? Fernández-Villaverde: At this moment, I would say 2055. In 2055, the world population will start going down. Thompson: If you go back to the 1960s and 1970s, it was common for public intellectuals to predict that the global population would rise and rise until the environment buckled and we suffered ecological disaster and widespread famine that wiped out billions of human souls. That has not happened. Global fertility has declined significantly. It’s falling faster than practically anybody predicted, certainly folks like Paul Ehrlich, author of the infamous book The Population Bomb. Why do you think these so-called experts were both so confident and so wrong? Fernández-Villaverde: The wording of your question already tells you a lot about the answer, because you used the word public intellectuals. You didn’t use the word demographers. I’m a professor at Penn, and we have—sorry to brag—what I think is one of the best demographics groups in the world. Had you gone to our population study center in 1968 or 1969 and asked professional demographers what they thought about Ehrlich’s book, they would have probably said, “Eh!” I would argue the book was not very good at the time, and what a lot of the public intellectuals were saying was not really what the best demographers were saying. Thompson: But your research also seems to disagree strongly with expert demographers today. You’ve said that you think the United Nations is overestimating the total fertility rate of many countries. Why are today’s experts wrong? Fernández-Villaverde: The Population Division of the United Nations was created because there was a serious concern that we were having a population bomb. It’s very difficult for an institution that has spent 60 years saying we had a population bomb to wake up and say, “There is no population bomb.” In fact, the UN has three scenarios: low fertility, middle fertility, high fertility. My scenario and their low-fertility scenario are on top of each other. It’s not that I’m very far away from the UN. We are already fighting about the second decimal. The problem is that these things, even at the second decimal, accumulate over half a century. Thompson: I think a lot of people believe that falling fertility is mostly a rich-country phenomenon. But you point out that’s a misconception. Total fertility rate is lower than that of the U.S. in Mexico, Brazil, Colombia, and Thailand. Why is this happening at a global level? Fernández-Villaverde: There are several hypotheses on the table, and I’m going to list them in what I think is their relative importance. First, there’s been a huge change in social norms worldwide. This probably has a lot to do with social media and cellphones. If you’re in a country like South Korea, or in many Latin American countries, where household work allocation is very unequal, suddenly a lot of younger women are looking at the world and saying, “Why am I going to be working for my husband 24 hours a day?” Social media has really changed that perception. Second, we have moved to an economy that is much more service-based. Service-based economies, even in India and Africa, mean people don’t work in factories that much anymore, or even in agriculture. They work in shops; they work in offices. Those are jobs much easier for women to have, because they don’t depend on physical strength. In Mexico, Brazil, or Colombia, if you are a woman 22 or 23 years old with a decent job in the service sector, and a guy comes to you and tells you, “If we get married, I’m going to be the macho in the home, ruling everything; you are going to work for me all the time, and we are going to have three kids,” you tell the guy no. Third is what I have called the educational arms race. People are staying much longer in school. They are marrying or forming partnerships much later in life. When they are thinking about their kids, they understand they will need to maintain their kids and educate their kids for many, many years. This is particularly true in Asia—in China, Korea, and Japan, where [there is pressure for] your kid to excel in high school and college. Those are the countries with the lowest fertility rates. The last is housing. In many countries, not in all, housing is at historical heights in relative price. That also limits the ability of families to have more children. Thompson: Two other issues I want to put on the table. First, contraception. Second, socialization rates in the West and throughout East Asia have gone down. People socialize less, they couple up less. When you put all of this together, having kids has gone from being a necessity or a predestination to a choice. Fernández-Villaverde: At the very basic level, I fully agree. That’s why I already forecast back in 2001 that fertility was going to drop a lot. But if you stopped the Jesús of 2001 and told him Colombia’s fertility was 2.8 or 3 then, and asked me where I thought Colombia’s fertility would be in 2026, given all these mechanisms, I would have probably said 1.8, 1.7. What the Jesús of 2001 would have been enormously surprised by is that it’s not 1.8 or 1.7. It’s 1.1. That’s what has surprised me, that we have not gone from seven to two. We have gone down much, much further. You were mentioning contraception. The U.S. was around 1.9 in 2000. There was lots of contraception in the U.S. in 2000. And in 2000, the U.S. was already a service-based economy. It was already a world where women were empowered, maybe not as much as today, but not very different from today. So why have we gone from the 1.9 of 2000 to the 1.57 of today? That is the mystery. Thompson: More education for women is good. More freedom for women is good. I’m very pro–access to contraception. So the reasons for the decline of fertility are a mix of, I think, quite clearly good things and arguably bad things. Similarly, the implications of the decline of fertility combine both upsides and downsides. Let’s talk about the upsides first. Fernández-Villaverde: In a world where population doesn’t grow or where population starts going down, we will consume less energy, or the growth of energy consumption will be smaller. That’s good for the environment. Second, it will help us redesign a lot of cities across the world. I’m originally from Madrid, in Spain. A lot of the residential neighborhoods in Madrid are ugly. People don’t see those when they come to visit Madrid, but they are really ugly, because in the 1960s and 1970s when population was growing very fast, you had to build these horrible high-rises just to put people under a roof. We are not going to need those ugly high-rises. We can demolish them. Thompson: What are the downsides? Fernández-Villaverde: The obvious thing that comes to mind is Social Security. Everything related to retirement benefits, Social Security payments, the equivalent of Medicare and similar health programs for the elderly across the world, that’s going to impose a tremendous amount of cost on the planet. But also you are going to start being forced to close primary schools. The school district here in Philadelphia, where I live, was just forced to announce a couple of weeks ago that they are closing a lot of primary schools because there are no kids. That’s a serious disruption for a lot of local communities. You will be forced to close hospitals. You will be forced to close a lot of other public services. Finally, if fertility really stays at 1 or 1.1 for a long time, I don’t think we appreciate how big a change this is. Now I’m going to make a crazy forecast, and I want everyone to understand this is a crazy forecast. Let’s suppose Thailand keeps its current fertility rate of 0.8 for 200 years. Thailand right now has 63 million people. At the end of 200 years, it will be around 2 million people. Thompson: Sorry, 2 million? Fernández-Villaverde: Two million. How do you wind down a society of 63 million people into 2 million? When population starts falling a lot, countries may do crazy subsidies for having kids—things can change. Maybe the people who are still having kids tend to have more kids, and they grow as a share of the population. All of those things can happen. I’m just highlighting that these things compound over time. You are going from a society that has 63 million people to a society that has 2 million. It means you need to close 98 percent of the hospitals of the country. It means you need to close 98 percent of the schools of the country. Thompson: It also seems to me that the politics of immigration become a significant and unavoidable part of sustaining the welfare state, because what do you need to sustain a welfare state? You need taxable income. Where does the income come from? It comes from people. And if you’re running out of people, you need to import people, and that’s called immigration. But in my experience as someone who lives thousands of miles away from Europe, it seems to me like practically every country that allows immigrants to become a certain share of their population almost always has a populist backlash. Slashing Social Security creates another backlash. So you find yourself in an environment where there is no long-term popular solution to your political problems. That’s what I see as an outsider. Fernández-Villaverde: Exactly. Japan right now is around 98 percent ethnically Japanese. If we wanted to keep the population of Japan constant in 200 years through immigration, in 200 years Japan will be 5 percent Japanese and 95 percent non-Japanese. This is not about bringing in a few immigrants. This is about changing your country. That country will not be Japan. You may say, “I’m perfectly fine. I’m not attached to the idea of Japan in the abstract.” But I can see a lot of Japanese say, “This is not about being a xenophobe. This is not about being anti-immigrant. This is about not having a country anymore.” In Spain, in addition to Spanish, we have regional languages like Catalan. The problem is Catalonia is getting a lot of immigrants. The immigrants are not Catalan speakers. Their kids may learn Catalan in school, but they don’t speak Catalan. Given the current level of immigration, Catalan, I have forecast, is doomed as a language. It will not exist. Some people will always speak it in a small village in the mountains, but as a working language of day-to-day life, Catalan is doomed. If you’re a native Catalan speaker, this is existential. So this is not about being anti-immigrant because I’m a nasty guy. This is not about being racist. This is just about saying, “Don’t I have a right to my language to still exist?” I’m an immigrant myself, so it’s not that I’m against immigration. But like everything, it needs to be within a reasonable degree. Thompson: You said only two things matter in the world. One is fertility. The other one is deep learning—AI. How do these trends intersect? Fernández-Villaverde: They intersect to some degree, but not as much as sometimes people think. If, thanks to artificial intelligence and robotics, a lot of jobs can be done by computers and robots, and that generates a lot of economic growth and that helps us to pay for Social Security, that will make the transition much easier. I’m a bit of a techno-optimist in that sense, and I’m glad this is happening. I think it’s going to give us more degrees of freedom to adapt our society. But coming back to my point before, this is just not about GDP. My wife and I love to go to a small village in England to spend some time on vacation. It’s a lovely English village. They recently closed the local pub because of population decline. The problem is the local pub in an English village is not just the place you go for a beer. It’s the place where you meet your neighbors. It’s the social gathering place of the village. How are you going to substitute that with artificial intelligence? This article was adapted from a post on Derek Thompson’s Substack.

item.title: The Most Important Breakthroughs of 2024
item.description:
Source: Derek Thompson | The Atlantic Score: 4.02
This is my third time honoring what I see as the year’s most important scientific and technological advances. In 2022, my theme was the principle of “twin ideas,” when similar inventions emerge around the same time. Just as Alexander Graham Bell and Elisha Gray both arguably conceived of the modern telephone in 1876 (and, by some accounts, on the same day!), the U.S. saw a cluster of achievements in generative AI, cancer treatment, and vaccinology. In 2023, my theme was the long road of progress. My top breakthrough was Casgevy, a gene-editing therapy for patients with sickle-cell anemia. The therapy built on decades of research on CRISPR, an immune defense system borrowed from the world of bacteria. This year, my theme is the subtler power of incremental improvement, which has also been a motif of technological progress. Although nothing invented in 2024 rivals the gosh-wow debut of ChatGPT or the discovery of GLP-1 drugs, such as Ozempic, this year witnessed several advancements across medicine, space technology, and AI that extend our knowledge in consequential ways. An Ingenious Defense Against HIV Around the world, 40 million people live with HIV, and an estimated 630,000 people die of AIDS-related illness every year. The disease has no cure. But whereas patients in rich developed countries have access to medicine that keeps the virus at bay, many people in poor countries, where the disease is more widespread, do not. This year, scientists at the pharmaceutical company Gilead announced that a new injectable drug seems to provide exceptional protection from HIV for six months. In one clinical trial of South African and Ugandan girls and young women, the shot, which is called lenacapavir, reduced HIV infections by 100 percent in the intervention group. Another trial of people across several continents reported an efficacy rate of 96 percent. Clinical-trial results don’t get much more successful than that. This fall, Gilead agreed to let other companies sell cheap generic versions of the shot in poor countries. More controversially, the deal left out middle-income countries, such as Brazil and Mexico, which will have to pay more for access to the therapy. Lenacapavir works by targeting key “capsid proteins” that act as both sword and shield for HIV’s genetic material—protecting the virus’s RNA and allowing it to invade our cells. Lenacapavir stuns the proteins and disarms their sword-and-shield functions, which makes the HIV viral particles harmless. In naming lenacapavir its breakthrough of the year, the journal Science reported that the same technique could disrupt the proteins that protect countless other deadly viruses, including those that cause common colds or even once-in-a-generation pandemics. The ability to break down the structure and function of these viruses by targeting capsid proteins could help us cure even more diseases in the long run. The U.S. Enters the Age of Rocket-Catching For six decades, the U.S. has been pretty good at using propulsion technology to toss heavy objects into space. But catching them when they fall back to Earth? Not so much. Until this October, when a SpaceX booster plummeted from the sky at 22 times the speed of sound, hit the brakes, slowed down over the same tower that had launched it, and settled into its two giant mechanical arms for a high-tech hug. Sixty-six years after America blasted into the age of rocket-launching, it has finally entered the age of rocket-catching. So what is this rocket-pincer technology—nicknamed “chopsticks”—actually good for? SpaceX, founded and run by Elon Musk, has already cut the price of getting stuff into space by an order of magnitude. Making rockets fully reusable could cut that price “by another order of magnitude,” writes Eric Hand, a journalist with Science.
