According to news agency ANI, more than 5,000 applicants were vying for the post. The temple in Uttar Pradesh was inaugurated in 2024 by India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, fulfilling a key Hindu nationalist pledge. The temple site has been a controversial flashpoint because it was built on grounds where the 16th-century Babri Masjid, or Mosque of Babur, once stood. The mosque was demolished by Hindu mobs in 1992, triggering bloody riots that left nearly 2,000 people dead. Mishra's appointment comes after the Ram Temple became embroiled in controversy in recent months following allegations of theft involving donations and offerings worth millions of rupees. Mishra served as chief of the Indian Air Force's Western Command during the 2025 Indian military strikes, dubbed Operation Sindoor, which New Delhi said targeted "terrorist infrastructure" in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir. "I also consider this the blessings of Lord Ram that after 43 years of service to the nation in the Air Force, He has given me the opportunity to serve Shri Ram Mandir (temple) and Shri Ram bhakt (devotees)," Mishra told news agency ANI. Opposition slams move The appointment has also drawn political criticism, particularly in the wake of the donation-related allegations surrounding the temple trust. The opposition Congress party has questioned Mishra's appointment. "Will appointing a new CEO or bringing in new people in the Trust bring back the donations by devotees? Has action been taken against the thieves?" Uttar Pradesh Congress chief Ajay Rai said in an interview with ANI. "Will the retired Air Marshal take action against these thieves and send them to jail? When will the action be taken and the stolen money be brought back?" he added. Congress leader Imran Masood told news agency PTI that the job was for "saints and seers." "Now, instead of saints and seers working inside the Ram Temple, a retired Air Marshal will be doing the work," he said. US Secretary of State Rubio reacts to Modi- Pezeshkian meeting US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said he does not believe India and Iran are discussing a trade deal, two days after Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modiheld a bilateral meeting with Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the SCO in Bishkek. The Monday meeting between Modi and Pezeshkian was their first since the start of the Iran war. Rubio reacted to the leaders' meeting during an interview on "The Brian Kilmeade Show" on Fox News Radio on Wednesday. When asked by the host whether New Delhi and Tehran were pursuing some form of trade deal, Rubio said: "Well, I don't think there's a trade deal between India and Iran. Obviously, there are - countries all develop their own foreign policy, and many countries around the world talk to the Iranian regime." Later in the interview, the secretary of state issued a sanctions warning and reiterated US President Donald Trump's stance that no nation should help Iran evade sanctions. "No country should be out there helping them create mechanisms by which they can generate revenue that they will then use to sponsor terrorism and try to build a nuclear weapon. And if countries decide to do that, then we're going to have to sanction them too," Rubio said. Foreign Minister S Jaishankar arrives in Poland, next stop Ukraine India's External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has reached the Polish capital of Warsaw as he kickstarts an official visit to Poland and Ukraine on Thursday. During the three-day tour, which runs until Saturday, Jaishankar is scheduled to meet Poland's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski and Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha for bilateral consultations, the foreign ministry in New Delhi said in a statement. The ministry added that the visit is focused on "enhancing bilateral relations" and will also provide an opportunity to "exchange views on regional developments and issues of mutual interest." The foreign minister was greeted at the airport in Warsaw on Wednesday by India's ambassador to Poland, Neeta Bhushan. Jaishankar's trip to Poland comes amid speculation about a visit by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to India. Earlier in August, Poland's top envoy to India said that Tusk's visit, which would be his third to New Delhi, would send a strong signal for cooperation. There is yet to be formal confirmation of Tusk's India tour. The visit also reflects broader efforts by New Delhi to deepen engagement with Central and Eastern European partners. Following the Poland leg of his tour, Jaishankar will head to Ukraine. Jaishankar's Ukraine visit comes after key Modi-Putin meeting The Ukraine leg of Jaishankar's tour comes days after Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Russian President Vladimir Putin during the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on Monday. During the meeting, Modi urged an end to the war in Ukraine. Ahead of Jaishankar's arrival in Kyiv, Ukraine's First Deputy Head of the Office of the President, Sergiy Kyslytsya, said on Tuesday that he had met India's Ambassador to Ukraine, Anjani Kumar, to discuss Kyiv-New Delhi ties and India's role in efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine. Kyslytsya said he discussed with Kumar Modi's message to Putin in Bishkek, in which the Indian prime minister urged a "move from endless war to end of war" in Ukraine. "We look forward to continued dialogue with India and to translating this shared interest in peace into concrete steps," Kyslytsya added. Welcome to our coverage This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our daily roundup of the biggest headlines making a splash in India. India's Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar is embarking on a trip to Poland and Ukraine today, where he is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with his counterparts. Jaishankar's visit comes on the heels of a meeting between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) earlier this week, where Modi urged close ally Putin to move from an "endless war" to "an end of war" in Ukraine. In more diplomatic news, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has reacted to a meeting between Modi and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian at the SCO summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. Meanwhile, in domestic news, Ayodhya's Ram Temple will now have an Air Force veteran as its first chief executive officer following a donation theft controversy. We will cover that and more in this blog.

item.title: Malaysia's middle path between China and US faces new tests
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.59
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has spent much of his time in office insisting that Kuala Lumpur will not be forced to choose between the United States and China. But two sets of comments last month have raised questions about how sustainable that position is as rivalry between the two superpowers increasingly spills into Southeast Asia. "I see Taiwan as part of China, period," he said in an interview with news outlet Al Jazeera that aired on August 16. Beijing considers democratically governed Taiwan part of its territory. While Chinese leaders say they favor "peaceful reunification," they have never ruled out using force to bring the island under Beijing's control. More controversially, Anwar appeared to accept Beijing's argument that force could be necessary. "If one province decides to break away. Do we use force? I think I will, [to] protect the sanctity and unity of the nation," he said. Regional concerns The comments drew an enthusiastic response from Beijing, while Taiwan's Foreign Ministry accused Anwar of effectively legitimizing the use of force against the islandand warned that his "one-sided support for China could negatively impact Taiwanese businesses' confidence in investing in Malaysia," including in the country's strategically important semiconductor sector. Two days after his comments on Taiwan aired, Anwar argued that Malaysia should strengthen its defenses in Sabah, citing the expansion of US-backed military facilities on the nearby Philippine island of Balabac. The Philippines is upgrading facilities on Balabac, roughly 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the Malaysian islands of Banggi and Balambangan. Balabac was one of four additional locations added in 2023 to the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement, which allows US forces to access designated Philippine military facilities, construct infrastructure and pre-position equipment. Taken together, Anwar's comments raised concerns that Malaysia is growing warmer toward Beijing while becoming more suspicious of Washington's military footprint in the region. A fundamental realignment? Kuala Lumpur has also been one of the region's strongest critics of Israel's actions in Gaza. Anwar has repeatedly accused the United States and European governments of hypocrisy and double standards for championing democracy and international law while failing, in his view, to hold Israel sufficiently accountable. But Malaysia experts warn against interpreting Anwar's rhetoric as evidence of a fundamental strategic realignment. "Malaysia still maintains very good relations with the US and other Western countries," Ngeow Chow Bing, director of the Institute of China Studies at Universiti Malaya, told DW. Those ties may sometimes be less visible than Anwar's increasingly warm public rhetoric towards Beijing, Bing said, but the underlying relationship remains strong. "It is certainly true that the space for maintaining its traditional balancing act between China and the US is narrower than before, but that space remains, and Malaysia will continue to operate within it," Bing added. A shift in tone, not strategy Anwar's comments about the Philippine military buildup are much more about an ongoing territorial dispute between Kuala Lumpur and Manila, Chee Meng Tan, assistant professor at the University of Nottingham Malaysia, told DW. The Philippines maintains a territorial claim over Sabah, which became part of Malaysia when the federation was formed in 1963. Malaysia rejects the claim and regards its sovereignty over the state as indisputable. Those tensions resurface regularly, and in August Kuala Lumpur lodged a fresh objection with the United Nations over a Philippine submission about its continental shelf. "A neighbor that claims part of your territory is building a military base 20 minutes offshore — any government would react," said Tan. Anwar called for the strengthening of Malaysia's own defenses, not for Chinese help, "and he went out of his way to say relations with Manila remain good," Tan added. Anwar also sought to lower the temperature over Taiwan after his initial comments. Speaking to Malaysian media after the event, he stressed that Kuala Lumpur wanted a peaceful resolution to cross-strait tensions and insisted that Malaysia's position had not changed. Malaysia has formally followed a "One China" policy since establishing diplomatic relations with Beijing in 1974. Chinese state media quickly interpreted Anwar's remarks through Beijing's preferred terminology, with Xinhua reporting that the Malaysian leader had "reaffirmed the one-China principle," something Malaysian analysts said isn't true. Malaysia has not abandoned its traditional position, but Anwar's rhetoric "has sometimes been more accommodating towards Beijing than necessary," Khoo Ying Hooi, associate professor of international relations at Universiti Malaya, told DW. "That can create the perception of a tilt even when Malaysia's wider strategic behavior remains more hedged and pragmatic," she added. Malaysia has less room to hedge The prime minister faces mounting political pressure after his Pakatan Harapan coalition suffered three consecutive setbacks in state elections. The defeats have intensified tensions within Anwar's broad governing alliance and speculation that he could call a snap general election. Yet beyond Anwar's rhetoric and domestic political calculations lies a more structural problem for Malaysia. Its longstanding strategy of hedging between the United States and China is becoming more difficult as Beijing's economic and military weight grows and Washington takes an increasingly transactional approach to foreign relations. "Malaysia is not abandoning its traditional balancing strategy, but the space for ambiguity is narrowing," said Hooi. Anwar is expected to visit China in late September, his first trip there in more than a year. He is reportedly due to attend the Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou and hold talks with Chinese Premier Li Qiang as Kuala Lumpur seeks to deepen economic ties with its largest trading partner. But closer relations with Beijing do not remove Malaysia's dependence on Western markets, investment and technology, or its own differences with China. Despite warm political ties, Kuala Lumpur continues to reject Chinese maritime claims in the South China Sea that overlap with waters Malaysia considers its own. In February, Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan reiterated that Malaysia would not recognize Chinese claims that conflict with its maritime boundaries in the South China Sea, while Anwar has recently insisted that Malaysian oil and gas exploration will continue in the waters despite objections from Beijing. For Tan of the University of Nottingham, Malaysia's ability to continue balancing the two powers ultimately depends less on Anwar's rhetoric than on Malaysia remaining valuable to both. "China wants friendly neighbors to keep trading with, and America needs Malaysian factories, where a big share of the world's chips is tested and packaged," said Tan. "Neither gains from pushing Malaysia toward the other." Edited by: Ole Tangen Jr

item.title: Russia's hybrid attacks on Germany: When is it 'war?'
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.55
Fortunately, nothing bad happened this time around. Had the attack succeeded, however, who knows what the consequences might have been: On the evening of August 4, a drone outfitted with explosives and a detonation device was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes in the security area of Leipzig/Halle Airport. The airport serves as a hub for military aid to Ukraine. The German government hesitated for a long time before publicly holding Russia responsible. But now it has announced its findings. On Tuesday, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters that the methods used in the attempted attack were consistent with those seen in other Russian hybrid operations, citing the drone's construction, various components, explosives and detonation technology. He noted that the attack had been planned with a "high degree of technical expertise and considerable organizational effort." In late August, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said of the incident: "The federal government will make the perpetrators of hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for this." At the time, he did not mention Russia by name. And even now, Merz himself has not commented on the matter. However, the price Russia will have to pay is relatively small. The Russian House cultural institute in Berlin is being shut down amid suspicions that it is serving as a cover for espionage. The Russian Consulate General in Bonn is also being closed. What's more, entry requirements for Russian citizens are set to be tightened, and Germany also plans to take tougher action against the Russian "shadow fleet" — the network of ships accused of circumventing fuel sanctions. Exactly how and when remains unclear, however. Mixed reactions to Germany's measures For the environmentalist Green Party in the Bundestag, however, the government's response was lacking. "The federal government's analysis came a bit late, and the steps it's taking aren't enough for me," said Sara Nanni, the Greens' security policy spokesperson, in a DW interview. "I don't think anyone in Moscow is afraid or giving it a second thought right now." As an example, she said Germany should be taking tougher action against the Russian shadow fleet. This would be necessary to "stop the flow of money to the Russian war machine," she said. Roderich Kiesewetter, security expert with Chancellor Merz' center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), is also dissatisfied. In the Handelsblatt newspaper, he called for the delivery of Taurus cruise missiles to Ukraine — and for the activation of Article 4 of the NATO Treaty, which requires allies to engage into consultations in the event of an external threat. He urged the German government to abandon "the politically convenient path of appeasement." However, wouldn't responding more assertively, as Kiesewetter has demanded, risk provoking a military confrontation with Russia, especially given that Russia has flatly denied responsibility for the Leipzig incident? On Tuesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin called the German sanctions against his country a "serious mistake" and accused Germany of fabricating evidence. The Foreign Ministry in Moscow announced that it would take countermeasures. Foreign Minister Wadephul sees Germany as a target Once again, the question of whether Germany is already at war with Russia is being raised — and this time with even greater urgency. But the federal government has unequivocally denied it. "We are not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," said Interior Minister Dobrindt on Tuesday, after he blamed Russia for the failed attack. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told German public broadcaster ARD that Germany is not at war but is a Russian "war target." A year ago, in September 2025, Chancellor Merz said — though without naming Russia: "We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace either." This came against the backdrop of increasing attacks on data networks, critical infrastructure and hybrid threats. Security expert Sönke Marahrens from the University of Kiel offered a more nuanced answer: "No, Germany is not at war at the moment. We are facing hybrid activities by other countries, but we are not at war." In Western countries, he noted, declarations of war are regulated by law. And in Germany, according to the constitution, the Bundestag must declare that the country is at war, and that applies only after a physical attack. "Nothing currently meets that definition," he said. However, the Green Party's Nanni fears Russia will continue to escalate the situation. "We are not yet at war with Russia, but Russia appears to be preparing for a war not only against Ukraine but against all of Europe," she said, calling the incident in Leipzig an "attempted terrorist act." Not at war with Russia From a legal standpoint, too, Germany is not at war with Russia. No declaration of war has been made, no recognized armed conflict exists, and no collective defense obligation has been invoked under NATO's Article 5. Furthermore, consultations among NATO members, which must take place before a collective defense obligation can be invoked, have not been scheduled under Article 4. But things look different when it comes to hybrid warfare, which is not as precisely defined. Numerous security experts have argued that Russia is already waging just such a hybrid war against Western nations. This refers to attacks on infrastructure, cyberattacks, disinformation and traditional espionage. However, the line between hybrid war and an open act of war are blurry. Marahrens believes Russia is using hybrid actions — such as the one in Leipzig — to advance its strategic interests in Germany, the second-most important supporter of Ukraine after the US. Had the attack at the airport been successful, it would have relieved pressure on the Russian front, Marahrens said. He went on to say that "if Russia succeeds in convincing the German public not to support these political decisions [to support Ukraine], that would also directly reduce the pressure on the front lines." AfD opposes further military support for Ukraine The state election on Sunday in Saxony-Anhalt is one current example of Russian strategic interests. Many observers believe that this election is the most important in Germany in decades. The key question is whether the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — which is classified as far right by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany's domestic intelligence agency — will secure an absolute majority and, for the first time, govern a German state. The AfD opposes further military support for Ukraine and would like to normalize relations with Russia. This resonates with many in eastern Germany, where the war in Ukraine is seen by many as none of Germany's business, and where there is a feeling that too much money has already been sent to Ukraine. This is why the federal government — composed of the conservative CDU/CSU bloc and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — is being careful about stepping up its rhetoric, as doing so could potentially help the AfD secure an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt. On the other hand, it can hardly afford to place the blame for the events in Leipzig on Russia while also responding in only a relatively mild manner. This dilemma may also be the reason why Chancellor Merz has so far refrained from speaking out to blame Russia. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: EU wants drones to spray pesticides, but it could backfire
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.43
In theory, the idea doesn't sound bad: Instead of using tractors to spray large quantities of pesticides over fields, drones could precisely spray herbicides, fungicides and insecticides only where they are actually needed. The plan would be to scan a field, identify affected areas and treat them selectively — significantly reducing pesticide use, according to the European Union's Omnibus X legislative package, which aims to simplify EU food and feed safety rules. After all, the bloc aims to halve the use of chemicals for plant protection by 2030. Until now, however, the EU had a decades-old ban on spraying pesticides from the air over agricultural land. Exceptions applied only to difficult-to-work terrain, such as steep vineyard slopes. Omnibus X is now set to change that. In May, the European Council gave the legislative package the green light. Drone use doesn't automatically mean less pesticides "I think it makes sense in principle to distinguish spray drones from conventional aerial application from a regulatory perspective," said Thomas Daum, an agricultural economist and human ecologist at the School of Global Studies at the University of Gothenburg. Daum studies new technologies and their impact on agriculture. Compared with an airplane or helicopter, he said drones can generally spray more precisely. However, Daum also cautioned that "the drone itself does not save any pesticide." He sees potential for using drones to respond more selectively to pest infestations — and thus reduce overall pesticide use. Another advantage for farmers could be the ability to respond quickly to an infestation "even when soils are wet or in difficult-to-access terrain." "At the same time, this flexibility lowers the barriers to treatment and could therefore also lead to spraying being carried out more frequently overall," Daum said. This could result in a technological lock-in — meaning that more efficient application could reinforce dependence on chemical crop protection. Omnibus X aims to save administrative costs, cash Chemical pesticides have been cause for concern for many researchers. Omnibus X is intended not only to make it easier to use spray drones, but also to change the way pesticides are approved. When the European Council approved Omnibus X in May, a group of researchers from 27 European research institutions voiced strong criticism. Among them was Carsten Brühl, a biologist at the Institute for Environmental Sciences at the Rheinland-Pfalz Technical University of Kaiserslautern-Landau. Brühl, who studies the effects of pesticides on the environment, called Omnibus X a "deregulation package" and is deeply alarmed by it. To date, pesticide active substances have generally been approved at the EU level for a period of 10 years. Once that period expires, manufacturers can apply for renewed approval and must once again submit data on the safety of the active substance. Since this review process was introduced in 2011, it has resulted in 59 active substances not being reapproved, as they were deemed harmful to human health and the environment. The main aim of the Omnibus X package is to cut administrative costs, reduce bureaucracy and "ensure fair treatment for companies while safeguarding fair competition within the internal market [...]," according to an EU press release. Researchers warn Omnibus X could harm people, environment European scientists have been critical of the EU proposal to cut red tape and deregulate the industry, because it could lead to many active substances being approved indefinitely, eliminating regular reassessments. They also say the transition periods after an approval expires would be extended from 18 months to three years. Brühl called the idea "reckless." It would mean that even active substances suspected of being harmful to human health could remain on the market — like weedkiller glyphosate, for example, which has been linked to cancer in humans. But the precautionary principle should apply, Brühl argued. This political principle holds that potential harm to people and nature should be prevented proactively, even when there is not yet conclusive scientific evidence. The scientific evidence on pesticides is already incomplete. The risks posed by an active substance are inferred from the results of laboratory studies, Brühl said. But how that substance actually behaves over the long term under different environmental conditions and in combination with other pesticides is unclear at the time of approval. That is why regular reassessments are so important. Brühl now fears Omnibus X could undermine scientific interest in studying these active substances. It would be unappealing for researchers "to engage with a system that can no longer be influenced anyway," he said. Agriculture can work without pesticides Brühl is certain the new EU legislation will not lead to lower pesticide use — not even with the help of drones and more targeted spraying. This approach, for example, does not work at all with fungicides, he pointed out. Fungicides combat fungal infections and have to be applied preventively because once a plant has become infected, it can no longer be saved. But Brühl stressed there is another way: doing without pesticides entirely, through what is known as "integrated pest management." And this isn't some hippie eco-fantasy, but rather a concept for the sustainable management of harmful organisms enshrined in German law in 2012. Shortly after the European Council gave the green light to Omnibus X and its new rules on drones and pesticides in May, the Scientific Advisory Board of Germany's National Action Plan for the Sustainable Use of Plant Protection Products reminded the German government of its own law in a statement. Brühl was the lead author. Researchers wrote that integrated pest management calls for the use of synthetic chemical pesticides only as a last resort. The goal is to secure yields and quality while also minimizing negative consequences for people and nature and preventing resistance to plant protection products. This can work if certain crop rotations are taken into account and mixed cropping is favored. Pests can be controlled by attracting natural predators through flower strips or hedges, while weeds can be removed mechanically. The problem: Spraying pesticides is often the less time-consuming and therefore cheaper option. There is also a persistent narrative that pesticides are necessary to ensure food security. What this narrative leaves out is that monocultures and ecosystems disrupted by pesticides make agriculture more vulnerable to changing environmental conditions. That threatens food security, said Brühl, "because you have a system in place that can't cope with climate change." This article was originally published in German.

item.title: Volkswagen to cut 100,000 jobs by end of decade
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.31
German automobile giant Volkswagen announced on Thursday that it would be cutting a total of 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade in what is set to be the biggest restructuring ever seen in the global car industry. The company said that management and trade unions had approved a plan involving the reduction of a further 50,000 jobs, in addition to 50,000 redundancies already agreed. "It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities," read a statement from the multi-brand Volkswagen group which, apart from VW itself, also includes Audi and Porsche. The total of 100,000 cuts amount to about 15% of Volkswagen staff worldwide. The cull eclipses the 50,000 job cuts General Motors made after it declared bankruptcy in 2009. Unions and management had publicly rowed before signing off on the plans, with the former accusing the latter of not being honest with the workforce after the figure of 100,000 possible job cuts surfaced in the media before being communicated internally. 'The motor of the entire region' What's more, Volkswagen also said the long-term future of four major German plants – in Hannover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm — could not be guaranteed. Their closure would mark the first full-scale shuttering of Volkswagen factories in its home country. "If this plant really were shut down, you could put a big black spot on the map," one long-term employee in Zwickau, Saxony, told the AFP news agency. "The plant and the jobs outside it, our suppliers, they're the motor of the entire region." Caught between US tariffs, Chinese competition and a sluggish growth in demand for electric vehicles, Europe's largest carmaker is in trouble. Company reforms to drive profitability However, CEO Oliver Blume insisted that the decision to cut 100,000 jobs sent "a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group." Volkswagen did not give details as to the timing of the cuts and how they would be distributed across the different regions where it has plants and offices, but the company said its focus will turn to North America and that it is looking to expand exports to the Global South. The plan also includes a three-digit-billion sum investment over the coming years as VW looks to improve technologically through research and development and become more competitive. Among the moves is a structural change that should bring about faster decision-making and a cut to the number of businesses and holdings it owns by about one-third. Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Germany's military wants to recruit tech-savvy gamers
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.28
Gamescom, which runs from August 26-30 in Cologne, is promoted as the world's largest video game trade show. Last year, two-thirds of its non-industry visitors were male, with over 40% of them between the ages of 16 and 25. Those are precisely the young people the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, is trying to reach as it urgently seeks to expand its ranks. Germany's military aims to have 260,000 active-duty soldiers by 2035. The German government has supplied hundreds of billions of euros to modernize the country's armed forces. Defense has become a priority for Germany in the face of the current global security situation. Career advice in camouflage The Bundeswehr set up shop at Gamescom for the first time in 2016. It's been back every year since. A brand-new, olive-green Caracal off-road vehicle is one of the main attractions. Alongside it are laptops belonging to the Bundeswehr's Center for Cyber Operations — tasked with cyber defense, among other responsibilities. Under a watchful eye, visitors can try their hand at hacking. At another station, visitors can put on VR headsets to get a glimpse into the working life of a soldier aboard a naval vessel. Pilots, aircraft mechanics and air traffic controllers present their professions in a 3D experience. Elsewhere, several fit mountain infantry soldiers stand beside a pull-up bar, where visitors are invited to test their strength. New this year is a career lounge where interested visitors can have what the Bundeswehr is calling "career counseling sessions." The atmosphere is positive, with soldiers promoting their jobs without being pushy, taking time to answer questions from visitors — who have primarily come to Gamescom to have fun, meet friends and play the latest games. Do gamers make good soldiers? A representative study by Germany's Bitkom digital association found that one in five people believed video and computer games teach skills that could be useful in wartime — training reaction speed and problem-solving, for instance. However, being a good gamer doesn't necessarily make for a good soldier. "We need people who are comfortable with technology," Lt. Gen. Robert Sieger, president of the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Personnel Management, told DW. "What we don't want are people who think we're playing an ego shooter or some kind of shooting game. That doesn't do justice to the seriousness of the situation at all. War isn't a game. As a soldier and a general, it is important to me that people understand the seriousness of what we do." For Sieger, educating people about the Bundeswehr and the range of careers it offers is a central reason for having a booth at Gamescom. "We're an integral part of our country's safety net. We have to simply be here and show what it means to stand up for the freedom of our country, be that as a soldier or a civilian." Criticism of Bundeswehr presence The Bundeswehr is represented alongside many other employers in the gaming trade show's Job Area, including Germany's federal police, retailer Edeka and software company DATEV. Gamescom is, however, still a video game trade show — and not everyone is comfortable with the Bundeswehr getting close to the gaming world. The German Peace Society — United War Resisters has criticized the Bundeswehr presence at Gamescom, along with booths operated by Germany's foreign intelligence service and defense companies such as Airbus and Rheinmetall. Peace campaigner Marius Pletsch said the Bundeswehr uses inappropriate slogans, designed to appeal specifically to gamers, and distorts the image of military service. "We think it's wrong to lure young people to the booth by appealing to their sense of adventure. We don't think the Bundeswehr should be represented at a trade show that is primarily about video games and leisure to boost its personnel numbers," he told DW. The peace organization will have a booth outside the trade show exhibition halls for two days, providing information about conscientious objection to military service. Bundeswehr: Not just any job "Being a soldier isn't a normal job," the peace initiative said in a statement. Lt. Gen. Sieger uses similar terms, but puts it somewhat differently: "Being a soldier isn't a job like any other. We put our lives on the line for the security of our people." Sieger reaches a different conclusion than the peace advocates, though. "It would be downright negligent for an organization responsible for our country's security not to be an inherent part of society," he said. "As an inherent part of society and a modern employer, of course we have our rightful spot here in the Job Area, just as we have over recent years." What did young Gamescom visitors make of the Bundeswehr's presence? "Morally questionable, but a good employer," said Dennis, a 22-year-old computer science student, although he said the Bundeswehr wasn't for him. Dominik, 26, said he was pleased that the German military was represented at Gamescom. "You can actually have a pretty good conversation with them. They're all very nice," he said. He said he may even consider working for the Bundeswehr's cyber defense division. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: The Dinner Party Has Left the Building
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 5.73
A few months ago, a small group gathered for a picnic during a retreat in upstate New York. In lieu of sitting on a grassy knoll with a checkered blanket, the diners huddled on a flat rock by a waterfall while the retreat’s co-organizer, Charles Michel, began priming its surface with vinegar before painting it with brushtrokes of vegetable purees and embellishing it with flowers and foraged elements to create an abstract composition. As an artist, chef, and self-described “food futurist,” Michel has been creating these food paintings for 15 years. But this painting in particular, he tells Eater, broke new ground for his practice with its fully nature-immersed setting — no tables, chairs, or even plates. “It also became the excuse to provoke interesting social dynamics,” Michel says; he references the relational aesthetic philosophy of French curator Nicolas Bourriaud that anchors his work, and which calls for the art world to create pieces that explore “human relations and their social context” in a more public way. In this instance, the picnic’s context encouraged childlike playfulness (scooping up vegetable puree with sourdough bread) and reverie (“Nobody rushed toward the food. There was a collective pause, [and] a moment of presence and gratitude before we began eating”). One bite from the puree-filled brushstrokes might be umami-rich, floral and delicate, or bright and acidic; much of the food was also reworked from the group’s retreat-sourced leftovers, such as the fibrous trimmings of grilled white asparagus they ate the day prior, now transformed into a delicate velouté for their collective palette. Michel’s work is a prime example of earthwork dining, an increasingly popular trend of curating experiential, artistic culinary moments designed around dining in (and with) nature. The traces of earthwork dining are everywhere, from multicourse dinners with dirt-made “placemats”’ to the collaborative dinner series The Ever-Changing Table, a series unfolding this month as part of the culinary program for Art Biesenthal where “leaves replace porcelain, vegetables become sculptural centrepieces, and the surrounding landscape becomes part of the table itself.” Earthwork dinners also have their sea legs, as evidenced by Banquet on the Sea, an aquatic dinner that took place a few months ago in the waters of Marseille, presented by Résidence Vue Mer and designed by the culinary artist Alix Lacloche. Every aspect of the event was either locally sourced or upcycled, as Lacloche explains in this interview with Ready to Host; the table was built from the panels of an old fishmonger’s cold room, and the menu was designed to pay homage to simple, seasonal offerings with a bouillabaisse-inspired, locally foraged seaweed soup, which was served with bread that the organizers baked in recycled leather flip-flops (a fun nod to Daniel Spoerri). Not only did the event go viral, but outlets and Instagram accounts made a point of underlining that it was not AI. In many ways, the blueprint for these earthwork dinners was laid decades ago. Consider Bread & Puppet Theater, the revolutionary 1960s puppet-activist group that has been feeding its audience house-made sourdough rye and pumpernickel loaves in the fields of Vermont since its early days, and continues to do so in the state’s rolling hills. The company’s underlying philosophy is that theater, like bread, should be consumed outside of a commerce-driven mentality, and dignified as a human-nourishing necessity. The farm-to-table movement of the 1970s reinvigorated the food world’s passion for placing local, seasonal ingredients front and center, undoubtedly laying the groundwork for larger-scale land art dinners such as Outstanding in the Field: a traveling, outdoor dinner series by land artist Jim Denevan that started in 1999 and continues to this day. Together, Denevan’s crew serves hundreds of diners at a single, sprawling communal table — on beaches, in fields, and in orchards — around the world, with the evening’s menu featuring seasonal dishes prepared by a local chef. This week, the culinary caravan went to Menorca for an eclipse dinner. Denevan’s tables, for all of their bucolic achievement, do rely on a more clearly demarcated indoor-outdoor contrast, a retention of certain dining decorum. At every dinner, one can expect rows of chairs and an impossibly long, tablecloth-covered table (complete with the comforts of cutlery and tableware) that becomes a visual foil to its surroundings. Works like Lacloche’s Banquet on the Sea and Michel’s rockface food-painting picnic, however, were stripped of some of those dining conventions. That meant “almost none of the rituals resembled the way we normally eat,” Michel tells Eater. “There were no individual plates, [and] no courses; No clear distinction between audience and participant. And yet everyone arrived hungry and left nourished.” Last fall, a similar experience unfolded at a dinner titled Farm Is Table at Treiber Farms in Peconic, New York, where the table and seating was literally carved into the dirt by organizers — there were plates, but no tablecloth in sight, and the weed-strewn earth was instead elevated to the elbows of the diners, who were served local oysters off repurposed irrigation pipes from the farm. Artist Allan Wexler was one of Farm Is Table’s co-organizers, and tells Eater that the event was one of 10 dinners building up to the March 2027 release of his new book in collaboration with Michael Yarinsky of Office of Tangible Space, which reinterprets The Futurist Cookbook. The content of the nearly century-old conceptual Italian cookbook is rich with relational aesthetic dining fodder; its concept of Aerofood, for example, asks diners to serve themselves food with one hand while the other strokes sandpaper or velvet. Farm Is Table leaned into that notion of a sensory-heavy, social-norm-disrupting dinner by carving 30-foot-long troughs for its 30 guests (tickets were $125) to dine on a multicourse, locally sourced dinner. Wexler drilled holes into the ground, and put candles along the entire length. “As the sun went down and the moon came up,” he says, “it was a gorgeous evening. It just became magical.” “It was very seafood-forward, and we really just worked with what was available locally,” Peter Treiber Jr., who co-runs Treiber Farms with his father, tells Eater. “There was delicata squash and mustard greens; we cooked tilefish, and Davy Jones Shellfish Co. delivered the oysters. It all created a bigger picture of what North Fork is about through the land and the sea.” As far as who attended the event, Treiber Jr. says it was a mix of friends, artists, and folks from New York City, with their common trait being an interest in a nature-driven, communal experience at the cross section of the arts and agriculture. “That cross section is something I’ve been exploring for years both as an artist and a farmer,” he says with a laugh, “it really is fertile ground.” That fertile ground, however, is not always sown with purely artistic intentions. In recent years, earthwork meals have also attracted adept marketing minds who know that the well-oiled mechanics of social media are best suited for thumb-stopping images, even if they’re no longer art for art’s sake and are increasingly promotional commerce and brand activations. A few years ago, a dinner in this remote Menorcan stone quarry for the fast-fashion brands like Mango went viral; this past winter, L’Oréal carved a table and seating into the snowy mountains of Savoie, France, for an influencer brand trip. These events, while visually captivating, feel less attuned to the low-waste ethos of most earthwork artists and more tapped into the type of virality-baiting digital content (or worse, AI slop) that envisions them as moments of exclusivity and luxury. Marketing has a history of mining the fringes of subcultures and art movements, but the ways in which these earthworks coax us into getting our hands and feet dirty feels especially precious in 2026. “It’s a pretty simple concept,” Treiber Jr. says about Farm Is Table, “but it’s pretty effective about getting people grounded. Being at root level.” Michel echoes this sentiment, explaining how such dining experiences can help us confront overconsumption, loneliness, and a growing disconnection from the land and people that nourish us. “That’s the message,” he says, “food is the Trojan Horse.”

item.title: Tea Is So Hot Right Now
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 4.93
In Los Angeles, Tea at Shiloh describes itself as a “late night teahouse.” Here, visitors can reserve slots from 7 to 11 p.m. to sip unlimited amounts of tea — at this hour, all herbal, with blends made by each day’s staff — and sprawl out in nooks of plush cushions, in a warmly lit loft with tall ceilings and exposed brick, while jazz musicians play in a corner. “I was looking for soft spaces in the evening,” says founder Shiloh Enoki, who opened the eponymous teahouse in 2022. Tea Is So Hot Right Now The success of bubble tea and matcha has opened the door for more tea businesses to gain traction Enoki previously worked in the music industry, and her experience with nightlife was often loud and centered on the more performative aspects of dating (“being perceived by guys,” she says). For her new venture, “All I wanted to do was drink tea, listen to jazz, be cozy, and still have the opportunity to meet strangers.” Tea felt like a conduit to an alternative space. While coffee shops tend to encourage a practice of grab and go, or of work or hustle culture, “that’s not the energy of tea,” according to Enoki. “Tea is like, I’m gonna sit here for hours and I’m gonna have a deep conversation with the person sitting across from me, and that’s so rare in our culture.” Despite tea’s astounding popularity globally, the United States has long lagged behind many other countries when it comes to tea consumption, and that conception of tea has mostly been limited to iced black tea. This, however, appears to be changing, with the U.S. importing far more tea — in the hundreds of millions of dollars — this decade than it did 30 years ago, with millennials in particular the most likely to be tea drinkers. Matcha is, obviously, everywhere; according to the New Consumer, it usurped chai as the leading specialty tea drink in cafes. A lot more tea, it seems, is about to follow, as new tea-focused businesses sprout up across the country and as tea sees increased applications as a flavor element in food, desserts, and cocktails in addition to its consumption as a standalone drink. Across the country, teahouses with a similar ethos to Enoki’s are catering to the desire for another kind of space: one that feels slower and more intentional than the average coffee shop, and which offers a different experience than yet another restaurant or high-end cocktail bar. In July, “tea salon” Han Cha opened in Chicago, serving a selection of nine teas from Chicago-based tea company Spirit in the format of British high tea. Over the course of the two-hour-long booking, guests might sip Taiwanese black tea with notes of quince and orange blossom alongside bites of English cheddar and Korean-style quick pickles, or Thai white tea with Japanese curry pimento cheese sandwiches. Heiji Black, who partnered with artist Theaster Gates (in whose Stony Island Arts Bank building the concept is located) on the venture, is compelled by the way tea “makes people slow down and savor the experience.” She cites the teahouses she grew up going to in Korea, which were “really about being social and meeting with people and connecting with them,” as inspiration for Han Cha. At Tea at Shiloh, Enoki also tries to emphasize being in the moment. While the cafe welcomes co-working, especially during the day, she says she wanted to design the experience at night such that people “don’t want to be on their laptop or their phone.” Rather than enforce a hard no-laptop policy, Tea at Shiloh offers other things for people to do with their hands, like games, clay, and watercolors. The dim lighting and communal seating also offer “subtle cues” that the space, at night, isn’t a place for being lost in a screen, she explains. Even teahouses that don’t serve matcha, like Tea at Shiloh, cite its importance in the current teahouse moment. In May, the artist Juno Shen opened Soft Hours, a teahouse in Manhattan’s Chinatown. (A laptop-free space, it draws inspiration from the Song dynasty, which Shen describes as a “culturally rich era” in which scholars “built rituals around slowing down and shifting your attention.”) “Matcha and boba have done something really important in making tea culture relevant to a younger generation, and I think we’re reaching a point where people are asking, What else is there?” Shen says. At Soft Hours, there is no matcha whisked in front of you, poised for a TikTok video. Likewise, “we don’t do boba; we don’t do cold foam. We moved away from all the performance that a trendy tea place would have.” Instead, Shen’s menu hews toward a selection of Chinese teas: streamlined but still showing range. There’s green tea fragrant with jasmine; two kinds of oolong, one oxidized in a way that gives it notes of plum and the other roasted over charcoal until it evokes toasted nuts; black tea with a honey-like body; and a deeply woodsy fermented pu’erh. Perhaps the main concession to trends is that every tea can be ordered as an iced latte as well, which Shen considers a way for people to “softly get introduced” to tea. “I’m not presenting something that’s extremely traditional, so I think I’m just the next step of [people] exploring a little bit more about tea,” Shen says. “I think the next stage of tea culture in America should move beyond individual ingredients becoming trendy [and into] the understanding of tea as this incredibly diverse seasonal category.” Tian Tea House opened in Kansas City, Missouri, in late 2025. Matcha drinks are far and away the most popular, according to co-owner Saranya Hubbard. “I really don’t have to advertise anything that much — it already sells itself,” she says. But similarly to Shen, Hubbard, who grew up in Thailand surrounded by the tea culture in Bangkok’s Chinatown, sees her teahouse as an opportunity to showcase the wider variety of Asian tea culture. Tian brews and offers classes on Chinese gongfu tea and serves lesser-known Thai tea, including one made with hibiscus and bael (a fruit that’s sometimes called golden apple or stone apple). To make the most of the space, the teahouse turns into Moon, a cocktail bar, at night. Tea bridges the gap between the two concepts: There are highballs infused with tea and whisky drinks made with matcha. Further proof of tea’s rising moment can be found in Heytea’s current expansion across the United States. The Chinese chain got global attention when it popularized cheese tea in the late 2010s, but it didn’t enter the U.S. market until 2023, when it opened its first store in NYC; now, it has more than 40 locations nationwide. With drinks like milk tea boba, fruit teas with inclusions, and black teas finished with fluffy toppings, the chain sits at the intersection of the growing cultural fixations on bubble tea, matcha, and highly customized specialty beverages of all kinds, including coffee and dirty soda. The chain describes itself as offering “new-style” tea, which senior PR manager Yinnan Shen explains to mean “experimenting a lot with what tea can become.” Some of its beverages, Shen says, take the approach of crafting a cocktail: What botanics can be added to the drink? What layers of texture and flavor? McDonald’s Sweet Tea this is not. In June, Heytea also opened the first U.S. location of its Teabar offshoot. The concept — which serves dine-in only pots of tea as well as tea ice cream and elaborate beverages like jasmine milk tea topped with a “matcha cloud” — rapidly drew massive crowds. Unlike Heytea shops, which offer a more grab-and-go feel, Teabar was, like some of those independent teahouses, intended to be more of a place to slow down. Together, the interest in Teabar in addition to the original Heytea concept, represent what Shen calls tea’s “continued evolution.” “What Heytea is trying to do is find the most accurate contemporary interpretation of people’s needs around tea,” she says. That seems especially pertinent in the context of the U.S., where the tea culture is nascent compared to China. Now, according to Nethra Rajendran, a beverage experience developer at Oatly, black tea, jasmine, and oolong are starting to “re-emerge in new formats,” particularly in mainstream chains. Instead of boba being the medium for these flavors, they’re increasingly popping up as part of the growing “refresher” category,” she explains. Of course, the interest in tea is no longer limited to the teahouse or tea bar alone. “We can see a very real application of tea beyond a [drink] base in the 2025 resurgence of Earl Grey,” wrote Rajendran, noting the popularity of Earl Grey syrups and creamtops for use in matcha and coffee drinks. Tea is no longer a standalone drink, but, increasingly, a freeform flavor element. When NYC’s ambitious new soft serve shop Unnecessary opened this summer, it launched with a “not-so-plain vanilla,” enriched with osmanthus oolong. Oolong also appears as the grounding basenote of its watermelon-mint flavor, which it developed to be more refreshing than what people might expect from typical milk tea. The argument has been made that we, as modern society, are on a hedonistic hunt for more flavors, our tastebuds “spoiled” by the glut of “maple-matcha-blackberry-thyme-yuzu-miso-caramel everything.” Every drink is involved in a way that only the early days of the Starbucks Frappuccino could have foretold; every dish is a referential mashup of a handful of other dishes or other cultural fascinations. Perhaps tea, with its global breadth barely tapped in the U.S., can provide further flavors to mine. Nearly every culture has a tea to explore, Rajendran adds: the osmanthus and oolong of East Asia, the masala chai and Assam teas of South Asia, the rooibos and kineliba of Africa, the hibiscus in the Caribbean and Latin America, the sweet tea of the American South. Tea has been around for thousands of years, but perhaps we’ve yet to see how far it can continue to go. As Heytea’s Shen says, “Tea is a living culture, and living culture changes.”

item.title: Why Anthony Bourdain’s Editor Wanted ‘Tony’ to Be Darker
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 4.23
There are two types of biopics: those that unconventionally show, and those that exhaustively tell. Thank goodness that Tony, the highly anticipated A24 biopic about the late Anthony Bourdain, takes the former route. “When we are writing a biopic,” screenwriter Todd Bartels told me, “[co-writer Lou Howe and I] are allergic to cradle-to-grave narratives. We like to pick a window on someone’s life that serves as a microcosm for their longer journey.” In this instance, that window is the summer of 1975, when a young Tony first cuts his chops in a Provincetown, Massachusetts, kitchen. “[It’s] more a movie about the relatable arc of knowing who you want to be but not quite knowing how to get there and raging against that,” writes Eater’s Bettina Makalintal in her review of the film, and “it happens to be a movie about someone we all loved.” Then again, successfully pitching a Bourdain biopic to his estate was always going to be a big swing. I spoke with Todd Bartels and Lou Howe about what made that swing possible (for one: bringing on Kimberly Witherspoon, Bourdain’s literary agent and friend, as an executive producer); which cast member demonstrated the best culinary chops; and who they could imagine playing an older, more seasoned Anthony Bourdain. Eater: How did you strike the balance between making a movie for the passionate Anthony Bourdain fans, and viewers who may know very little about him? Lou Howe: I was anxious about that [laughs], especially at the very beginning. But [we] just [tried] to make a good movie, and hope that the entertainment factor and emotional engagement hits the target well enough. We started this whole process as fans, so in that way we felt relatively comfortable servicing fellow fans. You want to write a good story that people can plug into no matter who the character is. Of course, there are some Kitchen Confidential Easter eggs. Such as? How did you manage to tap into the emotional, and not just factual, truths of Bourdain’s story? Todd Bartels: As [Lou] mentions, when we work on a biopic we’re very allergic to cradle-to-grave narratives. We prefer to focus on a window in someone’s life. The biography written by Laurie Woolever, who was Bourdain’s longtime assistant and collaborator, was essential at helping us answer questions like, How did this person “in need of a good ass kicking” — as Bourdain famously wrote about himself as a young man — become this enlightened figure for so many people? He wrote that he treated the world like his ashtray, that he was narcissistic and insufferable. How do you go from little shit to guru? How did you gain the trust of Bourdain’s estate? LH: That was a multistep process. We knew we had to go to the estate first, and our executive producer, Emily Rose — who is also a big Bourdain fan — chased down Kimberly Witherspoon, Bourdain’s literary agent and someone who helped build his career as a writer. Witherspoon and Ottavia Busia-Bourdain are the executors of the estate, and [Rose] was finally, after much chasing, able to get us a meeting with them. What was the elevator pitch? LH: That it would be a love letter: a Provincetown summer coming-of-age story that ends in a clambake. [Witherspoon and Busia-Bourdain] were kind of like, “Well, that’s different from what we’ve been getting pitched,” which was a lot of stuff focusing on his later years, and trying to understand his death. We rejected that consciously. They liked that idea, but basically said, “Prove it,” so we then went back to them when we had a script, and A24 involved, and [co-writer and director] Matt Johnson and Dominic Sessa; those two kind of came on board as a team. [Witherspoon] also came on board as an executive producer and was very creatively involved throughout everything. Was anyone else considered to play Bourdain? LH: It was always Dom. Who do you think could play an older version of Bourdain? TB: That’s such a fun thing to think about, and no one has asked us that yet. I have two thoughts, amongst many, but a friend once suggested Bobby Cannavale. I can see it. LH: And [Cannavale] would really have the voice down. Kim Witherspoon knew Bourdain so well. How did her input impact the film? TB: She’s really one of the keepers of his legacy, and would help us to gut-check these moments where we’d be like, “Okay, does this feel like your friend?” We were always surprised at how she wanted us to get even darker. She’d say, “No, don’t make him so nice. [At this stage] he was a punk.” We were showing the devil and angel on his shoulder, as represented respectively by the characters Sal, who was played by Leo Woodall, and Ciro, the chef played by Antonio Banderas. She insisted that we really not sanitize that [journey]. LH: She didn’t want him to look like the innocent little victim of bad influences. The whole idea of having Eric Ripert make a cameo was also her idea. What was Eric Ripert like on set? That must have been emotional. TB: Well, Ripert is a Buddhist, always wearing his mala beads, and was extremely humble and just curious about the acting process. At no point was he swaggering around like the grand chef from Le Bernardin that he is [laughs]. LH: It was such an honor. With him and [Witherspoon] being involved, it really just felt like we had the people who loved him honoring him the right way. Can you tell me more about the on-set food logistics? TB: Christine Tobin was our food culinary consultant, and was there every day making all the food in a little shack behind the kitchen. I think Dom [Sessa] ate like, eight lobster rolls at a time [laughs]. Leo Woodall also became unbelievable at shucking an oyster. He made it look effortless, which is also such an important aspect of his character. LH: Antonio [Banderas] is also a restaurateur. Leo [Woodall] and Dom [Sessa] trained beforehand in kitchens, but [Banderas] didn’t need any help. In fact, during a lot of scenes, he’s actually off to the side making paella. Wait, Antonio Banderas was literally just always making paella on set? LH: Yeah! Incredible, right? He just loves to do it — which, again, was also so perfect for his role as the chef as well. Were there any other scenes or moments you would have loved to show in the movie? LH: I have one that comes to mind that was never shot. Bourdain’s favorite hot dog stand is this spot called Hiram’s in Fort Lee, New Jersey, and in earlier drafts of the script we see him head to this place — a real childhood favorite, and a true greasy spoon haunt — to see the amount of joy that it gives him. It’s a first insight into his relationship with food. TB: Provincetown’s history as this Portuguese fishing town, too, is also [front and center]. There’s a kind of melancholic, longing singing known as fado in Portuguese culture. If you pay attention, you can hear it in the background during the striper run scene and when Tony and Ciro are sitting by a bonfire. At one point, we were going to have an actual fado singer’s character who was perhaps the unrequited love of Antonio [Banderas’s] character. But we wanted his character’s backstory to be more mysterious. How did you familiarize yourself with that old-school Provincetown energy? TB: We hung out for the better part of two days at Bourdain’s favorite dive bar, the Old Colony Tap, which is still there on the main drag of Commercial Street, and covered in all of its maritime flotsam and jetsam, Red Sox [memorabilia] glory. I’d say it’s the best bar in America.

item.title: Google's new AI weather model uses live satellite data for higher-resolution forecasts
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.82
Google's new AI weather model uses live satellite data for higher-resolution forecasts WeatherNext 3 is also supposed to be much better at predicting precipitation. Google DeepMind has released the WeatherNext 3, an updated version of its last AI-powered weather model that it claims offers even more detailed forecasts across key variables like temperature, moisture and wind speed. DeepMind notes the new model should be particularly useful to companies working in renewable energy production, because of its ability to forecast "100-meter wind speeds (roughly at turbine-height) for precise wind-energy output, alongside high-resolution cloud cover and sun radiation levels to help solar farms." WeatherNext 3's ability to offer hourly and higher-resolution forecasts (in a 5-kilometer square grid rather than the 25-kilometer square grid of WeatherNext 2) is all due to the new data it's trained on, DeepMind says. Rather than primarily relying on data from numerical weather prediction models, which include a six-hour lag, WeatherNext 3 incorporates live satellite data, which gives the model "a rich, continuously updating view of the atmosphere." The model's ingestion of sparse weather station data means it can also offer more detailed forecasts of variables like humidity, which can usually change dramatically from one kilometer to the next. Combining precipitation data from NASA and Google's own satellite analysis also means WeatherNext 3 is better at predicting things like rain and snow. DeepMind says the model produces "up to 50 percent more accurate precipitation forecasts — with the greatest improvements in regions where forecasts have historically been less reliable." WeatherNext 3 will power weather experiences in Google Search, the Gemini app and Google Maps, along with the Google Maps Weather API and the Google Earth Engine. If you're curious about experimenting with the model yourself, you can give it a spin right now in the Google Weather Lab. If you want to take the next step and build something with Google's model, the original WeatherNext model is also open-source as of August 2026.

item.title: Epic Games brings cross-platform voice chat to Fortnite and its services
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.48
Epic Games brings cross-platform voice chat to Fortnite and its services Game and yap from across Epic’s ecosystem. Epic Games is expanding its options for chatting with friends while playing its titles. A new feature called Epic Parties allowers players to enter voice chats across platforms and games. Fortnite, the Epic Games Store and the Epic Games app all support Epic Parties, and there's also an option to transfer a voice chat between those places. In other words, you could start a chat while in Epic's app and then seamlessly transition the call when you enter a Fortnite match. Epic Parties is also cross-platform, so people can communicate no matter what hardware each of them are on. The chat can also continue in the background when on mobile or when playing other titles from the Epic Games Store. People who accept an Epic Party invite will automatically be placed in the same Fortnite lobby together when in-game. The new voice chat options expand on the text chat communication options that the company began rolling out to its services last year. Players can invite each other to a party from their friends list, and there will be an option to move an existing text chat to voice with a "Start Party" button in the chat window.

item.title: Google rolls out AI-powered voice capabilities for Gmail, Docs and Keep
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.42
Google rolls out AI-powered voice capabilities for Gmail, Docs and Keep The features are out of beta and available for all Google AI subscribers. Gmail, Docs and Keep Live are now out of beta and are generally available to paying Google AI subscribers. Google started beta testing Gmail Live in June as part of the company's efforts to replicate the experience of using Gemini Live on its popular apps. You can use Gmail Live to look for specific information in your emails using natural language. It understands questions like "When is my kid's next school event?" and answer follow-up inquiries, such as "Does he need to bring anything for the field trip?" Like real conversations, you can interrupt Gmail Live and change the subject or switch gears anytime, if you have other questions. The feature will display the transcript on screen so you can read it, as well as link to email sources. It's now available to Google AI Plus, Pro and Ultra subscribers on Android and iOS. As you can guess, Docs Live can help you organize your thoughts and structure your document, based on what you tell it. If you decide to give it permission to access your Drive and Chat, it can also draw information from there, in addition to your Gmail account and the web, to write a draft for you. You'll be able to access Docs Live on Android and iOS if you have a Google AI Pro or Ultra plan. Finally, Keep Live can write up lists and notes based on what you say out loud. It can understand what you mean even if you don't give it explicit instructions, such as listing grocery items under "ingredients for pesto pasta" without you telling it to or adding more items to your existing grocery list. This one is Android only for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, at least for now.

item.title: Anthropic automatically signs out Claude users to protect them from hackers
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.35
Anthropic automatically signs out Claude users to protect them from hackers Infostealer malware apparently had harvested active Claude login sessions from users' PCs. Anthropic has been signing users out of their accounts, deleting saved payment cards and refunding charges after attackers used stolen browser data to burn through victims' usage limits. That's according to an email the company sent to affected users last week, which has since been shared publicly on Reddit. As reported by SecurityWeek, the AI giant points to customers' own computers rather than any breach at Anthropic, telling affected users that infostealer malware had harvested active Claude login sessions from their own PCs. Once inside affected accounts, the attacker(s) could burn through usage limits and make unauthorized Claude charges. "If your usage limits looked like they refilled and then drained while you weren't using Claude, this was likely the cause," the email reads. In response, Anthropic said it forced sign-outs of affected sessions, removed the card on file and refunded any extra usage charges it tied to the activity. While this stops the stolen sessions, Anthropic told affected users that this doesn't remove the malware. Both Windows and macOS users are affected Anthropic has identified six malware families as responsible for the hijacked sessions so far: Vidar, Lumma, StealC, RedLine, Acreed on Windows and Atomic Stealer (AMOS) "on a small number of Macs." None of these infostealers has been built to target Claude specifically; they're general-purpose stealers that usually come bundled with malicious downloads. Once running, they scoop up saved passwords and browser cookies, which then allows threat actors to hijack accounts. In this case, the infostealers copied Claude session cookies, the tokens that a browser keeps after login so Claude doesn't demand a password on each new page load. An attacker replaying a stolen cookie then picks up the victim's session mid-stream, already authenticated, so password and two-factor authentication requests aren't triggered. Anthropic's recommended fix is to remove the malware before logging back in to Claude, then lock down the email address attached to the account with a new password and two-factor authentication. Only then, Anthropic says, should payment methods be re-added to affected Claude accounts. What makes a Claude account worth hijacking? Stolen Claude logins have serious resale value at scale. Adam Meyers, senior vice president of counter adversary operations at CrowdStrike, told Axios in August that a trade has grown up around hijacked AI accounts, with criminals trafficking credentials for Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini. Meanwhile, findings by Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 have traced hijacked accounts to proxy services known as transfer stations. These pool stolen credentials and resell access to AI services at a much lower cost than retail. Anthropic doesn't publish exact figures for its Claude usage limits, but every prompt has a compute cost, which the company absorbs when a stolen session is doing the prompting. An attacker that has hijacked a session with a card on file can also buy extra usage on the victim's account, which is why Anthropic deleted saved payment methods instead of only terminating sessions. The company doubled Claude Code rate limits for paid users in May because demand kept outrunning capacity. Anthropic can invalidate every stolen session it finds and cover every fraudulent charge, but until the infostealer is gone from a customer's machine, the next login produces a fresh cookie for the same attacker to collect. We've reached out to Anthropic for comment on this story but did not receive a response. We'll update if we do hear anything.

item.title: Adobe brings 70+ tools from Photoshop, Illustrator and more to Slack
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.35
Adobe brings 70+ tools from Photoshop, Illustrator and more to Slack Prepare for a lot of chatting with Slackbot. Adobe announced a new integration with Slack, adding more than 70 tools from its popular apps to the communication service. The capabilities include features from Adobe Firefly, Adobe Express, Photoshop, Premiere, Acrobat, InDesign, Illustrator, Stock and Lightroom, which means a pretty comprehensive set of new work can happen without leaving Slack. If that number sounds familiar to you, it may be because Adobe announced a ChatGPT plugin that allows users of OpenAI's platform to access "more than 70 tools across Adobe's creative and productivity suites." The implementation appears to be near-identical between the two platforms. Adobe for Slack is available now for Slack Business+ and Enterprise+ customers on web, mobile and desktop versions of Slack. It follows similar integrations with Canva and Figma that were introduced when Slack first added Model Context Protocol support to Slackbot in June. Interestingly, an Adobe account isn't required to use its Slack app, but having one will allow more full access to the tools in question. Once the Adobe app is installed on the platform, users can message Slackbot with a task and the chatbot will use the most relevant Adobe tools to complete the assignment. Slackbot will be able to draw on content from within Slack channels and Canvases as well as from Adobe Creative Cloud assets. Possible uses of these new integrations include turning a spreadsheet into a visual, creating marketing or social media content from templates and executing bulk edits on a large number of images.

item.title: Rogue OpenAI agents took over a German coding forum in a previously undisclosed hijacking
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.19
Rogue OpenAI agents took over a German coding forum in a previously undisclosed hijacking OpenAI says it's investigating the incident after a group of researchers disclosed their findings. Rogue OpenAI agents appear to have been involved in a previously undisclosed incident that saw them bypass their sandbox restrictions to hijack a website this past spring. Per Reuters, a group of researchers on Friday published findings showing that AI agents with affiliation to OpenAI made more than 15,000 edits to DseWiki, a German-language Wikipedia-style website originally intended to assist human coders, starting in late May. The agents had names like "OpenAIResearcher," and repurposed the site into a message board, where they shared tips on how to "cheat" on tasks, mask their actions and bypass OpenAI's restrictions. OpenAI reportedly only learned of the incident weeks ago, but Reuters claims company executives chose to keep quiet about what had happened amid the fallout of the previously disclosed Hugging Face breach. During that incident, a collection of OpenAI models, including GPT-5.6 Sol and what OpenAI described at the time as an "even more capable pre-release model," escaped their controlled environment and hacked the LLM repository after they became hyperfocused on solving an evaluation problem. OpenAI did not immediately respond to Engadget's comment request. The company told Reuters it had not yet reviewed the report, on account of its authors not sharing early access to their findings. "We will carefully review its contents upon publication and take any necessary next steps," an OpenAI spokesperson told the outlet. According to Reuters, some OpenAI employees wanted to investigate the DseWiki incident closely, but those efforts were reportedly met with resistance from other parts of the company, including from OpenAI's legal advisors. "Claims that our legal team discouraged investigation of the incident are false," an OpenAI spokesperson said, adding the company has been working openly with outside experts to disclose security incidents. Sydney Von Arx, the CEO of AI safety nonprofit Nightingale and one of the authors of the report, speculated it was "extremely unlikely" OpenAI wanted its agents to hijack DseWiki. "I doubt they're supposed to be coordinating with each other," she said. "I doubt they're supposed to be writing on the open internet." The agents that posted on DseWiki appear to have been intensely focused on solving technical problems that are typical of the kind of questions AI labs use to test and evaluate their latest models. The researchers uncovered the hijacking in August using only the information the agents wrote on the wiki. "Analysis including the chain of thought would likely provide much more evidence about the motivations and strategy of the AIs during this incident," they wrote. The disclosure comes just one day after OpenAI announced its latest frontier system, GPT-6 Astra, which it's marketing as "the most intelligent and aligned model in the world." Astra earned a perfect score on ExploitBench, a benchmark designed to determine a model's ability to exploit software vulnerabilities, though OpenAI says it built the new system to not comply with advanced cybersecurity tasks. Last month, in the aftermath of the Hugging Face incident, OpenAI announced it was briefly pausing model training to implement additional safeguards. Following this latest disclosure, the company is likely to face renewed questions over its safety practices.

item.title: Audacity's new look is finally here, along with its largest feature update in years
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.13
Audacity's new look is finally here, along with its largest feature update in years The popular free audio editor gets a colorful dark mode and granular editing tools. Audacity released its Version 4.0 update today, bringing a fresh coat of paint and a number of new features for the popular free and open-source audio editor. This is the biggest update since Version 3.0 caused a ruckus over five years ago, and users have been waiting to see how radically the software would change with this latest release. But while the update includes plenty of departures from the way Audacity has traditionally worked, its Muse Group developers seem to have focused on maintaining continuity for users who don't want to relearn the program. The biggest change most users will immediately notice is the new look, which finally gives Audacity a dark mode. The interface is more playful overall, with colored audio clips and more vibrant accent colors on UI elements like gain sliders. If it's not to your liking, don't panic. The classic Audacity look has been preserved as an option which can be enabled during setup, so you never even need to see the new design if you don't want to. New editing workflows are here, too. Non-destructive editing, first explored in Version 3.2, is greatly expanded. Clips can finally overlap, and trimming back will reveal the covered-over audio if you go too far. Multiple clips can be selected and trimmed at once by dragging a single handle. They can also be grouped for complex edits. Anyone who has used the automation features inside of Ableton Live or ProTools will instantly recognize the new envelope tool in Audacity 4. Users can click to create a draggable control point for things like gain. Waveforms will show changes on-screen in real-time, so you can see, for example, whether you're redlining one portion of a clip. There's also a new splitting tool for one-click clip cutting. It should feel familiar to anyone who uses other creative software (not just audio software) as everything from Adobe Premiere to Logic Pro include a similar capability. It's yet another way in which Audacity 4 feels like a leap forward for what has traditionally been a basic audio editor.
