China’s leaders also objected loudly to American missile defense plans, and over the past decade Beijing has sought to guarantee that it can overwhelm any U.S. defense by roughly doubling its nuclear stockpile and fielding an air-launched ballistic missile and a new submarine-launched missile to complete a triad. China has also practiced the launch of key strategic systems into the Pacific—in September 2024 it conducted its first full-range ICBM test in more than 40 years—and developed an orbital bombardment system that could evade U.S. radars and attack the United States. Both Russia and China have built and tested weapons that can threaten the satellites on which U.S. missile defenses depend. Enmity alone does not induce an arms race. There is always a lag between identifying an alarming shift in the strategic balance and developing a response to it. Budgets and bureaucracy can move at a glacial pace, and internal politics often determine the weapons and strategies a country pursues in surprising ways. In the 1970s, for instance, the Soviet Union developed a new generation of seemingly more accurate missiles, the SS-18 and SS-19—large, silo-based ICBMs that could each deliver multiple warheads to targets across the United States. The program was the outcome of a years-long bureaucratic battle in the late 1960s over how to respond to Washington’s development of the multiple-warhead Minuteman III missile. Chinese engineers, meanwhile, began exploring ways to counter U.S. President Ronald Reagan’s proposed missile defense system, the Strategic Defense Initiative, in the 1980s. But plans to improve China’s space-based capabilities languished for years until the 1999 U.S. bombing of the Chinese embassy in Belgrade. The U.S. government said the attack was accidental—the target was a Yugoslav arms procurement agency—but the uproar loosened Chinese funding for various defense programs, including the development of an antisatellite weapon that Beijing finally tested in 2007 by smashing one of its own weather satellites in orbit. It’s too early to understand fully how internal politics are driving Russian and Chinese decisions about arms development today. Yet leaders in both Moscow and Beijing clearly see a need to respond to a U.S. defensive buildup. They may have overreacted after 2002, given the underwhelming nature of the missile defenses the United States has actually deployed and the efforts of U.S. officials across several administrations to reassure their Russian and Chinese counterparts that the purpose of those defenses was protection against North Korea and Iran, not to neutralize Russian or Chinese nuclear forces. But now, the Trump administration has explicitly embraced the goal of defending against “peer and near-peer adversaries”—a phrase that in Pentagon usage means Russia and China. This has surely made Moscow and Beijing believe that they were right all along. FICTION NO MORE The United States’ Golden Dome project will supercharge this competition. The space-based interceptors at the center of the U.S. proposal would attack Russian and Chinese missiles in their first minutes of flight, before they released their warheads and decoys, threatening to thin out the retaliatory strike that each country relies on to deter a U.S. attack. Russia and China will be seeking new missiles, warheads, and delivery systems that can breach those defenses. Even if there is some doubt about the viability of the Golden Dome, Russian and Chinese officials are obliged to take it seriously. When Reagan introduced the Strategic Defense Initiative in 1983, it was widely derided as “Star Wars”—science fiction. At the time, satellites were too large and launching them was too expensive to send an enormous cluster into orbit, as the project proposed. But today, SpaceX’s Starlink network, composed of thousands of relatively small satellites, demonstrates that very large constellations are feasible. Launching swarms of small, light interceptors to defend the United States from incoming nuclear missiles may no longer be so far-fetched. That is not to say the Golden Dome does not face problems. Missile defense systems have always struggled to be what analysts call “cost-effective at the margin.” An attacker can usually build and deploy a missile (or another warhead or a decoy) more cheaply than a defender can build and deploy enough interceptors to stop it. At the moment, the U.S. military plans to use four interceptors to target each warhead in space, and the kill vehicle—the technology that locates and collides with the warhead to destroy it—is particularly expensive. When North Korea paraded six mockup ICBMs in 2012, the United States responded by ordering 14 more interceptors. What those launchers and any missiles cost Pyongyang is unknown, but it was surely a tiny fraction of the roughly $1 billion Washington spent in response. Nor will the cost problem likely be solved with space-based interceptors. In theory, space-based interceptors might be cheaper than ground-based ones because an interceptor already in orbit does not need a large booster and can target a missile early, while it is moving slowly and easy to track. But even though satellite launches are getting cheaper, just a thin defense against the simplest targets will require thousands of satellite-based interceptors that must be continuously refreshed. A few thousand could easily turn into tens of thousands if the interceptors’ boosters do not accelerate quite as quickly, their sensors are not quite as sensitive, and communication with them is not quite as smooth as U.S. military planners anticipate, requiring a greater quantity to make up for shortcomings in quality. Relatively inexpensive efforts by Russia or China to increase their missile stocks or improve the effectiveness of their warheads would make it necessary for the United States to deploy even more interceptors. Starlink satellites may only cost a few hundred thousand to a million dollars, but they do not have an expensive kill vehicle built in. Those that have that capability are enormously expensive. The last space-based interceptor the United States designed—the Near Field Infrared Experiment, developed two decades ago—cost roughly $65 million per unit, adjusted for inflation. THE DANGER MOUNTS It is tempting to take comfort in the slow pace of an arms race. It is entirely possible that by the time these new systems are ready to be deployed, the conditions in which they might actually be used will have passed. Consider AUKUS, the 2021 agreement reached by Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States, to jointly produce a nuclear-powered submarine in response to China’s military buildup. When the first boat enters service in the early 2040s, a China led by a 90-year-old Xi Jinping—if he is even still alive—will be vastly different from the China of today. But slow is not the same as stable. The United States, Russia, and China are now all able to harass one another’s satellites in ways that have real consequences. Private companies would find it harder to operate commercial satellites if international cooperation on tracking space objects deteriorates amid this hostile maneuvering, and they would be on the hook for billions of dollars’ worth of assets that are not and will not be insured against acts of war or sabotage. All three countries are also locking themselves into decades-long force postures without knowing exactly what their adversaries’ forces will look like and despite the fact that space capabilities and frontier artificial intelligence models are advancing on much faster timelines. No one can really predict what technologies will be available in the early 2030s, when the U.S. Air Force hopes to deploy the first Sentinel ICBMs, which will replace the 1970s-era Minuteman III in 400 silos as the land-based leg of the U.S. nuclear deterrent. By then, Chinese missiles may be accurate and numerous enough to threaten those silos. AI-enabled reconnaissance could make mobile and concealed forces far easier to find. Or perhaps new space capabilities or AI-enabled cyberattacks will make space-based sensors, on which U.S. early warning depends, vulnerable in ways no one has anticipated. There is a risk that in their efforts to develop capabilities that threaten their adversaries’ space assets, one of the main players could wind up with a temporary incentive to strike first in a crisis—even if it would prefer not to strike at all. If Russia, for instance, places nuclear weapons in orbit, which it appears interested in doing, it might attempt to use those weapons to wipe out satellites to blind the United States at the outset of a conflict. China may similarly develop dangerous methods for destroying large numbers of satellites, including ground-launched “pop-up” boosters that could loft a nuclear warhead into space and detonate it before U.S. defenses could respond. Chinese military scientists have already published models of such a nuclear detonation. The blast would damage any unshielded satellites in line of sight and, as a 1962 U.S. test demonstrated, leave behind a belt of radiation that would continue killing satellites for months. Because this kind of mass attack in wartime would very likely degrade U.S. nuclear command-and-control systems, Washington would have to take seriously the prospect that such a strike in space could be the precursor to a nuclear strike on Earth. The mere possibility of losing its critical space assets in a surprise attack could push the United States to use its forces early or to delegate launch authority in ways that raise the risk of an accident, to avoid the devastating consequences. TIME TO TALK The fear that rapid technological advances could threaten nuclear stability is not new. U.S. and Soviet planners had the same concern in the 1960s, when missiles capable of carrying several warheads (known as multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles, or MIRVs), antiballistic missile systems, and antisatellite weapons became available all at once. The solution they chose was arms control. Arms control agreements aimed not only to reduce the number of nuclear weapons in U.S. and Soviet arsenals but also to provide a predictable basis for force planning. The effort met with mixed success. The 1972 SALT agreement limited the number of U.S. and Soviet missile launchers, and later treaties gradually reduced each side’s deployed strategic warheads from more than 10,000 then to 1,550 today. In the 1972 ABM Treaty, Washington and Moscow even managed to rein in some of the defensive deployments that can induce an adversary to develop its offensive capabilities—which is why the nuclear strategist Thomas Schelling, writing in Foreign Affairs four decades ago, identified that agreement as the “high point” of arms control. But negotiations stopped short of limiting MIRVs or antisatellite weapons, and arms control efforts stalled in the early 1980s; after Reagan unveiled his Strategic Defense Initiative in 1983, the project became the chief obstacle to reviving them. A renewed arms control effort can slow today’s arms race. The last remaining arms control agreement between Moscow and Washington, New START, lapsed in February, and for the first time since 1972, nothing limits Russia’s and the United States’ expansion of their offensive or defensive nuclear forces. Both countries—and China—are largely making decisions on the basis of fear and suspicion, not the joint pursuit of nuclear stability. Both Moscow and Beijing clearly see a need to respond to a U.S. defensive buildup. For now, U.S. plans for space make a comprehensive deal difficult to imagine. Moscow is at least conditionally open to one: Putin proposed in September 2025 that both sides informally observe New START’s limits for a year after it expired, and when Washington did not respond, Russia announced that it would hold to those limits only as long as the United States did. Beijing is less enthusiastic, but Chinese officials have been hinting at what they call a “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” Writing on social media this year, Trump expressed interest in a “new, improved, and modernized Treaty that can last long into the future”—a treaty that administration officials have suggested might constrain all nuclear weapons, strategic and tactical, and include China as well as Russia. Yet the U.S. president is equally enthusiastic about the Golden Dome. Ultimately, these ambitions are in tension: Trump can have the treaty or the dome, but not both. Neither Moscow nor Beijing will limit their offensive forces or growing space capabilities without at least some predictability regarding the American defenses those forces are intended to defeat. Limiting offenses without also limiting defenses might allow the United States, in a crisis, to attempt a surprise attack on Russia or China and then rely on its powerful defenses to neutralize any surviving forces. This would leave Russia and China unable to retaliate and, as a result, vulnerable to coercion. The good news is that because most countries have a stake in expanding the commercial use of space, they have reason to try to reduce the dangers in that domain alongside efforts to negotiate a new treaty to limit strategic arms. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, to which the United States, Russia, and China are all parties, already bans placing nuclear weapons in space. It lacks verification, but this problem could be addressed if the signatories agreed to inspections of payloads either before launch or, in extraordinary cases, while in orbit. Every country with satellites in orbit should support a ban on antisatellite weapon tests that result in debris and pursue cooperation on space traffic control to reduce the risk of collisions. All of this becomes more feasible with some defensive limits in place. The idea of restricting defenses against nuclear attack has long been a third rail in American politics, especially among Republicans. But many former Republican orthodoxies have proved negotiable; the party staunchly supported free trade and NATO, and opposed Russia just as strongly, until Trump decided otherwise. An agreement, moreover, does not have to eliminate defenses entirely. The ABM Treaty allowed each party to maintain two missile defense sites, later reduced to one. What a new deal needs to do is to place verifiable limits on defenses that give the other parties a sense of predictability. Without such limits, the United States, Russia, and China are likely to continue expanding their offensive forces, developing ever more exotic delivery systems, and pursuing new ways to attack each other’s satellites. All three will blame their adversaries for making the buildup necessary, but in truth each country will be racing itself, driven by its own fears and internecine politics. It’s hard to imagine how anyone wins such a race—other than by not running at all. item.title: The Future of Ukraine’s Drone Democracy
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.77
On August 19, the Ukrainian parliament voted overwhelmingly to confirm Ukraine’s new defense minister, ending weeks of uncertainty at a crucial phase of the war. For more than a month, Ukrainians had taken to the streets of Kyiv and other cities to protest President Volodymyr Zelensky’s firing of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. His successor, Yevhenii Khmara, is a special operations officer, best known for leading Operation Spider’s Web, the successful attack on Russian strategic bombers deep inside Russia. But the political fallout from this summer’s upheaval is not over. The removal of Fedorov, whom many Ukrainians considered highly effective, set off a series of decisions by Zelensky to reshuffle the cabinet, and more consequentially, the heads of military and law enforcement agencies. Shortly after dismissing his defense minister, Zelensky sought to quell the public backlash by also firing Oleksandr Syrsky, the unpopular commander of the armed forces. As a result, the president was simultaneously replacing the two figures—the defense minister and the head of the military—officially responsible for Ukraine’s defense against Russia. That this was happening at the very moment Ukraine was gaining the advantage on the battlefield has made the changes all the more fraught. For one thing, the large-scale protests themselves mark a new stage in Zelensky’s relationship to the electorate. Unlike any previous protests since the full-scale invasion, Ukrainians directly challenged the president’s handling of the war, introducing a dynamic that is unlikely to go away. Perhaps even more consequential, on the eve of the parliament’s vote on Fedorov’s successor, Fedorov released a controversial video address in which he declared that Ukraine needed a “system reboot” and called for wartime elections—the first time that not merely a prominent Ukrainian figure but a member of Zelensky’s inner circle and one of his former closest allies had done so. Until now, most Ukrainians have dismissed the prospect, since elections cannot be held while the country is under martial law. Amid these developments, something else has become increasingly clear: one of the unforeseen consequences of Ukraine’s transition to drone-centered warfare has been the expansion of civil society in new ways. The embrace of a decentralized, technology-driven defense strategy has required new forms of cooperation between military and civilians, giving far more people a stake in matters of national security and military strategy. And that has created a new reality for the country’s leadership. A DIFFERENT WAR A crucial factor driving the events of this summer is the evolution of the military confrontation with Russia into a drone war. This reality, which began to take hold in 2024, has accelerated Ukraine’s transition from foreign-supplied to domestically produced weapons: some 95 percent of drones are now assembled inside the country. Moreover, although Ukraine remains heavily reliant on its scarce supply of American interceptors to defend against ballistic missile attacks, it is far less dependent on foreign systems and intelligence than it was at the start of the war. The shift to a drone-centered battle space has fundamentally altered combat tactics, the expertise required of soldiers, and the way arms are purchased. It has also rendered some kinds of legacy systems, such as armored vehicles and short-range artillery, increasingly obsolete. Yet it is not the drones themselves that have made the shift so dramatic. To exploit the full potential of unmanned warfare, Ukraine has adopted an integrated digital architecture linking unmanned platforms with situational inputs and intelligence. It has also pursued an unprecedented level of digital coordination, as well as decentralized production and procurement of weapons and of digital technologies themselves. Fedorov was one of the key architects behind the deployment of this drone infrastructure. Unlike many other officials or military leaders, he not only possessed an acute understanding of the battlefield, the weapons deployed in it, and the data streaming from it, but he also had the ability to build, coordinate, and continually upgrade a comprehensive digital system to manage it. Although he served as defense minister for only six months, Fedorov had driven this shift as the head of the Ministry of Digital Transformation, a government agency he created in 2019 and ran until 2026. Drawing on a team of specialists, the agency had set out to replace traditional bureaucratic procedures across government with more efficient digital platforms; a secondary goal was reducing corruption. After Russia’s full-scale invasion, Fedorov’s team became a driving force within the government for Ukraine’s drone program. Since the acquisition of drones initially fell outside formal procurement, the agency was able to largely run the process through its own “Drone Line” initiative. At the same time, it began building a new digital infrastructure to manage drone warfare. Some of these capabilities, such as Delta—a cloud-based system for managing the entire battlefield—had been designed earlier by volunteer-led civic initiatives. But the Ministry of Digital Transformation gave them crucial government support. It also introduced rewards for army units that successfully deployed drones and, later, for those operating unmanned maritime systems and ground robots, as well. Some military analysts worry that these kinds of incentives risk “gamifying” the war or that they oversimplify operational realities. Yet by providing continuous feedback, the programs provide valuable real-time battlefield intelligence, as well as sophisticated data sets for assessing the performance of weapons and units. Fedorov’s team, relying for a time on Zelensky’s backing, pushed for new policies and funding mechanisms to accelerate the military’s digital transformation. It also set out to streamline the military bureaucracy and bring greater transparency to wartime procurement, which has been highly vulnerable to corruption. Over 900 Ukrainian companies now produce thousands of drone models and components. To manage this huge and fragmented sector, the ministry introduced new systems to coordinate logistics, certification, and deployment. Overall, these changes have been significant. Step by step, drones have allowed Ukraine’s armed forces to acquire or sustain capabilities that have traditionally come from missiles and airpower. In 2025, Ukraine had reached parity in the air domain with Russia along the frontline; by 2026, Ukrainian drones and missiles were also able to reach Russian command-and-control centers, cut off logistics, and prevent some Russian assaults. Although Moscow can still outcompete on resources, using oil revenues and vast state spending to finance its aggression, Ukraine’s new digital architecture has enabled it to do more with less, multiplying the effect of particular weapons by connecting sensors, operators, and strike platforms into a unified system. NEW WEAPONS, OLD WAYS Despite their undeniable value, these innovations have often come from outside Ukraine’s military establishment, and sometimes in opposition to it. Overshadowed by the large number of civilian recruits after 2022 is the fact that the Ukrainian army began the war staffed by professional soldiers, with inherited doctrines and lines of command. Although the military established the Unmanned Systems Forces as a separate branch in 2024, its traditional mechanized, infantry, and armored brigades still bore the brunt of the fighting while integrating drones at their own pace. And as with any large national armed forces, the existing hierarchy has resisted wholesale change. Many commanders have embraced drones as weapons—just as they would tanks or guns—yet without fully understanding the structural changes needed to make them effective. Similarly, Ukraine’s established defense industry, which has long counted on existing relationships and contracts, has also resisted the overhaul. Until recently, drone contracting has remained a comparatively small sector. Even though it involves hundreds of millions of dollars, expensive traditional capabilities such as artillery and other conventional weapons systems continue to consume most of Ukraine’s defense budget. Over the past year, however, the balance has shifted: the military’s procurement priorities and the financial interests surrounding them have begun to adjust to drone-centered warfare. And that has created new forms of pushback. Almost from the beginning of his tenure as defense minister, Fedorov and his team were targeted by smear campaigns on anonymous Telegram channels. These have linked him to various military scandals and alleged corruption in the drone industry. Fedorov blames the attacks on entrenched interests—defense contractors and powerful insiders—who were threatened by the shift in war priorities. As one example, he has cited his successful efforts to reduce the price of a procurement deal for short-range artillery that was becoming obsolete, given the expanding kill zones. He also said that Zelensky had received persistent complaints that the digital reformers were breaking a functioning system and disrupting the delivery of essential equipment to frontline troops. At the same time, as large amounts of funding, especially from Ukraine’s international partners, have been directed at drone technology, established defense contractors and well-connected political actors have sought to gain a piece of the pie. They are now moving aggressively to compete with drone startups on drone contracts. Taken together, these tensions brought pressure on Zelensky to move more slowly on the military transformation—which Fedorov had been pushing to accelerate. But the president had failed to understand just how much the public had become invested in Ukraine’s new way of war, and the remarkable results it had begun to achieve. PRESSURE FROM BELOW By the spring of 2026, if defense contractors had misgivings about Fedorov, the Ukrainian public had become increasingly dissatisfied with Syrsky, Ukraine’s commander in chief. Syrsky had notched several strategic victories, including the battle for Kyiv and the liberation of the Kharkiv region during the first year of the all-out war. He had also embraced drone warfare, expanding drone procurement and battlefield integration, although that was part of the army’s broader evolution. Yet many soldiers saw him as a commander who emphasized discipline and was prepared to sacrifice lives when he considered it necessary to achieve a military objective. Within the military, Syrsky had long taken pride in staying close to the frontlines, sometimes to the point of micromanaging the battlefield. But there was also a growing sense among officers and soldiers that he was beginning to value personal loyalty within the command structure above military effectiveness. He had a tendency to sideline talented younger officers and to use his control over promotions and resources to consolidate his own influence. According to some soldiers and officers, these habits risked undermining battlefield readiness, including on the most critical sectors of the front. Then, in June, Ukrainian journalists published a bombshell investigation uncovering horrific allegations of abuse in an assault regiment—a unit that had been given privileged support by Syrsky. The revelations included evidence of violence and unlawful killings within the unit. Although a formal military investigation followed, public criticism remained intense and serving military personnel spoke out. Many laid the blame on Syrsky personally for allowing this to happen. It was after this scandal that Zelensky made the ill-timed decision to fire Fedorov. In the eyes of many Ukrainians, the president was siding with those who opposed reforms. Almost immediately, thousands of people took to the streets of Kyiv and other cities. To contain the public outcry, Zelensky then moved quickly to fire Syrsky and install Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi as his replacement, a choice that was broadly welcomed. Drapatyi, 43, had entered the military in 2014 as a battalion commander and risen through the ranks, while taking part in many defining battles. He is known for embracing new approaches, including the digital battlefield promoted by Fedorov, supporting promising officers, challenging army leaders when necessary, and championing operations that minimize casualties—a priority that Ukrainians value. Meanwhile, Zelensky named Khmara to replace Fedorov. Since 2011, Khmara—in his late 30s or early 40s—had served in Alpha, the Security Service of Ukraine’s special forces unit, and was considered to have an unblemished record. (He had to leave active military service and formally become a civilian before assuming the post, which by law must be held by a civilian.) Yet Zelensky’s moves failed to resolve the underlying tension between the Defense Ministry and the military’s general staff. By law, the defense minister is supposed to nominate the commander in chief to the president. But this time, Zelensky once again effectively selected the commander himself, creating a situation in which the general staff continues to see that it answers to the president, not to the defense minister. LOST MOMENTUM? A larger question is how this political upheaval will affect the war. Fedorov was fired just as the reforms he had been advocating for were helping Ukraine turn the tide against Russia. By spring 2026, Ukrainian long-range drone strikes were beginning to erode one of Russia’s greatest strategic advantages: its oil sector. Kyiv also continued to disrupt Russian logistics in the south, particularly in Crimea, while also attacking oil refineries across the European part of Russia, including Moscow and St. Petersburg. But many wonder whether Fedorov’s dismissal will slow that progress. In Russia, pro-war commentators openly celebrated Zelensky’s decision, viewing it as a rejection of one of the main architects of Ukraine’s military modernization. Hours after his dismissal, representatives of several foreign governments and international technology firms, including the Italian minister of defense and Palantir’s CEO, Alex Karp, offered him positions, which he declined. Zelensky has also offered him several alternative roles in Kyiv, but Fedorov has refused them all because they came with limited decision-making power. Still, he seems almost certain to gain an important place within the government or defense sector sooner or later. Despite Zelensky’s appointment of innovation-minded leaders to replace Fedorov and Syrsky, the future of Ukraine’s digital war ecosystem remains uncertain. Unlike Khmara, who takes office without an established cadre, Fedorov brought to the defense ministry the team he had already built at the Ministry of Digital Transformation. Although only a few of the digitization specialists Fedorov brought to the Defense Ministry have left so far, many more may be pushed out. By calling for elections, Fedorov signaled a move into opposition, raising questions about whether his relationship with Zelensky would deteriorate—and what this would mean for close associates still holding official posts. By design, Ukraine’s digital battlefield infrastructure has the capacity to rapidly evolve in response to changing combat demands. The system can function without Fedorov or his team, but it remains unclear whether it can maintain the pace of evolution needed to stay ahead of Russia. The immediate risk is lost momentum. DEMOCRACY IN THE BALANCE The democratic culture that took hold in Ukraine in 2014 and drove the protests this summer continues to be one of the country’s greatest military strengths. Many of Ukraine’s most important military adaptations have come from below—from individual soldiers and commanders but also from civilian entrepreneurs. Hundreds of private initiatives have advanced technologies, software, manufacturing, and logistics in ways that have dramatically improved the way Ukraine fights. Too many military units, entrepreneurs, engineers, and civic activists are now invested in this ecosystem for a single political decision to dismantle it. But the disruption could affect Ukraine’s ability to iterate new advances on the battlefield—at a moment when the overall dynamic of the war hangs in the balance. For Zelensky, the political damage of his decisions this summer cannot be undone. Ukrainians have largely remained united behind the president in the face of external pressure, including after Donald Trump’s return to the White House in 2025. Nonetheless, he has shown more than once that he is out of step with ordinary Ukrainians. Already a year ago, his effort to restrict the role of Ukraine’s anticorruption authorities provoked major protests and significantly diminished confidence in his leadership. Now, his decision to fire Fedorov has only reinforced that perception. Until this summer, Fedorov had avoided attention, presenting himself as a manager, not a politician. Yet Zelensky’s abrupt decision to dismiss him—for reasons the public still does not understand—made Fedorov one of Ukraine’s most popular figures almost overnight. Now, Fedorov’s call for elections has significantly raised the stakes. In his video address, Fedorov—without mentioning names—again spoke about powerful vested interests that have meddled in government and defense and resisted the changes Ukraine needs to maintain its military advantage. He also asserted that, with no end to the war in sight, Ukraine needs a broader debate about political accountability and decision-making. Clarifying his initially vague but surprising address, the former minister pledged to outline the technical and security logistics of wartime voting—specifically for soldiers, refugees, and frontline residents—to enable a realistic debate on holding elections. Under martial law, elections are barred. Until now, only external powers—Russia or the United States—had questioned Ukraine’s political legitimacy without elections. Most Ukrainians deemed wartime voting dangerous and impractical, fearing that staging elections would simply divert attention, funds, and effort from the front. But Zelensky is in his seventh year as president, under a constitution that permits two consecutive five-year terms. Having made consequential, unpopular decisions, he has increasingly given the sense that he has stopped reading the country’s mood. Fedorov’s announcement may not precipitate an immediate change, but it has started a debate that could play out in the coming months and years. Until now, when it came to the question of holding elections, it had seemed that Ukraine would know when the moment arrived: at some point, in an active, outspoken society, even during war, Ukrainians themselves would demand democratic accountability. This does not mean that Fedorov will automatically gain popularity if he decides to run. His call for wartime voting has alienated some public figures and politicians who backed him as defense minister. They see his intervention now as less a push for accountability than an open political challenge to Zelensky—one that risks draining attention from the reforms that Fedorov had previously championed. With the war likely to continue for the foreseeable future, the urgent question facing the country now is to what degree the people should be given a direct say in the war’s course: how it fights, by what means, according to what strategy, and with what broader vision for its defense. The rise of drone warfare has made military strategy more inclusive, giving a wider range of people—from civil society representatives and tech innovators to members of frontline military units—the expertise and leverage to shape it. That means, on a popular level, more engagement in the war than ever. But for the country’s leaders, it has also created a powerful new set of voices to be reckoned with and be held accountable to—ones that, in the future, may well demand an even greater say. item.title: How Taiwan Can Win the Strait
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.22
Separated from China by a roughly 100-mile-wide strait, Taiwan relies on its navy as the first line of defense against a potential invasion. It must be able to prevent an assault by a Chinese force carried across the Taiwan Strait in large amphibious ships. Taiwan has traditionally favored large ships such as destroyers and frigates to form the core of its fleet, both as visible symbols of state power and as tools for signaling resolve in the face of Chinese coercion, and Taiwan’s current shipbuilding plans include replacing an aging surface fleet with large and expensive new ships. Yet large surface ships are vulnerable in the narrow waters of the Taiwan Strait—a problem compounded by advances in technology that are making them easier to detect, track, and attack. China has invested in cutting-edge intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (collectively known as ISR), as well as electronic warfare systems, drones, and missiles. Taiwan’s large surface ships are now a liability. But Taiwan has an advantage: these same technologies make China’s large amphibious ships more vulnerable in restricted waters, and those ships cannot be replaced by smaller, stealthier alternatives. Taipei can take advantage of this mismatch by replacing its destroyers and frigates with a greater number of smaller surface combatants that are more likely to survive an initial wave of Chinese strikes and remain capable of attacking a Chinese invasion fleet. The Taiwanese navy is planning to invest heavily in large surface combatants, including a new 7,000-ton warship and as many as 12 3,000-ton light frigates. These large ships are impediments to the radical transformation of the Taiwanese navy that the Chinese threat requires. Building ships of this size with stealth features and defense systems to survive a battle in the Taiwan Strait would be prohibitively costly; without these features, they would be too vulnerable to play a major role in the navy’s primary wartime mission of denying a Chinese invasion force the use of the Taiwan Strait. Efforts elsewhere to build similarly capable ships have proved costly and difficult. The U.S. Navy’s Constellation-class frigate program, for example, budgeted roughly $1 billion per ship; the cost eventually rose to about $1.5 billion each before the Constellation program was canceled, and even at that price the ships lacked the capabilities needed to fight an advanced adversary in restricted waters. In comparison, the spending on Taiwan’s entire shipbuilding program is projected to be $1.5 billion annually. Rather than spend resources on large ships, Taipei should build stealthy corvettes weighing between 700 and 1,000 tons, armed with missiles and drones, that are harder to detect and target but can retain enough firepower to attack Chinese ships crossing the strait. Combined with current plans to build shore-based mobile launchers, aircraft armed with antiship missiles, and eight submarines, Taiwan can create a dispersed and hard-to-destroy defense system that can withstand Chinese attacks and repel a potential amphibious assault. SITTING DUCKS Large ships may be potent signals of national power, but they are relatively easy to target and politically costly to lose. When ships are fighting in narrow waterways under heavy surveillance, visibility quickly becomes a deadly liability. The sinking of a large ship can also have consequences beyond an immediate military setback. A highly visible and costly loss may make political and military leaders more cautious about risking additional warships as conflict continues. Major naval engagements over more than the last four decades suggest that any navy expecting to fight near an enemy’s coast should be wary of building its force structure around expensive, irreplaceable hulls. The 1982 Falklands War between Argentina and the United Kingdom, for example, showed how a single successful strike on a warship can constrain an entire surface fleet. Argentina entered the Falklands conflict with powerful ships, including the cruiser General Belgrano and the aircraft carrier Veinticinco de Mayo. But after a British submarine sank the Belgrano, Argentina decided to keep much of the rest of its surface fleet, including the carrier, closer to coastal waters or in ports for the rest of the war. In the Persian Gulf six years later, the U.S. Navy’s ability to combine surveillance, aircraft, ships, and precision weapons devastated Iranian naval forces during Operation Praying Mantis. In a single day, U.S. forces sank or badly damaged several Iranian surface vessels operating in the confined waters of the Gulf, including two large frigates. Whereas the Falklands War illustrated the political consequences of losing a major warship, Praying Mantis highlighted the danger for ships facing an adversary with a much more effective “kill chain”—the sensors and communications to detect, identify, track, target, and attack an opponent’s fleet. For Taiwan, the lesson is that the combat power of large warships is irrelevant if they cannot survive long enough to fight, and an early loss could have cascading effects on the navy’s sustained combat operations. A restructuring of Taiwan’s surface fleet is within reach. Losing a smaller ship is less costly politically and militarily than losing a larger warship. In 2006, for instance, a Hezbollah cruise missile struck the Israeli corvette Hanit, which was operating in the waters off Lebanon. The ship had not been warned of the threat and had little time to detect and respond to a missile launched from shore 12 miles away, and some of its defensive systems were not fully activated. The missile killed four sailors and damaged the ship’s equipment, but the crew contained the damage and the Hanit limped home. The attack did not lead Israel to abandon corvettes; instead, it built larger, better-armed corvettes. Most important for Taiwan, Ukraine’s Black Sea campaign after Russia’s invasion in 2022 showed that a weaker power can constrain a stronger one in contested waters without commanding the sea or possessing a comparable fleet. The campaign combined land-based antiship cruise missiles, swarms of uncrewed surface vessels, aerial drones, and external intelligence to impose heavy costs on Russian naval operations in the Black Sea. These attacks helped push much of Russia’s fleet farther from Ukraine’s shores. The sinking of the flagship Moskva, for example, showed that even a ship equipped with layered air defenses was vulnerable to an adversary’s kill chain. The ongoing war in Iran reinforces this pattern: the United States and Israel severely damaged Iran’s surface navy early in the conflict, but they have had difficulty eliminating dispersed missiles, drones, patrol craft and mine-laying boats. The result is that Iran, despite losing much of its conventional naval power, has retained the ability to threaten shipping and disrupt access to the Strait of Hormuz. SMALL IS BEAUTIFUL As these examples show, a less powerful navy does not need to control its coastal waters to deny a stronger adversary the ability to use them. In the Taiwan Strait, therefore, the goal should be “sea denial”: preventing China from using the waterway freely enough to carry out an invasion. Achieving sea denial does not require Taiwan to abandon its surface navy. But it must build a different kind of fleet—one based on a greater number of smaller ships that can operate independently while sharing information and coordinating their attacks, making the fleet more likely to survive an initial assault and repel an invasion force. Finland and Sweden are good models. Both countries must deter and defend against a larger, more powerful adversary—Russia—and they are simultaneously contesting sovereignty challenges to areas they control and preparing for potential amphibious attacks on their coasts. With navies built around corvette-class-sized ships, Finland and Sweden have successfully stood up to Russian pressure, harassing Russian submarines that have violated their territorial seas. They have escorted away Russian ships that entered their waters and lodged diplomatic protests with Moscow. Both countries have extensive, sophisticated, and steadily improving surveillance, communications, and decision-support networks. A restructuring of Taiwan’s surface fleet is within reach. In July, Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te attended the commissioning ceremony of the navy’s eighth and newest missile patrol ship—a lightweight but heavily armed corvette built in Taiwan with an innovative catamaran hull that makes the ship faster and more stable—and four more of these vessels are scheduled to be commissioned by the end of the year. Taiwan’s shipbuilding industry can rapidly produce these vessels, and the more it builds, the more efficient it will become. Sustained production would bring costs down, and each successive batch of vessels can incorporate new weapons, sensors, and uncrewed systems as they develop. Each of these ships has been delivered to the navy for less than $200 million, whereas a single 7,000-ton warship will cost an estimated $2 billion. These changes should be combined with a broader upgrading of Taiwan’s armed forces’ network of sensors, communications tools, drones, and missiles. Taiwan is already making some of these investments. Its most recent special budget and the next round of its naval plans strengthen the kill chain with maritime surveillance drones, upgraded command-and-control networks to direct and coordinate military forces, and artificial intelligence–assisted combat decision support systems. These are the essential building blocks of an effective system to deny China the ability to freely navigate the Taiwan Strait. But the same technologies that make Taiwan’s kill chain more effective also make its large surface ships susceptible to attacks. Only by restructuring and upgrading its surface fleet can Taiwan be ready for a potential invasion. A restructured Taiwanese surface fleet would also support plans to build eight new submarines, the first of which is already in sea trials. Submarines are slower but stealthier than corvettes. Missiles and drones launched from corvettes can disable ships by hitting them above the surface, and torpedoes launched from submarines can sink them. Changing its approach to its surface fleet is a key part of how Taiwan can make its other naval investments more effective. RIGHTING THE SHIP The obstacles to the transformation of Taiwan’s navy are more institutional than technical. Because they are highly visible, large ships are attractive to politicians. They bring contracts for shipyards, ribbon-cutting ceremonies, a sense of national achievement, and visible proof of the government’s commitment to national security. By contrast, the public cannot see a warehouse full of drones or a mobile missile launcher hidden in the mountains. For navy leadership, too, the status quo is easier than pushing for major change. Taiwan’s destroyers and frigates, many of which are based on 50-year-old American designs, are well understood and therefore institutionally safe choices. But rather than continue to upgrade these obsolescent, if not obsolete, ships, Taiwan should progressively decommission them and redirect scarce resources toward the lighter surface ships it needs. Moving away from familiar platforms will require political and military leaders to take risks and overcome the setbacks and criticism that accompany any institutional change. Production of Taiwan’s first domestically built submarines, for instance, is currently behind schedule. But such challenges are inevitable when dealing with complex vessels and should not derail necessary investments. Government and defense leaders need to sustain support for these programs and justify their importance to the public, even when opposition politicians criticize them. After years of stagnation and decline, Taiwan’s defense spending is finally increasing. Taiwan’s proposed 2027 defense budget is likely to surpass three percent of GDP, and the legislature also passed a $25 billion special defense budget in May (a significant sum, albeit down from the $40 billion originally proposed by the executive branch). But Taiwan will not be more secure if these resources are spent on outdated defense concepts and a small number of vulnerable large warships. The country needs a dispersed, agile, and lethal force structure to defeat China in the Taiwan Strait. Such a navy will not look as impressive during a fleet review, but it will be a more effective deterrent against a potential Chinese invasion. item.title: The Road Through Damascus
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.13
In early April, a convoy of 299 Iraqi fuel tankers crossed into Syria on its way to the Mediterranean port of Baniyas, one of the few remaining paths to international markets amid the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. It was the first time Iraqi oil had crossed through Syria legally since 2003, when the U.S. invasion of Iraq effectively shuttered the cross-border flow of oil from Iraq to Syria. In late April, Iraq expanded the route, reopening its northern Rabia crossing with Syria, a crossing that had been closed for more than a decade during Syria’s civil war. Between April and late July, more than 2.1 million metric tons of Iraqi fuel moved to the Syrian coast. Before Syria’s civil war began, in 2011, the country had served as a commercial crossroads between Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon, Turkey, and the Mediterranean, connecting Gulf states to European markets. But after 2011, Syria turned into a different kind of transit hub. Trade became dominated by Iranian weapons and logistics support on their way to Hezbollah in Lebanon, as well as fuel, narcotics, and other illicit trade that filled the coffers of the country’s dictator, Bashar al-Assad, but provided few benefits for Syrians. After Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, the militant group once led by Syria’s new president, Ahmed al-Shara, toppled the Assad regime at the end of 2024, regional trade began to trickle back in. By August 2025, as many as 327,000 trucks carrying over seven million tons of cargo crossed into Syria, according to estimates by Syria’s customs agency. Jordan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey began to normalize relations and do business in the country. Damascus’s new authorities moved quickly to restore the country’s ties with a wide variety of regional and international partners, with the aim of ending Syria’s economic isolation. Although significant, this is not nearly enough to rebuild the country after over a decade of civil war. In 2025, the World Bank estimated that Syria’s reconstruction would cost $216 billion, nearly ten times Syria’s projected GDP for 2024. Syria’s leaders are now positioning the country to benefit from a resurgence of regional turmoil. Since the outbreak of the Iran war, in late February, the opportunities for new foreign investment in Syria have proliferated. Because alignment with the United States and Israel and reliance on the Strait of Hormuz carry ever-greater risks of retaliation from Iran, many countries are turning to Syria, which has a variety of well-placed land and sea routes. Syrian authorities are using the potential rush of capital and trade to create a new source of revenue, allowing the state to recast the country’s image from a source of refugees, terrorism, and regional disorder to a transit power that plays a dominant role in regional connectivity. But the speed and scale of investment could also overwhelm the institutions needed to manage it. If not properly scrutinized or fairly distributed, the rush of new investment that seems so promising now may destabilize the country’s fragile recovery. AFTERSHOCKS The need for better and more diversified transit through the Middle East is not new, but for nearly 15 years, Syria’s civil war made transit through the country impossible. In 2009, the Saudi and Turkish governments began discussions around redeveloping the Hejaz Railway route, built by the Ottoman Empire and largely destroyed in World War I, but they abandoned these plans with the outbreak of Syria’s civil war. Between 2010 and 2021, Syrian exports fell by roughly 90 percent. Major transit routes through the country closed entirely as the state fragmented into competing zones of control. In 2023, India, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the United States, and European partners proposed the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor as a way to spur intraregional and interregional connectivity and integrate Israel, a node on the corridor, with its neighbors. Disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has made expanding these projects even more urgent. In April and June of this year, the Jordanian, Saudi, Syrian, and Turkish governments agreed to redevelop the Hejaz Railway within three to four years. Analyses of comparable regional rail corridors, such as that by the Atlantic Council, estimate that the railway could initially carry around 1.5 million containers annually, potentially rising to three million with track and port capacity expansion. This proposal resonates with Shara’s loose vision, laid out at an informal EU summit in April among leaders from Europe and the Middle East, for a Four Seas and Nine Corridors initiative that places Syria at the center of a network connecting the Persian Gulf, the Caspian Sea, the Black Sea, and the Mediterranean, facilitating ground- and sea-based trade in goods, electricity, and oil. Then, in July, Iraq and Syria agreed to rehabilitate the Kirkuk-Baniyas oil pipeline, which was destroyed during the U.S. invasion of Iraq in 2003, to create a permanent Mediterranean outlet for Iraqi oil. If the pipeline goes online within its four-year estimated timeline, it could transport two million barrels per day by 2030, equivalent to roughly 60 percent of Iraq’s crude exports before the Iran war and an estimated nine percent of the total oil that moved through the Strait of Hormuz. With new routes also planned through Turkey, Iraq is positioned to route more than 80 percent of its export volume around Hormuz, ending its near-total dependence on Gulf terminals. These trends, however, are not guaranteed to improve Syrians’ economic and political fortunes. Although Syria’s geographic position gives it geopolitical leverage with foreign actors seeking to diversify export routes, it also places the country in the middle of emerging rivalries, as Saudi Arabia and Turkey align on security, the UAE increasingly takes a commercial role in ports and logistics, and Israel attempts to prevent Turkey from establishing influence near its borders. Competition over who finances, operates, and protects these respective corridors could pull Syria into contests it is not stable enough to sustain. Syria could get pulled into contests over trade that it is not stable enough to sustain. Damascus has tried to limit this exposure by working with nearly every power willing to support its reconstruction and reintegration, including Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the UAE, and the United States, as well as China and Russia. But this strategy is proving more difficult as time wears on. The influence of Syria’s greatest financial supporters is drawing Damascus toward a Qatari-Saudi-Turkish constellation. If competition over the corridors grows faster than Syria’s capacity to manage it, the country could fall victim to greater foreign control and extraction. Israel may also prove to be a significant obstacle to Syria’s reemergence as a reliable passageway for trade. The reconstruction of the Hejaz Railway, if successful, will decrease Israel’s importance to the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor and as a Mediterranean gateway for Arab states. Israel may well try to resist this development. In February, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned of an “emerging radical Sunni axis” as Syria drew closer to Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey, and in June, Israeli Transport Minister Miri Regev warned that regional trade and energy partnerships designed to bypass Israel posed “a genuine strategic threat to national security,” placing Syria’s emergence as an alternative trade corridor within Israel’s wider threat perception. And Israel has demonstrated its willingness to use force against those countries; in 2025, it bombed a Hamas compound in Doha, carried out extensive attacks across Syria (including on air bases being scoped by Turkish military teams for deployment in Syria), and seized additional territory in the south of the country. In August 2026, Israel struck Syria’s Abu al-Duhur airbase after alleging that Damascus was preparing to permit a Turkish deployment there intended “to harm Israel,” in the words of Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz. Damascus, which cannot afford a war with Israel, has avoided military retaliation and sought an Israeli withdrawal by participating in U.S.-brokered negotiations. Such a tempered approach, however, may not deter Israel from expanding its illegal occupation of Syrian territory, targeting Syrian infrastructure, or fomenting instability through its ties with Syrian minorities, all of which are hampering projects critical for Syria’s recovery. As the Middle East analysts Shira Efron and Danny Citrinowicz have argued in Foreign Affairs, the attempts by Syria’s new government to counter those operations could result in Israel and Syria becoming lasting adversaries. Such attempts will also require even more support from foreign actors. PAY TO PLAY The growing influence of foreign powers in Syria also affects important political dimensions of the country’s reconstruction. Throughout the civil war, Assad granted countries that supported his repressive regime access to Syrian territory and economic assets. Russia built military bases and received lucrative phosphate, oil and gas, and port concessions. Iran used Syria as a land bridge to Lebanon and stationed thousands of troops in the country. Efforts to reassemble the Syrian state after Assad’s fall have unfolded under this shadow. The government led by Shara has largely ended this method of outsourcing Syrian sovereignty, ousting Iranian and Hezbollah forces from Syria, dismantling networks that sustained Iran’s military corridor in the country, and reclaiming control of formerly Russian-held military bases, although the bases will still be jointly operated. But the risk of outsourced sovereignty has not disappeared. Damascus is still grappling with a fragmented system of national governance. For years, customs administration systems across Syrian territory were governed by separate competing state and nonstate actors, chief among them the Kurdish-led Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria. Although Damascus has regained authority over the border crossings with Iraq in territory once led by the Kurdish minority, the main crossing into Turkey from that territory has yet to reopen. To attract the funding necessary for Syria’s reconstruction, the new government has lowered the barriers for regional and international powers to access and invest in Syria’s routes, ports, and territory, projects that could serve to connect its disjointed regions. Last June, Shara signed a decree permitting foreign investors full ownership rights in most sectors, an unrestricted ability to repatriate their profits, and extensive tax and customs concessions. The decree concentrates authority over investment licenses, access to state land, and eligibility for major tax incentives in institutions closely tied to the president, giving him considerable power to determine who can invest in Syria’s postwar economy. This centralization will likely help streamline investment. But without independent oversight into such decisions, oversight that Syria has yet to establish, centralization could also revive the Assad-era practice of offering economic access as a reward for political loyalty. Such a system could make reconstruction a new source of political patronage, undermining the new government’s legitimacy in the eyes of Syrians who lose out and possibly reproducing the same inequalities that helped fracture the country in the lead-up to the civil war. Long-term concessions give foreign companies considerable influence over critical infrastructure. The French-owned shipping company CMA CGM holds a 30-year concession of Syria’s largest port, Latakia, an arrangement that gives the Syrian government 60 percent of the port’s revenue. The UAE-based logistics company DP World will finance and build new infrastructure at Syria’s second-largest port in exchange for operational control over the facility for 30 years, after which control will return to Damascus. But it remains unclear, in the absence of any published revenue-sharing terms for this deal, how much income the state will receive, or how that income will be managed and distributed. The scale of Syria’s reconstruction makes foreign financing difficult to resist. Although the World Bank has directed nearly $500 million in grants toward public service projects targeting electricity, water, health, and financial institutions, that will cover less than one percent of the country’s reconstruction needs. In October, Shara said that his government had attracted $28 billion in commitments from a mix of Turkish and Gulf investors during its first ten months, roughly 13 percent of Syria’s total estimated needs. The largest commitments, however, favor government-awarded infrastructure and development projects—power plants, ports, airports, telecommunications, and urban real estate—but pay little attention to restoring basic services and destroyed homes in Syria’s hardest-hit communities. Moreover, much of the sum comes from preliminary agreements. Shara’s government has created two funds to manage the reconstruction: the Syrian Development Fund, for donations and grants for rebuilding public infrastructure such as roads, bridges, and water and electricity networks, and the Syrian Sovereign Fund, modeled after the Gulf sovereign wealth funds, to manage state assets, invest in public property, and take stakes in strategic projects. Dedicated reconstruction funds are common in postconflict states, and a sovereign wealth fund may be justified to streamline the management of fragmented, distressed, and historically poorly managed public assets. The concern, however, is that under its current formulation, the Syrian Sovereign Fund concentrates the management of public assets directly under the president without independent oversight and with limited public disclosure around its structure and management, as similar reconstruction programs in Afghanistan, Iraq, and Somalia have done. Even reforms intended to strengthen accountability are centralized under the president. The planned center for arbitrating investment and commercial disputes, for example, will sit within the Syrian Investment Authority, which is itself attached to the presidency. This architecture could give the president undue influence over which investors, regions, and communities benefit from recovery. In a country that has suffered from the state’s abuse of power and wealth since the 1960s, this pattern of control is uncomfortably familiar. PAYING DIVIDENDS Transportation corridors and investments cannot generate durable returns if renewed fragmentation preserves the disconnect between a strong, wealthy Damascus and a poor, underdeveloped periphery. Ultimately, whether Syria can convert foreign investment into local gains depends on whether Damascus can establish a predictable political order. So far, the government seems to be making steady gains, but it still has a long way to go. Over the past two years, Shara’s campaign to reunify the country has been violent. Fighting along the Alawite-majority coast, in the Druze-majority Suwayda region, and across the Kurdish-led northeast has deepened mistrust between the state and the communities it seeks to govern. Renewed confrontation between Damascus and the Syrian Democratic Forces—a U.S. backed, Kurdish-led coalition that governed much of northeast Syria after pushing the Islamic State (also known as ISIS) out of the area—offered the clearest warning of renewed civil war. Although the central government and the SDF signed an agreement to merge in March 2025, disputes over military integration and Kurdish autonomy at first prevented its implementation, leading to an outbreak of fighting in January that displaced more than 170,000 people. After a U.S.-brokered cease-fire halted the government’s advance north, Damascus and SDF leadership signed an agreement that mandated the transfer of control of border crossings, oil and gas fields, and local institutions to Damascus and the integration of SDF fighters into the Syrian military. In August, after months of gradual implementation, the SDF commander Mazloum Abdi announced the coalition’s dissolution as an independent force and the end of Kurdish-led self-governance in Northeast Syria. Even infrastructure and resources under the Kurds’ de facto control is now being handed over to Damascus. On paper, the January agreement between Damascus and the SDF provides a framework for resolving informal wartime boundaries and closed routes and for harmonizing competing duties and parallel systems of governance. If the Kurdish majority living in the northeast perceives this reintegration to be insufficient or failing to preserve Kurdish rights and representation, however, they may begin to resist, obstructing Damascus’s attempts to consolidate full control over the country and its transit corridors. The repatriation of millions of Syrians further raises the political stakes. By the end of May, an estimated 1.67 million refugees and 1.92 million internally displaced Syrians had returned to their home communities. Many are returning from protracted poverty in neighboring states to communities already struggling to meet residents’ basic needs, which has intensified competition over housing, employment, and public services and which may create new sources of local grievance and conflict as the process continues to unfold. To successfully integrate these returnees, Damascus must empower governorates and municipalities with the resources and autonomy to solve problems pertaining to service delivery, job creation, and education in real time. To avoid reproducing a rentier economy dependent on transit fees and foreign concessions, the Syrian state must reinvest project revenues in local economies. Assad’s dependence on Iran and Russia narrowed his room to maneuver, but the new government can negotiate with Europe, the Gulf states, Turkey, the United States, and international institutions seeking access to Syria’s markets and transit routes. Competition among these partners gives Damascus leverage to negotiate terms that keep as much of the investments’ value in Syria as possible. But using that leverage effectively will require transparent agreements tied to clear state policy priorities for reconstruction and recovery. To better connect the capital with faraway cities and towns, the central government must invest in improving roads and electricity connectivity and require foreign investors to support local hiring and revenue-sharing agreements. It will also need to forge durable and equitable settlements with minority leaders and tribal communities to strengthen domestic trust. Renewed interest in Syria as an advantageous transit point for regional trade has presented Damascus with income, relevance, and leverage at a time when it needs all three. But these resources are not immutable. Damascus’s challenge is to use the dividends from its newfound importance in regional trade to build functioning institutions, distribute resources for recovery, and overcome historical animosities. Otherwise, after decades of exclusion, Syria could return to the regional map merely as a fragile conduit for others’ commercial exploits.
