item.title: Research: How Curveball Questions Can Surface the Insight You’re Looking For
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.87
Research: How Curveball Questions Can Surface the Insight You’re Looking For Summary. Traditional “tough” questions often elicit polished talking points rather than candid answers. A more revealing approach is the curveball: a question that is closely tied to what We’re all taught to ask tough questions. Interviewers are coached to use open-ended prompts to get beyond rehearsed answers. Managers press for specifics when employees speak in generalities. Journalists and negotiators follow up when someone evades the point. The aim is the same: to uncover information the other person may be reluctant to reveal.

item.title: You Need to Understand Your Employees’ Caregiving Responsibilities
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.50
You Need to Understand Your Employees’ Caregiving Responsibilities Summary. Employees regularly balance work with caregiving responsibilities, whether it is child care, eldercare, or caring for another family member. Yet many organizations lack visibility into who their Most of us are caregivers. Seventy-three percent of all U.S. employees, and 71% of employees globally, identify as caregivers with responsibilities to look after children, aging parents, or other family members. Fifty-four percent of employees in their 40s identify as sandwiched caregivers, providing for the needs of parents aged 65 and older while also raising children or providing for a young adult child 18 years and older.

item.title: Do Your B2B Customers See the Value You Deliver?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.00
Summary. Many B2B companies suffer from a “value gap”: Customers benefit from their products but cannot clearly measure, articulate, or defend that value to stakeholders within their companies. Most B2B companies have long harbored a costly blind spot: a gap between the value they create for customers and the value those customers can see, measure, and defend. For many, early strong growth masks the problem until sales slow or competitive alternatives drag down margins. Closing that gap is an executive decision—and one most leadership teams have never explicitly made.

item.title: Mt Baden-Powell Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.87
Steady switchbacks up the PCT give you a spectacular taste of the Angeles National Forest’s high peaks, with a 1,500-year-old limber pine tree along the way. It’s a classic hike and here’s everything you need to know to do it safely. Distance 8 mi Difficulty Hard Total Climbing 2800 ft Time 4–5 hrs Who It's ForStrong intermediate hikers. Biggest RiskSpring snow and ice on trail. Exposed summit catches afternoon lightning. Check Highway 2 conditions before driving. When to GoMay-October for snow-free conditions. Winter snow requires traction devices, Highway 2 may close. A third party is now charging $5 for trailhead parking and is not accepting parking passes. You can park across the street for free. Be careful crossing the road. Mt Baden-Powell was named after Lord Baden-Powell, who founded the Boy Scouts. In the 1950s, local Boy Scout chapters restored the trail here and named the mountain in his honor. Before that, this peak was called North Baldy. Near the top, you’ll see the Wally Waldron tree, named after a Boy Scout leader who restored the trail and created the Baden-Powell monument at the summit. The tree is approximately 1500 years old and is considered the oldest living thing in the San Gabriel Mountains. Most of the hike follows the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT), which goes from the borders of Mexico to Canada. If you want more of the PCT without hiking its 2650 miles, read Wild: From Lost to Found on the Pacific Crest Trail, a best-selling book later adapted into a movie.

item.title: Garmin inReach SOS: How It Works & When to Use It
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.68
Garmin inReach SOS Guide Updated & Reviewed July 2026 The SOS button is the most important feature on a satellite communicator, and the one people understand the least. It’s not the same as calling 911. An inReach SOS routes to Garmin Response, a 24/7 center that coordinates with local rescue teams and messages with you the whole time. Here’s when to hit it and what to actually expect if you do. When to SOS - Unsure of a safe outcome? Hit it. The best advice I’ve heard, from an LA County search and rescue veteran: if you’re not sure you’ll be okay, press SOS. It’s two-way, so you can describe the situation, lost, stranded, chest pain, and Garmin Response helps you figure out what to do. - Not just for the backcountry. Garmin’s own SOS data is full of vehicle use: cars, boats, motorcycles. Carry it when you drive out of cell range, because a flat or a breakdown can just mean a tow, not a helicopter. - Medical issues and injuries are the top reasons people hit it. A pre-existing condition doesn’t disqualify you. If something feels wrong, ask. - More than half of SOS calls are for someone else. Like calling 911 as a Good Samaritan, hitting SOS for another person doesn’t make you liable. Just know that rescue insurance only covers you, not them. - Don’t abuse it. Being tired or having a sore stomach isn’t an emergency. Use common sense, same as you would with 911. Hitting the Button - There’s a countdown. Once you trigger it, the device counts down before the message goes out, and you can cancel during that window. - Sent one by mistake? Cancel it, don’t power off. Cancel the SOS on the device and reply to Garmin Response so they know you’re okay. Powering off leaves them assuming the worst, and a search may start anyway. - False alarms don’t cost you. Garmin doesn’t charge for an accidental activation you cancel. Cancelling isn’t an embarrassment, it’s the system working. - SOS can stay active on a suspended plan. On compatible devices you keep a working SOS button even with messaging suspended. Details on the subscription page. What Happens When You Hit SOS - A helicopter is not the default. Garmin’s data shows most rescues aren’t helicopters. They’re usually local volunteers organized by a sheriff’s department or park service. - It takes hours to mobilize. Even a helicopter rescue usually takes several hours. Be ready to wait, and carry enough to spend the night: an emergency bivy, extra layers, and food. - Rescue comes in many forms. It might be self-evacuation with guidance, a ground team, a cliff extraction, or just a ranger walking you down. I’ve seen that on Mount Whitney for altitude sickness. About 10% of people handle it themselves. - You stay in contact the whole time. Unlike a one-way PLB, Garmin Response keeps messaging you updates until help arrives. Rescue Costs Triggering SOS is included in every inReach plan, so there’s no charge to hit the button. The rescue itself is a separate question. Most rescues are free, but if a private helicopter or air ambulance gets involved it can run well over $20,000. That’s what rescue insurance is for, and I break down the options on that page.

item.title: Mt LeConte Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.61
Great Smoky Mountains National Park Mt LeConte Trail Updated & Reviewed August 2026
The hike to Mount LeConte from the Alum Cave Trail is considered the marquis trail in Great Smoky Mountains National Park. It’s a challenging hike but very doable by most folks. The trail is beautiful, easy to follow, and offers lots to see along the way.
- Distance - 11.2–12 mi
- Difficulty - Hard
- Total Climbing - 3050–3100 ft
- Time - 6–8 hrs
Who It's For Strong hikers who can handle all the climbing. Biggest Risk Lightning on exposed summit ridge. Turn back if afternoon storms develop, weather escalates fast. When to Go April-November. Winter can bring snow and ice.
Video Here’s a video I shot of what it’s like to hike the trail and what you can expect if you do it yourself.
Trailhead
Notes
- According to the USGS, Mt LeConte is named after Joseph Le Conte (1823-1901), a geologist and early conservationist. Le Conte was a co-founder of the Sierra Club with John Muir in 1892. He was such a popular guy that after he died in 1901, he became the namesake for Le Conte Glacier, Le Conte Canyon, Le Conte Divide, Le Conte Falls, Le Conte Mountain, and Le Conte Lodge. - But some people say it’s named after Joseph’s older brother, John, who helped measure the mountain’s elevation. - These mountains formed around 480 million years ago, making them some of the oldest in the world. The rounded peaks you see today are the result of 200 million years of erosion. Maps
Directions
Info The arch came into being as the softer rock underneath the harder rock was worn away by the cycle of freezing and thawing.
Info Alum Cave Bluffs is a vast overhanging cliff, named for the alum deposits found here in the 1800s.
Tip For a better viewpoint, continue straight past the summit on the short downhill.
Tip You can avoid the spur to Cliff Top and just go straight down.

item.title: Garmin Fenix 8 Review: Trail Tested
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.57
Garmin Fenix 8 Review Updated & Reviewed August 2026 The best all-around Garmin watch for the outdoors and everyday life. AMOLED maps and smartwatch features without the battery hit. After initial firmware bugs at launch, this is fairly stable and a great all-around watch for those who want a crisp AMOLED screen. The catch is aggressive auto-dimming at night with no override, which makes the screen harder to read on a tired glance. If you don’t need smartwatch features or care about AMOLED, the Enduro 3 costs less and lasts longer between charges. How I Earn I buy gear with my own money. It's the only way I can be 100% honest about what works. No sponsors, no free gear. Use the links below to buy, and you support these ad-free, independent reviews at no extra cost. Warning Lately Garmin hasn’t been great about providing stable firmware. Check the Garmin Fenix 8 support forum to see what the latest state of the software is. Video Here’s an update video after months using it and months of firmware updates. And this is my initial review so you can see it in action. Screen The Fenix 8 AMOLED runs at 454x454 pixels, 1000 nits. Outdoor daylight readability is excellent. Topo lines, trail names, and map symbols are crisp and easy to read. I have no issue preferring AMOLED over MIP for hiking. The one problem: automatic night dimming is more aggressive than the older Epix Pro on the same brightness setting. In low light or when you’re tired and want a quick glance, the screen is noticeably harder to read. There’s no way to shut the auto-dim off. Initially I thought it was a bug, but after months of others asking the same question, Garmin has said this is how they intended it to work. The workaround is to make all your data fields white on your watch face. It doesn’t up the brightness, but it does make the screen easier to read at night. Battery Battery is strong for an AMOLED outdoor watch. Features like always-on display, navigation, Connect IQ watch faces, and music cut into those numbers. In practice, I don’t worry about battery on multi-day backpacking trips with this watch. Real numbers from my use: - Smartwatch mode: 2-3 weeks - Activity tracking with multi-band + all GNSS: 56-78 hours - Mixed daily use with workouts: charge roughly every week Buttons Garmin redesigned the Fenix 8 buttons for better water resistance and dive compatibility. Shorter travel, lighter electronic buzz instead of a deep mechanical click. In practice, the longer travel on the older Fenix button feel was better for outdoor use. Cold mornings with gloves on, tired on mile 20, you want tactile confirmation you’ve actually pressed something. The Fenix 8 buttons are functional and you get used to it after a while. Flashlight Garmin quietly improved the flashlight without advertising the specifics. In my side-by-side comparison with the Epix Pro, the Fenix 8 throws a stronger, cleaner beam. It’s more useful for lighting up a dark trail or finding gear in a tent. Using the flashlight non-stop will drain your battery quickly, but it’s great for middle-of-the-night bathroom trips. Navigation Offline navigation is why I use Garmin watches. The Fenix 8 ships with preloaded maps including trail names, street names, and POIs. That’s still the feature that sets Garmin apart from every other smartwatch. Navigation has gotten more stable since launch. The early release had real problems. Recent firmware updates have addressed most of them. AllTrails also added Garmin integration, you can push a hike from AllTrails to your Fenix 8 through Garmin Connect, which is a handy workflow. The new menu layout is worse than the old UI. Garmin moved all navigation screens into a parallel swipe column. On previous Garmin watches, navigation screens lived in the same column as everything else and felt natural. The new layout requires a sideways swipe that doesn’t feel intuitive mid-hike. I’ve adjusted, but it’s not an improvement. GPS Accuracy GPS accuracy is excellent. In fact it’s often on-par or better than my Garmin handheld GPS accuracy. When I record my trail and document my trail guides, I often just wear my watch to get an accurate track. The Fenix 8 adds QZSS and BeiDou support beyond the previous Epix Pro’s GPS/GLONASS/Galileo. Phone Features The Fenix 8 adds voice commands to start activities, short voice notes (on-device, don’t sync to phone), a button to trigger your phone’s assistant, and call answering over the mic and speaker when your phone is paired. These features work but don’t feel polished compared to an Apple Watch. Call quality is serviceable. The assistant shortcut requires a button hold, no wake word. I occasionally use it to trigger Siri for a reminder. I buy Garmin for navigation and battery, not wrist calls. Recommendations Get the Fenix 8 if you want a great all-around outdoor watch with long battery life, a sharp AMOLED screen, health features, and offline maps. It’s the best Fenix available. Skip it if you’re coming from an Epix Pro and are happy with it, since performance is nearly identical. If you don’t need connected features, the Enduro 3 costs $300 less and has longer battery. If you mostly do casual day hikes and charge regularly, an Apple Watch Ultra with Footpath or WorkOutdoors is plenty.

item.title: Garmin inReach Subscription Cost: Which Plan Is Cheapest
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.56
Garmin inReach Subscription Cost Updated & Reviewed August 2026 Jump to a section A Garmin inReach subscription is required to use your device, and there’s a lot of variation in what you’ll pay. There are even inReach plans that Garmin doesn’t sell. Here’s how to figure out the best plan for you. | Plan | Best For | Price | |---|---|---| | Enabled | Pay only for what you use | $7.99/mo | | Standard | Sharing your live position with family on every hike | $29.99/mo | | ProteGear | Power users who want maximum flexibility | Pay per day | | Suspended | The cheapest way to keep 24/7 SOS (compatible devices) | ~$8/yr | Info I’ve paid for my own inReach device and subscription since 2014, when I got my first one. I buy all my own gear and don’t take sponsorships, so I’m free to use and recommend what works best. What You Get A Garmin inReach subscription is a monthly service plan, just like a cell phone plan. Two things have to be in place to get connected: an active subscription (these plans) and an inReach device to run it on. No plan means no SOS or messaging, even if you own the hardware. Here’s what a subscription unlocks: - Emergency SOS to the 24/7 Garmin Response center, who coordinate (but don’t perform) the rescue. Included on every plan, and still works when suspended on compatible devices - Two-way text messaging using satellite when you’re beyond cell range - Location tracking that shares a breadcrumb trail over satellite that others can follow on a map - Weather forecasts with hourly and multi-day outlooks, including a marine option - Photo and voice messages over satellite on inReach Plus-enabled devices like the Messenger Plus and Mini 3 Plus - Check-in messages, three preset “I’m OK” type messages you can send for less than a normal message Pricing Levels Pricing on each plan is purely based on how much you use it. The more expensive the plan, the more usage you essentially prepay for. | Plan | Price/mo | Annual | Texts/Weather | Photo/Voice | Live Tracking | Check-ins | Text Overage | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Enabled | $7.99 | $95.88 | $0.50 ea | $1.00 ea | $0.10/pt (10 min+) | $0.10 ea | $0.50/msg | | Essential | $14.99 | $179.88 | 50 | 25 | $0.10/pt (10 min+) | Unlimited | $0.50/msg | | Standard | $29.99 | $359.88 | 150 | 50 | Unlimited (10 min+) | Unlimited | $0.50/msg | | Premium | $49.99 | $599.88 | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited (2 min+) | Unlimited | N/A | - There’s a one-time $39.99 activation fee on all plans, charged on every device, including inReach smartwatches like the Fenix 8 Pro. - A weather forecast counts as one satellite text message. - Incoming messages count too, including replies to your check-ins. - Emoji reactions (tapbacks) to messages in the Garmin Messenger app are billed the same as check-ins: free/unlimited on Essential, Standard, and Premium, and $0.10 each on Enabled. - Messages sent over Wi-Fi or cell through the Garmin Messenger app don’t count against your plan. Only satellite messages do. - Live tracking points always go out over satellite, so they’re always charged, even if your phone has signal. - A group message counts as a single message, but each reply costs a message. - Photo and voice messages only work on inReach Plus-enabled devices like the Messenger Plus, GPSMAP H1i Plus, and Mini 3 Plus. - You can switch between plans at any time for free. You can also keep more than one device active on a single account (a new option since the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro), but each one needs its own activation fee and subscription. - Every plan includes Emergency SOS messaging through Garmin Response. - The plan prices are identical whether you carry a Mini 2, Mini 3, Messenger, or a GPSMAP. Garmin charges for the plan, not the device, so the “Garmin inReach Mini 2 subscription cost” is the same as the Mini 3 or Messenger. - Photo and voice messages only work on inReach Plus-enabled devices, so on an older unit like the Mini 2 those rows simply don’t apply. - Smartwatches with inReach (like the Fenix 8 Pro) add unlimited LTE messaging and calling when you have cell service. Cost Calculator Enter your estimated monthly usage and how many months a year you use the device, and this shows the monthly and annual cost for each plan. Click “Edit Charges” to adjust pricing for your local currency or region. Edit Charges Simply change the numbers here based on your currency. Overages | Plan | Monthly | Annual | |---|---|---| | Enabled | $0.00 | $0.00 | | Essential | $0.00 | $0.00 | | Standard | $0.00 | $0.00 | | Premium | $0.00 | $0.00 | Annual is your monthly cost times the months you use it, assuming you suspend for $0 the rest of the year. Year one adds a one-time $39.99 activation fee on every plan. - Most people: Enabled, about $146 a year. Full SOS, and you only pay for the tracking and messages you actually use. - Track every hike? Standard. Unlimited tracking beats Enabled once you pass about 36 tracking hours a month. - Essential rarely wins. It only makes sense for steady messaging with almost no tracking. Any real tracking, around 25 hours a month, pushes you to Standard. - Premium is niche. It’s only worth it above about 190 messages a month, or if you need 2-minute tracking, like guiding a team or sailing. - Seasonal user? Suspend. Keep SOS on a compatible device for about $8 a year instead of paying all year. Suspending You can suspend your plan for $0 for up to 12 consecutive months, with no reactivation fee. This is the move for seasonal users, and it beats canceling, which wipes your data and charges a fresh $39.99 activation fee to come back. The big deal is SOS. On compatible devices, Emergency SOS keeps working while your plan is suspended, even though messaging, tracking, and weather are off. That means you can carry a working SOS beacon in the off-season for almost nothing. To qualify, it has to be a compatible device, on the latest firmware, and previously on an active plan before you suspend. Not every device supports it, and the list keeps growing, so check Garmin’s current compatible-device list before you count on it. Older units like the original Mini and Explorer don’t qualify. After 12 consecutive months suspended, Garmin automatically moves the device onto the Enabled plan ($7.99/mo) to keep SOS alive. So the real cost of free suspended SOS is one paid month every 13: twelve months free, then the single auto-Enabled month before you suspend again. Call it about $8 a year. Third Party Plans A few partners resell the same Iridium connection with different pricing. ProteGear is the one worth knowing, and its whole angle is pay-per-day instead of per-month. - Pay-per-day. A €49 yearly base, then only the days you’re active, from about €1.50/day (safety) to €6/day (expedition). Flip it on and off yourself for free. - Same safety net. SOS still routes to Garmin Response, and you keep the Garmin Explore account and apps. - Extras Garmin dropped or lacks. Editable preset messages, a dedicated two-way email address, tracking down to 30 seconds, better weather reports, and Wikipedia or Google News over satellite. - The catches. The dashboard and setup are power-user territory and can be confusing, but human support is excellent and responsive. If you’re in Australia or New Zealand, TrackMeNZ is another third party option. inReach Rentals If you only go off-grid occasionally, renting can beat buying a device and paying for a plan. Outfitters will mail you a unit for your trip, usually around $10 to $15 per day with a few-day minimum. The typical flow: - Order online and choose a data plan and insurance. - The device ships to your home or a pickup location. - You get setup instructions by email. - Use it, then mail it back. I don’t have any specific company I recommend. Google “Garmin inReach rentals” and compare options. inReach Professional Garmin’s Professional plans are built for teams, organizations, and families that want one account across multiple devices. - Central management. Run multiple devices under one login, assign them to users, and monitor everyone from a single dashboard. - Best for. Guides, SAR teams, land managers, and anyone coordinating a group in the field. - Pricing. Tiered by how much messaging and tracking your team needs, billed monthly. See Garmin’s Professional plans for current rates. - Off-season. You can suspend Pro devices and still keep SOS on compatible units, so a fleet doesn’t lose emergency coverage when it’s stood down. Rescue Costs Your subscription pays for the SOS service, not the rescue itself. Most rescues are free, but if a private helicopter or air ambulance gets involved it can cost thousands, which is what rescue insurance covers.

item.title: Garmin inReach Tips and Tricks: Techniques I Rely On
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.53
Garmin inReach Tips and Tricks Updated & Reviewed July 2026 The inReach does a lot more than most people get out of it. These are the settings I actually change and the techniques I rely on in the field, sorted by messaging, tracking, and general use. This video covers the 10 tips I wish I’d known sooner. The list below has all of them, plus more I’ve added since. Messaging - Include your location with all your messages. Go to the Garmin Explore website and enable “Include a link to an online map with the location of my message” and recipients will get a map every time you send a message. It doesn’t cost anything extra. You can do the same thing for your unlimited check-in messages by toggling MapShare on when specifying recipients. - Send messages with your voice. Newer inReach models like the Messenger Plus let you record voice messages in the Messenger app. But there’s a technique that works on any inReach paired with iPhone or Android, enable voice to text. Then, in the Messenger app, tap the microphone icon on your keyboard, speak your message, and send, no typing needed. - Get your messages unstuck. Your inReach will try to get your location before sending a message. If you’ve been navigating or location sharing with your device, it’s already doing this, but if not, it can hiccup here. If my messaging isn’t going out I’ve found that going into my navigation functionality, dropping a waypoint (gets a GPS fix), then sending the message usually does the trick. Also note that the send priority for messages is SOS, most recent message, then track points. - Fix missing messages. If your message isn’t getting through, it could be them, not you. VOIP numbers, such as Google Voice, do not work if they are set up as virtual numbers. Some countries like Mexico, Romania and Saudi Arabia have restrictions. Check with this Garmin page for the latest on which countries might have issues. You should also check inReach System status to make sure the service is up and running before you head out. Send a test message to Garmin and make sure you are able to send on your end, you will get an automatic reply if it’s working correctly. - Enable audio alerts. I don’t get a lot of messages on my inReach, and if I do, it’s usually important. In my settings, I enable “ring until read,” which keeps beeping on the device until I read the new message. When sending a message, the device will continue to listen for replies for 10 minutes. After that, it will check for new messages every hour. If you’re waiting for a message back, do a manual mail check after 10 minutes. - Send inReach to inReach. Want to send messages to another inReach device when you’re out in the field? Have everyone share their inReach address beforehand and add it to your contacts. You can find it on the Garmin Explore website as “inReach Addr” under your account. It’s in an email format. Also note that inReach to inReach counts as a message. - Group messaging not working? You can only send group messages to phone numbers (not emails) through the Garmin Messenger app. All recipients must be using the Messenger app with a registered cellular number for it to work. Group messaging doesn’t support email addresses or inReach addresses. - Battery draining quickly? Make sure you turn your device off when indoors. Even if you have the Messenger app, which will try to use cellular or Wi-Fi to send a message, most inReach devices don’t have the smarts to know that, they’ll keep checking for messages over satellite. I learned this one the hard way. - Want to make it easy for friends and family to message you? Your inReach device doesn’t have a permanent phone number, and it can change. In Garmin Explore, enable MapShare (you can password-protect it if you want). Then turn on “Allow map viewers to send you messages.” Share your MapShare URL with the right people. I add mine to my contact card to make it easy. Just remember: your device needs to be on to receive the message. Tracking - Have a plan with unlimited tracking? On most devices, you can automatically start tracking when you power it on. Go to settings and enable Auto Track. Your device needs to get a GPS fix, so I power mine on as soon as I get to the trailhead and let it sit on the roof of my car. Location tracking can be an invaluable safety tool if you experience something catastrophic like a heart attack or stroke, rescuers can follow the breadcrumb trail to where you are. Tell your family they can report you missing as soon as they know you’re missing. They don’t have to wait 24 or 48 hours like on TV. - Tracking can be confusing. inReach has two types of tracking: internal (used to track an activity and for breadcrumb TrackBack) and satellite tracking to your MapShare page. They’re both called “tracking,” which adds to the confusion. In your settings, Send Interval controls how often your location is sent over satellite, while Activity Detail or Log Interval controls internal recording on the device. Internal tracking is what powers the breadcrumb trail used by TrackBack. I keep mine set to high detail so I have the most accurate path back in case I need it during an emergency. - Satellite required for tracking. Unlike messaging in the Garmin Messenger app, which can fall back to Wi-Fi or cellular when available, tracking always uses the Iridium satellite network, even if your phone is connected to the internet. - Check the weather ahead. You’re not limited to weather at your current location on most inReach devices. You can request a weather forecast for any point on your route. Look for “change location” or “add location” under weather and put the new spot in. It’s especially useful on multi-day or high-elevation trips where weather can shift fast. I use it to check conditions over mountain passes, at campsites, or near potential bailout points. - Always leave your device on when moving. It might be tempting to turn it off to save battery when you’re not actively sending messages, but if something catastrophic happens, rescuers have no way to ping your device if it’s off. When it’s on, it will continue checking for new messages every hour and updating your location. If you stop for the night and plan to turn it off, send a check-in first so there’s a clear record of your last known location. General Usage - Don’t let a surprise app logout ruin your trip. Before you leave your house, log into the apps paired with your inReach and make sure everything is synced and updated. Sometimes an app update will log you out, and if you’re already off the grid, you won’t be able to log back in. You can still use your inReach without the apps, but you’ll lose access to features like messaging from your phone or route syncing. - Ask a question. Use services like AskTopo, Backcountry Brain, and SatAI to find out about the weather, trail information, and even water sources. - Get proactive weather alerts. If there’s severe weather in your location, you get a weather alert pushed to your satellite communicator with Adiona Alert. - Offline maps for free. If your device pairs with the Garmin Explore app, you can download offline maps onto your phone, even if your inReach device doesn’t have maps (like the Mini 2). Just open the app when you’re off the grid and you’ll be able to see your position on a map using your phone’s screen. - Carry it correctly. If your inReach is in your pocket or buried in a bag, it’ll struggle to send and receive messages, and that drains the battery faster. The best setup is to clip it to your backpack strap using a carabiner, with the antenna pointing up toward the sky for the best signal. - Remote control with your watch. Some inReach devices can pair with your Garmin smartwatch, letting you control the unit remotely, including sending check-ins, messages, starting tracking, or even triggering SOS. Watches like the Fenix 8 even give you a small keyboard so you can type out a message right from your wrist. - Don’t get locked up. Satellite communicators are illegal in some countries, and that includes having one if laying over in transit. Your satellite enabled phone is fine, the hardware manufacturer will disable satellite in countries where it isn’t allowed.

item.title: Devil's Bridge Hike Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.41
Ranked as one of the best hikes in the USA, Devil’s Bridge in Sedona is a must-do. The trail can be crowded, but I’ll also show you a more pleasant route that’s easier to park at. Devil’s Bridge, the largest natural sandstone arch in the Sedona area, is doable by most folks, with only some steep stairs at the end. Here’s how to do it. Distance 4 mi Difficulty Easy Total Climbing 550 ft Time 2–3 hrs GearFitness clothes or light hiking gear is fine here. Bring a minimum of 0.5L of water. You can see all the gear I use on a hike like this here. There are two main trailheads for Devil’s Bridge: Dry Creek and Mescal. The hikes are about the same distance, but Mescal has advantages over Dry Creek. The Mescal Trailhead parking lot has about double the spaces of Dry Creek. Perhaps more importantly, for a pleasant hike, Dry Creek follows a dirt road halfway to Devil’s Bridge, open to vehicles. On the other hand, the first half of the Mescal route is on a regular trail with no vehicles and offers some incredible views along the way.

item.title: Bright Angel Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.38
The Bright Angel Trail Grand Canyon is the park’s most iconic hike, starting on the South Rim near Bright Angel Lodge and descending through millions of years of rock layers. In this guide, I’ll show you how to hike the Bright Angel Trail to the 1.5 Mile Resthouse, 3 Mile Resthouse, Havasupai Gardens, and Plateau Point. Not sure which one to aim for? Keep reading, and I’ll help you choose the right turnaround point and show you exactly how to hike the Bright Angel Trail based on your abilities. Distance 3–12 mi Difficulty Hard Total Climbing 1100–3060 ft Time 2–8 hrs Who It's ForFit hikers who can not only do the distance, but also do the tough climb after descending. Biggest RiskPeople worry about the edge, but it’s the heat that gets you. Especially if you are not fit enough to hike back up. When to GoSummer is brutally hot and potentially deadly. Fall through Spring is best time but trail can be covered in snow and ice. Here’s a video I made of the Bright Angel Trail showing you exactly what to expect on your hike. Options You can choose how far you want to hike down the Bright Angel Trail. Simply turn around and hike back up from the destination that you’re hiking to. The National Park Service doesn’t recommend continuing below Havasupai Gardens as a day hike for most hikers. Warning When you’re figuring out which option is right for you, know that 2,640 feet of climbing is 0.5 miles straight uphill and fairly tough for most folks. It’s not just the distance. Challenges Overall the Bright Angel Trail is safe. I’ve seen people of all shapes, sizes, ages, and fitness levels do these hikes. The trail is well-maintained, easy to follow, consistently about 4 feet wide, and has wider sections for passing. But you still need to be mindful of a few things. As you descend 1000 feet, the temperature will rise around 3.5°F to 5.5°F. So if you descend to Havasupai Gardens, the temperature could be somewhere around 18.5°F hotter than where you started. And the temperature will continue to rise until mid-afternoon. There are some shaded parts of the trail but not much, it can get very hot. You need to check park alerts and weather for the heat and plan accordingly. Leaving at sunrise is a great way to beat the heat and the crowds at the same time. The hike back up is much harder than going down. Many first-time Grand Canyon hikers overcommit on the easy downhill and pay for it on the climb out. A good rule of thumb: expect the hike up to take about twice as long as the hike down. Snow and ice can linger on the upper sections in winter, especially in the morning. Be prepared for slippery, frozen sections near the rim, so bring microspikes. An advantage of the Bright Angel Trail is that it follows the water pipeline. You should still carry water with you, and you can refill along the way. Check the park page before you go, the water is sometimes turned off in places. The trail is generally wide enough to hike comfortably and pass other hikers. Info Want to camp on the Bright Angel Trail? You can book a tent site at Havasupai Garden on Recreation.gov (Backcountry Permit > Classic GC Hike South Rim > Havasupai Gardens Campground). You can take free shuttles from a bigger parking area like the Visitor Center to the stop for Bright Angel Lodge. The closest parking is in the lot right next to the trailhead, which is next to the Bright Angel Lodge. I’ve had success here or on the street nearby when arriving early. The biggest lot nearby is Parking Lot D by the Backcountry Information Center. It’s a 5-10 minute walk to the trailhead from here and there are usually spots open. Did you know that the Bright Angel Trail used to be private and cost $1 (about $40 today) to hike? The path was used by Havasupai for hundreds of years but in the 1890s a settler claimed this land and started charging visitors to hike. Even after the Grand Canyon became a park in 1919 it was still private. The National Park Service was able to end private control by 1927. Hiking to 1.5 Mile Resthouse Info Pictographs = painted, Petroglyphs = carved Info These rest houses were built in 1935-1936 by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC). Hiking to 3 Mile Resthouse Hiking to Havasupai Garden Info Havasupai Gardens was formerly known as “Indian Garden” and you may see some references to that on maps or signs. Info Theodore Roosevelt (who rode down the Bright Angel Trail on a horse) ordered the Havasupai who lived here to leave in 1901 in order to make way for the park. Some left and some stayed, but in 1928 the Park Service forced the last Havasupai out of the Bright Angel area and onto a 518-acre reservation in Havasu Canyon. Info The fertile land at Havasupai Garden (around Garden Creek) has been cultivated since 300AD. Western tourists started arriving in the 1890s and as you know, the last natives were moved out of here in 1928. Today there is a ranger station, toilets, picnic areas, a campground, and water. Info Havasupai means “people of the blue-green waters,” referring to the color of the Colorado River, which runs through the Grand Canyon. In the early 1900s they worked as laborers here and created much of what you see at Grand Canyon National Park. Hiking to Plateau Point Hiking Back To the South Rim The downhill is over, the hard part is yet to come. Unless you’re going to float down the river, you’ll have to walk back up to leave the inside of the Canyon.

item.title: Enchanted Valley Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.33
Enchanted Valley Trail Updated & Reviewed August 2026 Deep in Olympic’s remote interior, the Enchanted Valley Trail delivers you 14 miles into a glacially carved valley where a Victorian chalet sits beneath cascading waterfalls. This 28-mile, 2-3 day trip requires a permit and crosses temperate rainforest to reach one of the park’s most isolated corners. - Distance - 28 mi - Difficulty - Moderate - Total Climbing - 3400 ft - Time - 2–3 days Info They don’t call this a rainforest for nothin’. The Enchanted Valley gets over 11 feet of rain a year, about 4 times as much as Seattle. It can rain anytime. Pack like it’s going to rain, and you’ll be fine if it doesn’t. Video Here’s a video that I made showing what the hike and backpacking is like so that you know what to expect when you do it yourself. Permits Info If you want to overnight here, you need an Olympic National Park Wilderness Permit. If you can’t get the dates you want, set up an alert on OutdoorStatus to snag an opening. | Itinerary | Details | |---|---| | 2 Days | Start early at Graves Creek Trailhead, hike all the way to Enchanted Valley, spend the night, then hike out the next day. | | 3 Days (Late Start) | Hike to Fire Creek on day 1, continue to Enchanted Valley on day 2, and hike out on day 3. | | Day Hike | If you have the fitness, you can tackle this in a day, no permit needed. The ups and downs make this feel tougher than the 3400 ft of total ascent. | | No Permit Camping / Short Day Hike | Do the 5 mile round trip to Pony Bridge. Combo with an overnight at Graves Creek Campground at the trailhead for a taste of the experience without any permits. | - Campsites aren’t numbered. Book an area and then individual tent sites are first-come, first-served. Permits reserve areas, not tent sites. - Every time that I’ve camped here, a ranger has checked my permit. - Primitive toilets are available at Pony Bridge, O’Neil Creek and Enchanted Valley. It’s easier to use these than to pack out your toilet paper (but you can bury your waste). In areas with no toilet, dig cat holes 6-8 inches deep and 200 feet (about 70 adult paces) from campsites, trails, and water sources. - Most campsites are close to water sources. - There are some small tent sites that are not listed in the permit areas (you’ll see them on my map below). If you have a permit for a nearby area, you’ll probably be safe camping there. Wildlife I’ve done this hike 6 times and the number one question that I always get asked by passing hikers is “did you see a bear?” I’ve seen people with multiple bear bells hanging off their pack (sounds like Santa), I’ve seen people with holstered bear spray at the ready. The reality is that the bears here are very mellow, are used to seeing hikers, and generally avoid humans. If you see one on the trail, stop, give it space, and let it pass. Make some noise by talking or clapping to let it know you are there without being aggressive. Do your part to keep the bears wild by using bear canisters. In addition to the bears that I mentioned already, the Enchanted Valley (and Olympic National Park) is home to 3,000-4,000 Roosevelt elk, which can get up to 1,000 lbs and are bigger than Rocky Mountain elk. They can be tough to spot, but you might hear their distinctive call. Like the bears, give them space and don’t get too close. The other herd animal that’s fairly common is mule deer. Info The river is home to beaver and river otter, but they’re much tougher to spot. Trailhead Getting to the Graves Creek Trailhead can be a challenge in itself. Even though it’s only 57 miles in a straight line to downtown Seattle, the Olympic Peninsula is known for being undeveloped and remote. I know some locals here and that’s how they like it. So it’s a long drive. Maps | Resource | What It’s For | |---|---| | CalTopo Map | Interactive map for planning and printing | | GPX Download | Put my route on your GPS | | AllTrails recent reports | What other hikers are seeing now | | Trailhead Weather | Forecast for the Graves Creek trailhead | | Enchanted Valley Weather | Forecast at the Chalet, about 1,700 ft higher | | Olympic NP Conditions & Alerts | Trail washouts, closures, river crossing status | Directions Info O’Neil camp is named after Joseph P. O’Neil, who was one of the first to really map and survey the interior of the Olympic Peninsula, which believe it or not, didn’t happen here until 1890. It gives you an idea of how remote this area is. Info The chalet was built in 1931 as a lodge for hikers and those on mules and horses. During WW2 it was used as an observation post for enemy aircraft. Since then the chalet has been open and closed at various times, and even moved away from the eroding riverside in 2014. Today it is on the National Register of Historic Places, the only structure originally built as a public resort that remains standing in the interior of the Olympic range, and, according to the ranger, infested with mice.

item.title: Garmin inReach Messenger Review: 28-Day Battery
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.27
Garmin inReach Messenger Review Updated & Reviewed August 2026 The inReach with the best battery life, but minimal navigation and heavy reliance on your phone. When the Garmin inReach Messenger first came out, I didn’t know who it was for. No real navigation, marketed toward car campers, and not even a clip or strap to mount it to a pack. After a few months of trail use, I have a clearer answer. It’s a solid inReach if battery life and price are your priorities and you’re comfortable relying on your phone for everything else. If you need backup navigation on the device itself, get the Mini 2 instead. How I Earn I buy gear with my own money. It's the only way I can be 100% honest about what works. No sponsors, no free gear. Use the links below to buy, and you support these ad-free, independent reviews at no extra cost. Video Why It Exists Garmin already has the Mini 2 and the GPSMAP 67i. The Messenger fills a different slot: more affordable (often on sale for $199), designed around phone pairing, exceptional battery life, and intentionally limited onboard navigation. Performance The Messenger uses Iridium, so you get 100% global coverage. I’ve had subscribers send messages from the South Pole. In my testing: - Messages went out faster than my Mini 2, usually within a minute. - Reliability in heavy canopy was better than other devices I’ve tested. - It supports GPS, Galileo, BeiDou, and QZSS, which helps with satellite lock in tough terrain. - You can stow it inside the brain of your pack. Keep it upright and near the top and it works fine without external mounting. A subscription is required for all satellite functionality. See the inReach subscription breakdown, including plans Garmin doesn’t advertise. The App The Messenger has a small screen and buttons for standalone use, but it works best with the Garmin Messenger app. The app handles two-way messaging, location tracking, SOS, weather forecasts, and device settings. A few things to know: - When connected to cellular or Wi-Fi, the app sends messages over data automatically instead of satellite. - You can start and stop breadcrumb tracking, trigger SOS, and pull weather from the app. - The Messenger does not pair with Garmin Explore, so there’s no app-based navigation. Trackback on the device is all you get. - Location sharing always goes over satellite regardless of connectivity. - Even when your phone is on Wi-Fi or cellular, the device still checks for messages via satellite every hour. Turn it off when indoors to avoid battery drain. You can also control the Messenger in a limited way from a Garmin watch. Battery Garmin claims 28 days in 10-minute tracking mode. In my testing: - Averaged 5% drain per day, even in cold weather. - On a 5-day trip with regular check-ins and tracking, I used less than 30% total. It charges via USB-C. Battery life is the strongest argument for this device over the Mini 2. Navigation The Messenger records your location every 10 minutes automatically. If you need to backtrack, you get an arrow pointing toward where you were 10 minutes ago. That’s it. It’s not a replacement for track navigation on a device like the Mini 2, and it’s not the same as location sharing via satellite to your MapShare page. If backup navigation matters as an emergency fallback, this device isn’t the right call. Who It’s For The Messenger makes sense if battery life and price are your top priorities, you always hike with your phone, and you don’t need the device to function as backup navigation. If your phone dies in the backcountry and you need to find your way back, you want a Mini 2 or GPSMAP device with that capability built in. For a specific use case, like thru-hiking where your phone is always on and you want the longest possible satellite battery, the Messenger is a strong option. Comparison | Feature | inReach Messenger | ZOLEO | inReach Mini 2 | |---|---|---|---| | Sale Price | $199 | $149 | $299 | | Messaging | Yes (2-way) | Yes (2-way) | Yes (2-way) | | Navigation | TrackBack only | No | Yes (but no maps) | | Battery Life | Up to 28 days | 200+ hours | Up to 14 days | | Display | Very small screen | No display | Small screen | | Weight | 4.0 oz | 5.3 oz | 3.5 oz | | Satellite Network | Iridium | Iridium | Iridium | | SOS Coverage | Global | Global | Global | | Weather Forecasts | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Reverse Charging | Yes | No | No | | Location Sharing | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Phone Required for Full Use | No | Yes | No |

item.title: Mt Mitchell Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.21
Blue Ridge Mountains, North Carolina Mt Mitchell Trail Updated & Reviewed August 2026
Reach the highest peak east of the Mississippi the right way, on foot. The Mt. Mitchell Trail climbs 3,700 feet over 12 miles, earning you what the summit road never will. I’ve hiked this a dozen times over the years. In this guide, I’ll show you everything you need to know to conquer Mt. Mitchell on the trail.
- Distance - 12 mi
- Difficulty - Hard
- Total Climbing - 3700 ft
- Time - 5–7 hrs
Who It's For Strong hikers who can do the climbing. Biggest Risk Extreme weather, including snow or thunderstorms at top. When to Go May-November. Summit much cooler than valley. Snow possible through late spring.
Video I made a video showing you what it’s like to hike the trail so you can be prepared when you do it on your own.
Trailhead
Maps
Directions
Info The summit’s Fraser fir forest has been decimated by the balsam woolly adelgid, an invasive insect. The standing dead trees are a visible reminder of this ecological loss.
Info Mt Mitchell is named for Elisha Mitchell, a professor who fell to his death here in 1857 while trying to verify the mountain’s height. He’s buried at the summit.

item.title: Do I Need SAR Insurance? Rescue Cost Coverage
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.20
Do I Need SAR Insurance? Updated & Reviewed July 2026 Your satellite communicator can call for a rescue, but it doesn’t pay for one. Most rescues are free, but that’s not always the case. Tip Quick pick: Overwatch x Rescue is what I use. It works on just about any device, including inReach and satellite-enabled phones. Rescue Costs Once you’ve asked for an evacuation, the rescue team will evaluate the situation and determine the best response. It could mean a ground team comes in and walks you out in a bucket, it could involve you self-evacuating to a meeting point, or could involve a helicopter rescue. If it does involve an aircraft, there can be a cost. The important thing to remember is that you don’t choose the response. - The rescue itself is usually free. Almost all search and rescue in the US is done by volunteers led by a sheriff or park team. If they have aircraft available, they can use it for the rescue and you aren’t charged. Some states will charge you for a rescue if you are negligent. - You pay for private services. The response may involve a private helicopter evacuation. It depends on the circumstances. Maybe a government helicopter is not available. Maybe your situation is so dire that you need a specialized air ambulance to take you directly to a specialized ER center. The average private air evacuation runs about $28,000, and you don’t get a say in whether one is used. - The hospital is separate. Once evacuated and admitted to care, your regular health insurance takes over. Rescue coverage gets you out of the backcountry, not the care that follows. Info Are you negligent? The test is the “reasonable person standard”: what a reasonable person would have done in your situation, which scales with your experience. Running a stop sign and causing a crash is negligent because a reasonable person stops. Hiking onto a closed trail or a route far beyond your ability can be treated the same way. Payment Options Knowing that a rescue could cost you, here are the options. - Health Insurance generally won’t cover an evacuation cost but it’s worth checking before you spend any extra money. - Local Cards are available for some areas. They support local SAR teams and cover any rescue costs. Two popular ones are New Hampshire’s Hike Safe card and Colorado’s CORSAR card. - Bundled Insurance with your device is usually an option for devices like ZOLEO, SPOT, and inReach. For inReach, Garmin sells SAR insurance plans from $39.95 to $999.95 a year depending on your needs. It’s insurance and you have to go through the claims process. - Overwatch x Rescue is like AAA for SAR, you pay one annual fee and that’s it. You can call them to coordinate a rescue or use Garmin Response, and unlike insurance, they simply cover the cost of rescue without a cumbersome claims process. - Other Options A simple Google search for SAR insurance will bring up lots of options, but I think for most users, the previously mentioned options make the most sense. Overwatch x Rescue This is the one I carry. I can put it on all my devices, their response center is the best I’ve come across, and it covers exactly what I need without a pile of fine print. Here’s what you get: - $79.99 a year, and it’s not insurance. It’s a fully funded service, so they pay the providers directly. No claim to file, no deductible, no reimbursement to chase. - Two fully funded responses a year, up to 10 days of assistance each. More than enough for most people. - Works on any satellite device, across more than one. A Garmin inReach, an iPhone or Android with satellite SOS, or a ZOLEO or SPOT, and you can cover several devices under one plan. - Risky sports are included. Mountaineering, rock climbing, skiing, and other hazardous summer and winter sports are covered for search and rescue and medical evacuation, with no surcharge. - It covers the whole way out. Search and rescue to the nearest hospital or safe harbor, plus medically necessary air transport to the nearest appropriate hospital. Your health insurance takes over from there. - International adds a lot. During foreign travel it also covers natural disasters, civil unrest, terrorism, wrongful detention, medical repatriation to a hospital back home, and flying a family member out if you’re hospitalized. Overwatch vs. Garmin | Feature | Overwatch x Rescue | Garmin Plan | |---|---|---| | Price | $79.99 | $39.95 | | Search & Rescue | ✓ | ✓ | | Medical Transport to Hospital | ✓ | ✗ | | Risky Activities Like Mountaineering | ✓ | $299.95 | | Above 5000m | ✓ | $999.95 | | No Monetary Limit per Response | ✓ | ✗ | | Family/Friend Hospital Visitation | ✓ | ✗ | | Home Hospital Repatriation | ✓ | ✗ | | Arctic & Antarctic | ✗ | ✓ | | Caving / Underground | ✗ | ✓ | | Intoxication, Self-Harm, War | ✗ | ✗ | | Can Purchase | Worldwide | US & Canada Only | | Claim | Pays Directly | You Pay & File Claim |

item.title: Guadalupe Peak Hike Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.14
Guadalupe Peak Hike Updated & Reviewed August 2026 With 3,000 ft of steep climbing, it’s not a beginner hike, and weather can make you turn around. At 8,751 feet, Guadalupe Peak is the highest point in Texas and one of the most rewarding hikes in the USA. You’ll climb the Guadalupe Peak Trail, starting in desert scrub and finishing above the clouds on an incredible summit ridge. It’s a tough but doable hike, and in this guide I’ll show you how to hike it safely yourself. - Distance - 8.4 mi - Difficulty - Hard - Total Climbing - 3000 ft - Time - 4–8 hrs Video I made a video of what it’s like to do the hike so that you can watch it and be prepared when you do it yourself. Trailhead Info Trailhead Address: Pine Springs Trailhead, Salt Flat, TX 79847. There is a fee to enter the park or use your National Parks Pass. Guadalupe Peak is remote. - There is no gas station between El Paso and the park, or Carlsbad and the park. - Bring all the food you need with you. - You can refill with water at the Visitor Center or at the campground by the trailhead. - Guadalupe Mountains National Park is situated right on the edge of two time zones (Mountain and Central Standard Time), and the time on your phone could be incorrect. Parking can be a big challenge for this hike. The main lot has about 44 spaces, but they can fill up quickly. Your best bet is to arrive at sunrise for the hike and you’re generally assured to get a spot. As the morning progresses it can get tougher and tougher, and often after 730am the parking lot can be full. If the lot is full, you’ll have to park at the Visitor Center (also not a big lot) and walk up from there. I’d say if you’re going to come all the way here to do the hike, get here around sunrise. Camping There’s a small backcountry campground about a mile below the summit, accessible only by hiking up the Guadalupe Peak Trail. It has a few tent pads and no water, so you’ll need to carry everything you need, including extra water for the night and descent. Camping here gives you a head start for sunrise or sunset at the summit, but be prepared for strong winds and cold temperatures, even in warmer months. Permits are required and available at the Pine Springs Visitor Center or on Recreation.gov in advance. Info After the first mile or so of climbing, the trail enters the Guadalupe Mountains Wilderness, and from there all human waste and toilet paper must be carried out. Bring a WAG Bag in case you have to “take care of business.” Maps | Resource | What It’s For | |---|---| | CalTopo Map | Interactive map for planning and printing | | GPX Download | Put my route on your GPS | | AllTrails recent reports | What other hikers are seeing now | | Trailhead Weather | Forecast at the trailhead, including wind | | Summit Wind Forecast | Elevation-specific wind speed near the top | | Park Alerts & Conditions | Current closures and hazard notices | Directions Mile 0 - 1.5: The Big Effort The first 1.5 miles is the hardest part for many hikers. It’s steep, rocky, and doesn’t offer many spots to catch your breath. Info The El Capitan Trail goes to a viewpoint below it. There is no official trail to the top of El Capitan. Mile 1.5-3.3: The Breather After the initial tough climb, the grade eases and you traverse a north-facing slope where the cooler temperatures allow for evergreens like Douglas Fir and Ponderosa Pines. Mile 3.4-4.2: The Last Push The last mile to the summit is steep and tough, especially if you’re not used to the altitude. Take your time and take breaks. Miles 4.2-8.4: The Descent The 4.2-mile descent is harder than most hikers expect. Focusing on footing the whole way down on steep, rocky terrain is tiring, and the constant downhill impact hits the knees. Trekking poles help a lot on this stretch.

item.title: State High Points: Which Ones You Can Actually Hike
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.04
State High Point Hikes Updated & Reviewed August 2026 Most lists treat all 50 state high points as one bucket list. They’re not. The majority are drive-ups or short walks. A handful are real trail hikes. Seven of them aren’t hikes at all: they require mountaineering, technical climbing, or glacier travel to reach the summit. Technical Peaks These peaks require skills and gear beyond standard hiking. Here’s the best hikeable alternative for each. Alaska Denali (20,310 ft) is obvious. The harder problem is finding any normal-hike alternative in Alaska. Even mid-elevation peaks in the 4,000–7,000 ft range typically have exposed sections I wouldn’t recommend to most hikers. Flattop Mountain (3,510 ft) outside Anchorage is the best option: maintained trail, one short scramble near the top, manageable if you take your time. Washington Mount Rainier (14,411 ft) requires mountaineering year-round. Mount St. Helens (8,363 ft) is the best alternative: forest trail, marked boulder field, steep ash slope to the summit. Open in late summer when snow clears. No technical skills required. Wyoming Gannett Peak (13,810 ft) requires glacier travel and is considered the hardest state high point after Denali. Medicine Bow Peak (12,018 ft) has an official USFS trail (#295) all the way to the summit. Cloud Peak and Fremont Peak are closer in elevation but involve off-trail travel and scrambling I wouldn’t universally recommend. Nevada Boundary Peak (13,147 ft) has a route, but the Forest Service describes it as requiring cross-country navigation. Wheeler Peak (13,065 ft) in Great Basin National Park is only 84 feet lower with a maintained NPS trail. The elevation difference is negligible; the experience difference is not. Montana Granite Peak (12,807 ft) involves exposed Class 4/5 rock climbing and is one of the hardest state high points in the lower 48. Trapper Peak (10,157 ft) in the Bitterroot Mountains has an official USFS trail and is a straightforward, if steep, full day. Idaho Borah Peak’s (12,662 ft) “Chicken Out Ridge” names the problem. Scotchman Peak (7,018 ft) in northern Idaho has an official USFS trail and is called the hardest Class 1 peak in the state. Hyndman, Castle, and Iron Creek Point are higher alternatives but involve scrambling and route-finding I wouldn’t broadly recommend. Oregon Every route to Mount Hood (11,249 ft) requires mountaineering. South Sister (10,358 ft) is the highest non-technical summit in Oregon, hikeable in late summer when snow clears. Loose and gravelly near the top, but no exposure and no route-finding. item.title: The Wave Hike Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.99
The Wave Hike Updated & Reviewed August 2026 Hiking to The Wave in Arizona can be overwhelming. There are permits, a remote location, and off-trail hiking. I’ll show you how to hike it safely and easily in this guide. Despite all the hassle, the Wave is spectacular and worth it. - Distance - 6.5 mi - Difficulty - Moderate - Total Climbing - 1000 ft - Time - 4–6 hrs Video Here’s a video I shot on the trails outlining what you need to look for and what the experience is like so you’re prepared when you get there yourself. Permits | Lottery Type | Details | |---|---| | 4-Month Advance Lottery | Rolling 4-month lottery, apply 4 months in advance of your desired date. 48 people allowed per day. BLM mails you the permit and info packet. No briefing or in-person pickup needed. | | 2-day Lottery | Applied through the Recreation.gov app, must be geofenced within the Page and Kanab area (won’t work from the Grand Canyon). 16 people per day. If you win, pick up your permit the next day in Page or Kanab and attend a safety briefing there. | Choosing the right time to do the hike is important. | Season | Notes | |---|---| | Spring and Fall | Peak seasons, cooler temperatures and decent weather. Advance lottery success rate is about 2%. | | Winter | Great time to go, lottery success rate jumps to around 10%. Snow and rain can make the drive to the trailhead impassable. | | Summer | Temperatures can be deadly, people have died from heat-related issues. Leave very early, even before dawn, to beat the heat, and don’t risk it if it’s too hot. Also monsoon season, when flash floods can occur. | You can also do a guided tour with an outfitter to The Wave, but know that you still need to obtain a permit on your own. Read the directions in this guide before you book. I do a lot of guides and this hike isn’t very doable without a guide service. Trailhead The Wave doesn’t fit nicely into any type of National Park or Forest. It’s located in Coyote Buttes North, which is part of the Paria Canyon-Vermilion Cliffs Wilderness, which is also part of the Vermilion Cliffs National Monument, which is not managed by the Park Service, but rather the Bureau of Land Management (BLM). Confusing? Yup… | Destination | Drive Time | |---|---| | Zion National Park | 2 hours | | Grand Canyon South Rim | 3 hours | | Las Vegas | 4 hours | | Phoenix | 5 hours | When planning your trip to The Wave, staying in Page, AZ or Kanab, UT makes the most sense. Both towns have plenty of lodging and food options, with Page having more and a Walmart. There are also two primitive campgrounds, Stateline Campground and White House Campground, which require driving down dirt and sand roads to reach. They are remote and don’t have any supplies or facilities nearby. The condition of the road to the trailhead can vary. Generally in dry conditions, it’s pretty tame. After rain or snow the mud can be extremely slippery, almost like ice. I’ve seen low-clearance cars at the trailhead over the years, so it is doable. But if you’re traveling here and renting, I highly recommend opting for a 4-wheel drive vehicle like a Jeep. It will take any anxiety about the drive out of the equation. Maps | Resource | What It’s For | |---|---| | CalTopo Map | Interactive map for planning and printing | | GPX Download | Put my route on your GPS | | AllTrails recent reports | What other hikers are seeing now | | Trailhead Weather | Extreme heat check, no shade or water | | BLM Permits & Alerts | Lottery odds, closures, road status | - The BLM will give you a printed guide with the landmarks along the hike. It’s helpful to bring this. - Some sections are on rock, and some sections are in the sand. You can follow the footsteps in the sand, but the rock is much harder. - I use my phone GPS with AllTrails Pro to make sure I’m in the right place. - I’ve seen some other guides recommend that you use offline Google Maps, but the trail line isn’t the same as the actual trail. - There are lots of other places to explore along the hike. I’ve included them in the map and GPX file below. Notes - Most of the rock you see on the hike is called Navajo Sandstone. Millions of years of wind and water shaped the rock. Oxidation of all the minerals created the colors. - The sandstone is fragile. Leave no trace. Take all your trash out, leave everything else as is. - How did The Wave get so popular? It was first featured in a German nature documentary in 1996 called Faszination Natur, which led European tourists on a hunt to surface the location. When Instagram exploded in the early 2010s, the spot became overrun, leading to the implementation of the permit system you see today.

item.title: Rim Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.91
The Rim Trail at the Grand Canyon is one of the park’s rare easy hikes, following the South Rim with nonstop canyon views instead of dropping steeply into it. You don’t have to hike all 13 miles. Instead I have three easy route options, starting at just 2.7 miles, that showcase the very best of the Rim Trail. Distance 2.7–8.5 mi Difficulty Easy Total Climbing 80–300 ft Time 1–4 hrs GearFitness clothes or light hiking gear is fine here. Bring a minimum of 1L of water. You can see all the gear I use on a hike like this here. WhenGenerally okay all year, but in winter path can be icy. People have fallen off the edge on the Rim Trail. 100% of the time it’s because they’ve left the trail to take pictures or explore. Use your noggin and stay away from the edge. Video Options # Name Distance Notes 1 Visitor Center to Bright Angel 3 miles Most crowded; do at sunrise or sunset to have viewpoints to yourself This stretch is the most popular part of the Rim Trail, connecting Mather Point and the Visitor Center with the Bright Angel Trailhead. It’s an easy, paved 3-mile walk with shuttle access at both ends, nonstop canyon views, and plenty of spots to stop along the way. Mather Point is named after Stephen Tyng Mather, the first director of the National Park Service. He pushed hard to make the Grand Canyon a national park in 1919. Today, it’s one of the most visited viewpoints in the entire park, about 90% of visitors see the canyon for the first time from here. Info The Yavapai Geology Museum is named after the Yavapai people, one of the Native tribes of northern and central Arizona. The word “Yavapai” comes from their own language and translates to “people of the sun.” Info Verkamp’s was a store from 1906 until 2008 when the NPS took it over. Info Hopi House opened in 1905, designed to resemble a traditional Hopi dwelling. It was built as a place for Hopi artisans to live, work, and sell their crafts Info If you’ve ever seen National Lampoon’s Vacation, the exterior of the hotel was used in the Grand Canyon scene. You’ll pass three more lodges, Kachina, Thunderbird, and Bright Angel. From here, you have some options: Hike back the way you came. Hop on a shuttle bus at the Bright Angel Lodge and go back to the Visitor Center. If you want to keep going, you can continue to hike 3 (to Hermit’s Rest) and hike as far as you’d like, taking a shuttle bus back when you’re done. If you have the fitness, you can also venture on the Bright Angel Trail. Hike 2: Visitor Center to South Kaibab Trail The stretch of the Rim Trail from the Visitor Center to the South Kaibab Trail is one of the quieter ways to see the canyon. This 2.7-mile paved section connects some of the best viewpoints, including Mather Point and Pipe Creek Vista, and you can hop on the free shuttle if you don’t want to hike it out and back. It’s a mellow walk with constant rim views and easy access from the main visitor area. Hop on a shuttle bus at the South Kaibab Trailhead and go back to the Visitor Center. If you have the fitness, you can also venture on the South Kaibab Trail to Ooh Ahh Point. Hike 3: Bright Angel to Hermits Rest The Rim Trail from Bright Angel to Hermit’s Rest is the longest and most spectacular stretch, about 8.5 miles of nonstop canyon views with far fewer crowds than the main village area. The hike passes every major west rim overlook, from Maricopa and Hopi Points to Pima Point, and if you get tired you can always catch the free shuttle that runs alongside the trail. It’s the best way to see the Grand Canyon’s South Rim without ever dropping into the canyon. Hermit’s Rest is named after “the hermit” of the Grand Canyon, a Quebecois, Louis Boucher. Boucher staked his claim here, carved out trails in the canyon, and eventually evolved his homestead to be a tourist destination.

item.description:

Bryce Canyon National Park Fairyland Loop Trail Updated & Reviewed August 2026
The Fairyland Loop Trail is one of the best ways to experience Bryce Canyon without the crowds. This 8-mile loop takes you deep into a quieter section of the park, winding through stunning hoodoos and rock formations. It’s a stunning area that gets overshadowed by the trails in the nearby Bryce Amphitheater. If you like hiking, the Fairyland Loop Trail is a must-do.
- Distance - 8 mi
- Difficulty - Moderate
- Total Climbing - 1600 ft
- Time - 3–4 hrs
Gear Fitness clothes or light hiking gear is fine here. Bring a minimum of 2L of water. You can see all the gear I use on a hike like this here.
When Summer can be hot, winter can have snow, check the weather.
Video
Trailhead
Fees: $20+ Park Entry Fee (or use your America the Beautiful pass) The Fairyland Loop is a hybrid hike combining Fairyland Trail and about 2.5 miles of the Rim Trail (to close the loop). I recommend starting at Fairyland Point and hiking counter-clockwise, which is also what the park suggests. That way, you’ll descend gradually into the canyon, do most of the climbing by the middle, and finish with a shorter, easier climb back to the rim.
Warning The shuttle bus does not run to Fairyland Point.
