item.title: RECCO Reflector Review: What It Is & Does It Work
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.60
RECCO Reflector Review Updated & Reviewed August 2026 Cheap, weightless insurance for being found, but only where rescue teams have detectors, and never instead of a satellite communicator. A RECCO reflector is a battery-free radar tag that makes you searchable to equipped rescue teams when you can’t call for help. After two years with one on my pack and talking to the SAR professionals who train with the detectors: if teams in your area carry them, it’s worth the $40. If they don’t, skip it. Either way, your primary is a satellite communicator; this is the passive backup that answers when every battery is dead. How I Earn I buy gear with my own money. It's the only way I can be 100% honest about what works. No sponsors, no free gear. Use the links below to buy, and you support these ad-free, independent reviews at no extra cost. Video What I learned in the two years since recommending the RECCO: what SAR teams told me, the documented rescues, and where it falls short. How It Works Crack one open and you’d find two foil antennas connected by a diode. No battery, no electronics, no registration. It’s a harmonic reflector, not an RFID tag. - The detector does the work. Rescuers carry a handheld detector, or fly a helicopter-mounted one, that broadcasts a specific radar frequency (917 MHz). - The reflector answers. When the signal hits the reflector, the diode doubles the frequency and bounces it back (1834 MHz). The detector hears that answer as a distinct chirp, so rescuers know it’s a RECCO and not a random piece of metal. - Closer means louder. The stronger the chirp, the closer the searcher is to you. The helicopter detector sweeps about a 300-foot swath and can clear roughly a square kilometer every six minutes. - False hits happen. Detectors sometimes get weak reflections off phones, radios, and other electronics, even powered off. A real reflector returns a much stronger, cleaner signal, and any ping still gives searchers a clue. Rescue Record Has RECCO found anyone? The question that matters, in three parts. - Documented live saves exist, all in avalanches. A skier in Spain was located alive under the snow in 2015, the first case published in medical literature. Another was found alive under 3.2 meters of snow in Switzerland in 2019. RECCO’s own count is 17 live saves through 2019, mostly in Europe, none in the US. - Recoveries are more common. Most confirmed finds are body recoveries, including climber Marc-André Leclerc (from the film The Alpinist) in Alaska in 2018, where rescuers who worked the search say RECCO was essential to locating him. That’s worth something on its own: it ends a search and gives a family an answer. - No documented live save of a lost hiker yet. The technology doesn’t care whether you’re alive, a reflector answers either way. The record is thin on summer rescues because few hikers carry reflectors and detector coverage is still growing. Every SAR professional I’ve talked to says the same thing: the tool works, the bottleneck is people carrying it. Coverage A reflector is only useful where someone has a detector. Check before you buy. - Check the coverage map. RECCO publishes a map of every team and resort with detectors that you can filter by handheld and helicopter units. If nobody near your trails has one, skip it. - US helicopter coverage is small but growing. Eleven US agencies fly the SAR helicopter detector as of mid-2026, including LA County Sheriff (the only one in California) and a new unit covering the Sierra out of Reno. Hundreds of ski patrols and SAR teams carry handhelds. - One reflector works everywhere. Detector frequencies vary slightly by country, but the same reflector answers all of them, US and Europe alike. Carrying It - You might already own one. RECCO has been sewn into ski jackets, pants, and helmets for over a decade, and it’s now showing up in backpacks and even trail runners. Check your gear for the logo before buying anything. - Old reflectors don’t expire. There’s no battery to die and nothing to wear out. A reflector in a 2012 jacket works like a new one. - Placement matters. Anything between the reflector and the detector weakens the signal, including your body, which is mostly water. High on your pack keeps it clear if you’re face down. The other school of thought puts it on your person (a belt loop) in case you’re separated from your pack. Or carry one in each spot. Be Searchable The reflector is one layer in a system. If you can’t hit SOS (heart attack, stroke, rockfall), these are the layers that get you found: - Leave a plan. Send someone your route link and a turnaround time. Searchers start where your plan says, not from the whole mountain. - Note your RECCO in your emergency details. Add “carrying RECCO reflector” to your inReach or PLB emergency notes and tell whoever holds your trip plan. SAR can only deploy a detector if they know to look for one. - Turn on tracking. inReach breadcrumbs give rescuers a trail to your last known point. - The RECCO is the last line of defense. A PLB’s homing beacon and your phone are useless after a few days of battery drain. The reflector still answers. From the comments: if everyone carries one, how do rescuers know who’s lost? They don’t scan the whole planet. They grid a defined search area for a missing person, and any return in that area gets checked. More reflectors make the tool stronger, not weaker. Worth $40? The materials inside are worth maybe $2, and yes, you could technically build one. What you’re paying for is a tested, sealed unit that’s part of a system rescue teams train on, and RECCO reinvests a portion of reflector sales into putting detectors in SAR hands, which is the only way coverage grows. For me the math is simple: a few grams and $40 for a chance of being found when nothing else on my pack works, and at worst, a faster answer for my family. I’m still carrying mine. If you hike where teams have detectors, it’s cheap insurance. If you don’t, spend the money elsewhere, and check the full gear list for where I’d put it instead.

item.title: Valley of the Moon Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.58
Valley of the Moon Trail Updated & Reviewed August 2026 The Valley of the Moon Trail offers a unique desert hike through some spectacular granite formations near the U.S.–Mexico border. Along the way, there’s a smugglers’ cave, abandoned mines, and a stretch of trail right on the border. It’s remote, rugged, and underrated. - Distance - 9 mi - Difficulty - Moderate - Total Climbing - 1700 ft - Time - 4–6 hrs Video Trailhead Info There is no fee to park here. Maps While the name might be Valley of the Moon Trail, there’s actually not a single defined trail per se. In fact, there are many different use trails and off-road routes here. It’s vital to have electronic navigation because it’s not as simple as turn-by-turn directions. Load the GPS file I provided onto your phone, have offline maps, and use them to make sure you’re in the right place. Safety This hike is generally considered safe, and all areas covered in this guide were deemed secure by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) at the time of writing. However, conditions can change rapidly in border regions due to various factors. - Before heading out, it’s advisable to check recent trip reports on platforms like AllTrails for the Valley of the Moon Trail and Blue Angels Peak to see current trail conditions and any user-reported issues. - Contacting the local CBP office can provide up-to-date information on safety and any advisories. When you call, mention your plans to hike in the Valley of the Moon area and inquire about any current concerns. While they may note that there’s always some level of risk, they can offer guidance on areas to avoid based on recent activity. - Remember that risks exist in many hiking areas, not just near borders. Personally, I’ve always felt secure hiking in this region, largely due to the significant law enforcement presence. While I’ve occasionally seen individuals crossing the border, they’ve consistently kept their distance or avoided contact. Directions Info Unlike most of my trail guides where I show you every intersection and turn, that wouldn’t be practical here at the Valley of the Moon because of the dozens, if not hundreds, of unofficial trails all over from here forward. I’ll show you the main landmarks and what to look for, but again, make sure you bring this route on your GPS or phone along with offline maps. Info If you’re lucky, you might spot some wild horses, burros, or cattle. The wild horses are allegedly descended from animals that escaped or were abandoned by Spanish settlers hundreds of years ago. This is not an official grazing area, so any cattle you see have likely wandered off from wherever they’re supposed to be. Info An old BLM web page has this description of Smuggler’s Cave: “A natural hollow in one of the boulders is known as Smugglers Cave. Many tales have been told about the cave. The earliest account ties the cave to the December 1875 holdup at the old Campo Store. According to this story, one of the bandits was wounded and chased by a posse to Smugglers Cave, where he was flushed out and finished off. Other accounts involve the smuggling of Chinese laborers and contraband across the Mexican border to the cave at the turn of the century.” Info In recent years, the area around Jacumba Hot Springs and the Valley of the Moon has been a hotspot for human trafficking. Activity had slowed down considerably when I documented this guide, but there have been times in the past when it was very active. Info The wind turbines, called La Rumorosa I, supply power to nearby Mexicali. Other turbines in the area also supply power to the United States. According to the Border Energy Forum, the La Rumorosa region has the second-highest wind energy potential in Mexico. Warning The BLM warns: Entering mines or mine shafts is dangerous. Poison air and cave-ins can and do occur. When you’re done at the top of the peak and at the mine area, continue back down on the trail you came up earlier. Info The actual border lies a short distance back from the fence. This area is in a state of change - new border wall construction has been approved, although I’m not positive if it affects this exact spot. The government has also been sending troops to the border, and this area could be closed to hikers at some point. As I mentioned earlier in the guide, it’s important to do your homework before showing up here. Desert View Tower Side Trip The real estate developer who built Jacumba also built this tower in 1922. It was originally built as a roadside attraction with a restaurant and gift shop. Today, it still stands and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

item.title: Mount Tammany Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.56
The Mount Tammany Red Dot Trail is New Jersey’s most popular hike for a reason. The steep, rocky climb to the top of Mount Tammany delivers big views of the Delaware Water Gap and the river below. But in this guide I’ll also show you how to get back down without wrecking your knees. Along the way, we’ll check out a waterfall and finish with a short stretch on the famous Appalachian Trail before it’s all said and done. Distance 3.6 mi Difficulty Hard Total Climbing 1200 ft Time 2–3 hrs GearFitness clothes or light hiking gear is fine here. Bring a minimum of 1L of water. You can see all the gear I use on a hike like this here. WhenSummer can be hot, winter can have snow, check the weather. Here’s the route I’m going to show you in this guide, and why. We’re going up the Red Dot Trail, which gets us to the top the quickest and has a view or two along the way. It’s iconic with some rocky climbs, but no challenging scrambles. Going down the Red Dot Trail is not very fun, especially for your knees. So we’ll take the more gradual Blue Dot Trail downhill, then join the Appalachian Trail for a short stretch. Why is it called Mt Tammany? It’s named after the Lenape Chief Tamanend, who negotiated a peace treaty with William Penn for the Lenape and European settlers to live in peace. About 50 years later they were displaced from the area under the Walking Purchase. Today, nearly 350 years later, the Lenape have been displaced to Wisconsin, Oklahoma, and Ontario (Canada). Directions Info If you’re peak bagging and want to reach the actual 1,527 foot summit, that point is about 800 feet behind the viewpoint in the woods. Info The original name of the Blue Dot Trail is the Pahaquarry Trail. Pahaquarry is a Lenape word for “the place between the mountains beside the waters.” Info On official topographic maps, the area where you parked is the former town of Dunnfield, which had a post office, train station, and thriving slate business. Today all that’s left is the parking lots.

item.title: Mount Minsi Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.40
The Mount Minsi Trail is a classic Delaware Water Gap hike with multiple jaw-dropping views of the river, a stretch on the iconic Appalachian Trail, and even the remains of an old fire tower. In this guide, I’ll show you how to hike Mount Minsi the easy way; you just bring the leg power. Distance 4.8 mi Difficulty Moderate Total Climbing 1080 ft Time 2–3 hrs GearFitness clothes or light hiking gear is fine here. Bring a minimum of 1L of water. You can see all the gear I use on a hike like this here. WhenSummer can be hot, winter can have snow, check the weather. Why is it called “Minsi”? The name comes from an alternate spelling of “Munsee,” one of the bands of the Lenni Lenape people who originally lived in this region. Info Did you know that rhododendrons are toxic? In humans eating them will get you anything from mild gas to severe nervous system issues. Info **In the 1960s the plan was to dam the Delaware River just north of here. **The Tocks Island Dam would have flooded the river valley, creating a lake 140 feet deep in places that would help control an overflowing river and provide water to New York and Philadelphia. The project was met with protest and eventually scrapped. The land acquired by the federal government became the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area. Info 28 out of the 2174 miles of the Appalachian Trail go through the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area. If you see backpackers going through, they might be on their journey between Georgia and Maine. This section is a little tricky, but both routes will get you in the right place. Info Around 100 years ago they built a steel tower here. It was used as a fire watch tower, radio tower, and airway beacon (a primitive series of lighted beacons used by airplanes before radar and radio). Today this is all that’s left.

item.title: Limestone Canyon and The Sinks Hike Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.37
Limestone Canyon Regional Park is an incredibly beautiful area to hike, but it’s also home to a famous area called ‘The Sinks,’ also known as ’the little Grand Canyon of Orange County.’ Limestone Canyon is not always open to the public, but this easy trail guide will show you how to visit and see The Sinks for yourself. Distance 9 mi Difficulty Moderate Total Climbing 850 ft Time 3–4 hrs GearFitness clothes or light hiking gear is fine here. Bring a minimum of 1L of water. You can see all the gear I use on a hike like this here. Limestone Canyon Regional Park is located in Orange County, CA, in the foothills of the Santa Ana Mountains.Before visiting Limestone Canyon Regional Park, you must register for an open event. Go to “Activities” and filter by “Limestone Canyon Nature Preserve” Find a match for the day that you want to visit. There are two types of hikes. Open hikes allow you to pick any open trails you’d like and hike freely. Docent-led hikes are traditional group hikes led by an expert. These hikes are great because you’ll usually get a guided tour along the way. Note that the hikes have difficulty ratings; you should find one that matches your level. Hikes can have different starting areas. The website has a downloadable map of the current trails and starting areas. Maps If you go on a general open day, I recommend hiking to The Sinks, aka the Mini-Grand Canyon, the main attraction. This guide has directions for that hike. There are many more trails and you could include others to choose your own adventure as well.

item.title: Humphreys Peak Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.22
Humphreys Peak Trail Updated & Reviewed August 2026 Humphreys Peak, the highest point in Arizona, is the classic hike in the area. From the summit, you can see all the way to the Grand Canyon. The trail takes you through pine forests and above the treeline, providing a truly unique Arizona experience. In this guide I’ll make the hike easy. - Distance - 9.6 mi - Difficulty - Hard - Total Climbing - 3360 ft - Time - 5–8 hrs Video Here’s a video I shot on the trail so you know what to expect when you get there. Trailhead Info The hike starts at the Arizona Snowbowl Ski Area, use this trailhead address: 9300 N Snow Bowl Rd, Flagstaff, AZ 86001 Info The hike starts at over 9200 feet. Expect the air to be thin. This area is known as “Arizona’s little Colorado.” Maps | Resource | What It’s For | |---|---| | CalTopo Map | Interactive map for planning and printing | | GPX Download | Put my route on your GPS | | AllTrails recent reports | What other hikers are seeing now | | Trailhead Weather | Forecast for the Snowbowl trailhead | | Summit Weather | Summit-specific wind and storm conditions | | Humphreys Trail No. 151 | Official trail status and regs | | Coconino NF Alerts | Fire danger and closures | Directions Info The area is named for the Hopi spirit beings, or Kachinas, some of whom according to Hopi mythology live here from July to December. Humphreys Peak is considered sacred by many Native Peoples including the Hopi, Navajo, and Apache. Info If you look up from the scree field, you may see some shiny objects in the distance, pieces of wreckage from a B-24 bomber that crashed here in 1944. After the crash, many visitors, not knowing it had been there for a while, kept reporting a new plane crash on the mountain, so the Forest Service blew up the wreckage in 1950. Some pieces still remain. Warning From here to the summit, it’s exposed. If you see bad weather coming in, it makes sense to turn around and head back.

item.title: Wheeler Peak Trail NV Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.16
Great Basin National Park Wheeler Peak Trail NV Updated & Reviewed August 2026
The hike to Wheeler Peak (NV) is tough, but it has its payoffs. On a clear day, you can see for 100 miles, and the scenery on the way to the summit is simply incredible. In this guide, I’ll show you how to hike to Nevada’s highest official hiking trail.
- Distance - 8.8 mi
- Difficulty - Hard
- Total Climbing - 2920 ft
- Time - 5–8 hrs
Who It's For Strong hikers who can handle altitude. Biggest Risk Altitude above 13,000 ft and afternoon lightning on exposed summit. Start early to avoid storms. When to Go Late June through October. Snow blocks upper trail until summer. Park road closes in winter.
Video Here’s a video I did of what the trail looks like and what you can expect.
Trailhead
Some notes if you’re visiting: - There is no entry fee for Great Basin National Park. - Get water and use the bathroom at the visitor center. The trailhead has no facilities. - If the parking is full, you can park down the road by the Wheeler Peak Campground. - The Wheeler Peak Scenic Drive is closed in the winter up to this destination. Check the park website to see if it’s open when you visit. - The park has no hotels or lodges, it’s camping only. Check the park website for more information. Maps
Directions

item.title: Peekaboo Loop Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.16
The Peekaboo Loop Trail takes you away from the crowds and into some of the most dramatic hoodoo scenery in Bryce Canyon. This scenic, up-and-down loop is a great way to explore the Bryce Amphitheater from below, with fewer people and nonstop views. In this guide, I’ll show you how to hike and get the most out of the Peekaboo Loop. Distance 5.2 mi Difficulty Moderate Total Climbing 1500 ft Time 3–4 hrs WhenSummer can be hot, winter can have snow, check the weather. GearFitness clothes or light hiking gear is fine here. Bring a minimum of 2L of water. You can see all the gear I use on a hike like this here. Fees: $20+ Park Entry Fee (or use your America the Beautiful pass) There’s a parking lot at Bryce Point with roughly 30 parking spots. In the summer Bryce Canyon NP usually runs a shuttle bus, and if you’re staying in Bryce Canyon City you can easily take the shuttle here and avoid the hassle. Warning Bring water with you before getting to Bryce Point; there’s no water fill station here. My trail guide follows the Bryce Canyon NP’s recommendation to do the Peekaboo Loop clockwise. Directions Info The Peekaboo is one of the only shared use trails (humans, horses, mules). You can bring your own horse or mule with you, or you can book a ride with the park’s official concessioner. The are also other ‘horse-only’ trails that are closed to humans. Info Once you pass the Wall of Windows, you go from Peekaboo Canyon into Bryce Canyon. Info If you want to connect to the Navajo Loop or Queens Garden Trail, you can do it at the bottom of this climb. See my guide for the Figure 8 Trail for more information. Info Do hoodoos fall down? They sure do, but usually it happens over a period of thousands of years, but given the amount of hoodoos at Bryce, it could really happen whenever. An iconic hoodoo called The Sentinel tumbled between 1980 and 2016.

item.title: Black Elk Peak Hike Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.08
Black Hills, South Dakota Black Elk Peak Hike Updated & Reviewed August 2026
Black Elk Peak is not only South Dakota’s high point, but it’s also one of the most beautiful hikes in the USA. This guide will show you a loop hike that takes you past Cathedral Spires, up to the Harney Fire Lookout at the summit of Black Elk Peak, and then back down past Little Devil’s Tower. It’s a classic hike that I highly recommend.
- Distance - 7.1 mi
- Difficulty - Moderate
- Total Climbing - 1480 ft
- Time - 3–4 hrs
Who It's For Hikers with moderate fitness. When to Go May through October. Area can be covered in snow in winter and spring.
Video Here’s a video I shot walking you through the entire hike so you know what to expect.
Trailhead Maps
Directions

item.title: Best Hiking GPS: Trail Tested
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 3.92
Best Hiking GPS Updated & Reviewed August 2026 Your phone does most of what a handheld GPS does, usually with a better screen. But when conditions turn harsh and battery life matters, a purpose-built handheld wins. I’ve tested them all since my Garmin GPS 12 in 1999, and I buy my own units and don’t take sponsorships, so I’m free to recommend what works best. | Option | Best For | |---|---| | GPSMAP 67 | Best all-around hiking GPS. Rugged, accurate, long battery, with inReach built in the 67i model | | GPSMAP 65s | This multi-band GPS is my budget pick, and it runs on AA batteries | | Enduro 3 | If you don't need a big screen, the Enduro does everything a handheld does on your wrist | | Phone + App | Casual hikers in tame conditions who are fine carrying a backup battery | My Picks Best All-Around Garmin GPSMAP 67i - My overall pick. I’ve used it for years on the trail and it’s the most accurate and longest-lasting handheld Garmin makes: multi-band multi-GNSS gets me around 6 feet of accuracy even in canyons and heavy tree cover, and I get about 140 hours of battery with 10-minute inReach tracking and messaging on (200+ in GPS-only mode). The inReach features give you SOS, non-emergency messaging, satellite tracking, and weather reports in one unit. ↳ REI ↳ Review Info I’ve tested the newer GPSMAP H1i Plus side by side, and the 67i is a better value. But if you want the latest and greatest, it’s the H1. Best Budget Garmin GPSMAP 65s - If you want the same multi-band accuracy without the inReach features or the price tag, get the 65s. It runs on two AA batteries that you can swap in the field, and you can also buy rechargeable AA batteries on Amazon. Accuracy is the same as the 67i in my testing. You lose the inReach, the longer internal battery, and USB-C, but it’s smaller and handles the essential navigation functions that you need. ↳ Amazon ↳ Review Best for Vehicle and Trail Garmin Montana 750i - A big touchscreen like a phone with a removable battery, great for a combined vehicle and dashboard setup with inReach built in. It’s too heavy to be my main hiking handheld, but if one device has to do overlanding and the occasional hike, this is it. ↳ Amazon ↳ Review Best on the Wrist Garmin Enduro 3 - The best hiking GPS watch I’ve tested. If you abandon the idea that the form factor has to be handheld, the Enduro 3 does everything my GPSMAP 67 does with the same accuracy. It has offline maps with trail names, offline navigation, and tracking. It also has solar and a battery that lasts weeks. The downside is that you only have a small screen to work with. If you do a lot of navigation on the fly in the field, this isn’t your best choice. But if you just want maps, navigation, tracking, and the ability to reroute in an emergency, this works well. ↳ REI | Amazon ↳ Review Phone As GPS For a casual day hike in good weather, your phone is probably the best hiking GPS you have. The screen is better, the apps are slicker than anything Garmin provides, and you already have it with you. Two apps I recommend: - AllTrails is the best starting point for beginners and for discovery. Huge trail database, user reviews, and simple offline downloads on the paid tier. I use it to find trails I haven’t done before. - Footpath is what I use when I want to draw my own route. Trace a line on the map with your finger, and it snaps to trails and estimates distance and elevation. Nothing else matches it for quick planning. - CalTopo is what I use for more hardcore planning. They have a mobile app but the navigation is basic, although effective if you know how to use it. The weak areas of a phone are battery and durability. Here’s how to address it: - Carry an external battery. Navigation will drain a phone faster than you think. - Put it in a durable case like an Otterbox Defender. A cracked screen in the backcountry is a real problem. - Download your maps before you leave service. Most apps make this easy on paid plans, but you have to remember to do it. Info In harsher conditions, rain, snow, cold, or multi-day trips, I use a handheld or a watch as my primary and use the phone as a backup. What to Look For Here are the key features that a handheld GPS should fulfill. - Give you directions to navigate a route - Have offline maps and routing so that you can do it on the fly - Have buttons that allow you to use the unit when wet, in gloves, etc. - Have a battery life of days not hours - Be durable enough to survive the outdoors, including extreme temperatures - Drop waypoints to mark camps, water sources, or bail-out points - Record your track so you have record of where you went - Customize and view key metrics like elevation, distance, and pace at a glance - Have enhanced accuracy down to 6-9ft, leveraging multiple GNSS systems and multi-band GPS The downside of a handheld GPS is that it’s another piece of gear you have to buy, charge, and update periodically. It’s generally heavier than you’d hope it would be, and the interface for many Garmin units will seem like a step back 20 years from your phone. Today there are dozens of phone apps that can handle navigation. But for me the question becomes is the phone something I can rely on when the conditions get really bad. When I’m in the backcountry I prefer to save my phone for “phone things” and use a GPS to do the heavy lifting on navigation, including any changes to plans. When you’re tired, wet, and need to get directions, the old clunky interface of a handheld GPS is much easier to use than hunting and pecking on a slick app interface on your phone. Testing Criteria I buy every GPS myself and navigate with it on real hikes before it earns a spot here. I test accuracy against known tracks in hard conditions (canyons, heavy tree cover), battery life against the spec sheet, and whether I can run the whole interface with wet hands or gloves. If a unit isn’t a meaningful upgrade in accuracy, battery, or reliability, it doesn’t make my picks, and I update this page as devices and firmware change. Here are the units I tested that didn’t make the cut. | Device | Why I Didn’t Choose It | |---|---| | GPSMAP 66sr | Still accurate multi-band, but the 65s does essentially the same thing for less money. | | eTrex Touch | Solid hardware and accuracy, but the battery claims fall apart on trail. | | eTrex 32x | Still works as a bare-bones AA trail GPS, but the 65s is worth the step up. | Maps If you have an older Garmin handheld that takes “add maps” or you want alternate coverage on a newer one, you can load free OpenStreetMap topo maps onto it. - Download your region from GMapTool, then install using the free Garmin MapInstall and MapManager apps. Connect your GPS unit and use MapInstall to send the maps to the device. Works on Mac and Windows. Check your unit’s spec page on Garmin.com to confirm it supports added maps before you start. - For worldwide maps, check this site. - To connect to newer devices that run on MTP mode, use OpenMTP. You can also create custom maps for your GPS using CalTopo. Using Your GPS Accuracy - Turn on multi-GNSS if you have the option. GPS is the USA’s satellite system, but there are others: GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (EU), BeiDou (China), QZSS (Japan), IRNSS (India). They all work on the same principles. The more signals your receiver can pick from, the better the fix. If battery doesn’t matter, turn them all on. If battery matters, run GPS-only. In my experience, GPS alone works well in the US. Galileo has also been reliable. - Get a multi-band receiver if you’re buying new. This is the biggest accuracy upgrade in years. Multi-band receivers pick up both the old public GPS signal and newer civil bands from modern satellites. In practice, that means better performance in canyons, slot canyons, and urban corridors where older single-band units lose the signal. The GPSMAP 65s, 67i, Fenix 8, and Enduro 3 are all multi-band. Some newer phones are too. - Do a GPS soak at the trailhead. When you get out of your car, power on your GPS and set it on top of the car for 2-5 minutes while you lace up and pack. Let it lock onto satellites before you start recording. You’ll get a cleaner track from the first step. Just don’t drive off with it up there. - Sync your device before you leave. Your GPS downloads an almanac file (Garmin calls it EPO) that tells it where the satellites are going to be. It gets this over satellite during use, but it’s faster over WiFi. Open Garmin Connect or Garmin Explore on your phone before the trip to update the almanac and firmware. - Enable WAAS or EGNOS if your device has it. These are correction signals that account for satellite drift and atmospheric distortion. They’ll improve accuracy at a small battery cost. If battery matters, turn them off. - Check the satellite screen. On a Garmin handheld, there’s a satellite page that shows a sky map of every signal you’re receiving. The center is directly overhead, the edge is the horizon, and there’s a 45-degree line in between. Ideally, you want satellites on all four compass points at or above that 45-degree line. If they’re all clustered together, your fix will be weaker. - Live with environmental limits. Canyons, thick canopy, and even solar weather can interfere with GPS. There’s a space weather report that shows how disturbed the ionosphere is. If accuracy really matters, get to higher ground with an open view of the sky. When the sky is blocked, no GPS is going to save you. Battery and Recording - Turn off smart recording for the most accurate track. On Garmin, smart recording drops track points based on movement detection, which can create big gaps. I set my recording to “every second” instead. Just remember to pause the unit when you stop, or you’ll get dozens of overlapping points from a device that thinks it’s moving. Unpaused, 10 feet of GPS noise over a minute stopped can add 600 feet of phantom distance. - Tracks are just the distances between points. If you and a friend record the same hike with different settings, your totals won’t match. More points, more chances for noise. Fewer points, more chances for shortcutting corners. Neither is wrong, they’re just different recording strategies. - Clean up your tracks after. Load the GPX into Basecamp, Garmin Connect, or CalTopo and delete any obvious outlier points. A single dropped signal can add hundreds of feet of distance. A minute of cleanup gets you a much more accurate record. - Kill what you’re not using to save battery. Bluetooth, WiFi, notifications, map shading, and the backlight all draw power. On a multi-day trip, turn off anything you don’t need. If your handheld takes AAs, lithium AAs last noticeably longer than alkaline. GPX Files - A GPX file is a plain text file that stores geographic data, specifically routes, tracks, and waypoints. It is the universal standard used to save your recorded activities, load trail plans onto a GPS device, or share navigation data with others. - Tracks are breadcrumb trails, routes are a series of waypoints that your device will calculate the path between. - Modern Garmin devices use something called a Course, which is a combination of a route and track. Course points are waypoints along your route. Navigation - Plan on a real screen. The best planning happens on a computer with CalTopo or the Footpath/AllTrails web app. Export the GPX, then sync or drag it onto your device. The mobile apps are fine, but nothing beats a big monitor for a complex route. - Carry it with the antenna up. On a handheld, clip it to a pack strap with a carabiner, antenna pointing at the sky. A unit buried in a pocket or stuffed in a pack fights for signal and burns battery doing it. - Drop waypoints at decision points. When you hit a tricky junction, a water source, or a campsite, take 10 seconds to mark a waypoint. On the way back, or if you get turned around, those marks can save you. - Use waypoint averaging for a precise fix. If you really need an accurate location, marking a cache, a trailhead, or a water source for future trips, use waypoint averaging. The GPS takes multiple readings over time and averages them for a much tighter position than a single drop. - Elevation is approximate. GPS elevation can be off by hundreds of feet. If your device has a barometric altimeter, use it and calibrate it from a known elevation at the trailhead. Treat all elevation numbers as a ballpark, not a measurement. General - How much accuracy do you actually need? Survey-grade GPS units get you centimeter precision and cost thousands. Follow the tips above and a consumer unit will get you 8-12 feet. That’s plenty for navigation, recording, and finding your way home. Unless you’re competing on Strava segments or doing real survey work, you don’t need more. - Sync apps before you leave the house. An app update can log you out, and if that happens off-grid, you’re stuck. Open every app paired with your GPS the night before and make sure it’s signed in and synced. - Know the difference between GPS and satellite messaging. A GPS is a receiver, it doesn’t broadcast anything. You can put it next to your head and nothing happens. A satellite communicator (like an inReach) actually transmits to a satellite. They’re different tools that often live in the same box. Here’s my sat comm guide if you want one device that does both. And of course, always bring a paper map as backup.

item.title: Garmin Enduro 3 Review: Trail Tested
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 3.88
Garmin Enduro 3 Review Updated & Reviewed August 2026 The best watch for hiking and backpacking, built around battery life and navigation instead of smartwatch features. Three weeks between charges with full offline topo maps, and I wear it from day hikes to multi-week backpacking without thinking about it. The catch is the high price and an MIP screen that looks washed out compared to a smartwatch’s AMOLED. If you want more detailed maps and can charge every 5-10 days, the Fenix 8 is the better call. How I Earn I buy gear with my own money. It's the only way I can be 100% honest about what works. No sponsors, no free gear. Use the links below to buy, and you support these ad-free, independent reviews at no extra cost. Battery The battery is the reason to buy this watch. The MIP screen draws almost nothing, and the solar ring offsets a meaningful amount of drain in full sun. In ideal conditions tracking with GPS only, Garmin rates it at up to 320 hours. That ceiling isn’t typical, but it shows you the possibilities if you tweak the settings. In fact, if I sit it on a rock in the sunlight all day, it can actually increase the battery percentage. The drain is minimal. Garmin tracks solar input in lux hours. Direct peak summer sun can hit 100k+ lux per hour. On your wrist, moving in and out of shade with a sleeve sometimes covering it, you’ll get a fraction of that. Overcast drops it to around 1,000 lux. For every 40-50k lux hours you accumulate, expect roughly 1% of battery drain offset. For me, using it for a long hike every week, daily exercise, and 24/7 tracking, I charge it around every 3 weeks. Here are the numbers I’ve been getting (averaged out): | Condition | Drain per Hour | Estimated Daily Drain | Hiking Days per Charge | |---|---|---|---| | No sun (forest/cloud) | 1-2% | ~15% | ~6-7 days | | Mixed sun/shade | 0.5-1.0% | ~10% | ~8-10 days | | Bright sun (above treeline) | 0.3-0.8% | ~3-8% | ~10-12+ days | Info Charging is quick via Garmin’s proprietary USB-C cable. From 10% to 99% takes about 2 hours and it plays nicely with low-output packs like Nitecore and Anker. Maps The Enduro 3 has full offline topo maps built in, no phone or connection required. Trail lines, elevation shading, trail names, and your position are all there on the wrist. I use it most at junctions where I need to confirm my direction quickly. Looking at a map screen and using navigation do drain the battery more than standard data screens, so I keep the map view closed unless I need it. For planning, I use Garmin Explore or Garmin Connect on my phone, then sync the course. Turn-by-turn prompts, distances to waypoints, and off-trail alerts all work once the course is loaded. On a shorter trip I’ll load courses for every day. On a longer backpacking trip, I skip that and just open the map at junctions. Waypoints for water sources, resupply, or bail-out points sync well and show up on the map page. Tip One practical tip: if you’re seeing GPS drift or inaccurate tracks, go to Settings > Sensors & Accessories > GPS and switch from auto-select to multi-band. Or just use GPS only if you want to save battery. Screen The Enduro 3 has a transflective MIP display. It’s always on, and never needs waking. The more ambient light, the better it reads. Direct sun is ideal. Forest shade or low light means you’re turning on the backlight, which you can set to trigger on wrist flick or button press. Side by side with the Fenix 8 AMOLED, the difference is obvious. 64 colors and 280x280 resolution versus 64,000 colors and 454x454. For trail decisions and nav data it’s fine. If you’re coming from an AMOLED screen, the adjustment takes a day or two and then you forget about it. If you want maps that pop and can live with charging every 5-10 days, get the Fenix 8. If you want a watch that disappears into your trip, get the Enduro 3. Comfort The Enduro 3 has a 51mm case but doesn’t feel big on trail unless you have a smaller wrist. The shape sits flat and balanced, and the UltraFit nylon band is a large part of why. Soft, fast-drying velcro closure that adjusts precisely. I’ve worn it for multiple weeks straight without irritation. Comparing it to the Fenix 8 on my wrist, the Enduro is noticeably more comfortable despite the close weight on paper. The band is the difference. If you end up with a Fenix, get the UltraFit nylon band separately. Reliability The Enduro 3 skips the smartwatch features on the Fenix 8: no mic, no speaker, no voice assistant, no dive support. Fewer settings, fewer things to break. On multi-day trips where you’re days from help, that simplicity pays off. My field use has been stable and predictable. Firmware updates have occasionally introduced minor bugs, but nothing that’s affected how the watch performs on trail. Other Features - The Enduro 3 has all of the top of the line health tracking features. These can be helpful to monitor your overall health and recovery, especially on a multi-day backpacking trip. Take it with a grain of salt. I’ve had my “body battery” down to 5 (lowest it will go while alive) and did a Grand Canyon Rim to Rim. Trust your body over the numbers. - The flashlight is useful. It doesn’t take the place of my headlamp but does work great when you have to get out of your tent to pee in the middle of the night.

item.title: iPhone vs Garmin inReach: Which to Trust
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 3.57
iPhone vs Garmin inReach Updated & Reviewed August 2026 iPhone satellite messaging has come a long way, but it doesn’t replace a dedicated inReach when it matters. The iPhone works in a handful of countries on phone battery while the inReach works worldwide on Iridium for days. I carry both: iPhone for easy messaging when I have coverage, inReach as the device I’d actually trigger an SOS on. For casual hiking in supported countries the iPhone alone is fine; for remote, international, or anything where reliability isn’t optional, get the inReach. Video Here’s a video where I test them both side by side so you can see the differences in real-world use. Comparison | Feature | iPhone | inReach | |---|---|---| | Durability | Not rugged | Rugged & waterproof | | Coverage | Limited to supported countries | Worldwide (Iridium) | | SOS | Standard 911 dispatch | Garmin Response coordination | | Battery | Hours | Days | | Use in Rain | Bad | Good | | Navigation | Needs separate app | Built-in on some models | | Weather | No | Yes | | Location Sharing | Manual via Find My | Automatic breadcrumb tracking | | Cost | Free (for now) | $10/month and up | | Messaging | Integrated with iMessage | Standalone via Garmin app | | Sending | Best pointed at satellite | No need to point | | Interface | Modern and easy | Simple but reliable | iPhone I’ve been using Apple’s satellite messaging since it launched and it’s worked well. You won’t always get an instant connection in canyons or dense forest, but the iPhone walks you through where to point and I’m usually connected within a minute or two. Only in the most extreme terrain has it completely failed, and that’s rare. One key difference from a dedicated device: Apple’s system requires you to manually activate satellite mode, and it won’t work in airplane mode. Since I usually hike in airplane mode to save battery, sending a message means flipping it off, waiting a few seconds, then connecting. Extra step, but manageable. When you do connect, messages go out fast and land in the standard Messages app, so recipients don’t need anything special. No new interface to learn. It just works. Tip Myth: you don’t actually have to point the phone at a satellite. It will still connect when lying on the ground, just slower and less reliably. inReach Garmin inReach devices are purpose-built satellite tools, not phones with SOS bolted on. The hardware is waterproof, dust-proof, shock-resistant, and rated for temperature extremes. The battery lasts days, not hours, which matters in a backcountry emergency. What the inReach adds beyond the iPhone: a dedicated SOS button that works even if your phone is dead, automatic breadcrumb location sharing, satellite weather forecasts, and navigation on some models. The feature I value most is the rugged hardware itself. Buttons with tactile feedback work in rain and cold without fail. No touchscreen to fight. If your life depends on it, the inReach just keeps working where a phone starts to struggle. Coverage Apple uses the Globalstar satellite network, which has solid technical coverage across much of the globe, but Apple only enables the service in specific countries due to regulatory restrictions. The regions where SOS works and where messaging works aren’t always the same. They’re expanding, but if you’re headed to remote parts of Alaska, the Andes, or the Himalayas, the service may not be available at all. Garmin inReach uses Iridium, which provides 100 percent global coverage including the poles. You don’t have to think about which country you’re in. If you can see the sky, it should work. Iridium is the same network used by militaries and professional maritime operators for the same reason: it’s reliable everywhere. Starlink Some iPhones now support Starlink’s Direct to Cell service, which lets your phone send standard SMS messages via Starlink when you’re out of cell range. No pointing required. In testing it worked some of the time, but coverage is spotty, message delivery is inconsistent, and replies can arrive out of order. Battery drain is higher than normal since the phone constantly searches for satellites, and like Apple’s system, it doesn’t work in airplane mode. It’s a decent secondary option that will likely improve, but not something to depend on in the backcountry today. SOS Apple’s SOS sends your emergency to a relay center that forwards it to 911 or local emergency services. In many cases that’s enough, but not all 911 centers have backcountry experience. Garmin inReach connects to Garmin Response: a dedicated 24/7 global rescue coordination center staffed specifically for remote and backcountry response. Apple has designed the SOS flow well. When you trigger an emergency, it walks you through a short questionnaire: injuries, number of people, terrain. That gets bundled with your GPS location and battery level before going to responders, which helps them prepare. Apple has been involved in several high-profile backcountry rescues including helicopter extractions from slot canyons. Garmin has a longer track record, with over 10,000 documented inReach rescues through its dedicated system as of Garmin’s last published milestone. One benefit of Apple’s approach: if you have any cell signal, even from another carrier, you can often dial 911 directly by voice, which is faster and more familiar than satellite texting. If your iPhone has Medical ID set up, that information is sent automatically during an SOS, giving responders your identity, conditions, and medications before they even contact you. Garmin inReach doesn’t offer this. Apple Watch If you’re an Apple Watch user, fall detection adds another layer. If something catastrophic happens and you fall, the watch can trigger an SOS on its own. Apple integrated this with the iPhone’s satellite capability: if your watch detects a fall and the paired iPhone is nearby, the phone will attempt to get help via satellite automatically. It’s a meaningful edge case that a standalone satellite communicator can’t replicate. Location With iPhone, you can share your location via satellite through the Find My app, but only when out of cellular range and only when you trigger it manually. No automatic tracking, and contacts need to check your location proactively rather than receiving updates. Garmin inReach offers automatic breadcrumb tracking that updates at set intervals, letting people at home follow your progress in real time. You can also attach your location to every text message you send. Depending on your Garmin plan, tracking may cost extra, but the functionality is far more capable than what the iPhone offers.

item.title: South Kaibab Trail Guide
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 3.54
South Kaibab Trail Updated & Reviewed August 2026 The South Kaibab Trail is a must‑do Grand Canyon hike with big views from start to finish. Follow the ridge to iconic spots like Ooh Aah Point, Cedar Ridge, and Skeleton Point, each offering a different perspective of the canyon. The NPS recommends Skeleton Point as the farthest turnaround for most day hikers, and there’s no water anywhere on the trail, so start early and come prepared. In this guide, I’ll show you exactly how to hike each section the easy way. - Distance - 1.8–6 mi - Difficulty - Moderate - Total Climbing - 600–2200 ft - Time - 1–5 hrs Info Kaibab is a word of Southern Paiute origin meaning “mountain lying down,” aka inverted mountain. Video I shot a video outlining what the trail looks like and what you can expect when you do this yourself. Dangers Overall the South Kaibab Trail is safe. I’ve seen people of all shapes, sizes, ages, and fitness levels do these hikes. The trail is well-maintained, easy to follow, consistently about 4 feet wide, and has wider sections for passing. But you still need to be mindful of a few things. - When people get into trouble on the South Kaibab Trail, it’s usually because of the heat. The trail is totally exposed with no shade, so in hot weather it can be brutal. Even in the shade, summer temperatures often exceed 100F (38C). Check the weather and park alerts regarding the heat. - The hike back up is much harder than going down. Many first-time Grand Canyon hikers overcommit on the easy downhill and pay for it on the climb out. A good rule of thumb: expect the hike up to take about twice as long as the hike down. - Snow and ice can linger on the upper sections in winter, especially in the morning. Be prepared for slippery, frozen sections near the rim, so bring microspikes. - Outside of the trailhead and Colorado River, there is no water anywhere on the South Kaibab Trail. You have to carry all the water you need, and in summer that can mean several liters per person. - The trail is generally wide enough to hike comfortably and pass other hikers. But people have also died after getting too close to the edge (taking pictures). Be conservative. - Mules also use the trail, so be ready to step aside in safe areas when they pass. Trailhead The road to the South Kaibab Trailhead (Yaki Point Road) is closed to vehicles. Here’s what I would recommend. - Take the free Orange shuttle bus from the Visitor Center. This is by far the easiest way to get back and forth to the trail. If you want to get an early start, take the Hiker’s Express Shuttle, which is set up for long distance hikers but can be used by anyone. Getting an early start is a smart way to beat the crowds and see the sunrise in the canyon. - You can also walk from the Visitor Center along the wide and easy Rim Trail. It’s about 2.2 miles and takes most folks around 40-60 minutes. - There’s a very small parking lot along Desert View Drive, not intended for hikers but rather as a turn-off for drivers. From here you can walk about 0.5 miles to the Rim Trail and then to the South Kaibab trailhead. Maps | Resource | What It’s For | |---|---| | CalTopo Map | Interactive map for planning and printing | | GPX Download | Put my route on your GPS | | AllTrails recent reports | What other hikers are seeing now | | Rim Weather | Trailhead forecast | | Inner Canyon Weather | How much hotter it gets below the rim | | Key Hiking Messages | Water status, heat risk, trail conditions | Directions Trailhead to Ooh Ahh Point Info The South Kaibab Trail was built by engineers in 1924-25 to create a smooth and direct route down to the river. It has been described as “a trail in a hurry to get to the river.” Info At the bottom of the canyon, the layers date back 1.84 BILLION years! To put that in perspective, the Earth is 4.543 billion years old. Info If this is your final destination, turn around and hike back from here. Ooh Ahh Point to Cedar Ridge Info While Cedar Ridge seems open and a great place to camp, no camping is allowed along the South Kaibab Trail. If this is your final destination, turn around and hike back from here. Cedar Ridge to Skeleton Point Info The South Kaibab Trail is part of the Arizona Trail (AZT), which stretches about 800 miles from Mexico to Utah.

item.title: Enduro 3 vs Fenix 8: Which Should You Buy?
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 3.48
Enduro 3 vs Fenix 8 Updated & Reviewed August 2026 Enduro 3 sticks to core outdoors features, Fenix 8 adds smartphone features on top. Same Garmin nav software underneath. I’ve hiked with both in desert sun and shaded rainforest, and the real differences are charging frequency and screen readability. The Enduro goes about three weeks between charges with a MIP screen that’s fine on trail; the Fenix 8 needs more frequent charging but its AMOLED makes maps and shading noticeably sharper. How I Earn I buy gear with my own money. It's the only way I can be 100% honest about what works. No sponsors, no free gear. Use the links below to buy, and you support these ad-free, independent reviews at no extra cost. Video Here’s me walking through both watches in real outdoor conditions: map visibility, solar charging, battery drain numbers, and how they feel on a long day. Which to Buy | Feature | Enduro 3 | Fenix 8 AMOLED | |---|---|---| | Charging Cadence | ~3 weeks | 5-10 days | | Display | MIP (always-on) | AMOLED | | Weight | 63g | 72g+ | | Mic / Speaker | No | Yes | | Dive Support | No | Yes | | Price | $900 | $1,199 | - Get the Enduro 3 if battery life and comfort are the priority. It focuses on core Garmin features (navigation, tracking, health) without trying to be a smartwatch. I charge mine around every 3 weeks with moderate hiking use. - Get the Fenix 8 if you want the AMOLED screen and smartwatch features like call handling and voice assistant. Battery life is still solid for a watch of its type, and the maps are noticeably sharper. - Also worth considering: get the UltraFit Nylon band from the Enduro and put it on a Fenix 8. I have this combo and it’s very comfortable. - The Forerunner 970 is worth a look if you want AMOLED and training features at a lower price point without needing multi-week battery. Battery The biggest difference between these two is battery. The Enduro 3’s MIP screen and efficient architecture give it a major advantage. I charge it around every 3 weeks with moderate hiking use. More time in direct sunlight means longer between charges. Solar doesn’t charge it to full. It offsets drain. Garmin measures solar input in lux hours, and you need around 50,000 lux hours to offset roughly 1% of battery. Pointing it straight at the sun is ideal; on your wrist in and out of shade you’ll get significantly less. Still, it adds up over a multi-day trip. The Fenix 8 AMOLED can’t touch that. AMOLED draws more power, especially with Always-On off. Expect to charge it every 5-10 days depending on how much you’re tracking. Info These numbers are from my real-world drain measurements with typical hiking settings: heart rate on, map use, pulse ox off, AOD off, occasional backlight. | Use Case | Enduro 3 | Fenix 8 51mm AMOLED | Fenix 8 47mm AMOLED | |---|---|---|---| | Smartwatch mode (per day) | 2-5% | 4-8% | 5-9% | | GPS only (per hour) | 0.7-1.0% | 1.0-1.2% | 1.3-1.6% | | All Systems + Multiband (per hour) | 1.5-1.7% | 1.6-1.9% | 2.0-2.4% | | Typical charging cadence | ~3 weeks | Every 5-10 days | Every 4-7 days | Screen The Fenix 8 AMOLED has 64,000 colors, 1000 nits of brightness, and 454x454 pixel resolution. Maps look sharp and detailed. Slopes show up with both contour lines and shading. I’ve seen complaints about it washing out in direct sun, but I didn’t find that to be an issue in my testing. I don’t make serious navigation decisions on a watch screen, but the extra detail does give me a better read of surrounding terrain at a glance. To maximize battery on the Fenix 8, I use gesture mode: screen stays off until you raise or flick your wrist. There’s a slight wake delay, longer than an Apple Watch, but you get used to it. The Enduro 3 uses a transflective MIP screen that’s always on. It relies on ambient light, so it looks great in bright sun. In shade or low light you’ll use the backlight. The screen is sharper than older Garmin MIP displays like the Fenix 7 or Enduro 2, but side by side with the Fenix 8 it looks washed out: 64 colors and 280x280 resolution. For reading numbers and navigating trails it’s fine. When I wore both at the same time, I always looked at the AMOLED first. Nicer experience, but not mission-critical outdoors. Comfort On paper the Enduro 3 is only a few grams lighter than the 51mm Fenix 8, but it feels significantly lighter on the wrist. Better balance, and the nylon UltraFit band is a big part of why. The velcro closure gives precise tension and dries fast. I liked it enough to buy one for my Fenix 8, and it made a real difference. The QuickFit silicone strap Garmin ships with the Fenix is fine, but it’s nothing special. If you end up with a Fenix, grab the UltraFit nylon band. Stability When the Fenix 8 launched, it had more bugs than the Enduro 3. The Enduro wasn’t perfect, but it was noticeably more stable out of the box. After several firmware updates both are generally reliable. Garmin still has a habit of introducing quirks with updates, and the Fenix’s added complexity makes it more exposed to those. The Enduro feels simpler and a bit more immune. Extras - Both watches have the LED flashlight. Surprisingly useful in camp; drains battery if you leave it running. - Both run the same Garmin UI, mapping, tracking, and health features. Core navigation is identical. The Fenix 8 adds a mic and speaker for calls and voice assistant when your phone is nearby, plus dive support. - I’ve used the voice assistant on the Fenix to engage Siri when my phone is buried in my pack. It works, but it’s nowhere near as integrated as a Pixel or Apple Watch. Dive support only matters if you need it. For hiking and backpacking, neither extra changes the decision.

item.title: Garmin Fenix 8 Pro Review: LTE + inReach Tested
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 3.44
Garmin Fenix 8 Pro Review Updated & Reviewed August 2026 The most capable Fenix. Best in LTE areas, but it isn’t a handheld inReach replacement. It’s built for trail runners and those who want LTE messaging and basic satellite coverage without carrying a second device. But in side-by-side testing I saw the Fenix 8 Pro’s LTE drop in clear-coverage areas where an Apple Watch on the same network connected immediately. If you need backcountry-grade coverage, pair a regular Fenix 8 with a Mini 3 Plus for more reliable results. How I Earn I buy gear with my own money. It's the only way I can be 100% honest about what works. No sponsors, no free gear. Use the links below to buy, and you support these ad-free, independent reviews at no extra cost. Warning Lately Garmin hasn’t been great about providing stable firmware. Check the Garmin Fenix 8 support forum to see what the latest state of the software is. Video Here you can see me actually using the Fenix 8 Pro on the trail to get an idea of what it’s like to connect. And here is a demonstration of the satellite connectivity between the Fenix 8 Pro and the Apple Watch Ultra 3. Fenix 8 vs Fenix 8 Pro The Fenix 8 Pro and the regular Fenix 8 are essentially the same watch (I’m using the 51mm version). Same processor (reportedly the same as the Fenix 7X per a teardown I found), same UI, same navigation performance. The main differences are the LTE-M modem and the Skylo satellite radio. | Pro 51mm | 51mm | |---|---| | AMOLED or MicroLED | AMOLED only | | ~2,000 nits (AMOLED); ~4,500 nits (MicroLED) | ~1,000 nits | | 16.5 mm thick, ~90–93 g | 14.7 mm thick, ~64–92 g | | LTE + satellite messaging | None | | 53h multiband | 62h multiband | | $1299 | $1199 | Plans You need a Garmin inReach plan to connect with the Fenix 8 Pro without a phone. Garmin updated their plans to include LTE alongside satellite. LTE usage is unlimited on all plans; the differences between tiers come down to satellite message counts. Key things to know: - Unlike standard inReach, coverage is not worldwide: both LTE and satellite are limited to certain regions, unlike traditional inReach with global Iridium coverage - LTE is unlimited on all plans - LTE roaming is supported if you subscribed in a different country - No separate carrier plan needed - 30-day free trial is available (note: cancels your existing inReach plan if you have one) - Without a plan, the watch works as a remote for your phone’s Messenger app over Bluetooth - Garmin now allows multiple active inReach devices per account Connectivity The watch connects three ways: - Through your phone: Bluetooth to phone with data connection, standard operation - Through LTE-M: low-power cellular for wearables, routes texts and voice calls over an IP address (no dedicated phone number) - Through satellite: manual trigger required, uses GEO satellites via Skylo LTE LTE performance in my testing was inconsistent. Messages and calls went through immediately sometimes. In developed areas with clear signal, it would still fail to connect. I ran side-by-side checks with an Apple Watch (T-Mobile) and every time the Fenix 8 Pro failed, the Apple Watch connected immediately. That’s not a coverage issue, it’s the radio or software. Two LTE modes worth understanding: - Always-On LTE: Checks continuously for messages like a standard cellular watch. Battery impact is severe. - Auto LTE (default): Only checks when you trigger it manually or use an LTE feature. Messages won’t arrive until you actively initiate a check. The practical problem with Auto-LTE: if someone messages you an emergency at 9am while you’re hiking in LTE range, you won’t see it until you manually run a message check. That’s a significant difference from a standard cellular watch experience. Always-On LTE fixes that behavior but brings the battery down to near Apple Watch Ultra levels. Satellite The satellite system is not Iridium. Garmin partnered with Skylo, which connects to geostationary (GEO) satellites from ViaSat and Inmarsat. These sit 22,000 miles above the equator, fixed in position. Traditional inReach uses Iridium low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites at ~485 miles altitude, moving across the globe, covering 100% of it. What that means practically: - No 100% global coverage - Coverage is solid in mid-latitudes, fades toward the poles - If you can’t connect where you’re standing, you can’t wait for a satellite to pass overhead, since they don’t move Satellite messages did go through in my testing, but not reliably enough that I’d trust it for SOS. Even under clear skies at 33 degrees north, well within coverage, I’d get full alignment and then sit at “searching” for several minutes, or get “poor signal” without an obvious reason. inReach Features What’s available varies by connection type: - Messages: Location-tagged messages, image receive, SMS to non-Garmin users, predictive text. Voice notes are the standout: recipient gets audio plus a transcription. Only available on LTE. - Calls: Watch-to-watch only via the Messenger app, not to any number. Mic and speaker quality were good; occasionally the audio was one-sided. - Location Sharing: LiveTrack auto-tracking worked well over LTE. Satellite has no auto-tracking, so every location share is manual. - Weather: Excellent over LTE (12-hour, 4-day, radar, air quality). Satellite requires requesting through the phone’s Messenger app. - SOS: Works on LTE with an active inReach plan. Incident detection only notifies contacts, and Garmin Response is not alerted unless you manually trigger SOS. Battery Real-world numbers from my testing: - GPS activity without LTE: ~1.9% per hour (matches Garmin’s 53-hour spec) - GPS activity with LTE LiveTrack: ~4.7% per hour (matches Garmin’s 21-hour spec) - Smartwatch with Auto-LTE, one workout per day, AOD off: 10-15% daily drain - Smartwatch with Always-On LTE, one workout per day, AOD off: 35-40% daily drain Always-On LTE puts battery life roughly on par with an Apple Watch Ultra 3. If you’re paying $1,299 for a watch primarily for the LTE connectivity and then running Always-On mode, the battery situation is worth thinking through carefully. Worth It? Get the Fenix 8 Pro if you want the most capable Garmin watch and plan to use LTE regularly in areas with coverage. It makes sense if: - You don’t want to carry a separate inReach like the Mini 3 - You understand the connectivity limitations - You’re already in the Garmin ecosystem - A check of the support forums shows no recent red flags Skip it if you need dependable backcountry coverage. Handheld inReach units have Iridium global coverage and connect more reliably. Pairing an Enduro 3 or Fenix 8 with an inReach Mini is still lightweight and a more reliable setup.

item.title: Garmin inReach Mini 2 Review: Still Worth It
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 3.40
Garmin inReach Mini 2 Review Updated & Reviewed August 2026 I carried this for three years before switching to the Mini 3 Plus. One of the most reliable inReach units Garmin has made and still a bargain. I’ve tested every major device in this category. The Mini 2 holds up: Iridium coverage, solid battery, physical buttons, no phone required. At full retail the Mini 3 Plus is the better buy now. It adds a touchscreen, voice notes, and photo messaging for $190 more, though battery life between the two is close enough that it’s not the reason to upgrade. But if you find a Mini 2 on sale as retailers clear inventory, it’s still a serious device that will do the job anywhere on earth. Get the GPSMAP 67i if you need onboard maps. How I Earn I buy gear with my own money. It's the only way I can be 100% honest about what works. No sponsors, no free gear. Use the links below to buy, and you support these ad-free, independent reviews at no extra cost. Video Features Here’s what the Mini 2 does well: - The SOS feature is the main reason I carry it. Hit the button and Garmin Response, a 24/7 backcountry emergency coordination center, coordinates with local search and rescue wherever you are in the world. - It works anywhere on earth. The Iridium satellite network covers 100% of the globe, including Antarctica, and is trusted by aviation, maritime, and military users. - Battery lasts days, not hours. Even with regular messaging, I’m not thinking about charging it mid-trip. - Two-way text messaging. “I’m running late, don’t worry” is the message I send most. It prevents false-alarm search and rescue calls and gives people at home peace of mind. - Real-time location sharing. Friends and family can follow along from home and message me directly from the MapShare page. - Weather forecasts via satellite. - Basic backup navigation: TracBack, waypoints, and off-route alerts when following a course loaded from Garmin Explore. - 100 grams. Clipped to my shoulder strap, I barely notice it. - Physical buttons work in gloves, rain, and exhaustion. More reliable than a touchscreen when conditions are bad. - USB-C charging. - Controllable from a Garmin watch for quick message checks without unclipping from the pack. Pair it with the free Garmin Messenger app for easier typing, conversation threads, settings control, and automatic switching between Wi-Fi, cellular, and satellite. Plans As of late 2024, Garmin offers three monthly plans, all month-to-month with no long-term contract. There’s a $39.99 activation fee for new or restarted service. | Plan | SOS? | Check-ins | Messages/Weather | Tracking | |---|---|---|---|---| | Essential | Yes | Unlimited | 50 | Extra cost | | Standard | Yes | Unlimited | 150 | Unlimited | | Premium | Yes | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited | Other options Garmin doesn’t advertise: - The Enabled plan is the cheapest option. Small monthly fee for SOS access, pay per use for everything else. You can switch to it when you start to cancel a regular subscription. - Protegear is a Garmin-approved reseller with flexible plans including pay-per-day options. Works globally. - TrackMeNZ offers alternative plans for users in New Zealand and Australia. - Garmin also offers professional plans for organizations or families with multiple devices. Activate at home before your trip using the Garmin Messenger app on your phone. You can’t activate over satellite. It needs Wi-Fi or cellular to complete setup. Messaging You can send messages to an email address, a phone number via SMS, or directly to another inReach device. Three message types: - Check-in messages: Three fixed Garmin templates (“I’m okay,” “Starting trip,” “Ending trip”). Free, don’t count against your monthly limit. - Custom messages: Type via QuickText, predictive text, or character entry on the device, or use the Garmin Messenger app for a much faster experience. - Group messages: App only. Send to up to five recipients at once and replies land in the same thread. Reliability Messages go via Iridium’s Short Burst Data system. Reliable, but not fast: - Under clear skies, most messages go through in 1-3 minutes. - In tree cover, canyons, or bad weather, expect longer. - Occasionally a message will fail and need a resend, though this is rare. The Mini 2 won’t transmit until it has a position fix. The multi-GNSS chipset (GPS, Galileo, QZSS, BeiDou) locks faster than the old GPS-only Mini, reducing pre-send delays even if transmission speed itself hasn’t changed. Tip: If a message isn’t going through, manually create a waypoint first, then retry. This often kicks a stubborn connection loose. SOS Holding the SOS button sends your GPS location and a distress signal to Garmin Response, a 24/7 emergency coordination center. A dispatcher starts messaging you directly through the device or app shortly after confirmation. Garmin coordinates with local rescue agencies based on your location: county SAR in California, maritime authority in international waters, and so on. Your emergency contacts get notified throughout. Covered scenarios per Garmin: - Injuries or medical conditions - Vehicle accidents or breakdowns - Stranded or lost - Weather events including wildfires and floods The Mini 2 also lets you trigger SOS for someone else. If you come across an injured hiker, you can call for help on their behalf without any financial responsibility. That Good Samaritan capability alone makes the subscription worth it for me. Tip: Don’t save this for backcountry trips. Keep it in your everyday bag. A breakdown or crash out of cell range is when you’ll be glad you have it. Rescue Costs In most cases, search and rescue is free. Many SAR teams are volunteer-run local agencies. But not always: vehicle rescues may include towing fees, and private helicopter transport or third-party emergency services can come with bills. - Garmin offers optional rescue insurance for U.S. and Canada users. Affordable, with tiered coverage limits. High-risk activities like mountaineering cost more. - I use Overwatch & Rescue for more comprehensive coverage. Unlike insurance, they pay the bill directly instead of reimbursing. Staffed by former military, law enforcement, and EMTs, with broader protections including evacuation during civil unrest. They’ve given my audience 15% off the first year with code HIKEGUY15. Traveling internationally? Check local laws before bringing your inReach. China, India, and Russia restrict or ban satellite communicators. Confirm with the destination embassy before you go. Tracking Tracking sends your position via satellite at a set interval: every 10 minutes to every 4 hours depending on your plan. Each point builds a breadcrumb trail on your MapShare page. You can share the page with anyone or password-protect it. Contacts can message you directly from the page without needing the app. Tip: If you’re worried about a medical event where you couldn’t press SOS, leave tracking on. It gives your last known position to anyone watching if you don’t come home. Navigation No maps on the device. Best used as a backup, not a primary navigator: - Drop waypoints for trailheads, campsites, water sources, and points of interest. - TracBack uses your recorded breadcrumb trail to guide you back to the start. - Load a course from Garmin Explore and the device will alert you when you go off-route. - The Garmin Explore app shows your position on a map via your phone’s GPS. Offline maps are free from Garmin. Nothing displays on the Mini 2 itself. Battery Garmin claims up to 14 days with 10-minute tracking, up to 30 days in power-saving mode with 30-minute intervals. Real-world results: - Around 200 hours with 10-minute tracking, occasional messaging, and open to mixed canopy. - As low as 30 hours in the same settings under thick forest or poor satellite conditions. To extend battery life: - Set a longer tracking interval (tradeoff: lower location resolution). - Turn off Bluetooth when you’re not using the Messenger app. - Disable high-detail activity recording in settings. - Use GPS-only mode (slower sends). Don’t turn the device off on trail. Even if you can’t press SOS, the Mini 2 automatically checks for messages every hour, passively sharing your location with Garmin. It’s a low-tech failsafe if something goes wrong. Earlier Video Setup - Download the Garmin Messenger app, tap Add a New Device, and follow the prompts to register your Mini 2. - Start this a few days before your first trip. Leave the device on so any firmware updates can download and install. You may need to confirm the install manually, so check the app. - If you’re getting Garmin SAR insurance or Overwatch & Rescue coverage, set it up before you need it. Neither applies retroactively to an incident already in progress.

item.title: Hiking Expert for Media: Cris Hazzard
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 3.39
Hiking Expert Media Contributor Updated & Reviewed August 2026 Cris Hazzard is the founder of HikingGuy.com, an independent hiking and outdoor technology resource focused on hiking safety, trail planning, navigation, and gear. With 26+ years of experience, a University of Wyoming guide certification, NOLS Wilderness Medicine training, and 20M+ YouTube views, Cris provides practical, consumer-first guidance and has been cited by outlets including CNN, FOX, ABC News, The Washington Post, and The Guardian.
