item.title: Eyeing a New iPhone 18 Pro? Do This to Get the Most Money for Your Old Phone
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.11
The iPhone 18 Pro is expected to hit this fall, and it's rumored to start at a steep $1,299, a whopping $200 more than the 17 Pro's debut price. If that price tag is a little hard to stomach, there is some good news. Apple also recently increased its trade-in values for the second time this year, making it a little easier to afford one of its new rumored iPhones. If you're preparing to trade in your old device to shave some cost off the upfront price, here's everything you need to know about Apple's boosted trade-in values and how to make sure your phone is prepped and ready to ship, so you can get the highest value in exchange. What's the Trade-in Value for an Older iPhone? Apple increased its trade-in values twice this summer, helping you get a little more money for your old device. If you have an iPhone 16, you can now get a maximum of $480 in trade-in value, an extra $20 since the last increase. Meanwhile, the iPhone 16 Pro could net you up to $630, up from $560. Similar increases have been added to the company's line of computers, tablets, and smartwatches. Here's the max value you can get for each type of iPhone: - iPhone 16 Pro Max: $720 (previously $695) - iPhone 16 Pro: $630 (previously $560) - iPhone 16 Plus: $485 (previously $465) - iPhone 16: $480 (previously $460) - iPhone 16e: $310 (no change) - iPhone 15 Pro Max: $530 (previously $490) - iPhone 15 Pro: $420 (previously $410) - iPhone 15 Plus: $340 (previously $325) - iPhone 15: $335 (previously $320) - iPhone 14 Pro Max: $405 (previously $375) - iPhone 14 Pro: $335 (previously $320) - iPhone 14 Plus: $235 (unchanged) - iPhone 14: $235 (previously $225) What to Do Before Trading in Your Old iPhone Now that you know the maximum trade-in value of your old phone, you'll want to take some steps to make sure it's backed up, unpaired, and cleaned up. Here are the steps you should take before you send in your old device. 1. Back Up Everything First, make sure you don't lose your data. Back everything up before you wipe it from your phone. To back up to iCloud from your device, go to Settings, select your name, and then choose iCloud > iCloud Backup > Back Up Now. To back up to your Mac, connect your iPhone and your computer via a cable or Wi-Fi. If you have macOS Catalina or later, go to Finder, select your iPhone, and then choose General > Back Up All of the Data on Your iPhone to This Mac > Back Up Now. If you have an earlier version or a Windows PC, you'd use iTunes. Open the program, click on the image of your phone, then select Summary > Back Up Now. 2. Unfind Your iPhone Apple’s Find My app can sometimes block activation by a new owner, so you should deactivate the app before you ditch the device. Though Find My is automatically deactivated when you erase all content and settings, which you'll do below, this is still a good step to take as a precaution. Go to Settings, select your name, then choose Find My and disable it for that device. Enter your Apple Account password and tap Turn Off. 3. Sign Out of Messages More than a decade ago, people who switched from iOS to Android without logging out of Messages on their iPhone found that texts were going to the old phone. The problem has since been fixed, but those still scarred by "iMessage purgatory" may want to go to Settings > Apps > Messages and disable iMessage. 4. Unpair Your AirPods Similarly, you can still connect your AirPods to a new iPhone without unpairing them from the old one, but it can't hurt to wipe the slate clean. Place your AirPods and iPhone near each other, then go to Settings > Bluetooth. Tap the information icon next to your AirPods, and select Forget this Device. 5. Unpair Your Apple Watch If you have an Apple Watch, save yourself a potential headache and unpair it from the iPhone you'll be selling. Place them near each other, then open the Apple Watch app on your phone. Go to My Watch > All Watches and select the info circle next to the watch you want to unpair. Tap Unpair Apple Watch and then confirm, which may require you to enter your Apple Account password. With a GPS + Cellular model, you're asked whether you want to keep or remove your cellular plan. Since you're selling the iPhone, you'll want to remove it. (If you don't plan to pair your watch with a new iPhone, you might need to contact your carrier to cancel.) Tap to confirm; you might need to enter your Apple Account password to disable Activation Lock. 6. Sign Out of iCloud You should sign out of iCloud, iTunes, and the App Store before selling your device. Tap Settings, select your name, and choose Sign Out. Enter your Apple Account password and tap Turn Off. 7. Wipe Your iPhone and Delete Data When your new phone is set up and you're ready to trade in or sell your old iPhone, head to Settings > General > Transfer or Reset iPhone > Erase All Content and Settings, then approve all subsequent prompts. 8. Remove the SIM Card (If You Have One) Apple went the eSIM route starting with the iPhone 14 lineup, but older devices will have a physical SIM card. In most cases, you can just deactivate your cellphone service on the device and trade it in with the SIM card intact. But that SIM card is the repository of your phone number, various bits of security data, and all the info needed for billing. It identifies you, your phone, and a lot of your activity on your phone. So you should remove it before you sell the phone. Fortunately, it's simple. Locate the SIM ejector on your phone, then insert a paper clip until the tray pops out. Remove the SIM card, replace the tray, and say goodbye to your old iPhone. The Best Places to Sell Your Phone I've also included some of the best sites for selling or trading in your phone. Some make it easy to send in your phone and get immediate cash, others let you control the price through bidding, and there are even options for receiving store credit from places you shop. To give you an idea of your trade-in power, I priced out what you can expect to get for an iPhone 15 Pro across all of them, and it varies wildly, as you'll see below. You can also trade your phone in with your existing carrier or switch to a new one. Many offer compelling trade-in promotions, so be sure to check out AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon, and others. Apple Trade In The Apple Trade In program pays you with a credit or gift card. If you pay for an Apple device in full up-front, a credit will be applied to your payment card once Apple receives your trade-in device and verifies its condition. If you're paying on an installment plan, the credit will be applied right away. Turning in an iPhone 15 Pro, for example, can get you up to $410 on a new iPhone now that Apple has increased some trade-in values by as much as $35. Best Buy If you're selling your iPhone and just want cash to buy electronics, you can cut out a step at Best Buy: Trade in your phone at a store or mail it in for a digital gift card. For a Black Titanium 512GB iPhone 15 Pro on Verizon in good condition, expect to get about $275. eBay To sell your device yourself, there's always eBay. The site has a quick walkthrough where you can input your phone's stats. After entering my example device, a Black Titanium 512GB iPhone 15 Pro in good condition on Verizon, the page recommended that I list the phone at $510. GameStop Are most of your iPhone apps games? Then you'll probably do well to turn in your iPhone in for some store credit at GameStop. You can also get cold, hard cash for it there. Bring your device to your nearest GameStop, get a price quote from a sales associate, and then receive store credit or cash on the spot. I recommend getting an estimate on the site before you make the trip. I found that a 512GB iPhone 15 Pro from Verizon in very good condition will get you $267.30 in cash or $297.00 in store credit. Swappa Swappa is a marketplace where you can sell your iPhone directly. Select your phone model on the site, upload some photos, and set a price. Once someone buys it, you're paid immediately via PayPal. You're responsible for safely shipping your phone to the buyer. According to the site, an iPhone 15 Pro is selling for an average price of $544, while a trade-in to one of Swappa's partners could get me $311. uSell Want to sell your iPhone fast? One option is uSell. Select your model, carrier, capacity, and condition to receive an offer. If you choose to accept it, you ship your iPhone to uSell for free. If your device is in the condition you said it was, you're paid by check or PayPal. A 512GB iPhone 15 Pro on Verizon in good condition is currently worth about $268. Editors' Note: Trade-in values were accurate at the time of publication. Your mileage may vary. Chandra Steele contributed to this story About Our Expert As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: Uber Lays Off 3,300 Employees, Cuts Down on Middle Managers
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.06
Uber is laying off 10% of its global workforce, or 3,300 people, to reduce managerial layers. Impacted employees were notified of the change via email, while Uber published CEO Dara Khosrowshahi’s message to employees in a blog post. “The changes we’re making today are designed to do two things: make Uber simpler and faster, and create more capacity to invest in our future,” Khosrowshahi says. “It will also generate savings that we intend to reinvest in growth, innovation, and the capabilities that will matter most over the coming years.” As part of the restructuring, Uber will reduce by 20% the number of employees who sit seven or more levels below the CEO and by 50% the number of micro teams that work with just one or two members. "I’m sure many of you have felt that you spend too much time 'aligning' rather than building, shipping, or serving customers," Khosrowshahi writes. Uber will also be realigning its delivery teams across its restaurant, retail, and direct services into single-threaded teams at the global, regional, and country levels. “Running these three businesses separately made sense in their early days, but that structure is no longer serving us at scale,” Khosrowshahi notes. Finally, the company will rearrange where employees work from and reduce the number of key work locations. Global teams will work from New York and San Francisco; tech teams will work from designated tech hubs; and regional and local teams will work from their respective hubs. Once realigned, only 1% of the company’s total workforce will work remotely. As Bloomberg reports, Uber’s restructuring comes after it committed $10 billion to its robotaxi business. The company plans to launch robotaxis in 28 cities by 2028, and over the past year, it has invested in several companies focused on autonomous driving, including Avride, Lucid, Nuro, and Rivian. Before the latest organizational cuts, Uber reportedly replaced 10% of its customer service staff with AI in July. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. item.title: Tesla's No-Steering-Wheel Cybercab Hits Austin Streets
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.94
Tesla on Thursday announced it is adding Cybercabs to its robotaxi fleet in Austin, Texas. First teased back in 2024, Tesla’s Cybercab is a fully autonomous electric vehicle that requires no driver intervention. In the absence of a steering wheel and pedals, the AV uses “camera vision and sensors to intelligently and safely navigate city streets, highways, complicated intersections, and parking lots,” Tesla says on a support page. It appears select customers in Austin can now choose between a Cybercab and Model Y when booking a ride via the Robotaxi app. Availability, however, may be limited as only 45 of Tesla’s 314 robotaxis operational in Texas are Cybercabs, The New York Times reports. Tesla says Cybercabs can be used for errands, commutes, and other purposes. Once the car arrives, its butterfly doors will automatically open as you approach it. You’ll also find options to enter the car, start a ride, or open its trunk, spacious enough for luggage, wheelchairs, golf clubs, and scooters, on the Robotaxi mobile app. Inside the car, you’ll find two bench-style seats at wheelchair height for easy entry and exit. At the center, you’ll see a giant 22-inch touch screen with access to entertainment and connectivity features, including music and gaming apps. From the mobile app, you can also adjust climate and media settings, and save them to your profile for future trips. Soon, these cars will also be equipped with V5 Starlink hardware for satellite connectivity. Initially, Tesla expected to sell the Cybercab to private owners and rideshare companies for about $30,000, but the sale of a car without pedals and a steering wheel has yet to receive regulatory clearance. You can still fill out an interest form on Tesla’s website, though. For now, Cybercab remains limited to Tesla’s robotaxi service in Austin. The company also offers robotaxi rides in Model Y vehicles in Dallas, Houston, and Miami. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Hacker Allegedly Stole 153 Million Driver's Licenses, Is Now Selling Them
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.93
In a disturbing find, a hacker has been spotted trying to sell access to over 153 million driver’s licenses from the US and Canada, including the IDs for US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and an FBI assistant director. The hacker created a site called Nexus to offer the IDs, according to cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs, who learned about the sales after the hacker offered Krebs' Virginia driver’s license as a free sample. The hacker also offered Hegseth's driver's license for $100. “A quick look around Nexus finds they are likely not exaggerating about that 153 million number: Running a blank search in Nexus (with no search parameters entered) returns approximately 11.5 million pages of results, with roughly 15 results displayed per page,” Krebs wrote. The hacker is advertising Nexus in the Russian-language hacking forum Exploit, writing, “We have been continuously exfiltrating new data for over a year into our private database.” The big question is how the IDs were stolen. Krebs suspects the hacker breached New Orleans-based identity provider IDScan.net, which counts FedEx, rental car company Hertz, video game retailer GameStop, and casino operator Caesars Entertainment among its clients. A cybersecurity researcher named Zach Edwards also found his driver’s license on Nexus and noted that his ID was recently scanned while visiting a marijuana dispensary in Las Vegas operated by Planet 13, which has a partnership with IDScan. If real, then the illegal sales could be one of the worst breaches in recent history, exposing millions of Americans to identity theft-related schemes. IDScan and the FBI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. But Krebs says both are already investigating. He adds that the mysterious Nexus website has since vanished from the dark web following his report, although it could always reappear through a new domain. item.title: Major AI Outage: Grok Trouble Blamed on Outage at Memphis Data Center
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.83
UPDATE 4 p.m. ET: SpaceXAI apologized to users and compute partners for the Grok outage, blaming "an outage at our Memphis compute center this morning." It says, "all systems have now been restored and are functioning nominally." Queries on Grok are now going through for us. UPDATE 3:15 p.m. ET: Claude appears to be back now. "All systems operational," the status page says. On Grok, however, we are still getting "Grok was unable to reply" errors. UPDATE 1:25 p.m. ET: OpenAI's status page now says it's fully operational. "We’re not aware of any issues affecting our systems." Reports on Downdetector have also dropped, and the chatbot is responding to queries. Gemini also appears to be up and running. Grok, however, is currently displaying a warning that says it's "experiencing issues," and warns that "Some features may be slow or unavailable." It's telling people to check status.x.ai for updates, but the page doesn't currently show any service disruptions. On Claude, we're getting "This response didn't load" to any queries. Original Story: If you’re trying to use AI tools today, you are likely experiencing problems. A widespread outage affecting thousands of users is ongoing across OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini, X's Grok, and other AI platforms. As shown on Downdetector, outages affecting OpenAI services began around 10:30 a.m. ET, ramping up quickly over the past hour. The outage appears to be widespread, with the peak number of reports exceeding 36,000. The OpenAI status page says it has applied a fix and is “monitoring the recovery” after 24 minutes of downtime across ChatGPT and Codex. One PCMag reporter who was experiencing issues says their service returned soon after the fix, but is now working slowly. OpenAI has yet to say what caused the outage. Google Gemini saw a similar spike in reports around the same time, but Google has yet to acknowledge an outage. Another PCMag reporter found that any prompts entered into Gemini returned an error, although reports on Downdetector are significantly smaller, suggesting it isn't impacting all users. Issues with Anthropic's Claude began earlier in the day with a small spike in reports at 8:30 a.m. ET before surging an hour later with more consistent issues. The first problem directly affected Claude Sonnet 5, while a second wave hit many more models, including Mythos/Fable 5.1 and Opus 5. Anthropic says it has issued a fix for its issues, which is now rolling out to users. It says the currently affected models are restricted to Opus 5 and Opus 4.8, with recoveries happening across Fable models and Opus 4.6. X’s AI platform, Grok, also appears to be down, alongside the smaller AI agent service Cursor, with both seeing spikes on Downdetector. Meanwhile, despite reports on Downdetector, Cloudflare says it is not experiencing downtime. “Cloudflare is not experiencing any significant service disruptions at this time. Our services are operating normally, and any reporting that deviates from this is incorrect.” This is a remarkable outage to hit all of these services at once, especially since it doesn't seem to be affecting other businesses outside the AI space. We'll update this article with more information as we hear it. Disclosure: Ziff Davis, PCMag's parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in April 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems. item.title: Apple Tests iOS 27 Handoff Feature That Supports Same Number on 2 iPhones
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.83
Apple is reportedly testing an iOS 27 iPhone Handoff feature that allows you to switch between two iPhones without changing your eSIM number. The feature was briefly mentioned on a slide during the WWDC 2026 keynote, and an iPhone user recently spotted it on their device, MacRumors reports. On the site’s forum, the same user also shared a video demonstrating how iPhone Handoff works. When available, users can enable iPhone Handoff in Settings > Cellular. While setting it up, you’ll be asked to keep the iPhones close and choose which one retains the main eSIM and which one gets the companion eSIM. Only the main iPhone will be able to modify Cellular Settings from then on. The feature allows you to share your eSIM with another iPhone and switch between them as needed. Each time you unlock an iPhone, a notification will indicate that cellular service has been transferred to the currently active device. A support article for developers also describes an “iPhone quick switch” feature that enables transfer of active services, “such as login credentials and persistent state from a formerly active iPhone to a newly active iPhone.” As with Apple’s original Handoff feature, this should allow you to pick up from where you left off on another device. Of course, Apple doesn’t control all aspects of the iPhone Handoff feature. You’ll be able to use the feature only if your carrier supports it. According to MacRumors, T-Mobile in the US and Deutsche Telekom in Germany might support the feature at launch. We should have more details about it soon. While iOS 27 is still being tested with public and developer betas, the stable version is expected to launch with the new iPhone 18 Pro and the foldable iPhone sometime next week. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Don't Want to Pay for Whoop? Screenless Luna Band Costs $149, No Subscription
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.67
Screenless fitness trackers are the new battleground in wearable tech, with recent releases like Garmin’s Cirqa Smart Band and Google’s Fitbit Air arriving to compete with the market leader, Whoop. Now, there's an alternative, and it's cheaper than most of those rivals. The Luna Band comes from smart ring maker Luna. The screenless fitness tracker minimizes distractions while giving you a full picture of your health, tracking activity, sleep, skin temperature, SpO2 (blood oxygen), women's health, Vo2 Max, heart rate variability, and more. The device has a rectangular design and no display, and is attached to your wrist with a nylon strap with a metal frame. Your color options are Aloe Green, Desert Beige, or Onyx Black. Some other sources report the availability of a blue version, but it’s yet to appear on Luna’s website. The device is also water-resistant up to 5 ATM (about 164 feet deep). As it's not powering a screen, Luna’s tracker can offer up to 10 days of battery life from a single charge, which it says takes around 60 minutes. That works through a proprietary charger, which is included in the box. Unlike the Whoop 5.0, the Luna Band doesn’t require a monthly subscription to access features. It’s a flat fee of $149 to buy the tracker, though some of its software doesn't appear to be as advanced as its rivals'. The Luna Band was first unveiled at CES 2026, then entered a limited preorder period, which meant some customers got their hands on the fitness tracker in late July. Now, Luna is ready for a full launch, including immediate availability across the US. You can buy the Luna Band from its official website, with shipping beginning today, Sept. 4. The Aloe Green version will ship on Sept. 7, Luna says. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Microsoft Is Forcing Memory Integrity Changes That Could Harm Your FPS
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.59
In its October patch release, Microsoft is set to enable Memory Integrity in Windows 11 by default, Windows Latest reports. That might harm your gaming frames per second, but the security boost is almost certainly worth the trade-off. Memory Integrity is a core isolation feature that uses a virtualized environment to verify kernel-mode drivers before they execute, ensuring they're safe. It prevents malware from exploiting an older, vulnerable driver to reach the system kernel, where it can do whatever it wants. In the early days of Windows 11, turning this off or never enabling it was one method to boost gaming FPS, as software calls on older hardware for this feature could cause performance dips. But from Intel's 7th generation and AMD's Ryzen 2000 generation onwards, hardware-level acceleration means there's almost no performance difference with this feature enabled. That's especially relevant for this new patch, because it's going to turn Memory Integrity on for a range of platforms, but only those that meet the minimum system requirements. And those are all modern enough to have the hardware acceleration to avoid FPS drops. Memory Integrity requirements include: - Intel 8th-generation processor or newer - AMD Zen 2 processor or newer - Qualcomm Snapdragon 8180 SoC or newer - At least 8GB of RAM on x64 systems - At least 64GB of SSD storage space - A BIOS with virtualization enabled. That pretty much describes any PC purchased in the past five or six years, and even some that are older than that. So if you aren't already running Windows 11 with memory integrity enabled, you can certainly do so, and the patch update will likely enable it if it isn't already. The only instance in which this won't happen is if you have already explicitly disabled Memory Integrity via the registry or a Windows Group Policy change. If you use older drivers for legacy devices, you may still want to do that since there's a chance Memory Integrity can break older drivers that need to interact with memory in insecure ways. Just be aware of the security trade-off you're making before doing so. How to Check if Memory Integrity Is Enabled There's a good chance you already have memory integrity enabled, in which case you won't notice this rollout. To confirm your status, navigate to Windows Security > Device Security > Core Isolation details. There, you'll see a heading titled "Memory integrity." If it's set to On, it's enabled. If it's off, you can either turn it on manually now or wait for the patch. If you really don't want it enabled, you can always return here and disable it after the update. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: CSI: Living Room? Dyson's New $1,200 Robot Vacuum Uses UV Light to Hunt Down Invisible Stains
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.45
BERLIN–Maybe I've been watching too many murder shows lately, but Dyson's latest robot vacuum reminds me of a detective. Unveiled at IFA, the Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV uses an ultraviolet LED to find invisible stains on your floor, like something out of "CSI: Crime Scene Investigation." "Specifically, [it can detect] real nasties, things like pet urine, spilled milk, alcohol, beer," Dyson engineer Guy Turner told me. "As they dry on the floor, they become transparent; they're really hard to see." The UV light causes those invisible dried stains to fluoresce, or glow. The Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai, introduced last year, uses a green laser to detect invisible dust, but the R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV is the company's first model to use UV light as well. After locating such gunk, the robot uses a roller mop on the bottom to wash it away. While rare, this feature isn't entirely new. The Shark PowerDetect UV also uses ultraviolet light to seek out otherwise imperceptible stains. Dyson's R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV has already received FCC approval, and is slated to go on sale in the US on Sept. 15 for $1,199. It debuts alongside the Costco-exclusive Dyson R2 Nurovi Wash+Dry ($699), which features triangular mopping pads for thorough corner cleaning, and the vacuum-only R1Nurovi Dry ($549). While Dyson's latest models are unaffected by the foreign robot vacuum ban, the long-term future of autonomous floor cleaning in the US remains to be seen. I asked Turner about Dyson's reaction to the ban, and he said the company, which is based in Singapore, has always taken privacy and data custody "incredibly seriously." "The US is one of Dyson's biggest markets," Turner said. "Of course, we're really committed to bringing all of our new technologies and products to American consumers. We will do what it takes to make sure that happens." item.title: Hacker Who Spread Malware to 80,000 Freelance Workers Finally Nabbed
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.43
A hacker who sent malicious Excel attachments a decade ago, circulating malware to 80,000 freelance workers, has finally been caught, according to federal investigators. A grand jury had indicted a 40-year-old Russian national for a malware campaign that targeted freelance workers in 2016 and 2017, the Justice Department announced Tuesday. Searzhudin Tamirlanovich Aktulaev allegedly exploited a “well-known freelance employment technology company” in California to spread malware to approximately 80,000 users between June 2016 and November 2017. To spread the malware, Aktulaev used about 255 fake accounts to send messages containing malicious Microsoft Excel attachments. “When opened, the attachments prompted users to run a macro, which then downloaded malware from the internet,” the Justice Department said. These Excel macros can be powerful and dangerous, as they can run a full set of automated commands, making them potent tools for secretly downloading and executing malware. In this case, the malware involved two variants, TeamSpy and DarkVNC. Both were designed to exploit legitimate remote access software, TeamViewer and VNC Viewer, enabling a hacker to secretly access a victim’s PC and steal sensitive data. In 2017, antivirus provider Avast warned about the TeamSpy campaign circulating through malicious Excel files. “When the macros are enabled by the targeted person, the infection process begins, running completely in the background, so the victim doesn't notice anything,” Avast said at the time. In reality, the macros will download a maliciously configured version of TeamViewer that quietly acts as spyware, without tipping off the user. “Once the machine is infected, the criminals have full access to the computer. They can steal and exfiltrate sensitive data, download and execute arbitrary programs, and more,” Avast added. Allegedly, Aktulaev and his unnamed co-conspirators used the malware to loot user data, such as logins and personal information, to commit fraud and other criminal activities. The malicious Excel attachments likely didn’t trick all 80,000 freelance workers. Still, federal investigators discovered thousands of computers infected by the TeamSpy malware. “According to the indictment, approximately half of the victims were in the United States, many of whom were located in the Northern District of California. A database found on the command-and-control domain revealed thousands of victims,” the agency said. The indictment against Aktulaev was filed in 2021 but was finally unsealed on Monday. He was arrested in May 2025 in Cyprus. Federal investigators then successfully extradited him to the US, where Aktulaev made his initial appearance in a federal court in San Francisco on Monday. If convicted of all the fraud and computer hacking-related charges, Aktulaev could face over 35 years in prison under a maximum sentence. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: LA Schools Join NYC in Blocking Student Access to Generative AI
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.32
From coast to coast, AI is getting a failing grade this academic year. Days after New York City announced a one-year moratorium on AI tools for students through 8th grade, the Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) said students will be barred from using AI tools on district-provided devices this academic year. While NYC’s ban leaves some room for high school students to explore the tech with vetted programs, LAUSD seems to have shut off access completely. Students will be able to see Google’s AI summaries on top of search results, but they won’t be able to interact with the AI tool any further, The New York Times reports. The move comes as part of the district’s broader effort to reduce student screen time. Earlier this year, LAUSD banned digital devices for young kids and enforced strict screen limits for others. Some board members were reportedly surprised when the decision was announced at Wednesday’s committee meeting. The ban is temporary, and the committee will make recommendations on AI policy at the end of the school year, an LAUSD spokesperson tells Bloomberg. At both LA and NYC public schools, teachers will be allowed to use AI tools. And students can use AI chatbots on personal devices, so it remains to be seen how effective this will be. The bans arrive amid concerns that a growing number of students are using AI for homework and bypassing the learning process. AI tools are also notorious for providing inaccurate information and entertaining inappropriate conversations. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Stop Resizing Windows! This Built-In Windows 11 Trick Will Double Your Productivity
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.00
Managing open windows shouldn't feel like a full-time job. With Windows 11's Snap Layouts, you can instantly organize your workspace without the endless clicking, dragging, and manual resizing. Whether you're juggling two apps or managing a multi-monitor grid, this guide covers everything you need to master Snap Layouts, tweak your settings, and increase your daily productivity. How to Master Snap Layouts in Seconds To get started with Snap Layouts, simply hover the mouse cursor over the Maximize icon near the upper-right corner of a program window. You’ll see a choice of window layouts. Click a position to instantly snap the window to that location on the grid. The precise layout options here depend on the display you’re using. Common options include two side-by-side windows and a four-quadrant grid. Windows shows layouts for arranging three windows side by side if your PC has a high-resolution display, too. You will see the Snap Assist grid with previews of your open windows after selecting a location for the first window. Click them to quickly choose which windows you want in each position on your screen. It’s much faster than hunting down and resizing application windows one by one. Additionally, Windows lets you use Snap Layouts with drag-and-drop gestures. Drag and drop a window’s title bar to the left or right edges of the screen to place it on either side, or drag it into one of the four corners of the screen to place it in that quadrant. You can also drag and drop a window to the top of your screen. You’ll see the Snap Layouts options, and you can drop the window in your desired position on your preferred layout. This works on a touch screen, too: Place your finger on the window’s title bar and drag it to your desired position on your screen to start snapping. After you create a Snap Layout with a group of windows, you can see an app’s position in that arrangement via its taskbar thumbnail. Windows 11 also shows combined window groups in the window switcher (Alt + Tab)and Task View (Windows Key + Tab) overlays, allowing you to quickly switch between groups of windows. Ditch the Mouse: Lightning-Fast Keyboard Shortcuts Press the Windows Key + Z to start snapping a window from the keyboard. Snap Layouts will display numbers in a grid, and you can press a number to quickly assign a window layout. Additionally, Windows lets you move windows around the grid with Windows key shortcuts. Press the Windows Key + Left Arrow or the Windows Key + Right Arrow to snap the current window to either edge of your screen. You can also use the up and down arrow keys. For example, to snap the current window to the bottom-right quadrant of your screen, hold the Windows Key, press the Right Arrow key, then press the Down Arrow key. You will see the familiar Snap Assist interface after snapping the first window. You can use the arrow keys and the Enter or Space key to quickly make a selection. You can also press Esc to cancel Snap Assist. Tweak the Settings: Customize Your Snapping Workflow Microsoft lets you configure Snap Layouts from the Settings app, and you can even turn it off if it gets in your way. Go to Settings > System > Multitasking, then expand the Snap Windows section to see the available options. If you toggle the Snap Windows off entirely, you won’t even be able to snap a window to the left or right sides of your screen. Other options here let you turn off Snap Assist suggestions, Snap Layouts pop-ups, and the overlay that appears when you drag a window to the top of your screen. Additionally, you can hide groups of snapped windows from the app switcher view and the taskbar, if you prefer. The Multitasking settings window also has a toggle for a feature called Title Bar Window Shake, which lets you grab a window’s title bar with your mouse and shake it to minimize all other windows. Microsoft originally called this feature Aero Shake in Windows Vista, and the Snap feature was originally called Aero Snap alongside it. The Title Bar Window Shake option is off by default. Go Pro With FancyZones: Total Desktop Control If Snap Layouts isn't flexible enough for you, try the superpowered FancyZones utility included in Microsoft’s free PowerToys package. It lets you create custom layouts for window arrangements, which might be especially useful on higher-resolution monitors. You can create multiple sets of custom layouts and switch between them with keyboard shortcuts, quickly snapping your open windows to different arrangements. After you install PowerToys, FancyZones is active by default. Simply hold down Shift while dragging a window to see layout options for snapping it to a zone. It's possible to customize the keyboard or mouse actions that trigger FancyZones from within the PowerToys app, too. For more ways to upgrade your desktop experience, check out these hidden Windows 11 features. About Our Experts I've been testing PC and mobile software for more than 20 years, focusing on photo and video editing, operating systems, and web browsers. Prior to my current role, I covered software and apps for ExtremeTech and headed up PCMag’s enterprise software team. I’ve attended trade shows for Microsoft, Google, and Apple and written about all of them and their products. I still get a kick out of seeing what's new in video and photo editing software, and how operating systems change over time. I was privileged to byline the cover story of the last print issue of PC Magazine, the Windows 7 review, and I’ve witnessed every Microsoft misstep and win, up to the latest Windows 11. I’m an avid bird photographer and traveler—I’ve been to 40 countries, many with great birds! Because I’m also a classical music fan and former performer, I’ve reviewed streaming services that emphasize classical music. I've been writing about technology for more than 15 years and using it in earnest for over twice as long. As a member of PCMag's software team, I focus on Windows coverage, but also write about other key desktop operating systems and system apps. (I used Windows 3.1 upon its release and have followed every subsequent release closely). Prior to joining PCMag, I wrote for How-To Geek starting in 2011, and my articles amassed over a billion page views. I went on to run the publication as editor-in-chief for four and a half years. I have also contributed to Computerworld, Fast Company, PCWorld, Reader's Digest, The New York Times, and many other outlets about everything from AI to PC hardware to Windows. I founded and ran my own direct-to-reader Windows-focused newsletters, Windows Intelligence and The Windows ReadMe, working in partnership with Thurrott.com.

item.title: Uber Launches UK's First Robotaxi Service in London, But There's a Catch
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.49
Robotaxis are finally available in the UK. After months of testing, Uber began offering public robotaxi rides in London earlier today. Customers in the city who book an UberX, Uber Electric, or Uber Comfort ride may now be matched with a Ford Mustang Mach-E vehicle equipped with Wayve’s AI Driver tech. Interested customers can accept Uber’s robotaxi offer at no extra cost or decline it and ride in a non-autonomous vehicle as usual. When the car arrives, follow the instructions in the app to open the door and initiate the trip. For safety reasons, Uber’s initial robotaxi trips will have a supervisor behind the wheel, and the company will operate just 15 vehicles in its fleet. More vehicles will be added “thoughtfully over time in line with rider demand, readiness, and regulation,” but if you’d like to increase your chances of being matched with a robotaxi, you can set your trip preferences to AV by going to Account > Settings > Ride Preferences in the mobile app. Approximately 140,000 Londoners have already done so, Uber says. When it comes to the service area, Uber’s robotaxis cover all parts of London but not airports. It’s quite a challenging city for autonomous driving, since the roads are narrower and more irregular compared with orderly grid systems found in many modern cities. "This launch is a major milestone in scaling safe, accessible AV technology in a city with some of the world’s most complex roads," says Sarfraz Maredia, Uber’s head of autonomous mobility. Speaking of airports, Amazon-owned Zoox has extended service to Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, TechCrunch reports. In late July, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) gave Zoox a temporary exemption, allowing the company to finally begin offering commercial rides. This week, it also launched in Houston and San Diego. Google-owned Waymo, meanwhile, is expected to begin its robotaxi service in London soon. It began testing Wayve’s driving tech last year and may launch public rides in the city this year. Last month, Uber beat Waymo to become the first to launch robotaxi services in Europe with rides in Zagreb, Croatia. The company has committed $10 billion to its AV expansion and is targeting 15 cities by the end of this year. It is already operational in eight. This comes as Tesla is expected to unveil more details about its Cybercab at an event in Austin, Texas, tonight. First unveiled in 2024, the robotaxi is a smaller coupe with two butterfly doors, two seats, and a single band of headlights, similar to the Cybertruck. There's no steering wheel, pedals, or charging port, as it can charge via induction. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: HTC's New Smart Glasses Offer a Few Imperfect Fixes for the Pervert Problem
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.28
Privacy and smart glasses should go hand in hand, and with the $499 Vive Eagle AI, HTC seems to realize that. It's clear the company wants to avoid the "pervert glasses" stigma that Meta's smart glasses have earned, and it's taking notable steps toward that end, though the built-in camera remains on the Vive Eagle AI. I'm currently testing them, and a full review is coming, but for now, here's what I see with HTC's "privacy-first approach." Addressing and Anonymizing AI Like all AI glasses, the Vive Eagle has built-in voice-activated AI. Interface functions, like activating different features, are handled by HTC's Vive AI, and HTC says your data will not be used to train its AI. Frankly, I think all AI data training should be opt-in, not the opt-out-and-good-luck-finding-out-how-because-we-won't-tell-you approach of a lot of AI systems. Including AI systems you weren't interacting with in the first place, like Twitch. If you want general information beyond the glasses' core functions, the Vive Eagle supports Google Gemini and OpenAI's GPT. They're much larger systems that have basically scraped the entire internet for training data, and will certainly use your interactions as well. Considering how much Google is tied to our internet footprints, there's a reasonable concern that every Gemini-related thing you do with the glasses will be linked to your Google profile. However, HTC says LLM requests through the glasses will be de-identified. The company pointedly says it makes it "harder" to build a profile, but not impossible. Sadly, that's the current reality we live in, and no privacy or security feature is completely bulletproof. Welcome to the data economy. The Vive Eagle is also ISO 27001 and ISO 27701 compliant, which means it meets international standards for securing personal data and ensuring some level of user-side privacy control. The Camera Problem The Vive Eagle has a built-in 12MP camera that lets you take photos and 3K video, and provides translations in 96 different languages. A camera is always handy to have, but it's also the main reason "pervert glasses" has become a common phrase. Creeps, stalkers, and general jerks use camera-equipped smart glasses to surreptitiously record and harass people. To address the problem, HTC added extra privacy and security features to the Vive Eagle. First, its recording light uses multiple sensors to ensure it's always visible when the camera is recording. It will adjust its brightness based on ambient light to be easily seen, and the camera won't work if the light is obscured in any way. A recording light that you can't disable has become standard on major smart glasses with cameras, including Meta's, but I'm skeptical that it can't be circumvented in some way. Second, the camera will not record unless the glasses are being physically worn. This means someone can't take the glasses off and set them to capture from a hidden position. There could also be a workaround there, but it's another good step. Third, the camera will turn off if anyone nearby says "stop filming." That's kind of brilliant in its simplicity. If you know you're being recorded, you can stop it. Again, in theory. The fourth feature is less an anti-pervert-glasses fix and more about general user security improvements. Photos and videos taken on the Vive Eagle stay on the glasses' on-board 32GB storage until you manually transfer them to your phone or another device, and that data can't be accessed if you pair the glasses with a different device. When combined with the ISO 27001 and ISO 27701 certifications, anything you capture on the glasses should be safe from other people. Privacy, Security, and Uncertainty It's good that HTC is up-front and highlighting its privacy and security measures on the Vive Eagle. They aren't remotely guaranteed, since no information security measure is, but it's a start. Still, in an ideal world, we wouldn't have to worry about this at all. Security to prevent individuals from stealing your data is one thing. Preventing unauthorized system access by bad actors has been a vital part of information security for as long as information has existed. Thieves will always exist, so we find ways to deal with the threats. But the concerns about AI glasses go beyond those bad actors to the devices' own manufacturers, service providers, and users. The Vive Eagle doesn't anonymize your AI prompts to keep some random hacker from tracking you; it does that to keep Google and OpenAI from tracking you. HTC comes out and says Vive AI won't use your data for training, even though every major AI firm is using it for training, whether you like it or not. The glasses don't have a "stop filming" kill switch to keep your photos and videos out of others' hands; they have it to keep you from being a creep or stalker with them. These privacy and security features aren't simply necessary to protect us from criminals. They're necessary to protect us from the very services we rely on, and from ourselves (or at least other people using the exact same devices). HTC seems to be doing what it can with the Vive Eagle (besides removing the camera entirely), but the fact that these actions need to be taken in the first place? Well, that really sucks. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s home theater and AR/VR expert, and your go-to source of information and recommendations for game consoles and accessories, smart displays, smart glasses, smart speakers, soundbars, TVs, and VR headsets. I’m an ISF-certified TV calibrator and THX-certified home theater technician, I've served as a CES Innovation Awards judge, and while Bandai hasn’t officially certified me, I’m also proficient at building Gundam plastic models up to MG-class. I also enjoy genre fiction writing, and my urban fantasy novel, Alex Norton, Paranormal Technical Support, is currently available on Amazon.

item.title: Open and Neutral? Nvidia Says Don't Worry About Its Hugging Face Acquisition
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.16
Nvidia’s $13 billion deal to acquire Hugging Face might spark concerns about the future of the popular AI model platform, but both companies insist that Hugging Face will remain “open and neutral” for AI developers and enthusiasts. “We want to continue to work with all AI developers globally,” Nvidia’s VP for enterprise computing, Justin Boitano, said in a press briefing after the acquisition was confirmed this morning. “To make sure that they’ve got an open and neutral platform that interoperates with every cloud provider, every hardware company in the world.” “We think this operation, this announcement, will allow the world and AI to be more distributed all over the world, and to avoid too much concentration of power,” added Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue. The concern is that Hugging Face hosts numerous open-source and open-weight AI models, effectively operating as the "App Store of the AI world" for over 200,000 companies, notes PCMag’s Brian Westover. Nvidia, on the other hand, is the top seller of enterprise GPUs to power AI models and is preparing consumer-focused chips with its RTX Spark line to drive AI use on laptops. Will the Hugging Face deal push the platform to favor Nvidia technology? Boitano says no. The priority is to keep the platform open and neutral so that it can grow, which requires maintaining trust with the software developer community. In turn, Nvidia will benefit as AI developers and businesses buy its chips to run AI models. Boitano also addressed whether the deal might face antitrust scrutiny from government regulators, saying Nvidia’s role is focused on helping Hugging Face “scale and expand access to AI globally," adding, “We think regulators are going to see this as overwhelmingly positive because it's going to infuse AI into every country, into every industry." Hugging Face’s Delangue also noted that “the vast, vast majority of what we do is open-source, open models, open datasets, that are by definition, neutral. Everyone can take them. Everyone can optimize them, everyone can fork our open-source if they are not happy about it.” He added that a major goal is to grow the platform’s user base to 100 million AI software developers over the next few years, up from the current 18 million. “We think that this announcement is really going to be fantastic and massively impactful for all the players in the ecosystem, not just Nvidia, but all the players,” Delangue said. Still, analysts at research firm Forrester noted that the deal gives Nvidia significant influence over the AI ecosystem, including a potential competitive edge over other GPU designers. "Nvidia gains visibility into customers' preferences and the AI models they use. They can see which models are trending, what datasets customers are downloading, and the architectures that are gaining traction weeks before they hit mainstream tech news,” says analyst Naveen Chhabra. "Nvidia also gets data-driven foresight into what next-generation chip architectures they need to build based on developer habits.” About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: DLSS 5 Spikes Power Consumption
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.13
DLSS 5 doesn't just tank frame rates and weather faces; it might also spike power consumption on GPUs. Tom's Hardware tested various games with high-end graphics cards running DLSS 5 and found that, in some cases, power consumption jumped by hundreds of watts when the card had headroom. Where it didn't, performance fell further, suggesting the already fire-happy 12v-2x6 connector may be limiting performance with DLSS 5 enabled. DLSS 5, which brings AI-powered photorealism to PC games, launched today on NBA 2K27. Whether it actually makes games look better is still up for debate. It's more efficient than when we first saw it, but the RTX 5090 still loses nearly half its FPS. When running Hogwarts Legacy at 4K with ray tracing and DLSS set to Performance mode, Tom's Hardware found that the RTX 5090 FE jumped from 417 watts without it to 547 watts with it. For the RTX 5090 Lightning Z, with a much higher power limit, it leaped from 480W without DLSS 5 to 720W with it. In comparison, the Founders Edition 5090 performance dipped by 49% with DLSS 5 enabled, while the Lightning dropped by just 42%, and its 1% lows were much less impacted. You can argue the Lightning Z is the more powerful card, but it was only 3fps higher than the FE card without DLSS 5, so DLSS 5 has the biggest impact here. The same story was true in Cyberpunk 2077, where the Lightning Z version went from 580W to 723W, losing 39% of its overall FPS in the process. The 5090 FE went from 482W to 551W but lost 42% performance, dropping below 60fps even with DLSS on Performance. Control had the highest power consumption and, therefore, the greatest limitation on the FE card. The Lightning Z version went from 691W to 802W, while the standard 5090 pulled 563W and only 575W with DLSS 5 enabled. While both cards saw their frame rates drop by 42% with DLSS 5 enabled, the Lightning Z still held above 60fps average, while the 5090 fell to just 51fps. So, DLSS 5 appears to benefit most from the latest tensor cores and greater power limits. Like the original DLSS release, it is likely to be a multi-generational technology that will be far more useful in the years and generations to come. More powerful cards with faster tensor units, with greater power limits, may be needed to take full advantage of it. But Nvidia will have to address that connector if it tries to push even more power through these things. Maybe something extra stealthy like the BTF method? About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: Move Over, DJI: Hohem's Eyepic 4K Vlogging Camera Has a Massive Twist
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.03
Vlogging cameras are the hot ticket right now, and the space just got a brand new player. Hohem, a brand best known to date for its iSteady smartphone gimbals, is bringing its first-ever camera to IFA in Berlin. The Eyepic is a tiny 4K video camera that can be handheld, worn, or magnetically mounted to a three-axis gimbal—making it a true triple threat for content creation. A Pocket Gimbal That Snaps Apart for Underwater Action The Eyepic draws inspiration from the DJI Osmo Pocket series, which has proven to be the go-to choice for vloggers who want to record handheld video and has inspired competitors such as the Insta360 Luna Ultra. Like others in the class, the Eyepic has a long, skinny body that fits comfortably in your hand, a touch screen, and a small joystick to control its powered gimbal. The gimbal promises to keep footage smooth and steady, even for walk-and-talk shots, and the Eyepic camera records clips at up to 4K60 quality. That's not as ambitious as some competitors—the DJI Osmo Pocket 4P and Insta360 Luna Ultra both support higher frame rates for slow motion and include dual lenses for wide and telephoto views, while the Eyepic is a single-lens device. But the Eyepic does one thing that DJI and Insta360 can't—its camera works separately from the gimbal. It pops on and off with a quick magnetic attachment, so you can go between handheld vlogging and mounting the camera to an object in a snap. That makes the Eyepic the first gimbal camera that's also a waterproof action camera, one that works down to 32.8 feet underwater. It also makes it easy to switch between widescreen and vertical video—the camera mounts to the gimbal in either direction. Pro Audio Upgrade: The AI-Powered Hohem Mic 2 Kit Vloggers know that a video is only as good as its soundtrack. Built-in mics tend to sound hollow and pick up a lot of background noise, so the company is releasing a wireless mic kit for the Eyepic: the Hohem Mic 2. The kit ships with a receiver and two body mics, and supports up to four mics in total. It supports 48kHz/24-bit audio, has AI-powered noise cancellation, and promises an incredible 984-foot transmission range. Availability: Targeting CES 2027—And an Opening in the US Market Like many of the products making their debut at IFA, the Eyepic isn't quite ready to ship to customers, so we don't know how much it will cost or which regions it will be sold in. Hohem says it plans to release a general version in the first quarter of 2027, and we'll be sure to have more information closer to that date. The early 2027 timing is conspicuously timed with CES, which takes place in Las Vegas and is a traditional launchpad for the coolest consumer tech, so we're hopeful that the Eyepic makes it US debut then. On paper, it looks like a great choice for US-based vloggers and content creators who can't get the latest DJI Osmo Pocket models because of the FCC's ban on new DJI products. Stay tuned to PCMag for more information as it develops. About Our Expert Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 15 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones.

item.title: AG Promises to 'Track Down' Those Behind X Password Reset Requests
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.00
UPDATE 9/2: US Attorney General Todd Blanche today attributed the password-reset spree to "sophisticated cybercriminals" who targeted hundreds of X accounts. "X disrupted the attack to prevent user accounts from being captured," Blanche tweeted. "We are working closely with X to track down the criminals behind this week’s attack. There is no refuge for those [who] perpetrate their criminal schemes from behind computer screens." Original Story 9/1: Did you wake up this morning to multiple password reset requests from X? Dozens of users took to the social network this morning to report receiving at least 10 emails around 9:30 a.m. ET. The messages, which appeared in the inboxes of at least one PCMag staffer, looked legit; they came from [email protected] and included the six-digit confirmation code required to complete a password reset. "If you didn't make this request, ignore this email," it said. Easier said than done. The messages sparked a wave of concerned posts on X from people worried they had been hacked or targeted by a phishing campaign. X Product Engineer Mridul Singhai said the company is "actively investigating the issue and, so far, [has] found no evidence of any breaches. We apologize for the multiple emails and appreciate your patience as we work to resolve this.” Singhai attributes the concerning emails to X Money, Musk’s payment platform for X Premium subscribers that became publicly available in July. "Attackers appear to believe that, now that @XMoney is widely available, they can gain unauthorized access to accounts." How to Secure Your X Account If you’ve received suspicious emails, don’t click on any links. Go directly to the X mobile or web app to check your account status. If you don't have secondary security set up on your account, do that ASAP, whether it's two-factor authentication (2FA) or a passkey. Also consider enabling Password reset protect via Settings > Security and account access > Security > Password reset protect. "If you check this box, you will be prompted to enter either your email address or phone number, or your email address, then phone number if both are associated with your account, to send a reset password link or confirmation code if you ever forget it," X says. The same Security page is also where you'd go to set up 2FA or a passkey. For 2FA, you can use an authenticator app or a security key. To receive codes via text messages, you'll need to be a Premium subscriber, but we don't recommend using SMS for 2FA codes anyway. For more on passkeys, check out our explainer. About Our Expert I’m a New York-based writer currently serving as PCMag’s Editorial Intern. I cover the impact of technology and internet culture on our daily lives, with a specialization in video games and cultural criticism. I have written for Kotaku, The A.V. Club, Unwinnable, Aftermath, and more. In addition, I have a formal background in video game development and visual design. You can find all of my work on my website.

item.title: How ad-free streaming became so much less affordable
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.52
Ad-free streaming used to be one of the biggest benefits of cutting the cable TV cord. Now it’s become a luxury. Inspired by some new research into the growing price gap between ad-supported and ad-free streaming, I decided to calculate how much the cost to avoid commercials has increased over time. Depending on which services you have, you could be paying an extra $42.50 just to skip ads, up 60 percent from a few years ago. Not all hope is lost for affordable ad-free TV, but you might have to get a bit creative to get it. The increasing ad-free tax My impetus for writing this is a new report from Ampere Analysis about the growing gulf in price between ad-free and ad-supported streaming. The study found that globally over the past three years, the ad-free tiers of Netflix, Amazon Prime, and Disney+ have increased by $1.61 on average, versus $1.21 per month with ads. Those results actually understate the problem. When you look at the United States in particular, which includes more streaming services, the ad-free tax becomes even bigger. Let’s say you’re a subscriber to Netflix, Amazon Prime, HBO Max, Disney+, Paramount+, and Peacock. At the end of 2022 (when both Netflix and Disney launched ad-supported tiers), the total cost would have been roughly $44 per month with ads, or $70.50 without ads, for a difference of $26.50. Those same six services now cost roughly $63 per month with ads, or $105.50 per month without ads. While the overall price has increased on both sides, the difference between ad-free and ad-supported plans has jumped by 60 percent, from $26.50 to $42.50 per month. Here’s a closer look at how the price gap has grown over the years: | | Dec. 2022 (ads / ad-free) | Sept. 2026 (ads / ad-free) | Ad-free fee increase | |---|---|---|---| | Netflix (Standard) | $6.99 / $15.49 | $8.99 / $19.99 | +$2.50 | | Amazon Prime Video | $8.99: Ad-free only | $8.99 / $13.98 | +$4.99 | | HBO Max | $9.99 / $14.99 | $10.99 / $18.49 | +$2.50 | | Disney+ | $7.99 / $10.99 | $11.99 / $18.99 | +$4.00 | | Paramount+ | $4.99 / $9.99 | $8.99 / $13.99 | $0.00 | | Peacock | $4.99 / $9.99 | $12.99 / $19.99 | +$2.00 | | Total | $43.94 / $70.44 | $62.94 / $105.43 | +$15.99 | Amazon is the biggest offender. At the start of 2024, it started including ads in Prime Video and charged $3 per month to remove them. The ad-free price then jumped to $5 per month last March, with a plan that Amazon now calls “Prime Video Ultra.” Other companies were more subtle in pushing ads on users. Disney initially indicated that its ad-supported tier would cost less than the ad-free plan. When that plan arrived in late 2022, Disney raised the price of for ad-free streaming and slotted in its new ad-supported plan at the old price. Netflix, meanwhile, phased out its “Basic (Ad-Free)” plan in 2024, making the jump to ad-free streaming more drastic. And Peacock has raised prices so aggressively that even its ad-supported plan costs more than the ad-free version once did. In all cases, the dynamic is the same: As Ampere points out, subscription growth is leveling out in the United States, and streamers are increasingly relying on advertising to boost their revenues. While ad-free streaming becomes more of a luxury, the streamers still need to keep ad-supported prices low so they can bring in new subscribers and scale up their advertising businesses. Ad skipping still remains alive and well in the realm of live TV streaming services such as YouTube TV, Sling TV, and Fubo. Those services include cloud-based DVRs, so you can record live TV and skip the commercials. But as more viewers opt for cheaper standalone streaming services, the streamers are now ushering the DVR toward obsolescence. What you can do about it In some cases, bundling services together may provide price hike relief, even on ad-free tiers. Disney, for instance, has actually shrunk the price gap for its bundle of Disney+ and Hulu. That package cost $10 per month with ads or $20 per month without ads a few years ago. Now it’s $13 per month with ads, but still $20 per month without ads. The bundle of Disney+, Hulu, and HBO Max has also maintained the same $13 per month upcharge for ad-free over the past couple years, even as the overall cost has increased. (It’s $33 per month for all three without ads.) The growing price gap may also create an opportunity for more affordable ad-free services. I keep writing about how YouTube is taking over TV viewing in the United States, and it now has 125 million subscribers on its Premium or Music plans. If you just want to skip ads on YouTube, Premium Lite for $9 per month can look like a pretty good value compared to traditional streaming services. Keep an eye on Roku’s Howdy streaming service as well. At $3 per month with no ads, the catalog is heavy on B-movies and forgotten reruns, but has some hidden gems that remind me of Netflix’s early days. It reportedly topped 1 million subscribers in less than a year, and it continues to grow its catalog with new licensing deals. If you’re up for a more adversarial approach, you can also take ad-skipping into your own hands. I’ve previously written about PlayOn, which records video from ad-supported streaming services and lets you skip the commercials. Using it can be a hassle, as it requires either pay-as-you-go cloud recording credits or a Windows PC to run the recording engine, but the savings can be significant. If you’re willing to watch through a web browser, the Multi Skipper extension will attempt to fast forward through commercials on major streaming services for free. I’ve been using this on my still-experimental living room PC setup with great success, and while relying on a computer for streaming has its own trade-offs, it’s one of the last ways to retain some control in a system that’s increasingly stacked against its viewers.

item.title: Best of IFA 2026: 10 hot PC products and tech on the horizon
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.25
Like CES in Las Vegas, the IFA technology tradeshow that takes place every year in Berlin gives technology vendors and taste makers an opportunity to show off their latest and greatest wares, and consumers a chance to start planning their next purchases and saving their shekels. From a PC user’s perspective, the category that got the most love this year was monitors, and we’re here for it as innovations include esports-caliber OLED and truly affordable Mini LED. There are also some tasty laptops coming down the pike, some intriguing developments for consumer AI, and a few very promising hardware concepts that we’re praying will make it to market. Without further ado, here are the 10 products and innovations from IFA 2026 that have us most excited. Acer Vero 16 Acer IFA is generally a showcase for laptops, and this year the big news is those RTX Spark models due in October. But I’m wary of new Arm chips, and doubly wary of Nvidia. For my money (what little it buys in a laptop these days), Acer stole the show with its revamped Vero 16. Granted, Acer is mostly cribbing on Framework here. In addition to recycled components that were a highlight of previous Vero designs, this one allows tool-free access to the primary laptop component bay, replaceable hinges, replaceable battery, all while keeping at least some durability. You can swap out the SSD, too…but not the RAM, like most Core Ultra Series 3 laptops. With a standard OLED screen and a base Core Ultra 5 322 processor (up to Core Ultra X9 388H at the top end), respectable Arc B390 graphics, and a 71-watt-hour battery, this looks like a pretty good option for a mid-range, all-rounder laptop…though who knows how much all that extra engineering will add to the price. I can’t say I’d prefer the Vero to a Framework without getting my hands on it, but I’m happy to see more companies incorporate repairable designs. – Michael Crider Lenovo’s Project AeroBlade concept Mark Hachman / Foundry PCWorld was the first to break the story on the Frore AirJet cooling chip, and we’ve been following the technology for years. Now the Lenovo Project AeroBlade concept finally looks like it could bring the AirJet chip to store shelves inside a new 14-inch laptop. Fortunately, Lenovo concepts often end up as products — I’m guessing in 2027. Why is this important? An AirJet laptop stands to be both quiet (no fans, remember) as well as light — 1.83 pounds, in this case. It’s literally as heavy as a full 24oz water bottle. Lenovo is using Intel’s Core Ultra 200 chip inside it, so it stands to be moderately powerful as well. I can’t wait until I can take something like this on a business trip. – Mark Hachman Alienware AW2527HX 560Hz OLED esports monitor Alienware For me, the biggest story coming out of IFA was the deluge of fantastical new monitors, and the Alienware 25 560Hz QD-OLED Gaming Monitor (AW2527HX) captured my attention like no other. The upshot here? OLED is finally ready for the high refresh rates that esports sweats clamor for. That means that in addition to the blistering 560Hz refresh rate, this 24.5-inch 1080p display also offers all of OLED’s benefits, like luscious contrast, vivid colors with wicked accuracy, fast gray-to-gray pixel response times, and inky VESA DisplayHDR True Black 600 certification that ensures blacks deeper than the darkest soul. Typical esports monitors use ancient TN panel technology instead, which is fast but suffers in visual quality and viewing angles. You won’t find that here. Add in physical design feedback from the esports pros at Team Liquid — I dig the height markers on the stand for easily repeatable setup — and the Alienware AW2527HX looks ready to turn heads when it launches in the first quarter of 2027. – Brad Chacos Acer Nitro XV275U Z2 OLED isn’t the only big dawg in the display junkyard. Mini-LED offers many of the same benefits of OLED, but offers higher peak brightness and better text clarity at the slight expense of slower gray-to-gray response times. Bottom line? Mini-LED monitors look great — and now they’re shockingly cheap. Case in point: Acer’s Nitro XV275U Z2. It will cost just $329 when it launches later this year, giving you a stunning 1,000 nits of HDR brightness powered by 1,152-zone mini-LED backlighting, along with a Dynamic Frequency and Resolution feature that starts at 275Hz at its default 1440p, 360Hz at 1080p, and 520Hz at 720p (ick). Mini-LED doesn’t suffer from the pixel burn-in concerns like OLED, either. Look for the Acer Nitro XV275U Z2 to land before the holidays. – Brad Chacos Alienware 32 4K OLED Gaming Monitor (AW3226Q) Dell Mini-LED may have historically offered superior text clarity to OLED, but thanks to new “RGB Stripe” OLED technology debuting this year, those days may be over. And Dell created a killer-looking 4K monitor for work and play that leverages the bleeding-edge feature. The Alienware 32 4K OLED Gaming Monitor (AW3226Q) offers everything gamers could want, from its pixel-packed resolution and 165Hz running speeds to its stunning 1,000-nit peak brightness and VESA DisplayHDR True Black 400 and Dolby Vision certifications. The panel is factory-calibrated for Delta E<2 color accuracy and covers 99 percent of the DCI-P3 color space, which should make it appealing to creators and visual pros as well — especially paired with RGB Stripe’s improved text clarity. Heck, Alienware even packed in HDMI 2.1, so the display plays nice with consoles, too. Is this the One Monitor To Rule Them All? I’m drooling at the idea of testing this display when it launches for $699 — a shockingly low price tag considering what the AW3226Q offers — later this fall. – Brad Chacos Acer DualPlay Mini concept Acer Why would you spend $2,000 on a PC gaming handheld instead of a gaming laptop? Aside from the size and the controls, everything else is a compromise. But what if you could have…both?
