item.title: TSA brings its new 'e-gates' to Newark. But are you eligible to use them?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 7.12
TSA brings its new 'e-gates' to Newark. But are you eligible to use them? As the Labor Day travel rush kicks off, airport security may look a little different for travelers at one of the biggest airports in the New York City area. This week, the Transportation Security Administration brought its new "e-gates" to Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) for the first time. It's a new setup that allows passengers to pass through Transportation Security Administration without ever stopping to speak with an officer. The automated gates are live for certain United Airlines passengers passing through Newark's Terminal C. EWR is one of the nation's first airports to pilot this new high-tech security process. Earlier this summer, the TSA began trialing similar technology at Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT). I just tried the TSA's new e-gates: Here's what it was like Passengers using the e-gates no longer have to hand their IDs to a TSA staffer. Instead, they walk into a booth and have their photo taken, and then the translucent gates typically open in a matter of seconds. View this post on Instagram Who can use the TSA e-gates? In Charlotte, the e-gates are available to all passengers registered for TSA PreCheck. Access in Newark is limited to United flyers who have opted in to the faster TSA PreCheck Touchless ID program. That biometric program allows passengers to pass through security without showing an ID. Instead, the TSA snaps a photo and compares the image to passport information already on file. Travelers using the e-gates at Newark can essentially pass through the initial security line without pulling out an ID or boarding pass, or speaking to an officer. Then those passengers (and their bags) will be screened as usual. How to use the e-gates in Newark To use the TSA's e-gates at Newark, you'll need to be flying United. And, you'll have to opt in to TSA PreCheck Touchless ID with the airline. Here's how to do that. The TSA has now trialed e-gates at three major airports: EWR, CLT and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA). So far, the process has been slightly faster than a normal security line; the TSA has said the automatic gates save about 3 seconds per passenger on average. It may not sound like much, but as thousands of flyers go through security each day, those saved seconds add up. The e-gates also free up officers to assist travelers in other lanes. Travel lines go high-tech TSA isn't alone in turning to higher-tech processes to speed up airport lines. In recent months, the paid security service Clear has also rolled out its own version of e-gates at dozens of airports nationwide. It comes as airlines, government agencies and private security companies have increasingly been relying on biometric photos to cut wait times at major hubs. Earlier this summer, TPG reported that U.S. Customs and Border Protection was trialing camera capture technology for Global Entry. That new process verifies passengers' identity as they walk into the customs hall, eliminating the need for the fast-track program's blue kiosks. Meanwhile, some airlines have begun using facial recognition at certain airport gates, allowing flyers to board without scanning a boarding pass. At TSA checkpoints, passengers can always opt out of having their photo taken. Photography — and use of the new e-gates — is optional. The TSA hopes to eventually bring the e-gates technology to more cities. Related reading:

item.title: United is making it easier to get on an earlier flight — and have food waiting at your gate
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.66
United is making it easier to get on an earlier flight — and have food waiting at your gate United Airlines is on a roll. The carrier just announced an exciting 13-route global expansion, is fresh off introducing all-new Polaris business class suites, is on the verge of adding a fancy plane to the lineup, has improvements coming to the economy cabin, and will soon add some of its biggest-ever lounges to the network. But while new planes, lounges and business-class suites are impressive, sometimes it's the smaller day-to-day travel improvements that matter even more. To that end, United has two more announcements this week that could help when travel disruptions strike — or when you're simply pressed for time between flights and need something to eat or drink. Getting on an earlier United flight is becoming easier during disruptions When flight disruptions happen, getting on with your journey as quickly as possible is usually the main goal. United is making that easier with a new function in its app. It will allow delayed customers who are rebooked on a later flight to keep their confirmed seat while also selecting up to three earlier United flights to the same destination to wait for on standby. The big addition here is that United will actively monitor seat availability on those three flights and text delayed passengers if a seat opens up. Passengers can then decide whether to take the earlier flight or remain confirmed on the later one. This is a much easier process than running from gate to gate to ask about standby availability or obsessively refreshing the app to see if a seat opens up. Related: What to do in case your flight is delayed or canceled United is testing food delivery at the gate If you've ever wished you could have a meal, a drink or even something like a charging cord waiting at the gate when you landed, you may be in luck. At nine gates (gates C125 - C138) in Terminal C at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), United now offers functionality that allows customers to order a selection of sandwiches, salads, drinks, kids' meals, chips, candy and travel essentials (such as select over-the-counter medicine, travel pillows and charging cords). These orders will be waiting at a designated pickup shelf at the gate. Eligible customers will receive a predeparture push notification via the United app or an email with a link to place an order. Participating airport restaurants will include Nonna's Kitchen and Victory Grill. This test is scheduled to extend to Houston later this year, after which United plans to evaluate interest for possible future expansion to other airports. If that happens, United shares that it would integrate the service into seatback inflight entertainment screens. That would mean you could order a drink and a sandwich from the air to have waiting at the gate when you arrive. Bottom line In TPG's Best Airlines of 2026 study, United Airlines came in a very close second, just behind Delta Air Lines. With continued innovations and route expansions, along with improvements in a couple of metrics that dragged its ranking down, the airline has a very realistic chance of overtaking Delta in next year's report. In the meantime, though, it's often the less flashy improvements that make travel noticeably easier. Being able to hold onto a confirmed flight while United looks for an earlier option and having food waiting at the gate when you land are both improvements I'm personally very excited to see.

item.title: Chase Ultimate Rewards sweet spots: Best flight and hotel redemptions
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.25
Chase Ultimate Rewards sweet spots: Best flight and hotel redemptions Chase Ultimate Rewards points are one of the most valuable transferable currencies you can earn. Because of this — and Chase's 5/24 rule — many people start with an Ultimate Rewards points-earning card when they first get into points and miles. If you're new to Ultimate Rewards, you can redeem your points for travel through the Chase Travel℠ portal. However, the most valuable redemptions often involve transferring points to Ultimate Rewards airline and hotel transfer partners. This guide will cover some of the best Chase sweet spots to help you maximize your next redemption. Book luxury Hyatt hotel stays with Chase points Chase's partnership with World of Hyatt is great news for anyone collecting Ultimate Rewards points. That's because World of Hyatt's award chart is very generous: Standard rooms at top-tier Category 8 properties cost between 35,000 and 75,000 points per night, depending on whether Hyatt designates the night Lowest, Low, Moderate, Upper or Top. With some Ultimate Rewards-earning cards transferring to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, booking these properties at reasonable rates is easy, especially if you can travel outside of holidays and peak travel times. For example, on select dates, you can book some of the fanciest Park Hyatt properties in the entire portfolio, including the Park Hyatt New York and the Park Hyatt Sydney, for 35,000 points per night. Ultimate Rewards points are worth 2.05 cents each per our September 2026 valuations, so 35,000 points are worth $717. That's a great deal for hotels that sell for close to $1,000 per night, even when demand is low. There's also great value at the lower end of the Hyatt award chart. With Hyatt Category 1 hotels ranging from 3,000 to 9,000 points per night, it's no surprise this is one of the best ways to spend Ultimate Rewards points. Related: Best Hyatt hotels in the world to book with points Book Iberia flights to Madrid with Chase points You can score a great deal on nonstop flights to Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas Airport (MAD), operated by Iberia, by redeeming your Chase points through Iberia Club. Round-trip flights from Boston Logan International Airport (BOS); Dulles International Airport (IAD) near Washington, D.C.; Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport (SJU) in San Juan, Puerto Rico; and New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to MAD only set you back 32,000 Avios in basic economy, 50,000 Avios in comfort economy, 59,000 Avios in premium economy and 81,000 Avios in business class on off-peak dates. This deal is so good that it might be worth paying for a positioning flight to one of these airports. To get the lowest prices for each route, fly on off-peak dates. Look at the calendar, and see if any dates work for you and have award space. Note that the dates in red are peak, and all others are off-peak. Related: Best ways to redeem Avios through Aer Lingus, British Airways and Iberia Book flights to Hawaii via Alaska Airlines and American Airlines Another of our favorite Chase Ultimate Rewards redemptions is transferring points to British Airways Club at a 1:1 ratio and booking flights to Hawaii with Oneworld partners American Airlines and Alaska Airlines. While domestic flights within the U.S. can be found for as little as 13,500 Avios each way, West Coast flights to Hawaii on either American or Alaska start at 22,000 Avios each way. Related: Airlines you can book using Avios: How to maximize your points and miles Book Air France and KLM flights to Europe via Flying Blue Another great Ultimate Rewards sweet spot is transferring points to Flying Blue to book flights on Air France or KLM to Europe. Both airlines have substantial North American and European route networks via their hubs at Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) and Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS), respectively. While Flying Blue prices its awards dynamically, the program offers the lowest saver-level pricing for all one-way flights between the U.S. and Europe as follows, regardless of origin or destination, meaning you can connect at no extra cost: - 25,000 miles in economy - 40,000 miles in premium economy - 60,000 miles in business class However, keep in mind that Flying Blue is adding Light, Standard and Flex awards on Sept. 8, so the lowest-cost awards will soon be for Light fares. Remember, you could spend a few days in Paris or Amsterdam using the free Flying Blue stopover program. To book Flying Blue stopovers, you'll need to call Flying Blue at 800-375-8723. Also, look out for Flying Blue's monthly Promo Rewards, which offer discounts on select routes, classes and dates. Book short-haul flights to Canada using Chase points Though Air Canada's Aeroplan loyalty program still uses an award chart, it uses dynamic pricing for flights operated by Air Canada and select partner airlines. However, you can still find cheap short-haul tickets from the U.S. to Canada. Short Air Canada flights within North America start at 6,000 Aeroplan points. How to earn Chase Ultimate Rewards points You can earn Chase Ultimate Rewards points through spending on these Chase credit cards: - Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees): Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. - Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (see rates and fees): Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first six months from account opening. - Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees): Earn 75,000 bonus points after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. - Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (see rates and fees): Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Bottom line The myriad ways you can redeem your Ultimate Rewards points make them one of the most valuable and versatile transferable points currencies. Whether you're looking to travel domestically or indulge in international luxury, a transfer partner can help you get there. While these are some of the best Chase Ultimate Rewards redemptions, they're just the tip of the iceberg. If you play your cards right (pun intended), there are many other ways to get great value out of your Ultimate Rewards points. item.title: One of our favorite points brands just opened a hotel in Japan's premier ski destination
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.12
One of our favorite points brands just opened a hotel in Japan's premier ski destination Moxy is going to the mountains. Marriott today announced that its latest Moxy location is now open in Niseko, the heart of Japan's alpine ski region on the northern island of Hokkaido. The opening — one of the most anticipated points hotel debuts this year — is an interesting addition to Niseko's otherwise upscale hotel portfolio, which includes a Park Hyatt and a Ritz-Carlton Reserve. Moxy tends to be a more casual brand with a youthful vibe and a focus on lively shared public spaces (you often check in at the bar) and pared-down accommodations in creative configurations, some of which feature bunk beds for larger family or friend groups. The new hotel has 310 rooms, and from what we can tell so far, they only come in two categories: - Moxy Niseko Loft with one queen bed and two twin bunk beds - Moxy Niseko Twin with two twin beds The latter is a mere 194 square feet and, like you'll find in many other types of Moxy rooms, the sink is in the main room while the water closet with a toilet and walk-in shower is in a glassed-off space of its own. As for the Queen Loft room, it is also listed at 194 square feet and includes a queen bed by the window with a small sofa and a lofted twin-size bunk bed above it. There's no closet area to speak of in either room, but instead a wall with pegs, a folding table and a luggage rack, so it might be tough to find a place to stow your ski gear. As for the rest of the hotel, the interior design was inspired by Hokkaido's mountain landscapes with colorful touches of Kawaii, or "cute," pop culture references thrown in. The hotel has a grab and go counter for meals on the run, but its main restaurant is the Moxy Bar & Cafe, which is a laidback-looking space serving breakfast, lunch and dinner. The hotel also features a small 24-hour fitness center for folks who don't get their fill of exercise skiing in the winter or hiking in the summer. The new Moxy Niseko is located within the central Niseko Village ski resort with easy access to the Niseko Village gondola at the base of Mount Niseko Annupuri, putting the area's many ski trails in easy reach. Visitors will also find tons of nearby restaurants, shops and onsens to have a relaxing soak after a day out on the slopes. The hotel is also easy to reach from two different Japan Rail stations, which put it within a two-hour train ride from New Chitose International Airport (CTS), the region's main hub. So why bring Moxy to this particular part of Japan when many of the brand's outposts tend to be in major cities or near airports? (The four other Moxy locations in the country are in Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka). The brand has recently expanded to some other nature-first destinations such as Banff in Canada and a planned opening in Vietnam's beachy Phu Quoc. "Niseko's year-round appeal, global reputation and adventurous spirit make it a natural fit for Moxy," said Cristiano Rinaldi, Marriott's chief lodging product and services officer in Asia Pacific excluding China, in a statement. "This opening brings the brand's playful social energy to one of Japan's most celebrated mountain retreats, creating a stay experience that is approachable, design-forward and deeply connected to the destination." Moxy's entry into this particular hotel market also means travelers have another reasonable budget option for their next Japan ski (or summer hiking) trip, which is a boon considering how expensive some of Niseko's other accommodations can be. Rates at the Moxy Niseko in the next few months start at a mere $88 per night. Rates in January through March, when the powder tends to be best, start at $192 per night (though most nights are priced at $400). Points rates have not yet been made available. Compare that to the Park Hyatt Niseko Hanazono, where rooms start at a whopping $1,550 per night this January, and you might be willing to sacrifice a few creature comforts (and cram into a smaller room with your ski gear) in order to experience Japan's winter wonderland. Hopefully points rates will be loaded into Marriott's system soon. And when they are, you can bet several members of the TPG team will be looking into winter trips to Japan and how a stay at the Moxy Niseko measures up. Related reading:

item.title: Baby on board: Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards just made it much cheaper to fly with lap infants on award tickets
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.37
Baby on board: Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards just made it much cheaper to fly with lap infants on award tickets If you're looking to redeem points and miles for airline travel and have a lap infant traveling with you, Alaska Airlines' Atmos Rewards program just made an incredibly generous policy update. For long-haul international Atmos Rewards redemptions, including those operated by partner airlines, lap infants will now only be charged government-mandated international taxes when the award ticket is issued on "027" stock, meaning issued by Alaska or Hawaiian. Lap infants are defined as passengers under the age of 2 on the date of travel of all flights of the trip who do not require their own seat. They will continue to fly free on Alaska-operated domestic award flights (including Hawaiian Airlines flights) when accompanied by an adult. For some other airlines, lap infants are charged 10% of the adult revenue fare, plus taxes and fees, whether an adult passenger redeems miles or pays cash for international flights. On short-haul international services, where cash rates are just a few hundred dollars, lap infant costs are affordable. However, it becomes more expensive to redeem for long-haul business-class flights. So even if you find a sweet spot international business-class redemption for 50,000 points, for example, you'd need to pay 10% of the cash fare to bring a lap infant along. That means on a $3,000 one-way business-class fare, you'd spend $300 for a lap infant who doesn't have their own seat and probably won't eat or drink anything offered on board. If you are traveling internationally with a lap infant on an award ticket, this 10% fee, which is common across the industry, can be a significant added expense to your points and miles redemption. That's why this surprise policy change from Atmos Rewards is so generous and so welcome. It not only covers international flights operated by Alaska (which is steadily adding pins to its route map) but also the impressive roster of Atmos Rewards partner airlines, including British Airways, Japan Airlines, American Airlines, Icelandair and Starlux, giving you more choice to save when you travel with your family. Bottom line Atmos Rewards now has the most generous lap infant award policy of any major loyalty program. On long-haul international redemptions, you pay only government-mandated taxes and fees for a child under 2 traveling on your lap, which are usually very low, with no percentage of the adult cash fare and no points payable. That applies to Alaska and Hawaiian metal and flights operated by partner airlines, and lap infants must be added by phoning Atmos Rewards. Lap infants on international revenue fares are still subject to the 10% charge, so consider redeeming Atmos Rewards points instead. Related reading:

item.title: Ending soon: Highest-ever bonuses on no-annual-fee Chase Ink business cards
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.86
Ending soon: Highest-ever bonuses on no-annual-fee Chase Ink business cards Editor's Note Both the Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card (see rates and fees) and the Ink Business Cash® Credit Card (see rates and fees) are strong small-business options, with flat-rate or bonus-category earning structures that can add up quickly. And new applicants of either card can currently earn $1,000 in bonus cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. It's the highest welcome offer we've seen on either card, but the offers are ending soon. If you've been considering one of these cards and can comfortably meet the spending requirement, now may be a good time to apply. Keep in mind that these are business credit cards. You don't need a large company with employees to qualify — even freelancers, sole proprietors and those with side gigs may be eligible. However, you will need a legitimate business to apply. Turn cash back into Chase points While the Ink Business Unlimited and Ink Business Cash technically earn cash back, you can convert that cash back into Chase Ultimate Rewards points if you also hold a premium card such as a Sapphire card or the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (see rates and fees). Doing so can dramatically boost value, since points can be redeemed for travel at elevated rates or transferred to airline and hotel partners. (Note that while the Chase Ink Business Premier® Credit Card (see rates and fees) is also a cash-back card, its cash back cannot be converted into transferable points.) Ink Business Unlimited Credit Card Welcome bonus: Earn $1,000 bonus cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. This is the highest offer we've seen on this card, but it's ending soon, so don't wait to apply. Annual fee: $0 Earning rate: 1.5% cash back on all purchases Who should apply: The Ink Business Unlimited is a great option for small businesses and sole proprietors who don't have spending concentrated in specific spending categories. Regardless of category, you'll get a flat 1.5% on purchases. While it's not the best flat-rate option for business owners, it does come in handy if you have Chase Ultimate Rewards points-earning credit cards to turn that 1.5% cash back into 1.5 points per dollar spent (a 3.1% return, based on TPG's September 2026 valuations). To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Unlimited. Apply here: Ink Business Unlimited Ink Business Cash Credit Card Welcome bonus: Earn $1,000 cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. This is the best offer we've seen on this card. Like the offer on the Ink Business Unlimited, this bonus won't be around for much longer. Annual fee: $0 Earning rates: - 5% cash back at office supply stores and on internet, cable and phone services (on the first $25,000 spent in combined purchases each account anniversary year, then 1% cash back) - 2% cash back at gas stations and restaurants (on the first $25,000 spent in combined purchases each account anniversary year, then 1% cash back) - 1% cash back on all other purchases Who should apply: The Ink Business Cash is great for anyone who spends a lot at office supply stores and on internet, cable and phone services. These are common expenses for many small businesses, so most business owners should be able to maximize rewards with this card. To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Cash. Apply here: Ink Business Cash Ink Business Preferred Credit Card Welcome bonus: Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. According to TPG's valuations, this welcome bonus is worth $2,050 when you take advantage of Chase's transfer partners. Other redemption options include redeeming your points through Chase Travel℠ and for cash back, but these options offer less value: up to $1,750 (depending on your booking) and $1,000, respectively. This bonus is one of the better offers we've seen for the card, so any time it's offering at least 100,000 points (as is currently the case) is considered a good time to apply. Annual fee: $95 Earning rates: - 3 points per dollar spent on shipping purchases, internet, cable and phone services, travel, and advertising purchases with social media and search engines (on the first $150,000 spent in combined purchases across these categories each year, then 1 point per dollar spent) - 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases Who should apply: Small-business owners with significant spending in the above bonus categories will be happy to earn up to 450,000 points per year on those purchases. This card also provides access to Chase's airline and hotel transfer partners, so it can provide value even without pairing it with another Chase card. To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Preferred. Apply here: Ink Business Preferred Ink Business Premier Credit Card Welcome bonus: Earn $1,000 in bonus cash back after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. This has been the standard bonus on this card since it launched in late 2021; we have not seen any elevated offers, so now is a good time to apply. Annual fee: $195 Earning rates: - 2.5% cash back on purchases of $5,000 or more - 2% cash back on all other purchases Who should apply: This card is ideal for small-business owners looking for a card with a flexible spending limit. That means you must pay the bill in full each month and cannot carry a balance. If you can pay your balance in full each month, you'll enjoy the unlimited earning potential on this card. It's worth noting, however, that the rewards from this card cannot be combined with Chase Ultimate Rewards-earning cards. To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Premier. Apply here: Ink Business Premier Are these bonuses worth it? One of these cards could be worth considering if you have a major purchase coming up that you want to use to earn one of these welcome bonuses, or if you want to take advantage of their earning rates sooner rather than later. While these cards won't add to your Chase 5/24 total, you need to be under that number to apply for any cards with Chase. If you've opened five or more personal credit cards (from any bank) in the past 24 months, you will likely be declined when applying. Business credit cards — or cards with significant welcome bonuses — tend to have higher spending requirements to achieve the bonus. If you can meet that requirement, the welcome bonus is almost always worth the effort. Related: The ultimate guide to credit card application restrictions Are you eligible for a Chase Ink welcome bonus? Chase has different welcome-bonus eligibility rules across the Ink Business card family. For the Ink Business Cash and Ink Business Unlimited: If you've previously had either no-annual-fee card, you won't be eligible for the welcome bonus on the other. In other words, having the Ink Business Cash can make you ineligible for the Ink Business Unlimited bonus, and vice versa. This restriction doesn't affect your eligibility for an Ink Business Preferred or Ink Business Premier welcome bonus, provided you're otherwise eligible. For the Ink Business Preferred and Ink Business Premier: The restriction applies only to the specific card. If you've previously had the Ink Business Preferred, you may not be eligible for another Preferred bonus, but you can still be eligible for the Premier bonus, and vice versa. You can also still be eligible for a Cash or Unlimited bonus if you've never had either no-annual-fee Ink card. You'll also need to be under 5/24, meaning you've opened fewer than five new personal credit cards across issuers in the past 24 months. While Chase has never publicly acknowledged this rule, they do enforce it. Finally, you must have some type of business to qualify for an Ink card, since they are business credit cards. You don't need to own a fully-fledged corporation; freelancing, gig work and sole proprietorships may qualify. Bottom line If you can combine your Ink rewards with an existing Ultimate Rewards account, these welcome offers can become even more valuable since you'll have access to Chase's airline and hotel transfer partners. Just make sure you're eligible under Chase's welcome-bonus and 5/24 rules and can comfortably meet the spending requirement without making purchases your business wouldn't otherwise need. The welcome offers on the Ink Business Unlimited and Ink Business Cash are ending soon, so if you've been considering either card, now may be a good time to apply. Otherwise, the right Ink card for you will depend on your business's spending patterns and which earning structure best fits your needs. Apply here: Ink Business Unlimited Apply here: Ink Business Cash Apply here: Ink Business Preferred Apply here: Ink Business Premier

Reviews Citi / AAdvantage Executive review: Admirals Club access and premium travel perks Stephanie Stevens is an associate writer with TPG's credit cards team. She focuses on creating timely credit cards content for TPG readers. September 4, 2026 • 12 min read The cards we feature here are from partners who compensate us when you are approved through our site, and this may impact how or where these products appear. We don't cover all available credit cards, but our analysis, reviews, and opinions are entirely from our editorial team. Terms apply to the offers listed on this page. Please view our advertising policy and product review methodology for more information. Editorial note: This is a recurring post, regularly updated with new information and offers. Citi is a TPG advertising partner. Editorial disclaimer: Opinions expressed here are the author's alone, not those of any bank, credit card issuer, airline or hotel chain, and have not been reviewed, approved or otherwise endorsed by any of these entities. Related stories Quick summary A premium airline card offers complimentary lounge membership, travel credits and elite-status perks for frequent flyers of a major U.S. carrier. The card is best suited for those who regularly use airport lounges and value airline-specific benefits, including credits for vacation packages and inflight purchases. Authorized users can access lounges for an additional fee, and the card provides hotel and car rental elite status with select partners. Compared to alternatives, this card is ideal for travelers seeking unlimited lounge access, while lower-fee options may suit occasional flyers. What to consider The card carries a high annual fee, making it most worthwhile for those maximizing lounge and airline benefits. Some credits require booking specific vacation packages or meeting ride thresholds, and not all perks are automatic—enrollment may be required. A 48-month application rule restricts bonus eligibility for those who have recently received a bonus on this product. What you'll miss from the article A detailed comparison of lounge access, credits, and elite-status perks to help determine which travel card best matches your flying habits. Generated by AI with support from our editorial team. Earn 4x AAdvantage® miles for every $1 spent on eligible American Airlines purchases. 1X 1 AAdvantage® miles for every $1 spent on other purchases Intro offer For a limited time, earn 125,000 American Airlines AAdvantage® bonus miles Annual fee $695 Regular APR 19.49% - 29.49% (Variable) Recommended credit 670-850 Excellent, Good The (see rates and fees) stands out for its complimentary Admirals Club membership and credits for frequent American Airlines flyers. However, the $695 annual fee makes it worthwhile only if you'll use Admirals Club access and its other benefits. Card Rating*: ⭐⭐⭐½ *Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer. Citi / AAdvantage Executive: The basics The is Citi's premium American Airlines card, standing out for its complimentary Admirals Club membership. It also offers travel credits, elite-status benefits and Loyalty Point bonuses. Unlike flexible travel rewards cards, the Citi / AA Executive earns AAdvantage miles rather than transferable points, so it's best suited to travelers who regularly fly American Airlines or Oneworld partners and value AAdvantage miles. Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Elite pros and cons Pros Cons Complimentary Admirals Club membership Authorized user Admirals Club access ($175 for three) American Airlines Vacations, inflight and Admirals Club credits Complimentary hotel and car rental status High annual fee Several credits require effort AAdvantage miles aren't as flexible as transferable points Citi / AAdvantage Executive benefits The comes with benefits designed primarily for frequent American Airlines travelers. Admirals Club membership The marquee benefit of the Citi / AA Executive is a complimentary Admirals Club membership for the primary cardholder. The primary cardholder receives a full Admirals Club membership, which allows them and their immediate family or up to two guests access to the club when they have a same-day boarding pass for American Airlines or an eligible partner airline. The membership provides access to nearly 50 Admirals Club locations and more than 60 partner lounges worldwide when flying American Airlines or an eligible partner. This benefit has become even more valuable since American increased the price of Admirals Club memberships in August. At $695 per year, the card is a compelling alternative to purchasing lounge access separately, especially when factoring in its other American Airlines benefits. For TPG editor-in-chief Nick Ewen, lounge access is the primary reason he keeps the card. He'll use it on upcoming American trips with his wife and daughter, and appreciates being able to add authorized users with their own Admirals Club access. You can add up to three authorized users for $175 each. They receive Admirals Club access when flying American or an eligible partner and can bring up to two guests, though they don't access partner lounges. Since Admirals Club day passes cost $79, this can be a valuable perk for frequent American flyers. The Citi / AA Executive offers valuable airport and inflight benefits: Enhanced airport experience: You and up to eight travelers on the same reservation get priority check-in, airport screening (where available) and priority boarding. First checked bag free: On eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries, the first checked bag for you and up to eight companions is free when traveling on the same reservation. Since American typically charges at least $45 per bag each way, this provides meaningful savings even for occasional check-bag users. Inflight and Admirals Club credit: Receive up to $100 back annually on eligible purchases. Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit: Up to $120 statement credit when you pay an eligible fee with the card (once every four years). I recommend Global Entry, which includes TSA PreCheck. To receive the credit, book an eligible American Airlines Vacations travel package or experience through AAVacations.com using your card. Eligible packages must include at least two components — a flight and hotel, a flight and a rental car, or a hotel and a rental car. This isn't as flexible as a general travel credit, so don't book a package solely for the benefit. But if you already book vacation packages or bundle flights with hotels or rental cars, the credit provides significant value. TPG principal spokesperson Clint Henderson is particularly interested in this benefit because he already uses American Airlines Vacations: "I've been a huge advocate for AAVacations over the years and I will definitely take advantage of this new perk." Automatic hotel and rental car elite status The Citi / AA Executive also offers complimentary Omni Hotels & Resorts Champion Status (enrollment required), which includes an annual free night reward after a qualifying stay,* and Avis President's Club status (enrollment available through Aug. 31, 2028). *A qualifying stay consists of two or more consecutive nights booked directly through Omni Hotels & Resorts at omnihotels.com. Benefits of Omni Champion Status can include complimentary one-level room upgrades and early check-in and late checkout (when available), while benefits of Avis President's Club include car upgrades, expedited service and complimentary additional drivers. I wouldn't recommend adding the card to your wallet just for these perks, but they're valuable additions if you already stay at Omni or rent with Avis. You'll earn 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points at each milestone: 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points (up to 40,000 bonus points per qualification year). This benefit is most valuable for frequent American Airlines flyers who already earn enough Loyalty Points to reach these thresholds. Cardholders can receive up to $15 in Lyft credits per month, or $180 annually, after taking three eligible rides that month. I consider this one of the weaker benefits of the card because the three-ride requirement means you can't simply take one Lyft trip and receive the monthly credit. How to earn and use your rewards The is most rewarding when you use it strategically rather than putting all your everyday spending on it. Earning miles on the Citi / AAdvantage Executive With the Citi / AA Executive, you'll earn: 12 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings 4 miles per dollar on eligible American Airlines purchases 1 mile per dollar on all other eligible purchases Spend $150,000 in a calendar year and you'll earn 5 miles per dollar on American Airlines purchases for the remainder of that year. You'll also earn 1 Loyalty Point for every eligible AAdvantage mile earned from purchases. The boosted earning rate on American's hotel and car rental portals is attractive if you regularly use those services, particularly since these purchases also earn Loyalty Points. Clint uses AAdvantage Hotels and likes the elevated earning rate: "I end up booking a lot of AAdvantage Hotels because of the generous Loyalty Point earning rates, so this is an added benefit, too." However, don't use the Citi / AAdvantage Executive for most everyday purchases — the base earning rate is weak compared with many other cards. If you're trying to maximize flexible rewards, you're generally better off using a card that earns transferable points on everyday spending and reserving the Executive for purchases where it offers a meaningful bonus or benefit. Redeeming AAdvantage miles AAdvantage miles can be redeemed for flights on American Airlines and its Oneworld and other airline partners. Award flights operated by American and Fiji Airways are dynamically priced, so the miles required vary by flight and date. All other partner awards follow AAdvantage's fixed, region-based award charts. For example, you can book a one-way business-class award on Qatar Airways from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) to Hamad International Airport (DOH) in Doha for 70,000 AAdvantage miles (and just $35 in taxes and fees). Where the Citi / AAdvantage Executive falls short The 's biggest drawback is its $695 annual fee. It's easiest to justify if you regularly use Admirals Clubs; otherwise, you may struggle to offset the cost. The card also isn't ideal for everyday spending. Most purchases earn just 1 AAdvantage mile per dollar, and AAdvantage miles aren't as flexible as Amex or Chase points, which transfer to multiple airline and hotel programs. Skip this card if lounge access isn't a priority, or if you want flexible rewards across broader categories. Citi / AA Executive vs. Citi / AA Globe If you want American Airlines benefits without unlimited Admirals Club access, the (see rates and fees) is the clear alternative. For a lower $350 annual fee, the Globe includes four Admirals Club passes yearly. One pass covers one adult and up to three children under 18; passes work at multiple lounges within 24 hours on American or Oneworld flights. The Globe also offers preferred boarding, a free first checked bag on eligible domestic American itineraries, and an annual companion certificate (starting year two) with substantial strategic value. Choose the Globe if you're an occasional American traveler who wants lounge access a few times a year. Choose the Executive if you regularly visit Admirals Clubs — unlimited access easily justifies the higher fee. For a limited time, new cardholders can earn 125,000 bonus miles after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first five months from account opening. According to TPG's September 2026 valuations, that welcome offer is worth roughly $1,813. This is the highest offer we have seen in the card’s history, making now a great time to apply if you can comfortably meet the spending required to earn the welcome offer. Citi's 48-month rule prevents you from earning a welcome bonus if you've received one on this card within the past four years. The clock starts from when you receive the bonus, not when approved or activated. Citi also applies this 48-month restriction to certain conversions from other Citi accounts. Other cards to consider if you don't want the Citi / AAdvantage Executive The is a strong choice for frequent American Airlines travelers, but it isn't the right fit for everyone. Here are a few alternatives: If you want a lower annual fee: The Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® offers a straightforward way to earn AAdvantage miles while receiving core American Airlines benefits such as a free checked bag and preferred boarding. To learn more, read our full review of the Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select. If you want Oneworld perks without being tied to American: The is a strong option for travelers who want to earn Oneworld elite status while taking advantage of benefits with Alaska Airlines and its partners. To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Rewards Summit. If you want transferable points and lounge access: The (see rates and fees) earns transferable Citi ThankYou points and offers premium travel perks, including lounge access. It can be a better fit for American loyalists who want more flexibility from their rewards. To learn more, read our full review of the Citi Strata Elite. The information for the Citi Platinum Select has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Bottom line The is fundamentally an Admirals Club card, with additional perks that can help frequent American Airlines travelers offset its $695 annual fee. The card makes the most sense if you'll regularly use Admirals Club access and can take advantage of benefits like Loyalty Point bonuses and authorized user lounge access. But for travelers who rarely fly American, don't use airport lounges or prefer the flexibility of transferable points, there are better premium travel cards for your wallet.

item.title: Fly to Tokyo and London from 20,000 points with the September Atmos Rewards Global Getaways
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.14
Fly to Tokyo and London from 20,000 points with the September Atmos Rewards Global Getaways For a few days each month, Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards lets its members save up to 50% on award tickets to select destinations through its Global Getaways promotion. Global Getaways is part of the monthly Atmos Members Day promotion, held on the first Wednesday of each month. Here's a look at the September Global Getaways offers. But remember to jump on these deals soon, as you must book them by Sept. 5. September Atmos Rewards Global Getaways offers | Destination | Starting cost for one-way awards to/from the U.S. | Travel dates | |---|---|---| | Apia, Samoa | 25,500 points | Jan. 5 to Feb. 28, 2027 | | Athens, Greece | 25,000 points | Jan. 5 to Feb. 28, 2027 | | La Paz, Mexico | 20,000 points | Jan. 5 to Feb. 28, 2027 | | London | 20,000 points | Jan. 5 to Feb. 28, 2027 | | Taipei, Taiwan | 30,000 points | Jan. 5 to Feb. 28, 2027 | | Tokyo | 20,000 points to/from Hawaii 27,500 points to/from other parts of the U.S. | Sept. 2 to Nov. 18, 2026 | One example of a route covered by this month's promotion is the following itinerary from New York to London. It costs just 20,000 points and $26 in taxes and fees. While writing this story, we saw 20,000-point award options on this route on most dates. As an added bonus, if you have the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card, the partner bookings fee is waived, so your cost drops to just 20,000 points and $6. You'll also see ample availability to Taipei for 30,000 points. For example, you can fly from New York to Taipei for just 30,000 points and $26 in taxes and fees (or $6 if you are an Atmos Summit cardholder). Availability to Tokyo for just 27,500 points is much more limited, especially from the East Coast, but here's an example we found on Hawaiian Airlines from New York to Tokyo for just 27,500 points and $6 in taxes and fees. And if you can fly from the West Coast, availability is better. Plus, you can fly from Honolulu to Tokyo for just 20,000 points and $6 in taxes and fees. We even found less expensive awards than listed to La Paz, Mexico. Specifically, you can fly from Los Angeles to La Paz for 15,000 points and $64 in taxes and fees on select dates. However, we found no availability at the listed starting rates to Apia, Samoa, or Athens, Greece. So, don't be surprised if you don't find any awards at the starting rates for those destinations. How to book Atmos Rewards Global Getaways To book one of these Atmos Rewards Global Getaways, go to the Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines website, log in to your account, click the "Use points" box and enter your desired itinerary before clicking "Search flights." We also recommend clicking the "Flexible dates" box, which will load a calendar view of the lowest award rates for each date. If you aren't seeing the lowest award rates on your ideal route, consider whether it might be worth positioning to a major hub such as New York City, Los Angeles, Seattle or San Francisco. This can be particularly important when booking through Atmos Rewards since the program doesn't allow you to combine two partners in a single booking. So, while you can book an itinerary with Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines and one other partner, you can't book an award with two partners (such as an American Airlines flight that connects to a British Airways flight). Related: Which credit card should you use for Alaska Airlines flights? How to earn Atmos Rewards points There are multiple ways to earn Atmos Rewards points. You can, of course, earn them by flying Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines. The carriers also partner with over 30 airlines, including (but not limited to) members of the Oneworld alliance. The Atmos Rewards cobranded credit cards are also a good way to accumulate points. You can earn points on purchases with these cards, but their welcome offers are also a good way to boost your account balance. - Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card: Earn 70,000 bonus points and a $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) after spending $2,500 or more on purchases within the first 90 days of account opening. - Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card: Earn 70,000 bonus points and a $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) after spending $4,000 or more on purchases within the first 90 days of account opening. - Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card: Earn 80,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $4,000 or more on purchases within the first 90 days of account opening. You can also transfer Bilt Points to Atmos Rewards at a 1:1 ratio and Marriott Bonvoy points to Atmos Rewards at a 3:1 ratio. Related: Atmos Ascent vs. Atmos Summit: Which is better for Alaska and Hawaiian flyers? Bottom line The Atmos Rewards Global Getaways deals are an excellent opportunity for travelers who want to book travel to the highlighted destinations, can book their flights within a few days and can travel during the specified time period. However, you may want to book even quicker than the Sept. 5 deadline, as the best dates will likely disappear as other travelers book. And if you are striving for Atmos Rewards status, keep in mind that you'll earn status points on Atmos Rewards award tickets. So, it could be worth booking a trip to Tokyo before the end of 2026 if you're running short on status points.

item.title: The unusually muted Tesla Cybercab launch
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 5.10
At a private, closed-door event in Austin, Texas today, Tesla officially launched its gilded car of the future: the Cybercab. It’s a huge milestone for Elon Musk, who has been hyping the imminent arrival of driverless cars for years and has bet the future of his company on AI, autonomous vehicles, and humanoid robots. The unusually muted Tesla Cybercab launch Tesla has 45 Cybercabs registered in Texas, though it’s unclear how many of them will be doing passenger trips. It was an unusually muted event, with no livestream, no journalists, and a very short invite list comprised mostly of pro-Tesla content creators. Tesla influencers planning live shows with the event stream were left streaming the webpage that tracks the number of Tesla robotaxis in Texas instead. Tesla was keeping a tight lid on the event. Invitee Chuck Cook said the company had him sign an NDA and agreed to an embargo requiring to wait to post content until after the event was over. But if the goal was to blunt criticism, it didn’t work. On X, pro-Tesla accounts who weren’t invited grumbled about the decision; Not a Tesla App accused the company of “dropping the ball.” As of this week, Tesla has 45 Cybercab vehicles registered with the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles — though its not clear how many will be put into commercial service right away. Several vehicles were made available to Tesla influencers in Austin for content creation; the company has been testing them in various cities for months now. Tesla also launched a new website for its Robotaxi service, which includes the rules for riding in the new vehicle. (For example, children under the age of 13 are currently banned from riding in the Cybercab.) Several videos were posted on the company’s social feeds, highlighting the interior, crash test worthiness, and accessibility. (The accessibility video was especially befuddling, showing a wheelchair user getting up to fold and stow his own wheelchair.) But even with the launch of the Cybercab, Tesla’s robotaxi fleet is still a small player relative to some of its rivals. With the new Cybercabs, the company now has 256 unsupervised autonomous vehicles in operation across six cities, according to Robotaxi Tracker. By comparison, Alphabet’s Waymo is currently operating approximately 4,000 unsupervised vehicles across 14 cities. There were still many lingering questions about the Cybercab. Two years ago, Musk said the two-seater would be available for purchase, perhaps for a price as low as $30,000. But the company still has yet say when the Cybercab would go on sale. There is a new online form for those interested in “future Robotaxi opportunities,” such as purchasing a fleet of Cybercabs or building “mobility hubs and infrastructure.” But no word on when regular customers could buy one for themselves. (YouTuber Marques Brownlee says his hair is safe for now.) For the past year, Tesla has been operating a robotaxi service in Texas and Florida using several dozen modified Model Y vehicles, some of which are supervised by human safety drivers and some of which are not. With the introduction of the Cybercab, the company is embarking on a risky new phase that will pit Musk’s stripped-down, less costly approach to autonomy against more established players like Waymo. The Cybercab, which was first introduced in 2024, is a two-seat sedan with gullwing-style doors and eight cameras that it uses to navigate the world without a driver. The vehicle lacks traditional controls, like steering wheel, pedals, and mirrors — as well as sensors commonly found on other robotaxis, like radar and lidar. The Cybercab is also the lightest, most range-efficient vehicle Tesla has ever produced. According to documents filed with the Environmental Protection Agency, the Cybercab runs on a single front-mounted 219 horsepower permanent magnet motor with front-wheel drive, a compact 48kWh battery pack running at 326 volts, and a curb weight of just 3,113 pounds — making it roughly 700 pounds lighter than the lightest Model 3 on the market. That’s roughly the same as a gas-powered compact car, despite the fact that it’s still carrying a relatively heavy lithium-ion battery. For years, Musk has been promising the imminent arrival of Tesla’s driverless cars, only time and time again to fall short of those predictions. He claimed that 50 percent of the US population would have access to Tesla’s robotaxis by the end of 2025. Today, the vehicles are only available in six cities in Texas and Florida. (Tesla is running a human-driven ridehail service in the San Francisco Bay Area, but has yet to apply for a driverless testing permit from California.) For Tesla’s vehicle owners, there’s been a string of broken promises. In 2016, Musk promised that every vehicle Tesla produced from then on would have all the technology necessary for self-driving. Years later, he was forced to retract that claim, acknowledging that the hardware in some older vehicles was insufficient to support autonomous capabilities. Musk promised to retrofit those customers’ vehicles, but has yet to offer any details as to how that would work. Tesla is currently facing multiple lawsuits from customers and regulators claiming it has misled the public about its self-driving capabilities. Today, the company’s $99-a-month Full Self-Driving feature is still just a Level 2 driver-assist system that requires constant human supervision. During Tesla’s first quarter earnings call this year, Musk promised that “unsupervised” FSD would be available to customer vehicles by the end of 2026 “at the earliest,” admitting that complex intersections, bad road markings, and weather were likely to slow the rollout. Tesla’s fans will likely point to today’s Cybercab launch as a moment of enormous significance for the company. Investors already seem to agree, with Tesla’s stock price trading up nearly six points over the past five days. Analysts view robotaxis as one of the primary justifications for Tesla’s $1.18 trillion valuation, and the key that will unlock the company’s future. Tesla’s EV sales have slowed down in the face of rising competition, especially from China. And Musk has made massive investments in AI and robotics, with some speculating he could try to merge Tesla with the recently public SpaceXAI.

item.title: Nvidia will officially bring DLSS 5 to older GPUs — but won’t give gamers full control
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.94
Officially, Nvidia’s controversial DLSS 5 AI rendering was supposed to launch this evening with only a single game, only on Nvidia’s latest RTX 50 GPUs, and with developers in full control of their artistic vision. Nvidia will officially bring DLSS 5 to older GPUs — but won’t give gamers full control Nvidia won’t confirm that previously announced DLSS 5 games will still ship with the tech. But unofficially, modders have already ported a leaked version of DLSS 5 to run on just about anything while cranking sliders to the max. Now, Nvidia is changing its plans. DLSS 5 is still launching first on RTX 50 GPUs, but it’s officially coming to older RTX 40-series GPUs as well, Nvidia spokesperson Rajal Maharaj confirms to The Verge. “Our current focus is on optimizing performance for the GeForce RTX 50 Series with model updates expected later this fall. Once RTX 50 Series performance is more fully tuned, we plan to work on expanding official support to the GeForce RTX 40 Series,” reads part of Nvidia’s statement. What about earlier RTX 30 and RTX 20-series GPUs, which modders successfully targeted as well, assuming you count “not exactly playable framerate and plenty of crashes” as successful? “Right now the focus is of course on 50-series,” Maharaj tells me. “Once we feel like the 50-series is in a good place, we’re going to look at the 40-series.” Now that the cat’s out of the bag, will gamers get full control over DLSS 5’s sliders the way modders already do? Nvidia says no: “For gamers, DLSS 5 is a simple on-or-off toggle,” the company confirms. “The more granular artistic controls are for developers, including model selection, Structure Intensity, Tone Intensity, automatic masking and custom per-pixel masking.” That said, the company tells me that developers could pass along certain controls in their own settings menus, like they’ve done with other graphics tech. (Early DLSS Super Resolution was also just an on/off toggle, but today’s games let you pick between varying levels of quality or even an exact percentage, depending on the game.) Assuming you don’t mind DLSS 5, one of the benefits is that it’s easy to integrate. Developers don’t need to tell DLSS 5 which objects are “silverware” and which are “furniture” because the AI models can automatically recognize and isolate objects in a scene, distinguishing between faces, textiles, foliage, and more to apply different amounts of AI processing. Game engines that already know which video game objects are which can help DLSS 5, too: For more targeted control, semantic AI masking can automatically recognize scene objects, while engine-level masking allows artists to isolate specific props or groups of assets, such as glassware, water droplets or foliage, and apply custom neural lighting adjustments to those elements. Unreal Engine 5 has a native plug-in, and Nvidia also has SDKs. Nvidia says developers can apply DLSS 5 to their entire game this way, or do it differently for different scenes, cutscenes, or portions of gameplay, and the company tells The Verge that its DLSS 5 models run on every single frame, so there’s no minimum frame rate for it to work. We’re still waiting to find out if the early backlash against DLSS 5 scared away publishers and developers that had originally committed to the technology. Nvidia’s response to us today suggests that perhaps some companies have backed away. When we asked if the company could reconfirm that it will come to Assassin’s Creed Shadows, Hogwarts Legacy, Starfield, Resident Evil Requiem, and the other 12 originally announced titles, this was the company’s only reply: “More games are on the way. Many developers are actively integrating DLSS 5, and we’ll share updates on upcoming titles as partners finalize their integrations.”
